author: WoMin
title: From Mombasa to Yaoundé, the vision and the demand is for reparative justice
content:
Through WoMin’s work alongside African women organising against extractivism, against the drivers of the climate crisis and its impacts, the destruction of the commons through false solutions, unjust energy transitions (and generally a world order that serves a minority over the global majority), we have been asking: what is the full range of impacts and costs in the face of environmental and climate impacts? Who and whose work absorbs these impacts and costs? And what would repair mean from the perspective of women, their communities and the ecosystems they care for and are cared for at the frontline of the climate crisis, where centuries of continued systems of accumulation by dispossession and destruction meet?


Our experience shows us that reparations cannot simply be another form of compensation. They must confront the very systems producing the harm – extractivism, odious and illegitimate debt, colonial legacies, patriarchy, racism, and corporate power promoting more false solutions whose aim is not climate justice but profit. Reparations must indeed offer us all a real chance to build Pan African feminist futures that centre care, including the restoration of the commons, and the conditions that make life possible.


Connecting the “c-words” – colonialism to climate reparations


The recent

African Symposium on Climate Reparations

 in Mombasa, Kenya, started on that same note: “there is no “c-word” that we cannot bring into conversations on climate reparations”, argued a comrade in his opening remarks. And indeed, the current

climate disorder

1

 is a historical process, and Colonialism (the c-word that in other climate justice spaces some shy away from) is part and parcel of it. As is, we argue at WoMin, capitalism. What is more, not only do climate reparations need to address colonialism and neocolonialism, but also the solution to the climate crisis will not be found within capitalism. Or as Audre Lorde put it, “… the master’s tools will never dismantle the master’s house. They may allow us temporarily to beat him at his own game, but they will never enable us to bring about genuine change.”


Not only we need our own tools, but also a broad alliance, as broad, yet united in principles and analysis, as broad and urgent is the task ahead. And the symposium offered an important space to bring together many working for reparations across the continent and in the diaspora, in conversations navigated along four main tracks: rights of nature and ecosystems stewardship; finance, debt and tax justice; law and human rights; and lived realities from frontline communities.


And the timing matters. We are entering the Decade of Justice and Reparations for Africans and People of African Descent, while the debt crisis in Africa continues to exponentially grow and deepen climate vulnerability, false climate solutions continue to expand, further threatening the commons millions of Africans depend upon for their everyday subsistence, and the African Court considers an Advisory Opinion on States’ obligations in the climate crisis.


As powerful expressed in an

open letter

 which emerged from the symposium, a Pan African position and action plan for climate reparations is urgent, but it cannot be constructed only through states, legal and financial tools. Those at the frontlines absorbing the costs of extractivism, ecological destruction and climate disruption have to shape what counts as harm, what constitutes repair, and what must stop. And importantly, we need to organise at all levels the collective power to make repair possible.


African women united for climate justice and reparations


This was the task of the 4th

Women’s Climate Assembly

 (WCA) in Yaoundé, Cameroon, held in early October under the theme, “Our lands, our voices: African women united for climate justice and reparations!”. The Assembly convened over 75 women community leaders, activists, feminist organisations, civil society groups and allies from twelve countries including Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), Guinea-Conakry, Liberia, Namibia, Niger, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, Senegal, and Zambia.


Oh ancestors, watch over Africa and let everything return to Africa! If we are coveted today, if there are wars, it is because our ancestors bequeathed this land to us. They did not abuse its riches. They used them sustainably. So we ask our ancestors to guide us during this Assembly, so that peace and food …

author: Mada Masr
title: Lina Attalah in custody after court issues LE3 mn fine, orders Mada Masr’s closure
content:
Mada Masr Editor-in-Chief Lina Attalah was fined LE3 million by the New Cairo Misdemeanor Court, which convicted her on charges of managing an unlicensed website, issuing an order for the website’s closure. Attalah was taken into custody after the issue of the ruling.


Tuesday’s session at the ninth circuit of the New Cairo Misdemeanor Court, presided over by judge Mohamed Mubarak, was temporarily suspended for deliberations after Attalah’s defense counsel requested time to review the case file.


After the court returned from deliberations, the judge ordered the courtroom cleared of everyone except Attalah and her defense counsel, the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights’ executive director Hossam Bahgat, who was also present, told Mada Masr. The room then filled with plainclothes officers and guards, with a National Security Agency officer in attendance, he added.


The presiding judge and a Supreme State Security Prosecution representative returned to the session and the judge announced that the court has decided to stand by its rejection of all the procedural arguments presented by the defense, including requests to bring in any documentation or hear any witnesses.


The judge then asked the defense team to present its plea. The counsel insisted that it would not submit a plea as long as its requests were unanswered by the court.


The judge then abruptly asked for a lawyer unknown to any member of the defense counsel to be brought in, “in a move that astonished all those present,” said Bahgat, and announced that the court decided to appoint a lawyer for Attalah.


At that point, all members of the defense counsel cried out to reject the court’s appointment of a lawyer when the eight chosen lawyers were present. Attalah herself spoke to say she did not accept the court-appointed lawyer acting on her behalf, an objection the judge refused to have recorded in the session’s minutes.


“In an even more shocking move,” said Bahgat, the judge himself began to log down the requests of the court-appointed lawyer, without the lawyer having said a word. The judge then read out the conviction amid shouts and protests from the defense counsel.


The judge sentenced Attalah to the maximum possible penalty: a LE3 million fine, the closure of Mada Masr’s website and the confiscation of its property.


Security personnel then surrounded Attalah, lifted her off the ground and took her out of the courtroom, where she remains in custody in the courthouse.

author: Pierre-Christophe Gam
title: Who gets to dream the future?
content:
We are living in unprecedented times. The world as we know it is changing rapidly as progress in AI and biomedicine is promising to radically transform our lives. We hear talk of humans merging with machines; of the possibility in the near future of uploading our consciousness into the cloud; of editing our DNA to end all diseases and augment our physical abilities; of genetically modified human beings; of human clones and hybrids. We hear talk of lab-grown meat, bio-engineered food and seeds edited to be sterile, rendering us permanently dependent on their patent owners.

We hear talk of a digital grid of control superimposed on our lives; of a future without privacy, without private thoughts or actions, of social credit score systems constantly monitoring and managing behavior; of brain implants recording our thoughts and altering our perception of reality; of the end of government and the rise of AI-controlled city-states run by mega-corporations; and of the collapse of democratic rule in favor of a neo-feudal order shaped by a radical racist, ableist, eugenicist worldview.

All these dystopian scenarios are not merely the science-fiction-informed fantasies of the leading Silicon Valley tycoons. They are also real, circulating scenarios of the future promoted in mainstream media, podcasts, and elite discourse. Since the reelection of Donald Trump and his theatrical inauguration ceremony, surrounded by the owners of the worldʼs largest tech companies, a new ideology has gained ground. Presented as the core philosophy of Silicon Valley elites, the “dark enlightenment” is the name coined for a neo-reactionary project for society.

Think of it as an apocalyptic cult, a quasi-religious project of radical social destruction, committed to the abolition of the democratic values and ideals of inclusive governance and social equity of the post–Second World War era. It envisions a future world structured around rigid, top-down social hierarchies, central authority, and techno-authoritarian control. Peter Thiel, a cofounder of Palantir, is the movement’s best-known backer, and now, with J. D. Vance, his protégé, as vice president, and with Elon Musk, the self-styled transhumanist czar and the largest financial backer of far-right movements across the world, the realization of this vision has never felt more imminent.

Whatʼs perhaps most disturbing beyond the fascist ambitions of this nefarious project is the near silence surrounding it. We are all witnessing the rise of a radical, global movement, a project bent on the total reprogramming of our societies and the destruction of our social norms, and yet it seems as if no one is challenging it, or even acknowledging its presence. But who gave this small circle of socially maladjusted tech nerds the right to decide the collective future of humanity?

The answer is simple. No one.

But who gets to dream the future? Is the future self-arising, an unavoidable destination without possibility for rerouting or adjustment? The outcome of a natural movement, informed by the gradual evolution of sociopolitical and economic trends? I want to argue here that the future, like our present and our past, will be conceived and designed from our collective beliefs; it will be informed by the hopes and fears of people like you and me. Everything that exists in our world first started as an idea, as an invisible, immaterial thought in someoneʼs mind. Most of the things that we take for granted today, such as the cars we drive, the devices we use to communicate with one another, or the clothes we wear, first emerged as arbitrary propositions within the realm of our imagination, and it is only with time and repetition that they eventually became cultural norms and social standards to the point where it has now become difficult for most to imagine a life without them. In that same manner, what we call the future will emerge from our collective imagination. It will be informed by the stories we tell ourselves, about what we deem to be real, valuable, and possible. Imagination is the foundation upon which our entire reality rests. Beyond resisting the ongoing fascist onslaught, we need to expand the scope of our imagination. In order to set forward a different kind of future than the hellish project envisioned by the techno-fascist mafia, we must identify new colors, shapes, and contours within the confines of our imagination.

title: News Quiz Nov. 14 | What day is it?
content:
It’s time again for a news quiz. Come on in and test your knowledge of current events.


1.

Silu’s Taxi in Rankin Inlet recently announced it would no longer operate. Aside from giving rides, what charitable activity did the company help with?


A.

 It operated as a medical transport service for patients flying south for health-care appointments.


B.

 The company hosted mechanic workshops to teach students the trade when its vehicles needed repair.


C.

 The company helped facilitate pizza deliveries to Leo Ussak Elementary School to celebrate the last day of classes.

 What did Kuujjuaq commemorate this week with its Path to 100 festival?

 Remembrance Day

 The anniversary of the James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement

 One-hundred years of Winnie the Pooh

 What did people come together to celebrate Saturday at Annie Pootogook Park in Ottawa?

 International Inuit Day


B.

 Bison Day


C.

 National Bittersweet Chocolate with Almonds Day

. Critics of the way Nunavut handles foster care point to an Indigenous-led method of family services that has worked for decades in which jurisdiction?

 Alaska

 Hawaii

 Puerto Rico

 Northern store’s security guards in Iqaluit look a little different these days. What has changed?

 They dress for holidays throughout the year in an effort to spread cheer.

 They are in tactical gear, including body cameras and carry what appear to be retractable batons.

 The store is employing robot security guards now.


What are these two celebrating Saturday at Annie Pootoogook Park in Ottawa? (File photo by Nehaa Bimal)


Answers:


1.

 C — Silu’s Taxi did more than offer rides for money. The company also

partnered

 with Slap Shot Canteen to deliver pizzas to Leo Ussak School to celebrate the final day of classes.


2.

 B — The festival, hosted in Kuujjuaq from Sunday to Wednesday,

 A — This one should be a gimme. People

author: Sara Fayyazi
title: Supreme Court Rejects Trump Administration’s Bid to Restrict Gender Affirming Care for Incarcerated People
content:
On October 21, 2026, the Supreme Court rejected the Trump administration’s request to restrict medical treatment and accommodations for transgender people in federal prisons. The decision allows a lower court order blocking the policy to remain in place while the legal challenge proceeds. The ruling is an important development in the ongoing debate over transgender rights, access to healthcare, and the federal government’s authority over incarcerated people.

The dispute began after President Donald Trump issued an executive order restricting federal funding for certain medical treatments for transgender people in government custody. In response, the Bureau of Prisons introduced a policy that would end hormone therapy and gender-affirming surgeries for incarcerated people with gender dysphoria. The policy also sought to restrict certain accommodations for transgender prisoners.

Gender dysphoria is the distress some people experience when their gender identity does not align with their sex assigned at birth. The administration argued that these gender-affirming treatments were not necessary and that restricting them was justified by security and administrative concerns within federal prisons.

However, the policy faced legal challenges from three transgender people incarcerated in federal prisons, including one transgender woman and two transgender men. Their attorneys argued that the new restrictions would force the end of treatments that the Bureau of Prisons had provided to people with gender dysphoria since 1992.

The policy could affect nearly 1,000 incarcerated people in federal custody. The lawsuit raises questions about whether the government can discontinue established medical treatments for incarcerated people and what constitutional protections apply to people in its custody.

A lower federal court blocked the administration from enforcing the policy. The Justice Department then appealed to the Supreme Court, asking the justices to pause that ruling and allow the restrictions to take effect while the case continued. On October 21, the Supreme Court rejected the emergency request in an unsigned order. Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas stated that they would have granted the request. The decision leaves the lower court’s order in place, preventing the administration from immediately enforcing the restrictions.

However, the Supreme Court’s decision does not resolve the underlying lawsuit or determine whether the administration’s policy is constitutional. The legal challenge will continue in the lower courts.

The case highlights the challenges transgender people face when seeking health care in settings where the government controls their medical decisions. Incarcerated people depend on prison authorities for access to doctors, medication, and other necessary services so when a policy restricts particular treatment, people in custody may have limited options for obtaining care independently.

Although the ruling does not end the case, it prevents the Trump administration from immediately implementing the restrictions while the legal proceedings continue. The outcome of the lawsuit will have important consequences for transgender people in federal prisons if the restrictions are placed and as the case moves forward, it shows the importance of questioning how government policies affect vulnerable populations and how government decisions apply to people whose freedom and access to healthcare are already limited.

author: kelsie kilawna
title: The taste we’ve been missing
content:
Graphic by Lauren Marchand


The clanking of pots and pans and the ringing of laughter while moving around the kitchen were always calming sounds to me growing up. 


The most important lessons I’ve learned about food came as I stood at the hips of my grandmothers, watching them peel potatoes and listening to their stories.


I am a culinary storyteller of syilx foodways. In my work at

Smoke on the Plateau

, I teach through food. I share stories about my syilx/Okanagan homelands through a fully embodied experience bringing together taste, sight, smell and sound. My research has been lifelong and has taken place in kitchens, in berry patches, and while waiting for salmon and deer to return so I could help prepare it for the people. 


There is a beauty to this way of knowing and living, because it is what taught me to be slow and patient with the offerings of our land.


The work I do honours the relationships that collapse time and place into story. It is a way of ensuring we never forget the importance of our Four Food Chiefs system. In essence, this is a reaffirmation of our governance system. 


Now, today when you enter the Okanagan Valley, you see another food story being told. A palate cleanser for the gentrification of our foodways.


What’s missing from culinary discussions


A rising culinary hotspot, the Okanagan has dressed itself in words like “local,” “seasonal,” “farm-to-table.” While wine glasses clink and tasting notes are murmured, words like “terroir” roll off the tongue as a somewhat promise to its authenticity.

It is a beautiful and comfortable story.


Terroir is a French term embraced by the culinary industry to speak to “the taste of place.” The concept itself describes how the climate and land conditions of an area affect the flavour profile of local food crops. 


In the Okanagan this is popularized through the wine industry. It’s often the terroir of a wine that is showcased through wine tastings. It speaks to the soil, weather, topography and tradition that shape what consumers taste. 


“Local” has now become a premium label, “farm-to-table” has become marketing copy, and “terroir” has become a way to charge more for the same soil that syilx Peoples have been tending since the time of our Creation, without acknowledging who did the tending, or what was given back in return.


This is gentrification. 


Not just through the extractive wine industry, but it’s become the gentrification of taste itself. 


When terroir is extracted from its French roots and planted in the Okanagan, it lands on soil that is already alive with syilx knowledge and responsibility. 


First Foods Board, Smoke on the Plateau Catering, An assortment of homesmoked deer and elk sausages, cedar smoked candied salmon, accompanied by homemade xusem raspberry compote, and siya jam. Photo by kelsie marchand (kilawna)


As a syilx culinary storyteller, I am responsible for reminding people of this, that our foodways should not be minimized for the sake of an entertaining evening.


Our foodways have and always will be prayed over. Ceremonies of health, and gratitude are held for all our homelands offer us. Young people go through their Coming of Age ceremony learning to pray for the health of our waterways. All of this is the missing spirit of the term terroir.


So I’ve been working to name what’s missing. One word, something that can hold the weight of kinship, of reciprocity, of generations coiled into one. Something that reminds us we are part of the land, not separate from it.


So I call it by it’s name, tmixʷ.


tmixʷ is the nsyilxcen word for life-force, the aliveness of every being that makes a place what it is, it speaks far beyond just soil and climate. Rather it speaks to the kinships between all of it, our reciprocity, and our syilx/Okanagan obligation to give back, so that what you take can live again.


The syilx/Okanagan understanding of place is through tmxʷulaxʷ, which speaks to the life-force-place. It is a dynamic, regenerative relationship between all beings, which the culinary industry’s shallow “local” label cannot contain.


The Okanagan culinary industry wants you to taste place, so what they’re selling is terroir, but what its missing is tmixʷ.


What tmixʷ tastes like


Let me tell you a story about xusem (soapberries).


There’s a small spot in the Okanagan mountains that has the sweetest soapberries my family has ever tasted. 


The oldest person in my family shared that those berries are …

author: David S. D'Amato
title: La Via Libertaria all’egalitarismo
content:
Di

David S. D’amato

. Originale:

The Libertarian Road to Egalitarianism

, del 14 novembre 2014. Tradotto da

Enrico Sanna

.


Secondo uno

studio recente di Emmanuel Saez e Gabriel Zucman per l’Ufficio nazionale per la ricerca economica

, “

lo 0,1% delle famiglie [americane] possiede tanta ricchezza quanto il 90% meno ricco

”. Sempre secondo lo studio, la tanto declamata “ripresa” non ha raggiunto la classe media; i benefici sono andati alla cima della piramide.


Mentre una piccola frazione della popolazione ammassa gran parte della ricchezza nazionale, esperti e accademici accusano e offrono soluzioni. Com’è facile immaginare, si accusa il libero mercato di causare differenze crescenti di ricchezza e reddito. Fautori delle liberalizzazioni e del libero mercato, i libertari sono spesso accusati di vivere in un mondo di fantasia, di ignorare il problema della disuguaglianza.


Siamo noi stessi a farlo: quando si arriva al dunque, troppi si sentono a disagio, si difendono sostenendo che la disuguaglianza

non è

 un problema, e che bisogna invece vedere lo stile di vita o qualche altro parametro. “Il capitalismo è un bene per i poveri!” Invece i libertari dovrebbero accettare il semplice fatto che la disuguaglianza è un grosso problema.


Non dobbiamo vedere nella disuguaglianza un punto debole del discorso sulla libertà economica, o una questione irrisolvibile. Le attuali relazioni economiche non sono il risultato della libertà di scambio o della legittima proprietà privata. In fatto di disuguaglianza, la ragione sta dalla parte dei libertari. Libertà e eguaglianza sono di fatto complementari, si rafforzano reciprocamente: dalla prima deriva la seconda.


Anarchici individualisti come Lysander Spooner sostenevano che “ricchezza e povertà estreme” sono il risultato del “diritto positivo”, sostituiscono il diritto naturale con un diritto arbitrario, “danno vita a monopoli e privilegi”. Sotto il capitalismo, spiega, chi possiede un certo capitale ha un particolare potere economico che non ha niente a che vedere con la libertà di produrre, scambiare e competere. In un’ottica generale, l’intervento dello stato beneficia chi è ricco e ha appoggi politici, oltre alle élite che possono influire su chi scrive e applica le regole che tutti dobbiamo rispettare.


Il meccanismo non è perfetto, e per questo sopra il capitalismo monopolistico troviamo tutto uno strato di misure chiaramente intese a proteggere i lavoratori, i consumatori e i poveri. Ma nessuna di queste misure riesce a intaccare l’obiettivo di fondo dell’intervento statale, il quale espropria i legittimi proprietari e mette le masse al servizio dei datori di lavoro. L’obiettivo storico dello stato, in breve, è la lotta di classe permanente, l’uso del proprio potere per tenere al sicuro un’aristocrazia socioeconomica.


La sinistra istituzionale ha certamente ragione sull’uguaglianza, ma tende a sbagliare in fatto di libertà, diritti individuali e mercato. L’anarchismo di mercato è per la libertà

ma anche

 per l’uguaglianza, e vuole una società senza stato in cui la legge ultima sia la parità di libertà e autorità.


La vera competizione aperta è una forza che ha il potere di dissolvere e disperdere. I libertari dovrebbero smettere di giustificare le attuali sconcertanti disuguaglianze come se fossero il risultato del

laissez-faire

 e della sovranità individuale.


Le nostre traduzioni sono finanziate interamente da donazioni. Se vi piace quello che scriviamo, siete invitati a contribuire. Trovate le istruzioni su come fare nella pagina

Sostieni C4SS

:

https://c4ss.org/sostieni-c4ss

.

author: By Sophia Potsi, Contributor
title: Europe’s Broken Promise: From Open Camps to High-Tech Prisons
content:
Greek Islands – In 2015, the Greek island of Lesvos was the epicenter of the so-called migration crisis. With arrivals reaching 2,000 people per day, images from the island reflected the solidarity of the locals. Fishermen were seen pulling people out of the water and elderly women took care of newborns in village squares. The islanders’ response of solidarity with people fleeing war was so remarkable that they were nominated for a Nobel Peace Prize.


For a while, Lesvos was a place that functioned as an in-between, an island that people stayed for a little bit and then left to continue their journey to Europe. But after the EU-Turkey deal in 2016, the islands were turned from places that people passed to places that people were held. From passageways they became waiting rooms in closed camps on the edge of Europe. 


And this is how Moria was built, the camp that in the following years would become a symbol of Europe’s brutal containment and inhumane policies and treatment against refugees, migrants, and people on the move.


Moria: Suffering and Resilience


Moria camp, formally known as the Moria Reception and Identification Center, was the largest refugee camp in Europe. It was originally built to hold 3,000 people, and had help up to 20,000 people at peak times before it burned down in 2020. 


The conditions in the camp were horrible. There was no running water, no sewage system and almost no healthcare. People were living in limbo in makeshift shelters waiting years for their asylum decision. 


It was a place of suffering and a

mental health crisis

 unfolded with reported suicide attempts, self-harm, panic attacks and anxiety. 


Yet, the camp allowed the residents to have some agency. Showing resilience, the residents built a mosque, a barber shop, and a makeshift oven. 


Residents showed solidarity with each other and

organized themselves

 to push for better living conditions, cleaned up the camp, and ran schools.


“Welcome to Europe” graffiti on the outside walls of Moria camp. Photo contributed by Sophia Potsi.


The Fire


In September 2020 Moria camp burned to the ground. 


Six people, five of them minors, were arrested and charged with arson and were dubbed the Moria Six. Greek authorities claimed the fire was deliberately lit by camp residents. The Greek Minister of Migration and Asylum at the time, Notis Mitarachi,

posted to social media

 that “the arsonists of Moria have been detained [and] the safety of everyone is guaranteed.” 


However,

Forensic Architecture

 later reconstructed the events on the night of the fire from hundreds of videos and testimonies and found the fire most likely came from improvised electrical connections among flammable tent-like shelters in hot, dry, windy conditions. This conclusion was supported by Lesvos fire department’s own report. Prior to the September 2020 fire, there had been 247 fire outbreaks in the camp.


Of the six people charged, two were tried as minors and released after four years. The other four were initially found guilty but then released after three and a half years in prison after they were acquitted of the charges and cleared in

2025

.


As the chapter closed on Moria, the European Union

made promises

 that there would be “no more Morias.”


A wall at one of the entrances in Moria has writing on it that reads, “You cannot repaır the hell. Let’s people to be free! One Day.” Photo contributed by Sophia Potsi.


The Replacement Camp


What replaced Moria in Lesvos, supposedly as a temporary solution, was the Mavrovouni camp, often called Kara Tepe. Facing the sea just outside of Mytilene are rows and rows of the same white containers. It looks like every other camp in Greece with no sign that anyone has made the place their own. 


It exists to keep people in containers, fed and counted, and almost nothing else. Compared with the chaos and terror of Moria it is an improvement but there are still issues with sanitation, water and electricity.  


The biggest additions are the restricted movement of residents and the intensified surveillance. Security guards stand at the gate. No journalists or NGO workers can enter freely. 


Residents have their

life controlled

 by police, private security and various procedures with set times to come and go mediated by ID checks and bag searches at checkpoints.


While this model is far more restrictive than the one seen in Moria, the country has unveiled even more strict systems for future …

author: Unknown
title: “Gen Z Regulates” : A New Wave of Unrest in Germany?
content:
For months, unrest has been spreading across Europe. In

Spain

, a movement against evictions and gentrification culminated on November 11 in a countrywide general strike. In

France

, student revolt set off the most intense street confrontations since the

Yellow Vest movement

. Albania has seen wave upon wave of clashes since last February. On Halloween, the European youth protests finally reached Germany.


Under the motto

“Gen Z regelt”

 (“Gen Z regulates”), tens of thousands took to the streets of nearly 40 German cities on October 31. While a large-scale uprising like the

one

 in France remains unlikely, the first cracks in the pacification of society are starting to show. In this report, two anarchists describe their experiences in two different demonstrations and discuss the potential of the events.


More demonstrations on the same theme are scheduled for

November 20

.


A stylish banner in front of the “Gen Z Regelt” protest in Göttingen. What would Goethe have said?


Germany in Crisis


The demonstration on October 31 took place in a general context of crisis. In Germany, as elsewhere around the globe, inflation has run rampant over the last six years, driven by the pandemic, Putin’s invasion of Ukraine and the consequent loss of cheap natural gas from Russia, and, most recently, the US-Iran war.


Another growing influence on the economy is the climate catastrophe. It is

estimated

 that Germany will lose around 30 billion euros a year as a consequence of its impact. In one week, a heatwave at the end of June

killed

 close to 10,000 people. Unlike countries that have long-term experience with temperatures above 40 degrees Celsius, only 10% of homes in Germany have air conditioning; with the exception of intensive care units and operating rooms, most hospitals and nursing homes don’t have it, so people who experienced heat stroke were treated in overheated rooms. Senior citizens and those with preexisting health problems were especially hard hit: in at least one nursing home, temperatures

reached

 up to 50 degrees Celsius.


A protester in the German city of Essen asks to stop some of the impacts of climate change.


Who dies as a consequence of climate change is determined mostly by class. Germany also faces a housing crisis—

something like 53% of people live in rented homes

—and the cheapest flats are generally located right beneath the roofs of buildings several stories high. These buildings were built to keep heat in, so during heat waves, temperatures in the flats at night often stayed above the outside temperatures at same time.


On top of this, the government comprised of the neoliberal left (SPD) and Christian conservative (CDU/CSU) parties has introduced an unpopular austerity program in order to push through a massive increase in military spending, which started after the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022. It would take another article to list all the financial cuts involved. Workers and middle-class people will have many billions less in “social benefits”—in other words, they get less back from the work and resources that the state and capitalists take from them.


Some 12% of all jobs in Germany are

directly in state institutions

, in addition to fully state-owned companies and other organizations connected to the state, like the public health insurance agencies and public media companies. Many of these have stop hiring because of the financial situation. At the same time, German economic growth is stagnating. Consequently, “Gen Z” career entrants confront a context in which companies are trying to figure out how to use artificial intelligence to replace them amid an employment market that is already much worse than previous generations faced. This is undermining the last vestiges of a social contract between companies and the state on one side and segments of the youth on the other.


Study, get degree, and you can have a middle-class life? Not anymore.


Finally, some international fashions trends like ski glasses are reaching German youth.


Unemployment is rising among university and college graduates. The social situation isn’t as catastrophic as it has become in other countries, but by contrast with many other countries, people in Germany do not have much experience helping each other directly. German society has focused on the state as the only thinkable source of support when people lose their jobs or experience other setbacks.


As a result, anger has spread …

author: Slingshot robot #1
title: a14 – What’s fermenting underground – Jazz Dance with today’s zine scene
content:
Our collective can barely process all the correspondence coming our way. The least of which comes with scrappy limited edition zines. We endeavor to highlight them here when we can. Thankfully we have found a bright and wise ally who, when not tending to the garden warmly sits and reads deeply and widely freaky shit on paper. Maybe you will find a new life of reading zines, reviewing or even making them to thicken the plot we’re in.

Ear of Corn #66 24 pages – $2 foodfortunata@hotmail.com

It’s really endearing that even after 18 years, Ear of Corn still uses pasteup for the design, even as it’s moved to glossy paper. You can see on every page that Ear of Corn is still assembled old school and copied like we all used to do at Kinkos with glue sticks. The glue had a mild starchy taste, slightly sweet with a bitter finish; not unlike bad cheese pizza.

I have this conspiracy theory about this zine. I usually write reviews in batches, and I’ll often have multiple issues of Ear of Corn on my desk at a time. But I’ve never had any sequentially numbered issues. I’ve begun to suspect issues are not numbered non-sequentially or perhaps they are sequential, but aren’t printed in that order. Their practice of reviewing old and new releases side by side makes it impossible to know for sure; but they’re definitely up to something other than eating the glue.

Out From The Void #8 $5 – 70 pages outfromthevoid@yahoo.com

This issue goes places Out From The Void hasn’t gone before. The new topics are mostly adjacent to the core topic: the missing. So it’s the CAHOOTS program, police records requests, suicide, and police killings. But on page 51 begins a 6 page essay about Israel’s genocide in Gaza. It’s sober, historical and philosophical without trumpeting statistics.

In the middle of Issue #8 is a photo essay reprinted from the zine Here’s What I’ve Hidden Under My Tongue. Writer DJT was visiting an abandoned and mostly collapsed mental institution. In the introduction Brenton Gicker comments that he didn’t write any of the stories in this issue. I appreciate that Gicker puts his mission ahead of his ego to spread awareness of these topics but I do miss his voice as a writer. But until next time, we get more tales of the missing, the lost and the found.

The story of James B. Hunt and Fluke goes back to issue #16 of the infamous Fluke fanzine in 2018. Kudos if you kept that issue, it’s now a fine collectible. Even Maximum RockNRoll said so. They saw the future, perhaps even more clearly than I did. Gina Murrell always had a sixth sense for such things. But if you wake up feeling a bit goth, have a soft spot for monsters, or just like dead stuff, NXOEED might be for you.

If you don’t recognize his art that tells me you don’t skate bruh. His art appears on show flyers, album covers, websites, rad stickers and other greasy places. But among all that ephemera this issue is special. Usually Mr. Hunt lets the ink speak for him, but this time we actually get a few precious pages of text; our first sense of the man himself. He’s a geezer, like me, trying to do punk rock things, but to also go to bed on time. I feel that in my soul.

$20 – 192 pages inequitypress@hotmail.com

It’s hard to say that many poets are famous today. But as poets go, some of those published in Big Hammer are highfalutin people now like David Cope, Donald Lev, Chris Stroffolino, Ken Greenley, and Enid Dame (RIP). Others, like Michael Pingarron, are still writing for Big Hammer. They’ve found their layer of strata, and one would hope some sense of belonging.

The first issue of Big Hammer rolled off the press in 1988. That was 38 years ago, kids. Statistically most of you reading this weren’t even born yet. That zine was way underground, like the Lincoln Tunnel; like the FDR Train Car in the pitch blackness of Track 61 marooned below Grand Central since 1945. But Dave Roskos is still out there in the tunnels, in the darkness, still editing and publishing Big Hammer. He’s doing it his own way, and accountable to no one. Doesn’t it sound grand?

Zine content from the eighties makes more sense in the context of its contemporary punk 7-inches” like “Too scared to be queer,” “Be a Fag,” and “Forbidden Love.” So I queued up the Homocore Hit parade cassette, and pondered its place in history. Homocore ran for just 7 issues between 1988 and 1991. If you didn’t catch my drift, it tapped into two communities which still remain the core of the underground today: queers and …

author: Carla Habif
title: How Brazilians pulled off Lula’s surprise win
content:
This article

How Brazilians pulled off Lula’s surprise win

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


On Oct. 25, Brazilians made history by resisting hopelessness and achieving, for the first time since the return to democracy in 1985, a comeback in the runoff of a presidential election. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won reelection by more than 4 million votes after losing the first round to opponent Flávio Bolsonaro by over 2 million votes.


Lula, a former metalworker and union leader who co-founded the left-wing Workers’ Party,

was seeking his fourth term as president. Flávio, by contrast, was the candidate of the far-right Liberal Party and was running as the successor to his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, a Trump ally who was

convicted and imprisoned for attempting a coup d’état

.


The first round suggested that Flávio and his party were on track to gain an enormous amount of power. The party won

more seats in Congress than any other


—

 nearly a quarter of the lower house and more than a third of the Senate — which, together with other right-wing parties,

gave the right a majority in both houses

.


Two days after the vote,

Flávio said he would use that majority to “change the Constitution” and “re-democratize” the country. Asked what he meant, he

proposed

 limiting the powers of Supreme Court justices, lowering the age of criminal responsibility and ending presidential reelection, and he left open the possibility of extending the presidential term from four to five years.


“I really think the desperation and fear after the first round changed everything. There was a need to act with more urgency, and this desire to organize.”


In addition, whoever won in October would be able to

appoint up to four of the 11 justices of the federal Supreme Court

,

the same court that convicted Jair Bolsonaro. A Flávio victory would have given the far right control over all three branches of government, amid the advance of the far right in Latin America and the United States.


As a result, after the first-round results came in on

the night of Oct. 4, the mood among Lula’s supporters was one of deep discouragement and fear. But this fear quickly turned into forms of popular organizing that were diverse, complementary and consistently nonviolent — and they changed the course of the race. The mobilizations included a large-scale effort by politicians, activists, content creators and ordinary supporters to organize and amplify pro-Lula content on social media, and an equally massive occupation of the country’s streets in peaceful demonstrations.


Students took center stage in the street mobilizations, with thousands turning out for protests such as one

led by the National Union of Students, or UNE, at the Candelária

 church in Rio de Janeiro, and one led by UNE and the University of Brasília’s student council on the Esplanade of Ministries in Brasília. People in the streets and on social media acted together and complemented each other.


Beyond protests and online activism, people organized to make sure that those who had not voted in the first round would go to the polls, including elderly people and those who live far from their polling places. They also got off the internet and talked in person with undecided voters who had not yet made up their minds, a process that had a name: vira voto, or flip the vote.


For Gabriel Rochlin,

a director, actor and teacher who took part in a vira voto group in Rio de Janeiro, this was a way to get out of the social media bubble. “The work of vira voto has a lot to do with breaking through the algorithm,” he said. “The street has this real quality of not having an algorithm that separates people: you’re going to meet people you would never meet on your feed.” He saw the fear engendered by the first round as the turning point: “I really think the desperation and fear after the first round changed everything. There was a need to act with more urgency, and this desire to organize.”


From demoralization to esperançar


Given the collective feeling of fear and hopelessness after the first round of voting, the first challenge was to shift the mood of the left. It was on Oct. 5, the day after the results, that popular mobilization began in earnest.

We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.

author: Unknown
title: “How Has Serving Impacted You?” : Veterans of the US Military in Their Own Words
content:
What is it like to serve in the United States military? If only it were possible for those who are considering enlisting to learn the unvarnished truth. In 2019, a viral

tweet

 from the official US Army twitter account unexpectedly drew over 11,000 candid replies in the course of 48 hours. These responses offer a rare window into the real experiences of servicemembers and veterans. We present a selection of them here for the benefit of anyone who is thinking about joining the military.


This is a document of an

earlier era

 of social media, captured here before it

vanishes

. You can obtain a book collecting the first twenty-four hours of responses

here

.


Just before Memorial Day in 2019, the United States Army made a strategic blunder almost on par with invading Vietnam. They posted this inquiry on their official Twitter account:


In response, veterans and their family and friends posted thousands upon thousands of tweets recounting broken promises and broken people. They described cancer, PTSD, domestic abuse, unpaid college and housing loans, Gulf War syndrome, insomnia, sexual abuse, poverty, Agent Orange, racism, nightmare disorder, unemployment, burying loved ones, misogyny, orphaned children, burn pit syndrome, homelessness, debilitating injuries, divorce, alcoholism, disappearances, a Veterans Affairs department that was unwilling or unable to help, and suicide, suicide, suicide.


The United States military is one of the largest concentrations of power in the world. With

tens of thousands

 of missiles,

millions

 of firearms, and over

5000

 nuclear weapons—about 40% of all the nuclear weapons in the world—the US military can hold the entire world hostage.


The US military is also the largest employer in the United States,

employing

 almost 2,900,000 workers—roughly 17 out of every 2000 people. If we add private military contractors like Blackwater (250,000 workers), the employees of non-combat support companies like Halliburton who build military infrastructure, provide food, and the like (150,000-250,000), US-based war manufacturers like Lockheed Martin and Boeing (1,500,000), and

veterans

 who receive disability or pension payments (2,000,000), we find that roughly 1 out of every 50 Americans is economically dependent on US militarism.


As in all industries, without this workforce, the military would grind to a halt. It especially depends on regular transfusions of young blood—young people sold stories about adventure, duty, and upward mobility.


If we were to ask new recruits why they joined, we’d

likely

 hear a mix of narratives about gaining strength, seeing the world, paying for college, serving God and country, learning life skills, continuing a family tradition, escaping poverty or an unsafe home, obtaining housing, having fun, and protecting loved ones. Most people join the military because they think it will benefit them or because they believe they are serving a higher calling.


Some recruits get to live out their dreams. Some leave instability, danger, or deprivation for a more structured and economically stable life; some even gain a sense of belonging. If they’re lucky, they serve their time without incident, then move on to free college tuition, a no-down-payment housing loan, health insurance, and a free meal at Golden Corral once a year.


But thousands of veterans’ dreams become nightmares. The promises of recruiters, family members, and Hollywood movies offer a gamble at best—a roll of the dice that

frequently

 ends with being harmed physically, psychologically, and sexually. Military service can lead to

substance abuse

,

homelessness

, and

suicide

. It can also end in unspeakable acts of violence against others, whether those be the declared enemies of the United States, noncombatants, or veterans’ own loved ones.


It is striking how many of these responses speak of being hoodwinked out of college, housing loans, and medical care—how many describe the pain of family members lost to PTSD, alcoholism, or suicide after witnessing or committing atrocities.


American media bombards us with war propaganda. Almost every video game spreads the myth that combat makes us stronger: more powerful weapons, tougher armor, a bigger health bar, greater fortunes. Hollywood promises that the hero can weather any fight—or, if he can’t, his death will be meaningful and glorious.


Statistically speaking, the more we are exposed to combat, the more likely we are to be …

author: Admin101
title: Announcing Black Rose/Rosa Negra Locals in Austin, New York City, and Chicago
content:
We’re thrilled to announce the formation of three new Locals of Black Rose/Rosa Negra Anarchist Federation (BRRN)! From the Texas Hill Country, to the Great Lakes, to the Northeast, our organization is growing deeper roots and expanding our capacity to organize, struggle, and build popular power in communities across the country.


As you will read below, each new local grows out of its members’ deep involvement in the popular struggles of their neighborhoods, workplaces, and broader communities. What follows are brief introductions in their members’ own words — including their contact info and social media handles.


Austin, TX


The Austin Local has officially re-formed! Our members are primarily focused on labor and tenant organizing, as well as rapid response to ICE. We are also making preparations for an open reading group to discuss

BRRN’s Program

.


We welcome those with interest to contact us.


Email:

 austin@blackrosefed.org

Instagram:


@blackrose_atx


Chicago, IL


The Chicago local is back! Our logo honors the Haymarket Martyrs Memorial — a symbol of the organizers who made anarchism a powerful current in immigrant and women workers’ struggles of their time, as well as the place we gathered for our first event all together as a local. 


We carry their memory with us alongside others as we work in the social movements where we are rooted. These include tenant struggles on the South and Northwest sides, as well as labor organizing in the Chicago Teachers Union. We look forward to deepening our connections with comrades in our movements and others through collective study and struggle.


Email:

 chicago@blackrosefed.org

Instagram:


@blackrose_chicago

 


New York City, NY


Members of the New York City Local organize with tenants, neighbors, youth, coworkers, and parents to build Black, Brown, and working-class popular power throughout the city. Sites of social insertion include the Astoria Tenant Union in Queens, anticarceral youth and parent programs in Manhattan, immigrant defense coalitions in Brooklyn, the American Association of University Professors, and more. True to BRRN’s internationalist character, we also organize within the Palestinian and Sudanese solidarity movements.


From the Young Lords to Occupy Wall Street, we recognize the integral role that revolutionaries in NYC have played in past freedom struggles and look forward to reviving organized anarchism in the especifista tradition across the five boroughs.

BRRN’s Program

 serves as a blueprint for renewed efforts to confront imperial and capitalist violence as anarchist militants living at the nexus of US empire and global capital .


Email:

 nyc@blackrosefed.org

Instagram:

 @blackrose_nyc


Are you organizing at your workplace, on your campus, or in your neighborhood? Looking for a political home in which you can strategize with others about how to build power, force concessions, and push our mass movements in a revolutionary direction?


Black Rose/Rosa Negra could be right for you.


Read our

Join

 page and send us a membership inquiry!

Announcing Black Rose/Rosa Negra Locals in Austin, New York City, and Chicago

Black Rose/Rosa Negra Anarchist Federation

author: Publicación Abierta
title: El genocidio indígena de la «Campaña del Desierto» llegó a los tribunales argentinos
content:
Boletín de pueblos originarios a 534 años de la invasión europea


El genocidio indígena de la «Campaña del Desierto» llegó a los tribunales argentinos


Mario Hernandez


 


El genocidio a los pueblos originarios de la Patagonia en el marco de la Campaña del Desierto (1878-1890) llegó a la Justicia argentina. El 16 de agosto, Ivana Noemí Huenelaf, mujer mapuche-tehuelche, presentó la denuncia ante los Tribunales Federales de Retiro (Ciudad de Buenos Aires). Lo hizo junto a su abogado Fernando Cabaleiro, de la ONG Naturaleza de Derechos. “Para que se inicie un Juicio por la Verdad a los fines que se investigue la comisión de hechos atroces que encuadran dentro de la figura de genocidio: torturas, fusilamientos, desapariciones forzadas y abandono de personas, apremios ilegales, traslados forzosos, disposición y reducción a servidumbre de personas y sustracción de menores”, dice el texto de la denuncia, que tiene 80 páginas.


Lxs demandantes pidieron que “en ese marco procesal se dicte una sentencia declarativa en referencia a todo ese proceso como un Genocidio y se dispongan las medidas y actos reparatorios que por derecho correspondan”.


 


El sorteo de rigor hizo recaer la denuncia en la Fiscalía 7 (González) y en el Juzgado en lo Criminal y Correccional Federal 3, (a cargo de Daniel Rafecas) de los tribunales federales de Retiro.


“Hay jueces  fiscales que nos pueden escuchar”


“Mari, mari”, saluda Huenelaf al salir de los Tribunales de Comodoro Py. “Siento el Newen (fuerza espiritual) porque es muy importante para mi pueblo. Se va tejiendo esto. Hay jueces y fiscales que nos pueden llegar a escuchar, es un gran paso que se gesta con la resistencia. No venimos con rabia sino con dolor para sanar esas heridas, con la sabiduría y el conocimiento de la Mapu (Madre Tierra), con gente que cree en nuestra causa”, dice con calma y sonriente esta mujer indígena. Y aclara: “No es sólo una etnia sino todos en comunidad, con Norita Cortiñas que va a ser testigo de concepto si nos aceptan como querella. Su genocidio fueron 30 mil víctimas, el nuestro fueron 20 mil, van a tener que acostumbrarse a ese número”, agrega Huenelaf.


Tiene 49 años, es madre de seis hijos y abuela de siete nietos. Nació en un paraje al pie de la Cordillera, José de San Martín. Es mapuche y tehuelche, y acompaña las recuperaciones de territorio. Vive en Mallín Ahogado, en un territorio en comunidad llamado Tierra y Dignidad. Trabaja en la feria regional donde vende pan casero y es profesora de judo –primer Dan– de niñeces en Lago Puelo.


En la soleada mañana del martes 16 de agosto, llevaba su vestimenta originaria y un brillante trarilonco (cintillo) de plata sobre el pelo negro azabache. Le trajo problemas. “Ni bien entré (a los tribunales) me demoraron. Hice tres pasos y una policía me agarró para no dejarme ingresar. Con mucha tranquilidad lo tomamos, tenemos medio naturalizado que nos paren y nos discriminen por portación de rostro. Hubo un cruce de palabras entre la policía y mi abogado pero finalmente pasamos a hacer lo que veníamos a hacer”, relata.


Desde la Campaña del desierto hasta Benetton


Ivana estuvo en enero de 2017 entre la decena de personas que acudió solidaria a la Lof en Resistencia de Cushamen cuando sus miembros fueron reprimidos por Gendarmería. Con ferocidad, como durante el operativo de agosto de aquel año, cuando desapareció el tatuador anarquista Santiago Maldonado.


Nunca imaginaron la pesadilla que vivieron después, al ser baleadas, perseguidas y detenidas. Ivana y el grupo fueron tiroteados por policías de Chubut y empleados de Benetton. Ella sacó fotos y logró avisar a una abogada, poco antes de ser golpeada y detenida en la comisaría de El Maitén. Mientras tanto, el fiscal Carlos Díaz Mayer negaba una y otra vez que estuvieran allí.  Se habrían quedado mucho tiempo más si no las sacaba el abogado Carlos “Chuzo” González Quintana que andaba por la zona de vacaciones.


“Me tocó vivir un proceso con una estrategia no muy diferente a la de 1879 que comenzó el genocidio que hoy estamos denunciando en Comodoro Py”, dice Huenelaf. El colmo fue que todas estas víctimas terminaron acusadas por el empresario italiano de robo de ganado y posesión de explosivos. Años más tarde quedaron absueltas: les habían plantado las pruebas. Así funcionan algunas cosas en la Patagonia.

author: anred
title: Visita del Papa a Argentina: entre sotanas, negocios y memoria
content:
La visita del papa León XIV a la Argentina no puede analizarse por fuera de la historia política de la Iglesia Católica, sus vínculos con el poder, las denuncias de abusos sexuales, los cuestionamientos por encubrimiento y una realidad social cada vez más hostil para las mayorías trabajadoras. La visita dejó mucho más que ceremonias, discursos y fotografías junto a representantes del poder político. También abrió una discusión necesaria: ¿qué representa hoy la Iglesia Católica en una Argentina atravesada por el hambre, la desocupación, el ajuste y la pérdida de derechos?.

 Por Rocío Cisterna para ANRed


No se trata de cuestionar la fe de millones de personas ni la necesidad de encontrar contención espiritual en tiempos difíciles. Se trata de discutir el poder de una institución que, a lo largo de la historia argentina, mantuvo vínculos profundos con los sectores dominantes y cuya jerarquía eclesiástica arrastra responsabilidades históricas que no pueden quedar sepultadas bajo ceremonias y discursos de reconciliación.


UNA HISTORIA QUE NO PUEDE OCULTARSE


Los lugares elegidos para las actividades papales tampoco son ajenos a esta discusión.En Claypole, el Pequeño Cottolengo Don Orione, institución vinculada a la congregación religiosa del mismo nombre, ha sido escenario de denuncias y cuestionamientos por abusos y malos tratos contra personas con discapacidad. Las responsabilidades individuales e institucionales deben investigarse y no pueden quedar protegidas por el prestigio de ninguna congregación religiosa.


En Córdoba, la Fábrica Argentina de Aviones remite a una historia atravesada por el terrorismo de Estado. La antigua Fábrica Militar de Aviones estuvo inserta en el entramado industrial y militar de aquellos años, mientras La perla funcionaba como uno de los principales centros clandestinos de detención, tortura y exterminio de la provincia. También resulta imprescindible recuperar el papel de sectores de la jerarquía eclesiástica cordobesa durante la dictadura.


En Luján, la memoria de la desaparición de una profesional de la salud vinculada a la Colonia Montes de Oca en1985 exige investigación y reconstrucción histórica. Las responsabilidades y omisiones institucionales deben documentarse para evitar que la memoria se convierta en una versión conveniente del pasado.


Cuando estos hechos se ponen en perspectiva, aparece una discusión histórica ineludible: la responsabilidad de sectores civiles, empresariales, militares y eclesiásticos en la última dictadura cívico-militar. No hubo solamente uniformes. También hubo complicidades, legitimaciones y silencios.


Ni olvido, ni perdón impuesto, ni reconciliación sin justicia.


ENTRE EL PODER ECLESIÁSTICO Y LAS DENUNCIAS DE ENCUBRIMIENTO DE

 ABUSO SEXUAL Y PEDOFILIA: ALBERTO BOCHATEY, EL ANFITRIÓN DE LEÓN XIV


La visita papal también obliga a poner el foco en una figura de enorme relevancia dentro de la estructura eclesiástica argentina: monseñor

Alberto Germán Bochatey

, obispo auxiliar de La Plata, amigo personal de LeónXIV y uno de los referentes religiosos vinculados a la recepción y organización de su visita al país. Su relación con Robert Prevost, hoy León XIV, se remonta a los años en que ambos compartían formación religiosa y pertenecían a la Orden de San Agustín. No es una relación circunstancial: es un vínculo personal y de larga trayectoria que coloca a Bochatey en un lugar de cercanía con el actual pontífice. Pero detrás de esa cercanía existe una historia que merece ser discutida públicamente: los cuestionamientos sobre su actuación frente a casos de abusos sexuales cometidos dentro de instituciones religiosas y las denuncias periodísticas sobre posibles mecanismos de protección y encubrimiento. Uno de los casos más graves es el del Instituto Próvolo, en Mendoza, donde sacerdotes y otros integrantes de la institución fueron investigados y algunos condenados por abusos sexuales contra niños, niñas y adolescentes 2 sordos e hipoacúsicos.


En 2017, el Vaticano designó a Bochatey como comisario apostólico para intervenir en la Compañía de María para la Educación de Sordomudos, congregación vinculada a los institutos Próvolo. Su misión incluía asumir responsabilidades de gobierno institucional y participar de la respuesta eclesiástica frente al escándalo. Sin embargo, su intervención fue objeto de fuertes cuestionamientos.

author: Redação
title: Vitória: um cartão postal manchado de pó preto
content:
Há mais de meio século, a população da Grande Vitória enfrenta uma poluição carregada pelo vento que causa transtornos tanto à sua rotina quanto à sua saúde – o Pó Preto. O material particulado de cor escura, popularmente chamado de pó preto, é produzido a partir de processos industriais com minério de ferro, carvão e outros metais pesados que acontecem no complexo industrial de Tubarão, onde estão instaladas a mineradora Vale e a siderúrgica ArcelorMittal.


No segundo episódio de Big Problema, vamos viajar até o litoral capixaba para investigar de onde vem o pó preto que cobre a cidade de Vitória e por que, mesmo após décadas de denúncias, a poluição causada pela indústria ainda faz parte da vida de quem mora na cidade.


O Big Problema é uma série de podcast narrativo idealizada pela primeira turma de

trainees da

Agência Pública

, que investiga como grandes empreendimentos têm transformado a cultura, o cotidiano e a relação das pessoas com as cidades brasileiras.

author: Maríangeles Guerrero
title: Saquear y fugar: el mito del desarrollo a partir de las exportaciones
content:
Por Mariángeles Guerrero


El discurso dominante de la política económica argentina defiende la “inserción internacional” y la reprimarización de la economía. Sin embargo, un estudio reciente del

Instituto de Pensamiento y Políticas Públicas (IPyPP)

 demuestra cómo esos sectores primarios (agronegocio, minería, hidrocarburos) no solo no contribuyen al desarrollo nacional sino que, a través de las fugas de capitales, consolidan el mercado financiero global en detrimento del país donde explotan los bienes comunes. 

Molinos Agro, Minera Exar, Minas Argentinas, Pan American Energy, Tecpetrol, Pluspetrol, Vista e YPF

 son algunas de las firmas analizadas.


“La extracción de recursos naturales se articula con mecanismos de salida de divisas y una menor captación estatal de la renta generada, lo que plantea interrogantes sobre la contribución efectiva de estas actividades al desarrollo productivo nacional”, expresa el informe del IPyPP realizado por los investigadores Gustavo García Zanotti y Martín Schorr.


Que Argentina sea proveedora de materias primas (oleaginosas y cereales, minerales e hidrocarburos) y bienes derivados permitiría, según la narrativa hegemónica, aprovechar las oportunidades que ofrece la globalización y generar las divisas necesarias. Para algunas perspectivas, como la del neodesarrollismo, servirían para impulsar el desarrollo productivo. Para otras, como la del neoliberalismo, para pedalear la bicicleta de la especulación financiera. En ambos casos la base es la explotación de la naturaleza ("recursos naturales", según empresarios y funcionarios).


Pero el esquema de exportaciones “no cumple meramente una función de abastecimiento de divisas para el balance comercial, sino que funciona de manera simultánea como el principal canal de transferencia de ingresos y riqueza hacia los centros decisorios globales y las jurisdicciones de baja o nula tributación”, advierte

el estudio

.


Como resultado, indica, se configura en Argentina un extractivismo de múltiples dimensiones. No solo se extraen los recursos naturales, sino también las divisas generadas por su explotación y los ingresos fiscales que el Estado resigna mediante beneficios tributarios y regímenes promocionales (como el

Régimen de Incentivo para Grandes Inversiones

, RIGI).


Foto: COFCO


Extraer y evadir


El informe explica que las grandes empresas trasladan ganancias al exterior mediante la manipulación de los precios de transferencia. Este mecanismo consiste en fijar precios para las transacciones entre empresas de un mismo grupo económico que se apartan de los que habrían acordado partes independientes en condiciones comparables. 


Por ejemplo, una filial argentina puede vender su producción a una empresa vinculada radicada en el exterior a un precio inferior al de mercado. Posteriormente, esta última puede revender la mercancía a su precio de mercado y apropiarse de la diferencia. Cuando el intermediario se encuentra radicado en una jurisdicción de baja tributación (como es el caso de Uruguay) o con escasa transparencia fiscal, esta operatoria puede facilitar el traslado de ganancias hacia el exterior y reducir la carga tributaria del grupo económico. Así disminuye la entrada de divisas al país (o, en todo caso, aumenta la salida en caso de compras o pagos de servicios).


Los sectores presentados como motores naturales del desarrollo por su capacidad para generar divisas y aprovechar las ventajas comparativas, son también espacios privilegiados para la circulación internacional del excedente. La inserción exportadora, por sí misma, no garantiza que los recursos generados permanezcan en la economía ni que se transformen en nuevas capacidades productivas.


Durante el gobierno de Javier Milei, las transferencias de ingreso hacia los sectores exportadores se intensificaron. La fuerte devaluación de fines de 2023 y la reducción de los derechos de exportación para la minería y el agronegocio favorecieron a estos sectores primario-exportadores. En 2026 se flexibilizaron las restricciones cambiarias para la remisión al exterior de utilidades generadas a partir de 2025, en un contexto en el que actividades como la petrolera y la agroindustria encabezan las remisiones de ganancias hacia el exterior.


En paralelo, el contexto internacional, signado por guerras y conflictos geopolíticos, ha reavivado las expectativas en torno a un nuevo superciclo de los precios de las materias primas, con efectos favorables sobre los ingresos y la …

author: Rizomatica
title: Sobre la propuesta de modificación al artículo 13 de la ley indigena 19.253
content:
La propuesta de modificación al artículo 13 de la ley 19.253 impulsada en el gobierno anterior a través de la denominada Comisión para la Paz y Entendimiento, fue una iniciativa transversal de la clase Política que incluyó a personeros de todo el espectro político Chileno como propuesta para el desarrollo en materia indígena.


Está propuesta ha sido fomentada por el actual gobierno de tinte ultraderechista con la finalidad de instalarla cómo política pública para el pueblo mapuche. Prueba de ello es que hace pocos días se reunieron en Temuco diversos personeros del gobierno con la finalidad de promover una consulta para dar implementación a esta medida.


El artículo 13 de la ley 19.253 es la normativa que regula y contiene restricciones respecto del dominio y uso de los terrenos indígenas. Este artículo contiene una protección exigida por el interés nacional del cual son sujetos los terrenos indígenas que impide que estos sean sometidos a enajenaciones, embargos, gravámenes, ni ser adquiridas por prescripción, salvo entre comunidades o personas de una misma etnia.


En términos generales, hasta ahora, el artículo 13 ha sido una salvaguarda para el dominio de la tierra indígena en manos de los pueblos originarios, por cuánto la ley en este aspecto tiene un carácter imperativo y obligatorio de protección.


No obstante aquello, esto no ha significado una protección completa ya que a través de diversos artilugios legales se han registrado casos en que a pesar de sus diversas prohibiciones, si se ha logrado enajenar (

vender

) terrenos indígenas a personas no mapuche. Esto ha sido en virtud de vacíos contenidos en la normativa que dejan espacios a artilugios legales que diversos abogados han utilizado para realizar esas ventas en vulneración al espíritu de la ley.


Un caso emblemático a este respecto fue el mediático caso de la venta realizada por la viuda chilena de un mapuche después de su muerte en la comuna de Pucón al ex subsecretario Ubilla durante el gobierno del expresidente Piñera.


Está venta de un terreno indígena a un chileno dejó de manifiesto lo frágil de la ley respecto de la real protección a los terrenos indígenas cuando hay intereses económicos importantes de por medio. Esta venta se pudo realizar en el contexto de lo que en derecho civil se conoce como liquidación de una sociedad conyugal y adjudicación por disolución de esta.


Volviendo a la propuesta de modificación al artículo 13, lo que preocupa es el aparente sentido inocuo de dicha medida, ya que directamente no habla de

enajenación

 o

venta

 de un terreno indígena a una persona o entidad no mapuche, sino que el énfasis ha sido puesto en la posibilidad de

arrendamiento

 de un terreno indígena a personas

no indígenas

 o

personas


jurídicas

 de diversa índole.


Está situación es más compleja de lo que parece a simple vista porque abre una posibilidad de vulneraciones difíciles de prever a futuro.


Lo que señala la propuesta de modificación es que los terrenos indígenas podrán ser arrendados a cualquier persona no indígena o persona jurídica por un plazo de hasta 10 años y 25 años con consulta al órgano técnico encargado en materia indígena que es la Conadi.


El argumento para esto, es que en las condiciones actuales de restricción que contiene la propiedad indígena ha sido muy difícil incorporar estos terrenos a los beneficios que contempla la ley y a diversas medidas administrativas de los órganos y servicios del Estado en materia de fomento productivo, acceso a vivienda, acceso a crédito, transferencia tecnológica y oportunidades de desarrollo en general. En la visión de los promotores de esta iniciativa se sostiene que esto ha sido el principal elemento de tope que han tenido los mapuche para hacer productivas sus tierras e incorporarlas eficientemente al circuito productivo de la economía local y regional.


Para ello se propone bajar el nivel de restricciones que contiene la ley en materia de protección y permitir arriendos en condiciones de mercado actuales y competitivos.


Esto en teoría significaría regular de forma más eficiente situaciones de arriendo irregular que hoy pudiesen existir y por otra parte mejorar los promedios de los valores de los precios de arriendo para el arrendador y conceder garantías tanto de tiempo como de condiciones jurídicas que permitan al arrendatario realizar una labor productiva con seguridad en un tiempo acorde a dicha inversión, pudiendo ser por un lapso de hasta 25 años.

author: La Zarzamora
title: Lanzamiento de Black Onions, un listado de sitios web anarquistas y antiautoritarios con extensión .onion
content:
Publicado originalmente en Montréal Contre-information

Nos complace anunciar el lanzamiento de Black Onions, una nueva iniciativa que tiene como objetivo ofrecer una lista estable y actualizada periódicamente de sitios anarquistas y antiautoritarios con extensión .onion. Los sitios .onion son sitios web accesibles a través del navegador Tor mediante direcciones que terminan en «.onion».

En los últimos meses, algunos gobiernos han atacado las infraestructuras de comunicación de nuestros movimientos con renovado vigor; buena prueba de ello son la conferencia internacional sobre el «terrorismo de extrema izquierda» celebrada en Estados Unidos en julio, así como la inclusión del proveedor de servicios de alojamiento militante italiano Autistici/Inventati en una lista de sanciones relacionadas con el terrorismo a finales de agosto.

Para bien o para mal, la comunicación pública de nuestros movimientos tiene lugar en gran medida en Internet, lo que la hace vulnerable a los mecanismos tecnológicos de censura. A diferencia de los sitios web convencionales, los sitios .onion son menos vulnerables a la censura, ya que no utilizan nombres de dominio y permiten ocultar la ubicación del servidor, del mismo modo que el navegador Tor oculta tu propia ubicación al visitar el sitio. Consideramos que los sitios .onion son nuestra mejor baza para seguir comunicándonos en línea dentro del movimiento anarquista, especialmente si los intentos de censura se intensifican en el futuro.

El problema recurrente de los sitios .onion es que sus direcciones, compuestas por 56 caracteres aleatorios, son imposibles de memorizar. Black Onions tiene como objetivo resolver este problema. Te recomendamos guardar en los marcadores del navegador Tor, o en un archivo en tu ordenador, las direcciones .onion que utilizas habitualmente; pero si necesitas una dirección que aún no has guardado, ¡encuéntrala en Black Onions!

Accede a Black Onions a través de cualquiera de las siguientes direcciones:

– blackonions.gd – blackonions.li – blackonions.st – (próximamente, una dirección .onion)

Para establecer una base de confianza en esta nueva iniciativa, los siguientes proyectos anarquistas han avalado nuestra propuesta mediante declaraciones firmadas con PGP: Act For Freedom Now!, un proyecto de contrainformación activo desde 2008 , y el No Trace Project, un proyecto contra la represión activo desde 2021.

¡Utiliza sitios .onion! ¡Resiste a la censura!

author: Publicación Abierta
title: Siete millones «no son nada»
content:
Siete millones «no son nada»


Alberto Núñez Feijóo fue a un pódcast a hablar de vivienda y dejó una frase que retrata a toda una clase social: siete millones de euros, en España, «no son nada». Hablaba del ático de Chamberí que la empresa pública Planifica Madrid compró el 14 de abril por 6,3 millones de euros. Dinero público. Para la presidenta Ayuso.


Un ático que no puede ser una oficina.


La versión oficial dice que es un inmueble destinado a oficinas provisionales. Pero el planeamiento urbanístico de Madrid solo permite oficinas en determinadas plantas, como la baja o la primera, y la planta ático queda fuera. Es una vivienda de lujo, con calificación residencial. Hasta el propio Feijóo ha tenido que admitir que Patrimonio debería explicar por qué se compró un ático que no puede utilizarse como oficina. Y después, ante el micrófono, se le escapó que eso es calderilla.


La justicia ya mira.


Esta misma semana, el Tribunal de Cuentas ha acordado investigar la operación al apreciar indicios de un gasto de 6,3 millones de euros sin justificación legal y un posible perjuicio a los fondos públicos. Una compra sin memoria justificativa y con sospechas de sobreprecio. Ayuso, mientras tanto, ha preferido no dar la cara y poner el ático a la venta.


Vivir siempre del dinero de todos.


Para entender por qué siete millones no son nada para Feijóo, hay que mirar de dónde procede su sueldo. Entró como funcionario de la Xunta en 1985 y, desde 1991, encadena cargos políticos: secretario general en la Consejería de Sanidad, presidente del Insalud, presidente de Correos, consejero, vicepresidente y, durante trece años, presidente de la Xunta. Hoy lidera el PP. Toda su trayectoria profesional conocida ha estado vinculada a cargos remunerados con dinero público. Una vida entera cobrando de la caja común explica, quizá, que sepa contar millones, pero no lo que cuesta ganarlos. Ese dinero no sale de su esfuerzo. Sale del esfuerzo de las trabajadoras y los trabajadores de este país.


Y no es el único de su bando. Santiago Abascal encadena cargos públicos desde 1999 —concejal, asesor en la Subdelegación del Gobierno, parlamentario vasco y director de la Agencia de Protección de Datos de Madrid— antes de fundar Vox, un partido que en 2025 recibió unos 12 millones de euros de financiación pública. Es dinero del partido, no suyo, pero sigue siendo dinero de todos.


Currantes y jetas.


El 16 de octubre, en Toledo, prometió que durante toda la campaña no se dirigiría «a los jetas», sino únicamente a los currantes. Es el mismo Feijóo que, en julio, ante los empresarios vascos, llamó «cáncer» a las bajas laborales, sostuvo que todo absentismo por encima del 4 o el 5 % esconde un enorme porcentaje de fraude sin aportar un solo dato y planteó que quienes están de baja cobren menos. Divide el país entre «currantes» y «jetas», pone bajo sospecha a quienes enferman y, al mismo tiempo, considera una menudencia un ático de lujo pagado con dinero público.


La aritmética de la clase.


Hagamos cuentas, que a los de abajo siempre nos las piden. Una persona que cobra mil euros al mes en catorce pagas tardaría quinientos años en acumular siete millones de euros. Quinientos. Para quien se levanta a las cinco de la mañana para reponer, cobrar en una caja o descargar un camión, esa cifra representa toda una vida y la de sus bisnietos. Para Feijóo, no es nada.


Un problema, una herramienta menos.


Cuando un país tiene un problema grave, lo normal es crear herramientas para resolverlo: ministerios, planes y presupuestos. Feijóo hace lo contrario. Anuncia que, si gobierna, eliminará el Ministerio de Vivienda, cuando la vivienda lleva veintiún meses consecutivos siendo el principal problema del país y, según el último barómetro del CIS, el 55,7 % de la ciudadanía lo señala como tal. Anuncia también que eliminará el Ministerio de Igualdad, que, entre otras cosas, tiene la responsabilidad de combatir la violencia machista: decenas de mujeres asesinadas cada año por hombres que las consideraban de su propiedad. Una lacra que debemos erradicar de una vez por todas.


Dos problemas, dos herramientas que se eliminan. Esa es su idea de gobernar: no resolver los problemas, sino desmontar lo que sirve para afrontarlos. Y, mientras tanto, siete millones de euros en un ático de lujo le parecen una menudencia. La vivienda no es una prioridad para quien la ve como un negocio o como un privilegio.
