title: Uysal: Art's unifying and healing power can contribute to peace
content:
Theatre in Turkey is increasingly drifting away from its essence, influenced not only by longstanding structural problems but also by the political climate. Even plays that claim to be political remain under the influence of Turkish nationalist ideology.


The launch of the Peace and Democratic Society Process has sparked public debate about the role of art in the struggle for peace and the experiences of the past. For years, plays featuring racist rhetoric targeting the Kurdish people and other communities under the influence of war have been staged. The new process has also brought discussions about the need to transform the language of art.


Theatre director and dramaturg Abdullah Uysal spoke to ANF about the current state of theatre in Turkey and the role of art in the struggle for peace.


'Theatre is a technically and economically demanding profession'


Abdullah Uysal said that theatre has been affected by the cultural erosion experienced particularly under the rule of the Justice and Development Party (AKP), emphasizing that the problems facing theatre have economic, social and political dimensions.


Uysal said: "What is the state of theatre in Turkey? The situation is actually good, but at the same time, it isn't. It is difficult to fully grasp the cultural erosion that has taken place over the past 25 years, particularly under AKP rule, and its consequences. Theatre is already a technically and economically demanding profession. You create a work, an artistic aesthetic, and you need spaces in which to present it. You sell tickets to audiences who come to those spaces. This is directly connected to society's entire network of relationships and its economic and sociological structure. Theatre naturally finds its audience in places where people are comfortable, economic difficulties are not overwhelming and democracy is not under threat. People can create opportunities to relax and devote time to themselves. This directly affects theatre. Tickets are sold, and you can bring your work to audiences.


However, Turkey has struggled with economic problems since its establishment. Over the past 25 years, particularly under AKP rule, the economy has deteriorated dramatically and is now in a very poor state. As a result, theatre practitioners have either been forced to scale down their productions, performing in smaller venues with capacities of 30, 20 or even 15 people, or to reduce their expenses significantly.


For example, productions with large casts are no longer being staged. Look at what is being produced today: one-person plays, musical cabaret-style performances and stories that do not challenge audiences intellectually but instead distract them from everyday life. These are often what might be called 'cheesy' productions, built around cheap, stale narratives.


The popularity and celebrity culture that have emerged with the use of social media, along with people's reactions to momentary events, have changed the reasons audiences choose certain performances. There is a group in Turkey that claims to be producing theatre, and their tickets sell out. Let me give you an example. A simple story that has been adapted into films since the 1970s, staged perhaps 20 times and turned into television series is currently being performed in Turkey. They stage it in venues seating between 3,000 and 5,000 people, with tickets costing 5,000 Turkish lira, and every performance is sold out. Some viewers may even remember a theatre performance in Turkey where arguments broke out because people complained, 'I can't see my seat.' If you showed footage of that performance to someone abroad, they would conclude that Turkey has no audience problem and that theatre is thriving."


Uysal also said: "Yet at the same time, we hear that many theatre venues in cities across Kurdistan and in Turkey's major metropolitan areas are closing because of economic difficulties. As economic, political and class contradictions deepen in Turkey, and the cultural divide widens alongside them, it becomes increasingly difficult to speak of theatre's continued existence.


This raises a fundamental question: What is theatre, and what is not? Theatre, as we understand it, means producing works of art that touch society and have the power to transform it. It should enable people to look at communities, individuals, women, ecology, animals and the world with renewed hope, or give them the strength to change the world. Unfortunately, this kind of …

author: Kodao Productions
title: Waves of protests to welcome Trump, Bayan announces
content:
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. is so desperate to welcome Donald Trump to the Philippines that he will roll out the red carpet even if his US counterpart arrives so late for the ASEAN Summit and other ASEAN leaders have already left, Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (Bayan) said.


Bayan president Renato Reyes Jr. condemned possibilities of work and school suspension extensions following Department of Foreign Affairs’ announcement that the US leader is set to arrive on the 17

th

 just as the summit he was supposed to attend would be ending. Presidential spokesperson Claire Castro, meanwhile, said Trump’s late arrival is not within Malacanang’s lookout.


“Is Marcos now telling the people that their suffering, and the work and school suspensions, will have to be extended because Trump decided to arrive late for his Philippine visit?” Reyes asked.


Government has declared November 16 to 18 as non-working days to clear Metro Manila of its notorious traffic for its hosting of the biennial event it is hosting this year.


Reyes, however, foisted the possibility of Marcos Jr. extending the work and school holidays as Trump is only set to leave after his dialogue with the Philippine leader on the 18

th

.


“Marcos Jr.’s mendicancy and subservience are on full display now. He is desperate to get a nod from Trump, desperate to get Pax Silica signed, and desperate to get US backing for his isolated regime,” Reyes said.


The activist leader also criticized Trump who he said treats the Philippines “like a doormat, oblivious to the disruption and gross inconvenience his visit makes, on top of the neocolonial policies he wishes to impose.”


Meanwhile, Bayan announced its major rallies will start on Monday with a march to Liwasang Bonifacio where a protest camp will be erected before a rally near the US Embassy.


Tens of thousands of protesters will then march to the venue of the ASEAN Summit on Tuesday, participated in by delegations from all over the country, reminiscent of Trump’s first official visit to the Philippines in 2017.


A similar protest event will be held near Mendiola Bridge in time for the Marcos-Trump meeting in Malacanang on Wednesday.


“The Filipino people will make sure that both Trump and Marcos Jr will emerge as the biggest losers at the end of this week. We reject US imperialism and we oppose government subservience to it,” Reyes said. #

(Raymund B. Villanueva)

author: Alyssa Mae Clarin
title: Women, youth groups slam Sara Duterte over sexual advice to women OFWs
content:
One of the places where OFWs spend their rest day in Hong Kong. (Photo by Carlo Manalansan/Bulatlat)

“Instead of holding men accountable for their cheating and abuse, the advice places the burden on women to keep their partners through sexual performance.”

Women’s group Gabriela condemned Vice President Sara Duterte for telling female Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs) in Hong Kong to be good at sex to prevent their partners from cheating or leaving them, calling the remarks “misogynistic” and an example of “victim-blaming.”

In a video posted online by Filipino singer Jimmy Bondoc, Duterte told the Filipino women in the audience that they should be good at “esmeringhoy,” a Bisaya term used as a euphemism for sexual intercourse, to keep their partners from going astray.

Although the remark drew cheers and laughter from the audience, national women alliance group Gabriela said it should not be dismissed as merely tasteless banter, particularly because it came from the country’s second-highest official.

“Instead of holding men accountable for their cheating and abuse, the advice places the burden on women to keep their partners through sexual performance,” Gabriela said in a statement.

The national women’s alliance said Duterte’s remark reflects the same victim-blaming logic that women face daily, wherein they are made to question what they did or failed to do to supposedly warrant the violence, abuse, or betrayal committed against them.

Gabriela also stressed that the remark is profoundly detached from the realities faced by Filipino women, whose struggles are rooted in the lack of protection, decent livelihood, and respect for their rights—not in any supposed failure to please men.

Read: Citing women’s conditions, Gabriela Women’s Party questions Marcos’ UN statement

“A woman is never to blame for a man’s infidelity,” the alliance further added.

Bayan Muna Youth also criticized Duterte, saying that even when delivered as a joke, her advice to Filipino women migrants contributes to broader public discourse on women’s rights and gender relations.

“Humor does not remove the responsibility to challenge harmful gender stereotypes, particularly in a country where violence against women, sexual exploitation, economic abuse, and unequal domestic responsibilities remain pressing concerns,” the youth group said.

Gabriela urged women to reject the notion that their worth is measured by how well they serve and satisfy men. The alliance also called on public officials to stop dressing up patriarchal beliefs as concern for women.

Similarly, Bayan Muna Youth also urged public officials to move beyond jokes that reinforce misogynistic attitudes and instead push for concrete policies that uphold and protect the rights and welfare of Filipino women.

“Remarks that reduce women to instruments of men’s satisfaction have no place in a government that claims to protect them,” Gabriela concluded. (AMU, RVO)

author: Franck Dick Rosete
title: Harassment won’t stop a son’s search for his missing father
content:
Marklen Lariosa, son of missing Kilusang Mayo Uno (KMU) labor organizer William Lariosa, speaks during a rally in Davao City on the first anniversary of his father’s disappearance on April 10, 2025. Photo by Kath Cortez/Davao Today

“Family members searching for their disappeared loved ones have to endure threats and harassment from state forces on top of the terrible uncertainty and emotional turmoil they are already going through.”

Is it a mistake for a son to demand justice and accountability?

Marklen, son of disappeared labor organizer William Lariosa, raised this question following the recent incident of harassment and surveillance he experienced. Members of his family were alarmed after two unidentified individuals were looking for his residence on the night of October 25.

He told Bulatlat that this was the first time such an event had happened since his father, a labor organizer under Kilusang Mayo Uno (KMU) Southern Mindanao, was abducted in Quezon, Bukidnon, on April 10, 2024.

Marklen could not think of other possible reasons, suspecting that the incident may have something to do with his continuing involvement in campaigns and mobilizations that demand the surfacing of Lariosa. “Is it a mistake for a son to search for his missing father?” he further asked.

Read: After 2 years, son laments continuing disappearance of Mindanao labor organizer

Neighbors of the Lariosa family in their hometown in Davao de Oro province were the ones who encountered the two individuals. They reportedly wore helmets and were on board a black motorcycle, introducing themselves as “collectors” when they were asked.

For Marklen, the response and presence of the two raised suspicions. Aside from the fact that they visited the community around 7 p.m., which is outside the regular working hours, Marklen said that he did not apply for any financial loan.

After the incident, he was concerned for the safety of his family, prompting them to lodge a blotter report with the barangay. However, he stood firm that it won’t stop him from continuing his cause.

Desaparecidos, an organization of families and friends of enforced disappearance victims, denounced the incident, urging the government to put an end to this kind of harassment.

“Family members searching for their disappeared loved ones have to endure threats and harassment from state forces on top of the terrible uncertainty and emotional turmoil they are already going through,” JL Burgos, Desaparecidos chairperson, said in a statement.

Rights groups Karapatan and the Center for Trade Union and Human Rights (CTUHR) also expressed strong condemnations about what happened.

Marklen, a member of the National Board of Desaparecidos, has raised a possibility that the two individuals who recently visited their neighborhood might be connected to those who visited their house several times prior to the disappearance of his father.

He said they were visited by individuals who allegedly introduced themselves as state agents once in 2022 and three times in 2023, accusing Lariosa of being involved in communist insurgency. There were warnings, he added, that they would get dragged into it if they would not cooperate.

The series of visits was reportedly the primary reason why Lariosa was forced to take refuge in Bukidnon. Marklen affirmed that his father, who remains missing, had been a labor organizer.

On July 8, the Supreme Court required certain commanders and elements of Philippine Army units to comment on the petition for review on certiorari filed by the family.

Read: Military ordered to reply to missing Mindanao labor organizer’s case

Since 2024, KMU Southern Mindanao has documented 57 cases of human rights violations against its members and organizers.

The labor group released a statement on October 24, presenting the faces of some individuals, including former high-ranking New People’s Army (NPA) member Roberto Rosete Jr., who allegedly harassed KMU’s leaders and members.

Read: Groups decry surveillance of KMU office in Southern Mindanao

Marklen called for an end to any form of harassment and intimidation against families of the disappeared, pointing out that achieving justice is their only goal. (RVO)

author: Brian Hioe
title: Jensen Huang Scandal Likely to Serve as Pretext for Continued Chip Controls, Securitization
content:
NVIDIA FOUNDER Jensen Huang has suddenly come under scrutiny, with allegations that he was engaged in an affair with a purported Chinese spy, Alice Huang. Huang is an executive at a Singaporean data center company.

With Huang having now resigned from his position, Nvidia does not have a successor who can maintain the same public image. Still, most prognostications are that Nvidia’s role is bigger than simply Huang, and that the company will continue to grow.

Huang admitted to having an affair, something that has shattered his family man image in Taiwan. Huang is highly popular in Taiwan, probably due to his status as a returnee–seeing as he was born in Taiwan, but grew up in the US. Two other affairs by Huang later emerged, with other Nvidia executives.

A significant degree of media reporting on Huang usually focuses on when he visits night markets and other regular places during stints in Taiwan, as if to show that Huang–who was born in Taiwan but grew up in the US and has spent most of his life abroad–has maintained ties with his native land.

Huang’s background proves similar to that of many other Taiwanese tech entrepreneurs who, in fact, have spent most of their lives abroad. Morris Chang, the founder of TSMC, also has spent most of his life in the US and seems to identify as an American as a result. This has long been the pattern in Taiwan, with educated elites going abroad to America. Consequently, Taiwanese media often fawns over such figures when they return to Taiwan.

Even so, one notes how Huang was quite skilled at driving up Nvidia’s public image.A speech by Huang on the importance of Taiwan for AI sent Taiwan’s stock market up 362 points on the promise of AI development in 2024. This may attest to the significant market power of this single captain of industry. But Huang has also become increasingly understood as a Trump ally after frequent media appearances with the US president, including traveling to Beijing with Trump for a meeting with Chinese president Xi Jinping. After the scandal, Huang is now to be questioned by the US national security establishment.

It is to be seen if the scandal impacts perceptions of Taiwan–which is highly sensitive to Chinese spying–in the US. Still, with society roiled by such allegations, one notes how the Taiwanese media has delighted in tearing down a tech magnate that it had previously fawned over, not unlike the fall of, say, idol Wang Leehom after a messy divorce scandal.

It is possible that there will be a greater social reckoning with Chinese spying, however, or even Chinese spouses of Taiwanese, after the scandal, with the Lai administration using the scandal as pretext to strengthen securitization in society. Certainly, Huang is not the first Taiwanese tech magnate to face such scandals over an affair–Robert Tsao has also faced allegations of an affair with a Chinese woman in the past, but personal affairs come to dovetail with international geopolitics and great power politics easily in the current age of AI.

Regardless, with Republicans hawkish on China probably aiming to use the scandal as pretext to maintain chip controls on China, to avoid such individuals taking a skeptical view of US-Taiwan relations, the Lai administration will seek to appear as though it is taking quick action on the matter. The scandal also raises questions about information sharing between the US and its allies, with the Lai administration apparently not having been informed by the US. Reports suggest that Trump was aware of the affair ahead of time but did not choose to take action, and that the Singaporean government may have warned the US ahead of time, but did not receive a response.

title: The Enemy at Home
content:
The belief that Democrats will dismantle a system designed to serve the rapacious greed of the war machine and the ruling billionaire class is a mirage.


 


CHRIS HEDGES


Nov 12


 


Power does not rest in the Congress. It does not rest in the courts. It does not even rest in the imperial presidency. It rests in the hands of Wall Street financiers, Silicon Valley, private equity firms, the fossil fuel industry, the predatory health care and pharmaceutical giants, agribusinesses and, most of all, the war industry.


 


No mainstream politician, including Bernie Sanders, dares utter a word against our entrenched militarism. If you do, you end up like Ralph Nader, who was turned into a pariah by a compliant media and our corporate-indentured political parties. Nader spoke the truth. He paid for his honesty.


 


We are about to witness the

largest increase

 in war spending in American history with a proposed $1.5 trillion budget. The average taxpayer already shells out over $4,000 a

year


to the war industry as consumer and environmental agencies are

dismantled

, health care and education are defunded and programs such as

Medicaid


and

food stamps

 (the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program) are slashed.


 


The new Pentagon budget will

hand

 $58.5 billion to artificial intelligence and military command-and-control centers and see the effective

merging

 of the United States and Israeli military industrial complexes. Seventy-four percent of the increase in the proposed $1.5 trillion budget

will go to

 private contractors,

including

 those who are building massive data centers on military bases.


 


None of this is good for us or good for the planet. The Pentagon, powered by the fossil fuel industry, is the world’s

largest institutional polluter

, emitting an estimated

66 million metric tons


of carbon dioxide in 2024.


 


Americans, meanwhile, struggle with rising prices — nearly 30 percent of people go

into debt

 to buy groceries. An estimated 114,174. Americans

die

 each year due to lack of health insurance or inadequate health care while a single-payer universal health care system could cover every American, save more than 100,000 lives a year, and reduce annual health expenditures by $1.04 trillion, or nearly 20 percent. Twenty-five percent of Americans are

functionally unemployed

. The minimum wage remains frozen, despite Democratic Party promises to raise it, at $ 7.25 an hour.


 


The elites use war not only for personal enrichment, but to stifle class conflict.


 


War, as W.E.B. Du Bois said, diverts the poor from their real interests. It funnels national frustrations into the “heroic” battle against a common enemy. The nationalist cant, with its endemic racism, seduces those who are alienated or on the margins of society into feeling they suddenly belong. It entices them to sacrifice themselves for a “noble” cause. They becime the architects of their own enslavement. They march like sheep into war’s purgatory.


 


By the time they wake up, it is too late. They are cast aside, as so many of our

veterans

 have painfully discovered, like human refuse.


 


But as a tactic to consolidate power and enrich the billionaire class, it is unbeatable.


 


Wars will only be curtailed, if not halted, when we nationalize the weapons industry and dramatically reduce the military budget. Until then, nothing, absolutely nothing, will change.


 


Indeed, things will only get worse.


 


No one in Congress — or any other branch of government — will do this for us.


 


The masters of war sitting in the boardrooms of Boeing, General Dynamics or Northrop Grumman are not praying for peace in the Middle East or coexistence with China and Russia. The generals — who build their careers by orchestrating wars and post military careers enriching themselves working for defense contractors — are not seeking a cessation of global conflicts. They are seeking hundreds of billions in taxpayer dollars and government debt to fuel the self-defeating cycle of endless war.


 


The corporate vultures — especially the war makers — are, as I write, descending on Congress. They are meeting with Democratic Party leaders and holding out promises of millions in cash. They will corrupt, neutralize and compromise most. They will destroy the careers of the very few who refuse to do their bidding.


 


They hold the real power. They have no intention of surrendering it.

author: John David Parol
title: 1,000 puno sa Marikina puputulin para sa ₱8.5-B ADB bridge project
content:
Sa kahabaan ng St. Mary Avenue sa Provident Village, nakabalot sa mga puno ng Narra at Balete ang mga telang may panawagang: “Save me! Say no to tree-cutting!”

Para sa mga residente ng subdivision na sinalanta ng pinakamatinding baha sa kasagsagan ng Bagyong Ondoy at Ulysses, ang natural canopy at ugat ng mga punong ito ang huling buhay na panangga laban sa pag-apaw ng Marikina River.

Subalit sa ilalim ng Metro Manila Bridges Project (MMBP) ng Department of Public Works and Highways, puputulin ang mahigit 500 puno sa lugar upang itayo ang tulay na magbubuhos ng mga sasakyan mula Marcos Highway diretso sa loob ng kanilang komunidad.

Sa isang pamayanang dati nang nalubog sa pagbaha, pinangangambahan ng mga residente ang epekto sa kanilang kaligtasan ng naturang tulay na bahagi ng ₱8.5-bilyong proyektong pinondohan ng pautang mula sa Asian Development Bank (ADB).

Nangunguna sa barikada at pagtutol ang koalisyong Marikina Kontra Agos (MKA) sa ilalim ng panawagang “Save the Trees, Stop the Bridge!”

Unang lumabas sa Provident Village ang kanilang panawagan nang maimbitahan silang magsalita sa “PA-X-PLAIN: A Forum on Pax Silica” sa inisiyatiba ng Silangan Against Pax Silica noong, Oktubre 17 upang mas magpalalim sa malawak na ugnayan at banta ng Pax Silica at Luzon Economic Corridor sa lupa, kalikasan, kabuhayan, at pambansang soberanya.

Para kay Carlo Maningat ng MKA, ito ang kauna-unahang pagkakataon na nagbahagi ang grupo sa labas ng sariling subdivision upang ilantad ang banta ng proyekto.

​”Mawawala ang canopy cover sa tinatayang 17 ektarang lupain kung puputulin ang mahigit 1,000 puno sa Marikina na magpapalala sa init sa lungsod at bulnerabilidad natin sa baha.”

Ilan sa mga ito ay daan-taon na ang tanda (century-old) at itinuturing nang national heritage na hindi na makaliligtas sa earth-balling, dahilan upang igiit ng grupo ang interbensyon ng National Commission for Culture and the Arts (NCCA) upang protektahan ang mga ito laban sa pagputol.

Bukod sa mga puno, higit 70 kabahayan sa Marikina ang nakatakdang ma-demolish.

​Sa Provident Village, inireklamo ng mga apektadong residente ang isyu ng illegal taking at kabayaran: tanging ang mismong parte lamang ng ari-arian na gigibain ang babayaran ng gobyerno, habang iiwanang nakatiwangwang at hindi na mapakikinabangan ang natitirang bahagi ng kanilang tahanan.

​Kinuwestiyon din sa presentasyon ang ligalidad ng pagpapatupad ng pampublikong proyekto sa pribadong lupain nang walang kaukulang deed of donation, certificate of acceptance, o resolusyon mula sa konseho ng lungsod na nagpapatibay sa donasyon ng lupa ng Provident sa Marikina LGU, batay na rin sa legal precedent ng Korte Suprema sa kasong Quezon City Government vs. Rainier L. Madrid.

Hindi lamang isa, kundi tatlong tulay ang plano ng DPWH at ADB.

​Ang Bridge 1, na nagkakahalaga ng humigit-kumulang ₱1.69 bilyon, ang pinaka-kontrobersyal dahil direktang magbubuhos ito ng trapiko mula SM Marikina sa Marcos Highway papasok sa St. Mary Avenue.

​Kasunod nito ang Bridge 2, na mag-uugnay sa Homeowners Drive at A. Bonifacio Avenue. Tumatagos ang linyang ito sa mga barangay ng Calumpang, Tañong, at Jesus dela Peña.

​Sa hilaga naman, itatayo ang Bridge 3 na tatawid mula Kalayaan at Kabayani Street sa Nangka (Balubad) patungong Matandang Balara at Capitol Hills sa Quezon City.

Ayon sa breakdown ng MKA, aabot sa eksaktong 1,069 puno ang nakalinyang putulin sa pitong barangay: 514 sa Bridge 1; 232 sa Bridge 2; at 350 sa Bridge 3.

​Ang kontrata para sa civil works ng mga naturang tawiran ay naigawad sa mga kumpanyang mula sa Tsina, kabilang ang Hunan Road and Bridge Construction Group Co., Ltd.

Batay sa datos ng pagpopondo para sa Metro Manila Bridges Project, umaabot sa kabuuang ₱12.028 bilyon ang inilaang pondo para sa proyekto. ​Sa nasabing halaga, ₱8.5 bilyon ang magmumula sa pautang ng ADB, habang ₱3.52 bilyon naman ang magiging counterpart fund ng gobyerno ng Pilipinas. Nasa ₱3.36 bilyon pa lang ang kabuuang pondong nailabas para sa mga taong 2025 at 2026 upang pondohan ang implementasyon ng proyekto.

​Nagsimula ang mobilization at pre-construction activities noong 2024, habang nakatakdang tapusin ang konstruksyon ng Bridge 1 at Bridge 2 sa Setyembre 2027. Target namang makumpleto ang kabuuang proyekto, kabilang ang Bridge 3, pagsapit ng 2028 bago sumapit ang loan closing date.

​Ayon sa mga residente at grupo, hindi lulutasin ng tatlong tulay ang problema sa trapiko. Sa halip, magdudulot lamang ito ng …

author: Deaglan Godwin
title: Businessmen, not battlers, lead the charge for One Nation in NSW
content:
Pauline Hanson’s One Nation pretends to be a party of battlers, standing up for the little guy against the major parties. This narrative has been parroted by the mainstream media and even taken up by Hanson’s opponents. The party’s lead candidates for the March 2027 New South Wales state election paint a very different picture of who the party represents.

Take Mike Newman, newly-appointed NSW leader and candidate for Cessnock, the Hunter Valley seat One Nation considers winnable. Newman’s riches-to-riches story involves growing up in well-heeled Mosman on Sydney’s lower North Shore and attending the elite private school Cranbrook, along with billionaire James Packer. His father, Maurice Newman, was the chair of the Australian Securities Exchange and then of the ABC. 

Son followed father into the world of investment banking. After a long career as a banker in Tokyo, Newman landed a gig in the public service as NSW Senior Trade and Investment Commissioner in Japan. The wasteful inefficiency of the bureaucracy supposedly radicalised Newman and convinced him to go into politics. Curiously, during his three-year stint as commissioner, Newman racked up hundreds of thousands of dollars in expenses (funded by the taxpayer) for flights, five-star hotels and restaurant and bar bills, as was recently revealed by the

Sydney Morning Herald

. This spending included more than $20,000 for an extended stay in a Meriton Suite in Sydney.

Next up is Jeff Bacon, who will be second on One Nation’s ticket for the upper house. Bacon is the managing director of Oceana Precision, a weapons manufacturer based in Tamworth, his north-eastern NSW hometown. He ran as the lower house candidate for Tamworth with the Shooters, Fishers and Farmers party in 2019, then joined the Nationals in 2023 before defecting to One Nation in October 2025. 

In an interview with Tamworth’s local newspaper, the 

Northern Daily Leader,

 in January, Bacon alleged that every single one of Oceania Precision’s rifles was banned in NSW following firearms legislation passed by the state Labor government in the wake of the Bondi Massacre. Bacon would, apparently, be broke in six months if the laws weren’t repealed. Hanson has described him as her “go-to man on the firearms industry”.

Sure, you might struggle to pay grocery or electricity bills, or cover your mortgage or rent. But spare a thought for the owner of a medium-sized weapons manufacturer whose human rights have been trampled on by the Labor government. 

Stuart Bonds, the party’s lead upper house candidate, is more regularly held up as emblematic of the party’s battler credentials.

Bonds, a former Hunter Valley coal miner, won 21 percent of the vote for One Nation in the 2019 federal election. Bonds is critical of both renewable energy and the behaviour of multinational mining companies. He left One Nation in 2021 over its support for the Morrison government's industrial relations legislation that undermined casual workers’ rights.

Bonds, however, is more representative of your average bigot than battler. At an anti-immigration rally in early November, he espoused the far-right Great Replacement conspiracy theory. He told the protesters that, “we are being demographically replaced inside our own nation”, and warned them that this was part of a “socialist plan” to “tear down the fabric of your civilisation”. 

Bonds is also a bigot on other social issues. Many have rightly pointed out the irony of his misogynistic comments when he boasted: “I don’t have a woman boss, and I don’t have a gay boss, and there’s a reason for that”. The only problem for Mr Bonds is that he does indeed have both a woman boss in Hanson and a gay boss in James Ashby, the party director. Irony aside, the comments indicate the rank misogyny and homophobia that aren’t simply personal opinions, but party policy. One Nation boasts about being “pro-life” and is currently campaigning to restrict abortion rights in NSW. 

One Nation’s NSW state election candidates give you a glimpse into the actual character of the party. Rather than being the authentic expression of working-class grievances, the party is a Frankenstein-like combination of bankers, bigots and small business owners. What unites them is not their genuine struggles under the system, but their hostility to the gains made by oppressed groups and minorities, hatred of the left and commitment to a pro-business economic agenda.

author: Malik Miah, Barry Sheppard
title: United States: Trump and Republicans routed in mid-term elections
content:
The Democratic Party won sweeping victories in the United States midterm elections on November 3, in a dramatic refutation of President Donald Trump and the Republican Party he controls.

These results were not a vote of confidence in the Democrats but were a rejection of Trump and Trumpism. The majority of US voters do not trust either party.

Going into the elections, Republicans held small minorities in the House of Representatives and the Senate.

All 435 members of the House are elected every two years and the Democrats won a decisive majority of 254-256 seats with a few results still to be finalised at the time of writing.

One-third of the 100-seat Senate is elected every two years for a six-year term and the Democrats now hold a majority of 54-56 seats.

This is the biggest change in Congressional seats since 1974, when the Democrats swept to victory and Republican President Richard Nixon was driven out of office, in a scandal resulting from him sending thugs into the Democratic Party headquarters.

The Democrats also made sweeping gains in state and local elections.

In Texas, considered a Republican stronghold, Democratic candidate and Mexican American Gina Hinojosa was elected governor — the first Latinx elected to this office in any state.

In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed became the first Muslim ever elected to the Senate, despite facing a virulent Islamophobic campaign against him, where Trump called him a “terrorist”.

Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first African American woman elected as governor in Georgia, in the nation’s “deep South”.

Native American Deb Haaland was elected governor of New Mexico and Minnesota’s Peggy Flanagan became the first Native American elected to the Senate.

The first openly gay Senate candidate, Chris Pappas, was elected in New Hampshire.

In Mississippi, African American Senate candidate Scott Colom leads by a narrow margin in a race too close to call, and in Alaska, Native American Mary Peltola has a slight lead in the race for the Senate.

Eight candidates endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) were elected to Congress, including Chris Rabb (Pennsylvania), Rashida Tlaib and Donavan McKinney (Minnesota), Melat Kiros (Colorado), Angela Gonzales-Torres (California), Darializa Avila Chevalier, Claire Valdez and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (New York).

DSA candidate Nithya Raman won the race for Mayor of Los Angeles, Janeese Lewis George won the mayoral race in Washington DC and Claudia Jimenez in East Bay, California.

The DSA grew rapidly following Donald Trump’s election in 2016 and on the wave of support for self-described democratic socialist Bernie Sanders — who is not a member of DSA. DSA seeks to strengthen the progressive wing of the Democrats and is criticised by the revolutionary left for advocating progressive reforms within the capitalist system, rather than its overthrow. Nevertheless, Trump labels DSA and left Democrats as “communist” and the Democratic Party as “socialist”.

A large turnout from young people eager for progressive change, and from the Black and Latinx communities were key to the Republican defeat.

Black community organisers led in Southern states. They made it clear they were making the elections an act of defending Black people from the Republican drive to go back to “Jim Crow-type” oppression in the South.

There is no mass (even mini-mass) working class electoral party, or parties of the oppressed nationalities in the US and the Green Party is weak. So there is no other choice in elections than between two capitalist parties, and results have to be analysed in that reality.

Some of the main factors for the anti-Republican vote include that the Trump administration is the most corrupt in US history. Add to that the Iran war, Trump’s cruel anti-immigration policy against Latinx communities, and Trump’s tariffs on imports that have driven up inflation, outpacing wage rises and impacting living standards and affordability.

At the same time, Trump and his billionaire friends have gotten richer, as have millionaires and capitalists in general. Trump has increased his own wealth by more than $3 billion and his immediate family by another $3 billion, since he took office in 2025.

Trump’s tariffs have cost working class families, on average, a minimum of $1000 — which continues to rise.

Trump’s war on Iran has made the price of petrol and diesel skyrocket. Farmers, whose equipment largely runs on diesel, turned against Trump …

author: Jasmine Duff
title: Bosses are pushing for a hard-right government in Victoria
content:
Australia’s business elite and right-wing press are gunning to end Victorian Labor’s twelve-year reign and install a Liberal government. They’re pushing for harsh cuts to services for working-class people. Victoria’s Chamber of Commerce published a 

wish-list

 for the election, demanding exemptions from the payroll tax, reversing Victoria’s state debt, and drawing in data centre investment. The Murdoch and Channel 9 media conglomerates have helped the Liberals make crime and debt central election issues.

They’re pushing at an open door because both major parties are helping the bosses to generate a harsher right-wing political climate. Under Ben Carroll’s leadership, Victorian Labor has attempted to appease business. In his four months as premier, Carroll has launched a Royal Commission into the CFMEU, increased police funding, tightened bail laws, and cut services for kids with disabilities. Both Carroll and his predecessor Jacinta Allan attempted to suppress the wages of teachers during their recent enterprise agreement campaign.

But for Australia’s business elite, this isn’t enough. They want a change of government. And if the polls are to be believed, they’re going to get one. 

Victorian Liberal leader Jess Wilson has, for now, stabilised her party after years of embarrassing internal strife. Her campaign relies on heavy fear-mongering about youth crime and presenting Victoria as drowning in debt. Wilson is often described in the press as a moderate Liberal because she appears less socially reactionary. She matched Labor’s pledge to make abortions free, neutralising Labor’s attempt to make it an election issue. 

But Wilson is a blue-blood, ruling-class figure. She was raised in the Liberal Party and was backed by the hard-right Institute of Public Affairs (IPA) while head of the Young Liberals. Before being elected to the blue-ribbon seat of Kew, she served as executive director of policy at the Business Council of Australia. Her husband works for the IPA, and hard-right Liberal powerbroker James Paterson is a close collaborator and godfather to her children. In power, she’ll serve the interests of big business.

The Liberals have pledged to return Victoria’s budget to surplus by 2032. They also plan to lift the threshold for the land tax and payroll tax and cut the metropolitan payroll tax rate. These are all measures which would hand money to businesses and large landowners. They’ve also pledged to hire 3,000 new police officers. 

To pay off the debt while taking these measures would require drastic cuts elsewhere. While the Liberals have mostly avoided outlining where they would make cuts, they’ve already pledged to increase the workloads of civil servants through a hiring freeze covering thousands of positions. It’s likely they will propose further cuts that will affect social services and undermine working-class living standards. 

Alongside cuts, the Liberals want to create a more authoritarian political climate. Wilson has pledged to ban the slogan “globalise the intifada” and introduce move-on powers to crack down on protests. She will scrap the Victorian Treaty process. And she plans to introduce legislation that expands the list of offences for which children will be subjected to adult courts and adult sentencing.

It’s not just the Liberals. One Nation is also doing a service to the bosses by shifting the debate even further to the right. Despite the media’s portrayal of the party as “populist” disruptors, they’re on board with the agenda of reshaping Victoria in the interests of business. 

The bosses have faced little resistance so far in making their concerns central to the terrain of the election. This only serves to entrench a feeling of resignation about the impending right-wing wave. But if significant forces were prepared to launch a fightback, they could likely get a hearing. Only a small minority agree with the Liberals’ plan to scrap Treaty, but there have so far been no rallies to defend it. Progressive NGOs have not led marches against racism or to defend migrants. Nor have unions organised mass meetings or strikes to resist the bosses’ offensive. Instead, when Victorian teachers fought to improve their pay and working conditions, their union’s leadership encouraged them to back down and accept crumbs. 

The institutional weakness of the left and the decline of union militancy put the bosses and their backers in a powerful position. They’ve set the tone for this election, and the …

author: Coral Wynter
title: Standing with the women and girls of Afghanistan
content:
About 110 people from Australia and Britain joined Amnesty International (AI) in an on-line forum, on September 23, to hear about the human rights group's strategy to support women in Afghanistan. Kathy Allan from AI introduced the forum by saying that when Kabul fell on August 15, 2021, the United States handed over power to the Taliban, after the US Coalition, including Australian forces, had carried out a military intervention into Afghanistan for two decades.

The Taliban has 164 decrees targeting women and girls. Women have been barred from most jobs, and from working with non-government organisations (NGOs). Girls are banned from secondary school and university, parks, gyms and beauty salons. Women cannot speak publicly. LGBTIQ+ Afghans have been forced into hiding.

The Taliban is also attacking ethnic and religious minorities, as well as journalists and human rights defenders.

This institutionalised pattern of systemic domination and oppression based on gender has been labelled “gender apartheid”. Afghanistan is the only country in the world to impose this extreme form of gender discrimination.

Right now, international law has no statute that fully captures this situation. AI is calling for gender apartheid to be recognised as a crime under international law.

Muslima, an Afghan educator and writer, told the forum, “Almost overnight, the door to our classroom was closed. Just because you were a girl, you lost your classroom.

“I never imagined that my future would just mean I stay home ... simply because I was born a girl. Being at home every day felt like a prison, like being in jail. Where do I go? My human rights were wiped out.

“But now I have a computer, my classroom to the outside world. All that I have is a small screen in my room. If they find out, I can face charges.

“Thousands of girls have no access to a computer and internet, but I am lucky. Afghan women can’t talk about their stories, nor can they speak about these issues. Girls of 12 years of age are denied the simple right to education, to learn, to develop their skills, to make friends.

“The Taliban can’t build a strong future by excluding half of the population. Afghanistan is losing enormous [human] potential.

“I want the world to see something beyond our suffering. Women are still writing, working, advocating, creating, contributing and building. If you want to support Afghan women, you must listen to them.

“When the headlines disappear, Afghan women do not disappear.

“So my message is clear: make a space for us to speak. Share our voices.

“Sometimes solidarity begins with something as simple as a refusal to forget. Listen to the voices of Afghan women, who are denied their human rights,” Muslima concluded.

The next speaker was Shaharzad Akbar, a human rights activist from Afghanistan, currently living in exile. She talked about the Peoples Tribunal on Women of Afghanistan, which was held in Madrid, Spain, in October last year and hosted by four Afghan women’s organisations.

They are worried that the actions of the Taliban, as the de facto regime, are being normalised in the region. The Taliban currently have consulates in Germany, China, India and Turkiye, although only Russia officially recognises the Taliban government. Europe is now holding conversations with the Taliban regarding potentially deporting Afghan men and women.

Akbar said, “Women are not able to train as midwives or doctors ... Women will die from preventable diseases because there are not enough female health-care providers.”

Women are suffering from domestic abuse, but it is not considered a crime inside Afghanistan. Emotional, economic and physical abuses are not criminalised. Husbands are allowed by law to punish their wives for any offence.

Women can only go to a judge to make a complaint if they have obvious bruises or broken bones — and face many hurdles to do so. They are not allowed to leave the house alone and a male family member has to accompany them to the court. So a brother or father has to be convinced to support them.

The woman has to relay her message to the judge through a man. If she is believed and she has broken bones caused by her husband, he will be imprisoned for 15 days. He usually returns home only to repeat the abuse.

“We have had increased killing of women, increased suicides of women and a mental health crisis for women and girls in Afghanistan. They don’t see a future for themselves. They are imprisoned in their homes …

author: Jordan Humphreys
title: The “two souls” of the Spanish general strike
content:
A 24-hour general strike is set to take place across the Spanish state on 11 November, sparked by recent struggles over housing. In the lead-up to the general strike, 

Red Flag

’s 

Jordan Humphreys

 spoke to Germán 

P. Montañés

, a member of the revolutionary organisation Anticapitalistas, about the unfolding situation.

Red Flag

:

 Rising rents and house prices are affecting people across the globe. Why has it become such a flashpoint in the Spanish state in particular? What is the housing situation like there?

Germán

 

P. Montañés:

 Housing in the Spanish state has been a structural problem for a long time. One of the most visible impacts of the 2008 financial crisis was a wave of mortgage evictions. Today, mortgage-related evictions are less common, but renting has become much more widespread.

Even so, renting remains less common in Spain than in cities like Berlin or New York, where tenant voting blocs have played a major political role. In Spain, home ownership is the norm even among much of the working class. This stems from a strategy popularised during the dictatorship—echoing Margaret Thatcher’s later policies in the UK—summarised by a government minister’s famous quote: “I want a country of homeowners, not proletarians”. This high level of home ownership has somewhat cushioned the crisis; without it, the social situation likely would have collapsed much sooner.

Still, the crisis remains severe for two main groups: young people, who are locked out of home ownership and forced to pay exorbitant rents; and low-income workers and migrants, who face the worst housing instability.

The modern housing movement began around 2008 with anti-eviction campaigns such as the Plataforma de Afectados por la Hipoteca (PAH). Later, tenants’ unions emerged from these struggles—founded in 2017 in hubs like Madrid and Barcelona, and expanding across the Spanish state over the past few years.

A major tipping point occurred in late September, when police evicted 87-year-old María del Carmen (Maricarmen) Abascal from her home in Madrid. She had lived there for nearly 50 years under a rent-controlled agreement, but after an investment fund bought the building, her rent drastically increased. On the fourth attempt, police successfully removed her. This high-profile eviction sparked widespread outrage across the country. In response to the growing public backlash, the prime minister brought the general elections forward to 29 November.

RF

: 

Could you give us a better idea about the tenants’ unions—what kind of organisations are they, and what relationship do they have with the revolutionary left?

GPM:

 The emergence of tenant unions reflects the limits of the previous housing movement, which focused almost exclusively on stopping evictions. The problem with focusing on evictions is that the movement arrives far too late: by the time a family is facing removal, the police are already at the door.

The founding principle of the tenants’ unions was to adapt the most effective elements of trade unions to housing—arriving early to conflicts and organising people sooner. Rather than a diffuse social movement, housing activism needed a formal union. Members pay a monthly contribution, providing a financial base that allows staff to work full time and maintains an ongoing presence.

They also drew heavily on US labour tactics, focusing on entire buildings or properties owned by the same investment fund or landlord family to intervene long before eviction day.

They’ve been very successful recently in Madrid. Around September, they had about 2,000 to 3,000 members, and over the last two months of conflict, that number doubled to roughly 6,000. To clarify: these are financial members, not dedicated militants—there are perhaps 100 to 150 core militants—but the growth is significant.

The mainstream political left has no militant presence inside these spaces and does not control them; it tries to exert influence from the outside through government institutions and political pressure.

The revolutionary left isn’t broadly present either, though our organisation is the only one with a real foothold inside the unions. Our influence extends beyond raw numbers: we’ve maintained a dialogue with the union leadership for ten years. While the leaders come from autonomist or anarchist traditions, key militants in leadership positions allow us to maintain a solid presence. Our goal is to build a revolutionary current inside the …

author: Mazin Qumsiyeh
title: Palestinian ecologist tells COP31: ‘Peace is an environmental necessity’
content:
Mazin Qumsiyeh, from the Palestine Institute for Biodiversity and Sustainability at Bethlehem University, delivered this speech to an ancillary meeting organised at the 31st Conference of Parties (COP31) being held in Türkiye.

We cannot seriously address the climate crisis while ignoring war, militarism, occupation, and the enormous environmental costs of colonisation.

Here in Palestine, the colonial genocide and ethnic cleansing of our people since 1948 has resulted in half a million killed, and now 8.5 million displaced or refugees.

We are working now to get the United Nations to pass an ecocide convention similar to the genocide convention.

The ecocide is global problem and goes beyond borders.

There is no other area where more bombs were dropped relative to population size than Western Asia.

The ecocide is more than just war effect and it does go beyond borders. The Zionist drying up of the Jordan River basin affects four countries; the uprooting of millions of trees and the pollution from the war on the people of Gaza is spreading along the Mediterranean coastline resulting affecting habitats and people.

War is also a climate issue as military activities consume enormous quantities of fossil fuels, destroy infrastructure, generate toxic pollution and release greenhouse gases.

These are often poorly reported or excluded from national climate accounting.

The destruction of Gaza has generated enormous greenhouse gas emissions, both directly through military operations and indirectly through the destruction and future reconstruction of buildings and infrastructure.

A study published in March reported that 33.2 million tonnes of carbon dioxide (CO₂) equivalent had been produced in the destruction of Gaza — a tiny area of 365 square kilometres.

This conservative figure does not take into account the destroyed trees (we studied those by remote sensing), nor the jet fuel burned in countless United States/Israeli sorties to bomb Lebanon, Yemen, Iraq, Syria and Iran.

The 2026 One Earth study estimated that US deliveries of military equipment to Israel between October 2023 and January 2025 involved approximately 50,000 tonnes of supplies transported through 507 aircraft and 107 ship journeys.

The US, which remains the largest single cause of climate change emissions — and it is exempted from reporting on these, has nearly depleted its stockpile of missiles via deliveries to Israel.

Military infrastructure, walls, fortifications and security installations also require enormous quantities of concrete, steel and energy.

The long-term environmental costs is catastrophic: Contaminated soil and water, destruction of agricultural land, damaged wastewater systems, loss of vegetation and even more people dying from diseases and deprivation than those killed directly by these weapons.

More studies and public attention are needed on all of this.

The destruction of ecosystems, like has happened in Palestine, makes communities less resilient to climate change.

Destruction of trees, agricultural land and natural vegetation reduces carbon storage. Soil degradation reduces water infiltration and groundwater recharge.

The destruction of wetlands and natural habitats undermines biodiversity and ecosystem services. Damage to water, sewage and electricity infrastructure increases pollution and dependence on burning wood and diesel for fuel.

The destruction of agricultural systems undermines food sovereignty and increases dependence on imported food.

The UN Environment Program’s September 2025 assessment provides particularly disturbing evidence. By May 2025, 97.1% of tree crops and 82.4% of annual crops in Gaza had been damaged. Approximately 61 million tonnes of debris would require management.

Climate justice requires accountability, not selective accounting.

There is a fundamental contradiction in international climate policy. Governments demand carbon reductions from ordinary citizens, farmers and industries, while military emissions remain inadequately accounted for.

The Paris Agreement climate framework does not impose a comprehensive mandatory reporting system for military emissions. Thus we demand mandatory, transparent reporting of military greenhouse gas emissions, including arms production, military logistics, combat operations and reconstruction.

We often speak about saving the planet for future generations.

But what does that mean to a Palestinian child growing up in Gaza, whose home, school …

author: Jerome Small
title: Carroll’s royal commission: an attack on effective unionism in Victoria
content:
The Royal Commission into the Integrity of Major Public and Civil Infrastructure Construction Projects in Victoria was announced by Victoria’s Labor Premier Ben Carroll in August: his first act as the incoming premier. 

Carroll’s announcement was a response to a years-long media campaign against the CFMEU, the main construction union. It was also part of a wholesale lurch to the right by an already neoliberal Labor government. And it is a blatant attack on any idea that unions should act to raise wages. 

If proof is needed, just look at the first day of the current bloc of hearings. I attended the first day of the commission back in September and sat through the proceedings yesterday via livestream.  

Literally the main point of yesterday’s hearing was how terrible it was that the CFMEU stopped a major construction job—the Gap Road level crossing removal in Sunbury—for a day and a half in June 2022, and that this resulted in traffic controllers winning an increase in wages from the award rate (at that time $26 per hour) to around $49 per hour. 

The horror. This equates to a full-time wage of $1,862 per week, slightly above Australia’s average full-time wage of $1,835 in 2022. It’s an OK wage, though no king’s ransom. With allowances, shift and casual loading, and the plentiful overtime that construction sites run on, this can add up to a decent wage if you’re prepared to work long hours.

To listen to Chris Young, the counsel assisting the royal commission, a union winning this sort of wage for a blue-collar worker through industrial action in 2026 is a threat to all that is right in the world. So much so that two weeks of the royal commission’s rather expensive time is being devoted to investigating how this could possibly have come about, with the express intention of ensuring it never happens again. 

Young spent yesterday sifting through the circumstances leading up to this supposed affront to decency. The CFMEU had a lot going in its favour. 

Railway crossing removals happen on a tight timetable, planned up to a year in advance. The two companies doing the work—John Holland and CPB—wanted to deliver the job on time in order to secure further work. The labour market was tight in Victoria. The CFMEU had already been successful in securing enterprise agreements with most of the big companies doing this sort of work in Victoria. From the evidence led by counsel assisting, it sounds like the CFMEU judged the moment perfectly—just like any union which is serious about taking action to raise wages should, and historically has. 

Both the CFMEU and the Australian Workers’ Union (AWU) cover workers working on civil construction projects like level crossing removals, and since 2014 the CFMEU has been trying to expand its coverage at the expense of the AWU. The Victorian Labor government at that time was uninterested in helping the AWU maintain coverage over these jobs—like Gap Road—and over traffic control work in particular. 

This was a positive for the workers at Gap Road, and more broadly. The royal commission was told that Zoom Recruitment, one of the AWU-aligned labour hire companies providing traffic control at Gap Road, was operating on a long-expired enterprise agreement that paid only the legal minimum specified in the construction award. 

This is utterly consistent with the business model of the AWU for the past century or more in construction, which is to undercut the wages and condition of the CFMEU and its predecessor unions. And to their credit, for most of that time, the CFMEU and their predecessors generally ignored the AWU’s claims to coverage on “civil” infrastructure work (roads, rail, bridges and tunnels).

The commission heard yesterday that the Labor government’s largely hands-off attitude to this demarcation dispute in 2022, which effectively favoured the CFMEU over the AWU, may have been because of factional alignments within the ruling Labor Party. This is hardly a crime, or even a novel tactic in Australian union politics.  

The AWU has used exactly the same approach, of translating political clout in the Labor Party into industrial coverage (and vice-versa), for its entire existence. The conservative Shop, Distributive and Allied Union (SDA) follows the same path. The only difference is that the AWU and the SDA have an appalling record of lifting wages—in fact the SDA did the opposite, helping employers undercut legal minimums, until a path-breaking legal case in the Fair Work …

author: Tamara Pearson
title: Journalism and news in times of catastrophe and enshittification
content:
I pace my small apartment for almost an hour after interviewing a fellow journalist in Mexico who was kidnapped by organised crime groups. Another day, a source has been arrested, another dies in a suspicious car accident. Others tell compelling stories of saving rivers and stopping powerful corporations. I feel alive when I work. But often also worried, deeply sad, and overlooked.

I also work as a global features editor, and the news comes in throughout the day, announcing more horrific events. Another oil spill, more destruction of the environment, of cultures, of people's youths and their futures.

Committed with such impunity, it sometimes leaves me questioning the impact of my work. The repetitive and ongoing nature of such injustices can also make journalism feel routine and close to pointless.

These are tough times for people reading or listening to the news, and for those real journalists who challenge economic and political power rather than aligning with it. But we must continue to stay informed—ignoring the bad news won't stop it.

Courageous journalism is needed more than ever, but it is being smothered by online platforms. Social media, search engines, and the web are increasingly enshitified—inundated with advertising, incorrect information, AI delusions, and mundane, vacuous viral videos.

It is an information crisis and a justice crisis all at once. But just as excessive consumerism and the approximately 48,000 overflowing landfills across the world are a clear call to only use what we need, these crises also embody within them a call for deep change, for a reckoning.

AI dominance begs us to return to everything that is humanising, creative, and real. Injustice and the climate crisis call for structural action and a strengthening of good journalism. The mainstream outlets beholden to corporations and in denial of empire and inequality are increasingly and obviously, useless.

Media outlets and other sources of information, like search engines and social media, are skewing perceptions about what matters. The amount of attention and space given to different regions, issues, and people forges a hierarchy of concerns.

Issues covered tediously can risk desensitising, normalising,and numbing. But overlooked news and silence numbs in malevolent and long-lasting ways, infusing populations with extremely high levels of tolerance and deflection.

Mass hunger in a world that produces an excess of food is a raging nightmare, deserving of daily coverage and strike action until it ends. Yet most people are accustomed.

For the journalists and outlets with integrity, at times it can feel like there is nothing left to say; that we've reported the injustices over and over. That all we are doing is documenting how the house is falling apart. This is indicative of a need to take things to the next level.

So how do we do good journalism, when everything is at stake and none of the polluting and warring criminals are held accountable? How can our news reading and news producing be useful, even as long-term worry exhausts us and narrows cognitive flexibility and creativity? How do we ensure clarity and care, without also falling apart?

The algorithmic boosting of low-grade and commercial content, accompanies the burying of critical insight and investigation. Amid catastrophe, injustice, and repression, the key sources of information — rather than enlightening — are calculated to numb and dull people.

The social media, information, book, and media landscapes are rapidly deteriorating as ad load is growing to ridiculous amounts. Every other post is sponsored content or online recipes. Many articles are unreadable without a browser or tools that remove all the ads. Our feeds are industrial swamplands of sponsored content and viral AI videos and stories. And for some demographics, objectified images of women.

Even newsletter spaces like Substack boost existing privilege (almost all the top newsletters are by men) and seek profitability. Meanwhile AI search engine summaries are discouraging direct reads of alternative media outlets. First page search results are likewise dominated by corporations like Expedia, United States outlets (even for users who aren't there), and mediocre click-bait websites. It's hard to compete, and our in-depth reporting can feel like feeble feathers in a hurricane.

Further, people expect shorter and short content. Two minute videos are now too long. Scrolling and short formats promote …

author: Odessa Bishop-McMurray
title: “If they won’t give us a future, we will build one right here” - why the French revolt should inspire high-schoolers everywhere
content:
As one of the organisers of the upcoming nationwide 

Students Say No to Hanson

 demonstration on 12 November, I’ve had to endure a lot of inanity from the media and the right. Amongst snide remarks about the stages of brain development and warnings of the mortal dangers of missing two periods of class, one accusation keeps coming up: that we’re plotting to bring “French-style riots” to Australian cities. 

Right-wing journalists seized on an Instagram post we made on 11 October, conveying the inspiration we draw from French student protesters fighting government austerity and the far right. 

Cue an avalanche of hysterical headlines and news segments: The Murdoch-owned Adelaide 

Advertiser

 warned readers to brace for “walkouts ‘inspired’ by violent French protests”. Pauline Hanson went on Brisbane’s 4BC Radio to rip into us:

“...They are saying they are inspired by what’s going on in France. What? The 

looting

? The 

burning

? The 

destruction

? They’re 

inspired

 by that?”

Well, we’re not sorry for being inspired by French students. Everyone who wants to see a better world should identify with their struggle. 

Young people everywhere are facing a dire future, and revolt is rightly spreading. It’s clear even to some in the establishment that what’s happening in France is part of a global wave of protest with deep roots. As former UK Prime Minister Gordon Brown wrote this week in 

The Guardian

: “A global youthquake is happening. Promises we made young people have been broken—and they know it.”

Both far-right governments and “sensible centrists” are taking us on the same trajectory: more racism, more militarism, and more austerity. 

When states aren’t attempting to re-introduce conscription, as in Germany, they’re funnelling billions into the military-industrial complex while schools crumble. In France, students endure classrooms infested with cockroaches, mould and overcrowding, sometimes numbering 35 students to a class. 

We’ll likely never be able to afford secure housing or sufficient healthcare. We’ve watched politicians choose fossil fuel companies over the habitability of our planet. For many of us, the establishment’s unanimous endorsement of Israel’s genocide in Gaza was the final nail in the coffin.

It’s obvious that the journalists’ and politicians’ pearl-clutching about a few broken Parisian shop windows is a means of avoiding discussion of these issues. And their condemnation of violence rings hollow when they decline to comment on the vastly greater violence that the system inflicts on people daily. 

There’s the violence that is inherent in running such an unequal society. French youth linger without a future in the slums while the richest 500 families own nearly half the country. Schools and hospitals in France are crumbling, but the latest budget announcement includes 54 billion euros in further cuts to public spending. The police systematically brutalise Black and Arab working-class migrants. The high-profile killing of 17-year-old Nahel Merzouk, which sparked a nationwide revolt in 2023, is part of a long history of racialised policing. 

When these injustices generate resistance, there’s one public service the government can guarantee: the bludgeoning of protestors, tear gas, and potentially lethal stun grenades; exploding a student’s hand, breaking another’s jaw and leaving two 16-year-olds blinded for life. 

This is an inherent admission that the ruling class has no genuine plan to improve society. They just want resignation from ordinary people, and when that fails, tear gas is their backup plan.

But French students have shown that resignation gets us nowhere; Our power comes from the streets, and that’s a lesson the ruling class desperately does not want students to learn.

Already, France has shown small glimpses of how these movements can win real gains. While still hoping to crush the movement, the government has already been forced to make concessions. They’ve announced plans to cap class sizes, hire more teachers, and create more university places. This is a tiny fraction of what the movement is demanding, but it proves a timeless truth: a month of rebellion can win more change than decades of asking nicely.

A grassroots student movement in Serbia just ended the 14-year rule of the repressive Vučić regime. In Brazil, thousands of students flocked to the streets to successfully halt the advance of far-right presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro.

It seems like …

author: CMI Argentina
title: Pauny no se presentó a la audiencia y crece la incertidumbre sobre la continuidad de los 450 empleados de su planta de Córdoba
content:
Pauny, la fábrica de tractores, debía presentar un plan para afrontar la deuda salarial y reactivar la producción en la fábrica de Las Varillas. Lucas Sarmiento, titular de la UOM San Francisco, aseguró que adeuda dos meses de sueldos.


La crisis de Pauny sumó un nuevo capítulo este jueves, luego de que la empresa no se presentara a la audiencia convocada por la Secretaría de Trabajo de Córdoba para abordar la deuda salarial con sus empleados y la paralización de la actividad productiva en la planta de Las Varillas.


En diálogo con Cadena 3, Lucas Sarmiento, secretario general de la Unión Obrera Metalúrgica (UOM) de San Francisco, cuestionó la decisión de la firma y rechazó los argumentos expuestos en un comunicado empresarial, en el que se responsabilizó a los trabajadores por las dificultades para retomar la actividad.


La audiencia tenía como objetivo que la empresa presentara un plan para afrontar las obligaciones salariales pendientes y una propuesta productiva que permitiera reactivar la fábrica, prácticamente paralizada desde hace entre tres y cinco meses.


“Los trabajadores están acá en planta esperando justamente una propuesta de la patronal para reactivar rápidamente la empresa. Eso no sucede”, sostuvo Sarmiento.


Sarmiento precisó que Pauny tiene alrededor de 450 trabajadores directos y que la deuda con el personal no se limita a los últimos dos meses de salarios impagos: “Están adeudando los últimos dos meses completos, pero no es solamente eso. Los trabajadores fueron tomando deuda a lo largo de este año y del año pasado porque la empresa fue pagando a destiempo”, explicó.


Uno de los puntos más cuestionamientos del sindicato es la intención de la empresa de desprenderse de 150 trabajadores mediante un plan de retiros voluntarios o desvinculaciones, con el pago de parte de las indemnizaciones en 12 cuotas.


“Es ilógico que la empresa plantee un plan de retiro voluntario cuando ni siquiera junta la plata para pagar la deuda que tiene con los trabajadores”, afirmó Sarmiento.


El dirigente también puso en duda la capacidad de la firma para afrontar esos compromisos y mencionó la situación financiera de Pauny. Según los datos que dijo haber consultado en la Central de Deudores del Banco Central, la compañía registra obligaciones con distintas entidades bancarias por más de 50 millones de dólares y 206 cheques rechazados en los últimos 15 días, por un monto superior a los $1.500 millones.


“¿Con qué van a pagar? ¿Con cheques? ¿Quién va a aceptar cheques de Pauny? Es una locura lo que está haciendo la empresa”, cuestionó.

author: cnt.es
title: ¿Y ahora qué? Ahora a seguir
content:
Imagen

: 02:4055h. Piquete informativo en Mercavalencia | Fuente: CNT


La huelga general del 11 de noviembre ha sido un éxito. Pero, sobre todo, ha sido una demostración de que cuando quienes sostenemos la sociedad con nuestro trabajo decidimos organizarnos y salir a la calle, tenemos mucho que decir y mucho que hacer.


Desde CNT valoramos muy positivamente el desarrollo de la huelga y, especialmente, la respuesta que han tenido las movilizaciones en las calles. Miles de personas han expresado su hartazgo ante unas condiciones de vida cada vez más difíciles, en las que trabajar ya no garantiza poder vivir dignamente. La precariedad, los salarios insuficientes, la pérdida de poder adquisitivo y la imposibilidad de acceder a una vivienda digna no son problemas individuales: son problemas colectivos que requieren respuestas colectivas.


Pero ahora viene la pregunta inevitable: ¿y ahora qué?


Ahora, a seguir.


No podemos permitir que el 11N se quede en una fecha señalada en el calendario, en una jornada de protesta que se recuerde durante unos días y después se olvide. La huelga ha sido un paso, pero no puede ser el último. Necesitamos mantener la movilización, extenderla a más centros de trabajo, barrios y sectores, fortalecer nuestras organizaciones y construir espacios de lucha y solidaridad.


Las huelgas feministas de 2018 y 2019 nos enseñaron algo importante. Fueron capaces de sacar a la calle a millones de personas, visibilizar las desigualdades que atraviesan la vida de las mujeres y situar en el centro del debate social problemas que durante demasiado tiempo se habían considerado asuntos privados. No acabaron con el machismo ni con las desigualdades, pero abrieron un camino y demostraron la capacidad transformadora de la movilización colectiva. Su éxito no estuvo en resolverlo todo en un día, sino en poner en marcha un proceso que continúa.


El 11N debe ser también un comienzo.


Y tenemos claro algo más:

esto no lo va a solucionar ningún Gobierno.

 No porque no existan responsabilidades políticas, sino porque el problema va mucho más allá de quién ocupa los despachos. Vivimos en un sistema en el que las decisiones económicas están condicionadas por los intereses de quienes concentran la riqueza y el poder. Cambian los gobiernos, cambian los discursos, pero la economía sigue organizada para garantizar los beneficios de unos pocos a costa de las condiciones de vida de la mayoría.


No vamos a delegar nuestros problemas en ningún político a sueldo de los millonarios. No vamos a esperar a que quienes administran este sistema tengan la voluntad de cambiarlo. Nuestra fuerza no está en las promesas electorales ni en confiar nuestro futuro a representantes profesionales. Está en nuestra capacidad de organizarnos, apoyarnos mutuamente y conquistar nuestros derechos mediante la acción directa y la solidaridad. En nuestra ilusión por crear un nuevo mundo, más justo y con más respeto a la vida.


La vivienda, los salarios, las jornadas, las pensiones y unas condiciones de vida dignas no son cuestiones separadas. Forman parte de una misma realidad: la de una economía que antepone el beneficio a las necesidades de las personas.


Por eso, desde CNT hacemos un llamamiento a continuar las movilizaciones, a mantener viva la organización en los centros de trabajo y en los barrios, y a convertir la indignación expresada el 11N en fuerza colectiva y capacidad de lucha.


No hemos salido a la calle para pedir que nos escuchen y volver a casa a esperar una respuesta. Hemos salido porque sabemos que nuestros derechos dependen de nuestra capacidad para defenderlos.


El 11N no es un final. Es un comienzo.


¿Y ahora qué? Ahora a seguir.

author: Unknown
title: Li HABAŞê mudaxeleyî karkeran kirin: Gelek karker hatin desteserkirin
content:
Li Kargeha Hesin û Pola ya HABAŞê ya li navçeya Alîagaya Îzmîrê ku di teqîna 9ê Mijdarê de 19 karkeran jiyana xwe ji dest dabû, mudaxeleyî karkerên ku şertên xebatê û qedexeya telefona desta protesto dikirin, hat kirin.


Li gorî nûçeya ku îro (13ê Mijdar) hatiye weşandin, karkerên ku li ber kargehê çalakî li dar dixistin, bi lêdanê hatin desteserkirin.


Li dijî qedexeya telefonê neketin kargehê


Piştî teqîna ku li kargehê bû sedema mirina 19 karkeran, ji bo karkeran qedexeya ketina tesîsê ya bi telefona desta hat anîn.


Di agahdariya ku li ber deriyê kargehê hatiye daliqandin de, hat diyarkirin ku bi fermana Serokê Lijneya Rêveber a HABAŞê Mehmet Ruştu Başaran, mecbûrî ye ku xebatkar telefonên xwe radestî peywirdarên ewlehiyê bikin. 


Hat ragihandin ku karkerên telefonên xwe radest nekin dê di turnîkeyan re neyên derbaskirin.


Karkerên vardiya şev û sibehê yên ku li hember biryarê bertek nîşan dan, neketin kargehê û li ber deriyê ketinê dest bi sekinandinê kirin.


Karkeran dirûşmeyên “Rêveberî îstifa” û “Turk Metal îstifa” berz kirin. Ajokarên kamyonan jî bi lêdana kornayan piştgirî dan karkerên ku li ser rêya ketin û derketina kargehê kom bûbûn.


Karker: Heta kavil neyên rakirin em naxwazin bixebitin


Karkeran diyar kir ku piştî teqînê li kargehê xebatên lêgerîn-rizgarkirinê û rakirina kavilan didomin, lê tevî vê yekê li hin beşan hilberîn û şandina kelûpelan berdewam dike.


Karkeran xwest ku heta kavil bi temamî bên rakirin destûra bi mûçe bê dayîn, lêkolîneke serbixwe bê kirin û beriya ku tedbîrên tenduristî û ewlehiya kar bi kêmasî neyên girtin, dest bi hilberînê neyê kirin.


Karkeran her wiha îdia kir ku armanca qedexeyê ew e ku rê li ber derketina dîmenên derbarê xebatên piştî teqînê yên li kargehê de bê girtin.


Bi nûnerên sendîkayê re alozî derket


Di dema çalakiya li ber kargehê de di navbera nûnerên Sendîkaya Turk Metal û karkeran de jî alozî derket. Nûnerên sendîkayê ji karkeran xwest ku bikevin kargehê. Lê belê karkeran diyar kir ku piştî teqînê xebat û sewqiyat didome û li hember vê bangê bertek nîşan dan.


Piştî nîqaşa ku derket, di navbera peywirdarên ewlehiyê yên fabrîqeyê, nûnerên sendîkayê û karkeran de pevçûn rû da. Hat dîtin ku di dema çalakiyê de li hin kesan hatiye xistin.


Piştî aloziyê agahiyê mudaxele û desteserkirinê ketin rojevê.


Di lêpirsîna derbarê teqînê de neh kes hatin girtin


Di teqîna ku 9ê Mijdarê de li Kargeha Hesin û Pola ya HABAŞê pêk hatibû de, li gorî agahiyên ku heta 13ê Mijdarê di çapemeniyê de cih girtine, 19 karker mirine û 14 karker birîndar bûn.


Ji ber teqînê 11 gumanbarên hatibûn desteserkirin û ji wan 9 kes hatibûn girtin. 


Serokê Desteya Rêveber ê şîrketê Mehmet Ruştu Başaran jî di nav de 2 gumanbar jî bi şertê zîndanîkirina li malê serbest bûn. 


(FY/AY)

author: webdev@democracynow.org (Democracy Now!)
title: "It's Just Barbarism": Dr. Feroze Sidhwa Mourns Friend Killed in Israeli Hospital Strike in Gaza
content:
Israel’s latest bombing of Nasser Hospital in Gaza on Thursday killed six Palestinians, including surgeon Dr. Rizk Abu Shaira. He was featured in the recent documentary

American Doctor

, which follows international medical volunteers in Gaza’s battered hospitals as they work alongside Palestinian colleagues.


Israel claimed, without providing evidence, that it targeted a senior Hamas militant in the hospital strike. Israel has repeatedly bombed medical facilities in Gaza since the start of the genocide in October 2023, even though such attacks are prohibited under international law.


“It’s just barbarism. I don’t know why we’re supporting this,” says Dr. Feroze Sidhwa, one of the titular American doctors in the documentary, who demands accountability for Israel’s actions and a change in U.S. policy toward the country. “That’s an American-made bomb dropped by an American-made airplane burning American-supplied jet fuel.”


Sidhwa also comments on the catastrophic flooding in Gaza that has swamped the temporary shelters of tens of thousands of displaced Palestinians as Israel continues to block the entry of shelter materials into the territory. As a result, “babies are going to die of hypothermia in Gaza for the fourth year in a row,” Sidhwa says.
