author: Nahuel Lag
title: El suelo como espejo de la relación entre humanidad y naturaleza
content:
Por Patricia Fernández y Lourdes Gil Cardeza*


Somos muchas las personas, organizaciones e instituciones que reconocemos estar atravesando una crisis civilizatoria muy profunda. Hay tantísima evidencia que muestra cómo estamos sobrepasando los límites físicos que permiten nuestra existencia en el planeta Tierra. Hay un área específica de la economía que lo estudia: la economía ecológica. El estilo de vida que impone la sociedad occidental implica calentamiento global, una creciente y continua contaminación de suelos y aguas, y el constante despojo de tierras a pueblos indígenas y campesinos debido al avance del modelo económico, que pone en jaque a los procesos biológicos de la vida que han ido coevolucionando desde hace, al menos, 460 millones de años, cuando empezó a desarrollarse la vida fuera del agua.


El suelo es un espejo de los vínculos que lo conforman. Es la resultante de la convivencia evolutiva entre la roca madre, el clima y los seres vivos. En otras palabras, el suelo es parte de los procesos del planeta Tierra, el suelo es vida, el suelo está vivo. Tanto su color oscuro característico como ese olorcito que percibimos corresponden a la materia orgánica (componente fértil y vital del suelo), compuesta por los organismos vivos que lo habitan y por lo muerto en vía de descomposición que nutren de manera espiralada a los organismos y las plantas de las que nos alimentamos. El estilo de vida occidental pone en riesgo esa vitalidad.


El tipo de agricultura que domina al planeta no es un simple conjunto de técnicas para producir alimentos (y muchas veces commodities): es la materialización de una lógica de poder que entrelaza colonialismo, patriarcado y capitalismo. Así lo evidencian las voces críticas de pensadoras que ayer y hoy señalan cómo el avance sobre la tierra y la naturaleza es un reflejo de la misma lógica de dominación ejercida sobre los cuerpos de las mujeres y los territorios. Llegar a comprender la crisis o la degradación del suelo hoy, exige, en principio, desentrañar esta trama histórica y epistemológica que ha convertido a la naturaleza en un objeto de explotación ilimitada. 


Creemos que hacer el intento por desarmar esta trama (o trampa), es condición necesaria en el proceso de deconstrucción que elegimos, como dijo

Audre Lorde

, para transformar la ira en un proceso creativo. Con este texto buscamos traer a la actualidad, y a latinoamérica en particular, a Eve Balfour, una mujer de la aristocracia inglesa quien, con mucha claridad y simpleza, se atrevió a abordar temas invisibilizados en Europa y sus continentes colonizados, al publicar su libro

El Suelo Vivo

 (

The Living Soil

) en 1943. 


Foto: Matías sarlo - Minga


Esta tesis describe de manera sencilla los vínculos entre la salud humana y el cultivo de nuestros alimentos y pone la lupa en el suelo jerarquizando su rol como promotor de la salud toda. En palabras de Eve:

“La evidencia acumulada sobre la interrelación entre la vitalidad del suelo y la salud de las plantas, los animales y el ser humano es de tal importancia y de tan profundas implicancias que ya es hora de que el público en general tenga la oportunidad de estudiar y formarse su propio juicio al respecto”

.


La matriz del despojo


La crítica al modelo agrícola industrial debe partir de la constatación de que su origen no es meramente técnico, sino profundamente político. La antropóloga maya-kaqchikel

Aura Cumes

 sostiene que el patriarcado colonial llega desde Europa y se reconfigura en América para ejercer el sometimiento sobre las mujeres, las poblaciones indígenas y afrodescendientes convirtiéndolas en sujetos despojables y así validar la extracción del territorio y del cuerpo-territorio. Este proceso de dominación tuvo un pilar fundamental: la disociación del hombre respecto de la naturaleza, a la cual se feminizó para legitimar su conquista. "A partir de ello —explica Cumes— se atribuye la potestad de descubrirla, penetrarla, torturarla y convertirla en mercancía." 


Esta visión no es casual, sino que se fundamenta tanto en los textos bíblicos que otorgan al hombre el "señorío" sobre la creación como en el discurso científico que adoptó estos postulados como base de su conocimiento. En esta trama (o trampa), el capitalismo manifiesta la continuidad de las mismas lógicas que motorizaron al colonialismo al implementar la sustitución de ecosistemas enteros por una "biota mixta" europea (trigo, ganado vacuno, cerdos, malezas, microorganismos, personas) …

author: Unknown
title: Indigenous Action - Voting is Not Harm Reduction
content:
Author

: Indigenous Action

Title

: Voting is Not Harm Reduction

Date

: February 5, 2020

Source

: http://www.indigenousaction.org/voting-is-not-harm-reduction-an-indigenous-perspective/


 When proclamations are made that “voting is harm reduction,” it’s never clear how less harm is actually calculated. Do we compare how many millions of undocumented Indigenous Peoples have been deported? Do we add up what political party conducted more drone strikes? Or who had the highest military budget? Do we factor in pipelines, mines, dams, sacred sites desecration? Do we balance incarceration rates? Do we compare sexual violence statistics? Is it in the massive budgets of politicians who spend hundreds of millions of dollars competing for votes?


 Though there are some political distinctions between the two prominent parties in the so-called U.S., they all pledge their allegiance to the same flag. Red or blue, they’re both still stripes on a rag waving over stolen lands that comprise a country built by stolen lives.


 We don’t dismiss the reality that, on the scale of U.S. settler colonial violence, even the slightest degree of harm can mean life or death for those most vulnerable. What we assert here is that the entire notion of “voting as harm reduction” obscures and perpetuates settler-colonial violence, there is nothing “less harmful” about it, and there are more effective ways to intervene in its violences.


 At some point the left in the so-called U.S. realized that convincing people to rally behind a “lesser evil” was a losing strategy. The term “harm reduction” was appropriated to reframe efforts to justify their participation and coerce others to engage in the theater of what is called “democracy” in the U.S.


 Harm reduction was established in the 1980s as a public health strategy for people dealing with substance use issues who struggle with abstinence. According to the Harm Reduction Coalition (HRC) the principles of harm reduction establish that the identified behavior is “part of life” so they “choose not to ignore or condemn but to minimize harmful effects” and work towards breaking social stigmas towards “safer use.” The HRC also states that, “there is no universal definition of or formula for implementing harm reduction.” Overall, harm reduction focuses on reducing adverse impacts associated with harmful behaviors.


 The proposition of “harm reduction” in the context of voting means something entirely different from those organizing to address substance use issues. The assertion is that “since this political system isn’t going away, we’ll support politicians and laws that may do less harm.”


 The idea of a ballot being capable of reducing the harm in a system rooted in colonial domination and exploitation, white supremacy, hetero-patriarchy, and capitalism is an extraordinary exaggeration. There is no person whose life is not impacted every day by these systems of oppression, but instead of coded reformism and coercive “get out the vote” campaigns towards a “safer” form of settler colonialism, we’re asking “what is the real and tragic harm and danger associated with perpetuating colonial power and what can be done to end it?”


 Voting as practiced under U.S. “democracy” is the process with which people (excluding youth under the age of 18, convicted felons, those the state deems “mentally incompetent,” and undocumented folx including permanent legal residents), are coerced to choose narrowly prescribed rules and rulers. The anarchist collective Crimethinc observes, “Voting consolidates the power of a whole society in the hands of a few politicians.” When this process is conducted under colonial authority, there is no option but political death for Indigenous Peoples. In other words, voting can never be a survival strategy under colonial rule. It’s a strategy of defeat and victimhood that protracts the suffering and historical harm induced by ongoing settler colonialism. And while the harm reduction sentiment may be sincere, even hard won marginal reforms gained through popular support can be just as easily reversed by the stroke of a politician’s pen. If voting is the democratic participation in our own oppression, voting as harm reduction is a politics that keeps us at the mercy of our oppressors.


 While so many on the left–including some Indigenous radicals–are concerned with consolidation of power into fascists hands, they fail to recognize how colonial power is already consolidated. There …

author: Arnold Padilla
title: What’s at stake in Trump’s Manila visit?
content:
U.S. President Donald Trump’s upcoming visit to Manila for the ASEAN Summit happens in the wake of intensifying struggle between the U.S. and China for economic, technological, political, and military dominance in Asia. Washington aims to consolidate its strategic position in Southeast Asia, with the Philippines under Ferdinand Marcos Jr. playing an increasingly important role in advancing U.S. imperialist interests.

Trump arrives politically battered. The sweeping Republican defeat in the November 3 midterm elections, which handed both houses of Congress to the Democrats, represents a powerful repudiation of his administration’s policies. Trump’s unpopular U.S. war against Iran and his aggressive tariff policies and their disastrous economic consequences, such as rising living costs, contributed to widespread dissatisfaction among American voters.

The defeat further exposes the political crisis confronting U.S. imperialism. It reflects growing domestic opposition to policies that impose enormous economic and social costs on the American people while sustaining Washington’s aggressive military interventions and global ambitions.

But Trump’s weakened domestic position does not mean that the White House will abandon its imperialist agenda abroad. On the contrary, the administration may seek to demonstrate U.S. power through new military, economic, and diplomatic agreements. Trump could use his visit to Manila to project strength and secure strategic commitments to counter the political setback at home.

The central objective of Washington’s ASEAN agenda is to preserve U.S. supremacy in the face of China’s expanding economic and military power. Southeast Asia occupies a crucial place in this rivalry. It sits astride strategic maritime routes and contains vital manufacturing centers, mineral resources, emerging digital markets, and production networks essential to the world economy.

For U.S. imperialism, maintaining influence over ASEAN means safeguarding its military reach while securing access to markets, technology infrastructure, critical minerals, and industrial supply chains. The U.S. seeks to organize these strategic assets around its own economic and national-security priorities, particularly by reducing dependence on Chinese-controlled production networks.

At the same time, China is expanding its own economic and strategic influence through trade, investment, infrastructure, and military power. This competition between rival great powers seeks to expand their influence over the region’s resources, markets, territory, and political decisions.

Washington’s military agenda was made explicit during the ASEAN defense ministers’ meetings in Cebu in October, when Pete Hegseth, Trump’s so-called Secretary of War, proposed a new framework for U.S.–ASEAN defense cooperation.

Under the language of maritime security and interoperability, Washington seeks to deepen military coordination, intelligence sharing, joint exercises, and naval cooperation with Southeast Asian governments. The proposal complements the expanding network of U.S. military alliances and access arrangements across the Indo-Pacific. It aims to strengthen its First Island Chain strategy to encircle and contain China. On the sidelines of the Cebu meeting, U.S. and Japanese defense officials discussed implementing a more effective denial-defense posture along this chain.

With its geographical location, the Philippines has become a crucial platform for this strategy. Under Marcos Jr., U.S. military access under the Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement (EDCA) has expanded from five to nine designated Philippine facilities. Washington and Manila are also increasing joint military exercises and deployments of advanced missile and unmanned systems. These arrangements strengthen the capacity of U.S. forces to operate in the South China Sea and potentially respond to a Taiwan Strait conflict.

So far, only two ASEAN countries have formal defense treaties with the U.S., namely the Philippines and Thailand. But all the other members, except for Myanmar, have various forms of extensive defense or military cooperation arrangements with the U.S. However, unlike its Mutual Defense Treaty (MDT) and related pacts with the Philippines, not all agreements with other ASEAN countries grant U.S. troops access to military installations, allow combat deployments, or entail an obligation to support U.S. military operations.

author: Willy Mutunga
title: Book Review: From Mau Mau to Ruto-Must-Go: A Scrapbook of Essays on Kenya’s Struggle Against Imperialism
content:
I recently read a review of the book, 

From MAU MAU to RUTO-MUST-GO: A Scrapbook of Essays on Kenya’s Struggle Against Imperialism,

 

by Teddy Odira, a young lawyer in Nairobi who published in The Platform for Law, Justice, and Society. I shared the review with one of the co-editors of the book, Shiraz Durrani, and asked him what he thought. This is was his response via a WhatsApp text:


It’s a brilliant review, I think. He understands the undercurrents that the book explores and identifies key issues, like land, that have driven resistance. He also sees resistance as an on-going, incomplete struggle. Very well done!


What is well said by another is mine. In this review, I want to glorify the work of the artist movements in Kenya for breathing life into the Constitution of Kenya, 2010, particularly

Article 33

 that decrees freedom of expression. This freedom of expression has limitations. It is the freedom of artistic creativity that is glorified in two of the articles in the book. They glorify cartoonists and Social Justice Theatre (SJCCTT). Freedom of artistic creativity in Kenya is valued by others, including the two mentioned. The others include: poets, spoken word artists, graffiti artists, songwriters, singers, comedians, filmmakers, and others. Freedom of artistic creativity has been a radical site of struggle in the implementation of the Constitution of Kenya, 2010. Freedom of expression under the Constitution has been the subject of a recently published scholarly work.


This Constitution has been described as progressive and transformative because of the process of its making, its texts on objectives, purpose, and vision to reform, by non-reformist reforms, which maintain the status quo in Kenya. While the ruling elite find the Constitution inconvenient and abstract, these sites of struggle have used provisions of the Constitution to craft political demands, breathe life into these sites through uprising, robust public participation, mass action, and public interest litigation. The quest for an authentic patriotic alternative political leadership is a continuous struggle anchored in these constitutional sites of struggle that the ruling elite has refused to implement. It is argued that such an alternative political leadership that is authentic and patriotic will implement the Constitution by consolidating gains made, and rescuing the weaknesses that are encountered during the process of its implementation.


Glorification


A: In Praise of Cartoonists: Ruo Kimani-Ruo


Ruo Kimani-Ruo praises the cartoonists in words that should not be paraphrased:


…,

there has emerged an unprecedented form of political cartoons artwork which has been launched in Kenya with sizzling, scorching, blistering cartoon editorials and other graphics and caricatures of public figures that express the artists’ opinions, with celebrated cartoon artists Celeste and Maddo


being joined by Yoko and others-all freely and fearlessly expressing their opinions on public issues and the individuals in government and thereby shedding light on the public mood on issues.…


With these political cartoons, the artists have had a field day and typically combined artistic skills, hyperbole and satire to question authority. The cartoons have drawn attention to, among other things, corruption, electoral inequalities, political abductions and other social ills including violence- and the Consolidated Fund at Central Bank of Kenya (CBK) where billions of shillings are being ‘siphoned and stashed in offshore accounts in the West; and suspicions of embezzlement.


The genius of the cartoonists that I have encountered over decades lies in the interpretation of their work for the powers that be, and the citizens themselves. They are always armed with many interpretations of their cartoons. They use those interpretations to either stay safe when confronted by elites and their machinery of violence, or to mobilize the citizens around the key messages. They invariably keep their mouths shut and let their work engage both the enemy and the friend. Their work requires great critical thinking, taking ideological and political positions in breathing life into the provisions of the Constitution to energize non-reformist reforms.

Zachary J Patterson

title: Trump bombardea Irán en la madrugada de su derrota electoral
content:
Tal como lo descontaban los sondeos electorales y hasta los “mercados”, Trump sufrió una derrota de carácter aplastante en los comicios de este martes. A

 nadie escapa que en el telón de fondo del rechazo electoral a Trump se encuentra la guerra contra Irán y sus consecuencias económicas. Pero al referirse al resultado electoral, los principales voceros del partido Demócrata -y también los de la democracia imperialista europea- han ocultado la cuestión de la guerra por abajo el felpudo. Un largo posteo oficial de Obama ni la menciona, después de varias invocaciones a la “unión nacional”. La guerra imperialista en desarrollo, que comenzó bajo el mandato de Biden, está en el horizonte estratégico de republicanos y demócratas.

Para Trump, la continuidad de la guerra con Irán es también un recurso para prevalecer sobre la Unión Europea, en medio del agravamiento de la guerra entre Ucrania y Rusia y los acuerdos por «separado» entre Putin y el propio Trump.

Un escenario de escalada militar, por un lado, y mayor autoritarismo, por el otro, agravará la crisis política y los estallidos populares al interior de los Estados Unidos, en medio de una crisis financiera en ciernes. El eje de la crisis mundial pasa por el corazón del imperialismo.

Por Marcelo Ramal (Política Obrera).


Tal como lo descontaban los sondeos electorales y hasta los “mercados”, Trump sufrió una derrota de carácter aplastante en los comicios de este martes. La victoria demócrata, que se consideraba segura en Representantes (diputados), también tuvo lugar en el Senado, donde la composición final sería de 52 o 53 escaños demócratas contra 48 o 47 de los republicanos. Los reveses de Trump abarcaron a estados con un dominio histórico de su partido, como Carolina del Norte y del Sur -en este último caso, ganaron los demócratas después de 25 años de mandatos republicanos; también en el bastión petrolero de Texas, donde se impuso un senador demócrata después de 38 años, y lo mismo en Kansas, después de casi un siglo de hegemonía republicana. En Florida, bastión del exilio derechista cubano y venezolano y corazón del movimiento MAGA, la candidata republicana María Salazar había tomado distancias de Trump para salvar el voto migrante. A pesar de ello, sólo se imponía por una diferencia del 0,1%, en un escrutinio voto a voto. En Michigan, la victoria del candidato de origen musulmán Abdul El Sayed lograba prevalecer después de una furiosa campaña en su contra de Trump y del sionismo.


Significado


Ningún observador reconoce un liderazgo o fisonomía política definida en la victoria demócrata: el hilo conductor del resultado electoral es el golpe asestado a Trump -los electores, que concurrieron masivamente a sufragar en un país donde el voto es voluntario- desplegaron una movilización política en rechazo a la carestía desatada por la guerra, la represión política y el “estado de excepción” impuesto por Trump contra la población migrante. Las redadas del ICE llegaron a convertirse en un factor de desorganización económica, al imponer una zozobra que afecta a una parte de la fuerza laboral del capitalismo americano. La tentativa de “reindustrialización” del país a costa de sanciones comerciales extendidas tuvo pobres resultados y acrecentó la inflación. La carestía fue también estimulada por la instalación de los centros de datos para la oligarquía tecnológica de la IA. En sus campañas electorales, los gobernadores electos de Texas, Ohio, Georgia y Pensilvania hicieron de la oposición a la instalación de estas infraestructuras un eje de campaña. 29 jurisdicciones votaron este martes medidas locales de restricción a estas instalaciones, con apoyo abrumador de la población. La política MAGA, en definitiva, sólo hizo grande a los negocios de la camarilla trumpista y la oligarquía tecnológica. Para la población explotada, sólo trajo inflación, salarios a la baja y mayor zozobra en el empleo.


Entre Mr. Veto y los acuerdos


“Con mi nombre en la boleta, ganábamos en todos lados”. Esto posteó Trump después de la derrota, desconociendo u ocultando que él mismo se había puesto al frente de las elecciones que acababa de perder. Pero la alusión a su figura apunta a lo que viene: la pretensión de erigir un régimen de poder personal, a costa de decretazos y de vetos. Las mayorías cosechadas por los demócratas no tienen la contundencia para desconocer esos vetos -tampoco para hacer avanzar hasta el final un juicio político contra Trump. content:
Number 114

Defying the zio-global dictatorship!


The grim trail of ZIM terror


Banned from Canada


Why anarchists must confront totalitarian humanism


Peter Marshall: an organic radical inspiration


Acorninfo


1. Defying the zio-global dictatorship

!


by Paul Cudenec, who reads the article 

here


I am sure you don’t need me to tell you that we are heading into a crucial period of history.


Not only is the shadow of a possible world war looming over us, but our freedom is coming under rapidly accelerating assault.


Here in France, for instance, the system started out by simply ignoring schoolkids protesting against the poor condition of their schools and their lives, then went on to

gas

 and

beat

 them,

smear

 their uprising in the media,

team up

 with far-right street gangs to attack the ever-broadening revolt,

ban protests

 in city centres,

pass a law

 to make demonstrators pay for windows they did not break on the basis of some kind of assumed collective responsibility, place protesters under

house arrest

 as “terrorists”, constantly

lie

 about the size of the turn-outs,

manipulate

 social media algorithms so that people did not know about the demos and threaten to pull that communication plug

altogether

.


I should add that there is also the possibility that at least some of the protesters and looters were

agents provocateurs

In an article for

Le Monde diplomatique

La France insoumise

“Others suggested creating thousands of new places in prisons on the model of Nayib Bukele in El Salvador, of removing benefits from the trouble-makers’ families or of hardening the law against minors”.


Bréville notes that curfews were imposed in several cities, policed by drones and helicopters. “Gatherings are banned and in certain neighbourhoods it is even forbidden to walk around with a rucksack or hat”.


He adds that the French railways, SNCF, cancelled trains to prevent some people from attending demos and those arriving by road and rail were subject to police checks.


 “In Paris, the army was mobilised to supervise the demonstrators, along with the brigade of regional intervention, the RAID (

Recherche, assistance, intervention, dissuasion

) and the national gendarmerie’s intervention group (GIGN)”.


But in the face of all that, numbers on the protests across France did not drop away and the uprising is still going strong as I write!


All across Europe protests are

breaking out

Meanwhile, hitherto unthinkable restrictions are being placed on people’s international travel on the basis of them not being appreciated by the zio-imperialist mafia (ZIM).


Take, for example, the way that veteran anarchist and co-founder of Food not Bombs

Keith McHenry

author: Shannia Cabuello
title: Molbog community exposes agenda behind land-use projects
content:
They turned our ancestor’s burial sites into dumping grounds.

“They want to take everything so we insisted on coming here to express ourselves. We will embrace our land even if they harass us. We will not give it even if we get hurt.”

Molbog community member Anjilon Flores from Balabac Palawan stressed this point as Molbog indigenous peoples travelled to Metro Manila ahead of US President Donald Trump’s visit.

They aim to amplify their resistance against the Department of Environmental and Natural Resources’ Enhanced National Greening Program (E-NGP) and the Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement (EDCA).

Along with multi-sectoral groups and environmental advocates, they exposed the E-NGP and EDCA as tools of imperialist war and resource plunder, threatening the life, livelihood, culture, and ancestral lands of the Molbog people.

Long before Spanish colonial rule, the Molbog community have been the traditional stewards of Balabac island, depending on coconut farming, shifting cultivation, fishing, and harvesting seaweeds for livelihood.

“Palawan is a key biodiversity area and known to be the last ecological frontier of the Philippines,” Bianca Intia of Kalikasan Timog Katagalugan (TK) said at a press conference on October 26.

It shelters several endemic animal and plant species, including Philippine Mouse-deer which are exclusively found in Balabac and nearby islands.

Flores described their fields as prosperous with cassava, banana, corn, peanuts, and rice, making it their community’s main source of income for decades.

For them, lands are sacred that require ancestral permission before undertaking any activities like when entering the land, performing rituals, planting, harvesting, and cutting trees.

Born in Balabac, Flores cannot accept the prohibitions imposed by the E-NGP in using their resources. “They would restrict us from cutting trees which we use for firewood. This is also the livelihood for most of us. What will happen if they forbid us? Our livelihood will also be gone.”

Bangsa Molbog leader Emmanuel San Esteban lamented the encroachment of Balabac Air Base on their homes, sacred prayer grounds, and burial sites in Barangay Catagupan without any consultation with their tribal officials.

“They turned our ancestor’s burial sites into dumping grounds. The mountains where we do our rituals were flattened,” San Esteban said.

The local authorities said that the remains of their ancestors would be transferred to a different location. However, this is against the principles and culture of the Molbog tribe.

The indigenous residents dread the impact of both projects, as it begins to disrupt their peace, routines, and tradition.

They stressed that access to their land has been restricted, limiting the products they could gather from the forest.

According to DENR, the E-NGP was signed to rehabilitate the estimated 1.2 million hectares of the remaining unproductive, denuded, and degraded forestlands by 2022. It also aimed to maintain and protect existing forests.

This was already implemented by the DENR in several areas in Balabac where trees were planted in Barangay Catagupan, Agutayan, and Indalawan.

The communities worried about fines for damaging plants under E-NGP while clearing farmland. Cutting a tree must also be replaced with a hundred more trees and a Php 6,000 ($94) fine.

Kalikasan TK underscored that E-NGP did not aim to benefit communities but only to carbon offset the Ipilan Nickel Corporation’s deforestation and mining operations in Brooke’s Point, Palawan.

The Molbog people also expressed concerns that monocropping and fast-growing plant species under the E-NGP could affect forest biodiversity and native vegetation.

“The E-NGP is within our ancestral domain, for which we had applied for a Certificate on Ancestral Domain Title (CADT),” said San Esteban, questioning how the project progressed faster than their CADT application.

They first filed their CADT application in 2004 but the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples (NCIP) only certified the application in 2019. To expedite the process, the NCIP required them to pay at least Php 1.6 million ($25,092.33). Their CADT remains pending.

San Esteban said that Balabac Air Base in Barangay Catagupan also pushed through because of the NCIP’s manipulation of the Free, Prior, and Informed Consent (FPIC) process.

author: Kalundi Serumaga
title: The Rise and Fall of Uganda’s Human Rights “Revolution” (1986-2026)
content:
It would not surprise me to see the emergence of a woman-led, woman-centred, or women-only political party in Uganda over the next few years, if not before the next election.


It would surprise me even less if such a party were to then fizzle out, after a brief moment of intense popularity, during which time a whole lot of new neoliberal schemes would be sold to the population as “liberation”.


Neoliberalism is basically the stage of capitalism where it seeks to return completely to its founding work methods. New governments are installed and encouraged to sweep aside all public policy aimed at shielding the vulnerable from the worst effects of those methods, and to instead facilitate a more thorough exploitation of labour and natural resources. Everything becomes a commodity.


Such a political project would simply be a more concentrated distillation of the plastic human rights revolution Uganda has undergone between 1986 and today. Because the performance of a human rights gospel was the thing that enabled the then-incoming National Resistance Movement (NRM) regime to sell and endear itself to a significant section of the Ugandan public after it seized power in 1986.


It would also be an attempt by the elite leadership of the women’s movement to hang onto the place of security and advantage they acquired through their historical strategic alliance with the NRM after it took power.


The plastic revolution grew out of the centring of human rights violations in the years of the political campaigns against the Amin regime, and the truly horrific further such violations meted out on civilians by the second Obote regime during the 1981–1986 civil war. 


Such a focus on human rights violations suited the NRA/M well as it worked to divert political discourse away from the deeper and more critical questions of imperialist domination – and also infantilism politics – by centring on a very emotive issue.


Equally practically, the cohort of feminists did sterling service in helping the NRM regime consolidate itself between 1986 and 1996. Their “gains” were to have the career concerns of elite women hard-wired into national policy at the constitutional level.


It would be the last card played by the imperialists’ hand, and our arrival at the very heart of what has been the success in managing the social damage caused by the neoliberal economic project in Uganda: the Uganda women’s movement.


The revolution was plastic because it relied heavily on external funding; it absorbed external ideas quite uncritically; it was rooted in the understanding and aspirations of the Ugandan middle class; and it was self-contradictory in many aspects, the key contradiction being the idea that there would be prosperity under neoliberalism.


These realizations unfold from the recent drama in which elements of the security forces hunted down, abducted, and detained the celebrated veteran Ugandan feminist Miria Matembe.


This was no small matter. Matembe had been an activist since the days before the current government took power. She had been a parliamentarian for a long time and had even served as a minister in the government whose agents were now inconveniencing her.


Initially denied bail when she was finally brought before the courts, Matembe spent a night in remand prison before being released on bail the following day, leading to a spontaneous, energetic celebration by a gathering of Ugandan women activists singing their English-language “anthem”, while the main character in this drama walked triumphantly from court declaring, “Jesus is king.”


This journey to such a disparate mix of wrong destinations – from illegal detention to an unquestioning court, and thereafter to an eventual release attributed to the god well used by colonialism, all the while as the English-singing cohort of feminists misattribute the initial injustice to the oppression of women, despite there being many more male Ugandans still detained and disappeared – requires a map for sure.


Destination: opportunism


The immediate starting point was the government’s announcement of the intention to create a new law regulating the way in which funds from abroad could be received and spent. This was called the “Sovereignty Bill”. As the arguments behind it rested heavily on the ruling party’s now extremely threadbare “anti-imperialist” credentials, it was said to be about “preserving Uganda’s independence”. 


Uganda’s Non-Governmental Organizations that cluster …

author: James Crump
title: Spain Caps Rents and Protects Tenants After Four Million Join Protests
content:
Spain’s parliament has approved a package of reforms aimed at making housing more affordable, a day after four million took part in a

nationwide general strike

 over the country’s housing crisis.


The measures, proposed by prime minister Pedro Sánchez’s government, include extending eviction protections for vulnerable tenants and restricting speculative property purchases by preventing companies from buying homes for less than 70% of their assessed value.


Rent increases will also be capped at 2%, while those already above the government’s neighbourhood reference index will be frozen. A 10% tax on flats rented to tourists will also be introduced. 


The conservative Popular Party said it will repeal the reforms if it takes power in the 29 November elections, which were called by Sánchez after his government failed to pass similar housing measures.


“Yesterday, the right to housing won on the street and in workplaces, and I hope it will win again at the ballot box,” said interim housing minister Isabel Rodríguez after the vote on Thursday.


Spain has witnessed weeks of housing protests following the eviction and subsequent death of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal, who was forcibly removed from the flat she had lived in for 70 years in September after she couldn’t afford rent increases.


The country has a deficit of 750,000 homes, which is set to grow to over a million by 2028. The average rental price of a home, €1,176, is equivalent to 98.7% of the average young person’s monthly salary, according to the Youth Council of Spain.


“We won’t stop until we transform this country’s housing model from top to bottom,” said Alicia del Rio of the Madrid Tenants’ Union.


Trade unions reported 90% turnouts among dockworkers and carmakers for the 24-hour strike on Wednesday – Spain’s first general strike in 14 years –

with “total stoppages”

 at Volkswagen’s factory in Navarre and SEAT’s in Barcelona, organisers said.


Around 85% of meat industry workers, 82% of waste collection employees and 75% from the energy sector also took part. In healthcare and ⁠social services roughly 38% went on strike, while 35% of postal service workers also joined.

author: Unknown
title: İBB davasında 8 tahliyenin ardından Çelik'ten çağrı: 'Tutuksuz yargılama esas olmalı'
content:
Tutuklu Cumhurbaşkanı adayı ve İstanbul Büyükşehir Belediye Başkanı Ekrem İmamoğlu’nun da aralarında bulunduğu İBB davasında 8 kişinin tahliye edilmesinin ardından Yeni Parti İstanbul İl Başkanı Özgü, tutuksuz yargılamanın esas olması gerektiğini vurgulayarak açıklamalarda bulundu.

Tahliye edilen isimler arasında Ekrem İmamoğlu'nun avukatı Mehmet Pehlivan, Medya AŞ Genel Müdürü Fatoş Pınar Türker, Kültür AŞ Genel Müdür Yardımcısı Onur Aldı, Fatoş Ayık, Serhat Kapki, Ahmet Köksal, Volkan Ateş ve Murat Or bulunuyor.

Cezaevinde bulunan diğer tutuklu sanıkların da serbest bırakılmasını isteyen Çelik, duruma ilişkin "Bugün verilen tahliye kararı, iki yıla yakın süredir devam eden hukuksuzlukları ortadan kaldırmadı" şeklinde değerlendirmede bulundu.

Çelik, sosyal medya hesabından yaptığı açıklamada şu ifadeleri kullandı:

"Bugün İBB davasında tahliye olan 8 yol arkadaşımız için sevindik. Hepsine hoş geldin diyoruz. Ancak, tutuksuz yargılama esas olmalıyken, yol arkadaşlarımıza ağır tecrit koşullarında tutsaklık reva görüldü.

Bugün verilen tahliye kararı, iki yıla yakın süredir devam eden hukuksuzlukları ortadan kaldırmadığı gibi, ailelerinden, sevdiklerinden, çocuklarından haksız bir şekilde uzak bırakılan yol arkadaşlarımız halen zindanlarda.”

Cezaevinde haksız yere tutulan tüm isimler için de tutuksuz yargılama kararının bir an önce verilmesi gerektiğini söyleyen Çelik, “Halkımızın her gece evinde kurduğu vicdan mahkemelerinden tertemiz çıkan biziz… Fon vurguncuları ise halkımızın vicdanında çoktan mahkum oldu, mahkemelerin yargılamaya başlamasını bekliyor” dedi.

Çelik, “Biz bu ikili hukuk düzeniyle mutlaka hesaplaşacağız. Gün gelecek, adaletin terazisi gerçek suçlularla, masumları ayıracak. Gün gelecek, kısa çöp uzun çöpten hakkını alacak. Hak kazanacak, halkımız kazanacak, Türkiye kazanacak" ifadelerini kullandı.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Ming-Yeh T. Rawnsley
title: Making Hope Credible: Puma Shen and the Politics of Access in Taipei
content:
A HOME THAT can be renewed without repeated moves, a cultural allowance that continues into working adulthood, and an exercise service that comes to the neighbourhood: these are tangible reasons to pay attention to Puma Shen’s (沈伯洋) campaign for Taipei mayor. They also offer a way to test the comparison increasingly drawn between Shen and New York mayor Zohran Mamdani. Beyond the excitement surrounding an unexpected challenger, what would make the city more accessible to people with unequal resources?

Shen’s command of municipal policy has helped change how voters see him. Nathan Batto’s account dated September 28 describes how detailed answers helped him reach beyond his established image as a specialist in civil defence and Chinese information warfare. His appeal invites scrutiny of what that expertise could deliver for residents who find existing services difficult to use.

THE COMPARISON reportedly helped shape the contest itself. ETtoday’s Tao Ben-he (³³¥»©M) reported on October 29 that President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) drew inspiration from Mamdani’s unexpected rise when insisting on Shen’s nomination as the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) candidate. The reported connection poses a consequential question: if New York supplied inspiration for choosing a candidate, how much of Mamdani’s challenge to inequality has travelled with it?

Brian Hioe identified the distinction in New Bloom, also on October 29: Mamdani campaigned explicitly against socioeconomic inequality, while Shen has emphasised policy expertise and good governance. The proposals examined here suggest a distinctive contribution: reducing the practical burdens of using public provision. That could bring meaningful improvements, although its redistributive reach remains uneven, particularly where housing assistance depends on ownership.

Mamdani’s promises to freeze rents for rent-stabilised tenants, make buses free and provide universal childcare named household costs that government could reduce. His inaugural address on January 1 also connected childcare to taxing the wealthiest. Taipei need not reproduce those policies to learn from their political clarity: residents should understand whose circumstances will improve, who will contribute and what public authority will do.

Shen has offered a wide range of policy proposals. From that platform, I examine three areas—housing and urban renewal, cultural support for young adults, and neighbourhood exercise services for older residents—to assess how his proposals would change access to public resources. These examples reveal different relationships between administrative reform and inequality; they cannot establish the overall redistributive ambition of his platform.

HOUSING PROVIDES the hardest test. Taipei’s existing approach is not simply to leave residents to negotiate with developers. The city already promotes publicly led renewal and faster review through its urban renewal programmes. It also provides temporary accommodation and describes neighbourhood-based relocation as an objective, including arrangements involving social housing. Shen’s alternative must therefore demonstrate what it changes in practice.

His proposed circular urban renewal scheme (無限都更) changes the sequence of redevelopment. Willing owners would exchange existing property rights for a new home, or rights to use one, before their original site is rebuilt. The city would assemble an initial housing supply and manage the exchange; completed redevelopment would replenish resources for subsequent rounds. The objective is to avoid the familiar sequence of moving into temporary accommodation and moving again after reconstruction.

The scheme recognises disruption as a real cost, especially for older residents whose routines depend on nearby care and social relationships. It could make agreement easier without treating reluctant residents as obstacles. But Shen’s policy acknowledges limited initial supply. Its preference for nearby exchanges needs to be supported by identified sites and a realistic timetable.

Valuation is equally important. Shen’s scheme envisages settling differences between old and new property values, with loan assistance where needed. An older owner with little income may still struggle to bridge that difference. Independent valuations, accessible advice and safeguards against unaffordable debt would determine whether the exchange expands choice or mainly assists households already able to pay.

title: Συγκέντρωση ενάντια στο κλείσιμο του προγράμματος στέγασης «HELIOS JUNIOR», Πέμπτη 12/11, στις 18.00, στην πλατεία Βικτωρίας
content:
Κάλεσμα/Αφίσα από

Solidarity with Migrants:


Συγκέντρωση 12/11, 18:00, Πλατεία Βικτωρίας:


Ενάντια στο κλείσιμο του προγράμματος στέγασης «HELIOS JUNIOR»


Στις 9 Νοεμβρίου, το πρόγραμμα «HELIOS JUNIOR» τερματίστηκε επίσημα. Οι ένοικοι (περίπου 200 πρόσφυγες, ηλικίας 18-21 ετών) ενημερώθηκαν μόλις 5 ημέρες νωρίτερα ότι πρέπει να εγκαταλείψουν τα σπίτια τους, χωρίς να προβλέπεται κάποιο άλλο πρόγραμμα στέγασης. Επιπλέον, το Υπουργείο Μετανάστευσης δήλωσε ότι το κλείσιμο των δομών στέγασης αποτελεί πολιτική απόφαση, παρά το γεγονός ότι υπάρχουν διαθέσιμα κονδύλια από την ΕΕ. Μέχρι στιγμής, κανείς δεν έχει αποχωρήσει από το σπίτι του, ενώ οι άνθρωποι αυτοί αναζητούν εναλλακτικές λύσεις.


Την περασμένη εβδομάδα συναντηθήκαμε με αρκετούς από τους ενοίκους και αποφασίσαμε να καλέσουμε σε συγκέντρωση την Πέμπτη, στις 18:00, στην Πλατεία Βικτωρίας, για να αντιταχθούμε στο κλείσιμο του προγράμματος και να διεκδικήσουμε τη συνέχιση της παροχής στέγης για τους ασυνόδευτους νεαρούς πρόσφυγες στην Ελλάδα.


Η εκκένωση των κατοικιών με τόσο σύντομη προειδοποίηση είναι απαράδεκτη. Είναι ανεπίτρεπτο η κυβέρνηση να πετάει ανθρώπους στον δρόμο, χωρίς να προσφέρει καμία εναλλακτική λύση. Οι γειτονιές μας γίνονται όλο και περισσότερο στόχος θεσμικού ρατσισμού, ”εξευγενισμού” (gentrification) και της κρατικής βούλησης να αποκλειστούν οι μετανάστες από το κέντρο των πόλεών μας. Το κλείσιμο του HELIOS JUNIOR αποτελεί πολιτική επιλογή και απαιτεί συλλογική απάντηση.


Γι’ αυτό καλούμε σε συγκέντρωση την Πέμπτη, στις 18:00, στην Πλατεία Βικτωρίας, ως μια πρώτη δημόσια δράση.


Ενάντια στο κλείσιμο του προγράμματος στέγασης «HELIOS JUNIOR»


Στέγη για όλους – ντόπιους και μετανάστες μαζί.


Solidarity with Migrants


Gathering 12.11, 18:00 Plateia Victoria:


Against the closing of the HELIOS JUNIOR HOUSING Program


On November the 9th the HELIOS JUNIOR PROGRAMM officially closed. The residents (around 200 refugees in the age 18-21) were informed 5 days before, that they need to leave their houses and no further housing program is planned. Furthermore, the ministry of migration stated that it is a political decision that the housing structures are closing and that the money would be available from the EU. So far no one left their house and the people are trying to find other solutions


In the last week we met with several residents and decided to call together for a gathering on Thursday at 18:00 in Plateia Victoria against the closing of the program and to demand a continuation of a housing program for unaccompanied young refugees in Greece. The closure of the houses with such a short notice is not acceptable. It is not acceptable that the government throws people on the streets, without providing any alternative.


Our Neighborhoods are further and further targeted by institutionalized racism, Gentrification and the will of the state to exclude migrants from the center of our cities. The closing of HELIOS JUNIOR is a political choice and needs a collective answer.


Therefore we are calling for a gathering, Thursday 18:00 in Plateia Victoria as a first public action.


Against the closing of the Helios Junior Housing Program!


Housing for everyone, locals and migrants together.


Solidarity with Migrants

title: Incekara: Determination of young people proves that resistance is possible
content:
Protests launched by high school students in Paris against poor educational conditions have had a domino effect, spreading across France and to other countries. What began as a protest over education has developed into broader opposition to the system, encompassing the rising cost of living, declining wages and the housing crisis. These developments have also drawn attention to Turkey, where exploitation and inequality are even more deeply entrenched. University students took to the streets in Istanbul on the anniversary of the establishment of the Council of Higher Education (YÖK), an institution created in the aftermath of the fascist military coup of September 12, 1980. Students protested against the government's increasingly repressive measures. Demonstrations in Beyazıt Square and Beşiktaş were particularly marked by anger over a directive issued by the Ministry of Interior concerning universities in September. Istanbul University student Yasin Incekara spoke to ANF and said, "The determination shown by young people during the March 19 protests demonstrated that it is possible to resist the repressive regime being established in Turkey and showed how these blockades can be broken."


'Young people face similar forms of repression worldwide'


Yasin Incekara, a second-year sociology student at Istanbul University, said that young people taking to the streets across Europe and other parts of the world reflected the problems they share. Incekara emphasized that although Europe is often portrayed as a prosperous society, young people there also struggle with poverty and the problems created by the capitalist system. He said, "Over the past few months, we have seen young people taking to the streets against poverty, the lack of a future and repressive policies, not only in the Middle East but also in Europe, which is presented as prosperous. The youth uprising that has emerged particularly in France shows that young people face similar forms of repression not only in Turkey but in many parts of the world."


'March 19 showed young people's determination to seek freedom'


Incekara said that although resistance in Turkey has been weaker than in other countries, the March 19 protests demonstrated how young people could break through the restrictions being imposed on them. He described the March 19 protests and subsequent developments as evidence of young people's determination to pursue freedom in the face of oppression. Incekara said, "Through their determination to demand freedom against oppression, young people demonstrated during the March 19 protests that it is possible to resist the repressive regime being established in Turkey and showed how these blockades can be broken."


'Repressive directives seek to label revolutionary students as terrorists'


Incekara said that the authorities had intensified repression through various mechanisms in response to the determination shown by young people in their struggle. He pointed to the 17-article directive sent to universities by the Ministry of Interior in September, which he described as fascist, as the latest example. He argued that the directive sought to label students involved in progressive and revolutionary activities at universities as "terrorists." Incekara said: "The directive explicitly refers to providing private security personnel at universities with training similar to that given to police officers, as well as intensifying efforts to recruit informants and pressure students into becoming collaborators. It also opens the way for officers from the Anti-Terrorism Branch to set up information stands at universities under the pretext of awareness-raising and preventive activities, allowing them to conduct intelligence operations. Through these stands, the police aim to criminalize students involved in political struggle in the eyes of newly enrolled students, portraying them as marginal groups associated with terrorism and manipulating newcomers with warnings to 'stay away from them.' Of course, this does not reflect reality. If there is any group seeking to spread terror today, it is the capitalist state and the police themselves."


'Families are also pressured to inform on their children'

author: Rachel Evans
title: Anti-racists counter protest far-right ‘Australia Marches’ rally
content:
About 300 people joined the “No to Racism: Migrants and Refugees Are Welcome” rally at Sydney Town Hall on November 8. It was organised by the Refugee Action Collective Sydney (RAC) to counter the far-right Australian Marches rally against migration.

The far-right rally, which featured speakers from One Nation, Libertarian MP John Ruddick and other right-wing influencers, rallied at the Royal Botanic Garden and drew about 500 people.

Speakers at the counter-protest included Lynda-June Coe, Wiradjuri and Badu Island woman and NSW Greens upper house candidate; Nour Salman from Australia Palestine Advocacy Network; Ishita Chakrabarty from Hindus for Human Rights; Bidjigal/Gweagal activist Jordan Ryan-Hennessy; Ann El Khoury, from University of Sydney Staff for Palestine; Beau Lyon from Action for Public Housing’ and Anisa, a Somali refugee who was held in the Naoero detention centre.

Chakrabarty spoke about the racism faced by Indian migrants and linked One Nation and the Australia Marches rally to the far-right Narendra Modi government in India.

Ian Rintoul from RAC, who chaired the rally, said the United States midterm elections were a huge blow to the racist politics of US President Donald Trump, but said anti-racist campaigners still need to get organised.

“The tragedy is that the racist policies of Australia Marches and One Nation are being fueled by anti-migration and anti-refugee policies of the Labor government,” Rintoul said.

“Labor is linking migration with the housing crisis; cutting the numbers of international students; has introduced fees that will make it harder for refugees to seek asylum in Australia and is implementing an ICE-like compliance force to round up people on temporary visas.”

Lyon said those in power are pushing racism to distract from the real cause of the housing crisis, the for-profit housing system.

“Migrants are not responsible for the housing or cost of living crisis,” Rintoul said.

author: anred
title: ¿Qué pasó en Guernica?, el gobierno de Alberto y la represión a la última ola de tomas de tierras
content:
Sergio Berni, entonces ministro de Seguridad bonaerense, se jactaba de desalojar cinco tomas de tierra por semana. Era plena pandemia, cientos de miles de familias que no podían pagar alquileres o vivían hacinadas buscaron una salida en la ocupación de terrenos. Ocurría la última gran ola de “tomas de tierras” durante el gobierno de Alberto Fernández que terminó marcada por la represión, las promesas incumplidas y el abandono. Guernica se convirtió en el caso visible y emblemático de aquella crisis: la organización de más de 2 mil familias en tierras “compradas” en dictadura destinadas a un country, la resistencia al desalojo y la exposición mediática obligaron al gobierno provincial a abrir una negociación que estuvo atravesada por titubeos, dilaciones y propuestas que no resolvían el problema habitacional. Por ANRed | Imagen: German Romeo Pena


Primero es necesario contar que la “ocupación de tierras “ tras la dictadura fue una modalidad habitual de las clases trabajadoras más empobrecidas para adquirir sus viviendas ante la sucesiva falta de respuesta habitacional que dieron las democracias posteriores, es decir ni el Estado y menos el mercado resolvieron la crisis habitacional. Para aquel entonces los últimos datos eran delCenso Nacional de 2010, el déficit habitacional alcanzaba 3,5 millones de vivienda entre ellas 1,3 millones de viviendas faltantes y 2,2 millones de viviendas que no proveían  las condiciones mínimas para mantener un nivel de vida digno. 9 millones de personas que eran inquilinos, cifras que actualmente se han agravado en el último censo del 2022.


Luego el desenlace del conflicto en Guernica, disputa que estuvo atravesado por la crisis política y económica que sacudía al gobierno de Alberto Fernández. En septiembre de 2020, la disparada de los dólares paralelos, la presión empresaria y la preocupación oficial por la inestabilidad económica habilitaron una ofensiva política contra las tomas de tierras. Sergio Massa, junto con la intendenta de Presidente Perón, Blanca Cantero, impulsaron una posición de endurecimiento frente a las ocupaciones. Cantero convocó a intendentes del conurbano que reclamaban una respuesta judicial y policial, mientras se consolidaba un bloque político que exigía terminar con la toma y enviar una señal contra nuevas recuperaciones. Guernica comenzaba a ser presentada como un antecedente peligroso que debía clausurarse para evitar que se multiplicara.


14 intendentes piden desalojar tomas de tierras y Berni se publicita defendiendo la «propiedad privada»


La tensión se agravó en octubre con la ocupación de la estancia Casa Nueva, perteneciente a la familia Etchevehere, en Entre Ríos. La iniciativa fue impulsada por Dolores Etchevehere junto al Proyecto Artigas, con el acompañamiento de Juan Grabois y militantes vinculados del Movimiento de Trabajadores Excluidos (MTE), que proponía desarrollar un proyecto agroecológico en esas tierras. La reacción de empresarios y la derecha política que venía presionando por desalojar Guernica reaccionó de inmediato: el conflicto se convirtió en una bandera contra las recuperaciones de tierras y en una supuesta amenaza generalizada a la propiedad privada. La disputa con los Etchevehere intensificó la presión política y mediática sobre el gobierno nacional. Dentro del Frente de Todos también se profundizaron las diferencias: mientras un sector intentaba sostener la negociación y encontrar una salida habitacional, Massa, Berni y los intendentes reclamaban hacer cumplir la orden judicial. Las negociaciones impulsadas inicialmente desde Nación, con participación de funcionarios vinculados al Movimiento Evita, contemplaron una posible relocalización colectiva, pero naufragaron en medio de las disputas internas entre el Movimiento Evita y La Cámpora. Desde septiembre, Andrés Larroque quedó al frente de las conversaciones provinciales, cada vez más condicionadas por la presión judicial y política.


Finalmente, el 28 de octubre, cuando todavía se discutía una última prórroga y existían conversaciones para evitar una intervención violenta, la Justicia rechazó el pedido de postergación y la gobernación cancelo las negociaciones inventando justificaciones. En la madrugada del 29, unos 4.000 efectivos de la Policía Bonaerense.. La decisión terminó imponiendo la línea de Berni y de los intendentes: el desalojo como respuesta disciplinadora frente a las recuperaciones de tierras, antes que una solución de fondo a la emergencia habitacional. title: Women in Arzoxlî protest against delivery of solar panels
content:
The dispute over the construction of two solar power plants is escalating in the village of Arzoxlî (Turkish: Kervanpınar), in the Sur district of Amed (Diyarbakır). Although an administrative court has temporarily suspended the implementation of the Zenkar-2 project, preparations for the neighboring Zenkar-1 project are continuing. On the 23rd day of a protest vigil against the construction work, trucks delivered solar panels intended for the project to the site.


In response to the delivery, women from Arzoxlî gathered in the village square and marched together toward the construction site. Chanting slogans such as “Excavator operators, get off our grazing land,” “Axa me ava me hebûna me ye” (Our land and water are our existence), “Resistance leads to victory” and “No to companies in Arzoxlî,” they protested against the continuation of the project.


Soldiers block access to construction site


On their way to the project site, the villagers were stopped by Turkish gendarmerie. The soldiers blocked their access and prevented them from proceeding any further. The protesters expressed their anger at the soldiers’ actions.


Residents of Arzoxlî are demanding that construction work on the Zenkar-1 solar power plant also be halted. While a court order has already suspended construction of Zenkar-2, the villagers continue their resistance against the second project through a permanent protest camp.

title: Thousands of youth walk out against Pax Silica, Trump PH visit
content:
University of the Philippines Diliman (UPD) joined by an Ayta community and Kabataan partylist representative Renee Co during their walk-out and local protest action on November 13, 2026. Photo by Elisha Beatrice Umali/Bulatlat

By Elisha Beatrice Umali Bulatlat.com

MANILA – Thousands of students around the country joined the National Youth Day of Action against Pax Silica on November 13, denouncing the U.S. President Donald Trump’s upcoming visit to the Philippines and the U.S.-led Pax Silica initiative.

The National Union of Students of the Philippines (NUSP) stated in a Facebook post that thousands of students and youth groups nationwide walked out in opposition to the Pax Silica initiative. “The youth have united in defending our national sovereignty, natural resources, ancestral lands, livelihood, and human rights,” stated NUSP.

Youth Against Pax Silica, a nationwide network of individuals and student-led organizations, earlier announced 42 universities across nine regions to participate in the mobilizations.

Several state-wide university systems, including the University of the Philippines (UP), Polytechnic University of the Philippines, and Mindanao State University took part in the mass protests.

Kabataan Partylist Rep. Renee Co condemned the Philippines’ involvement in the war efforts of the USA during the local mobilization at UP Diliman.

“We will not allow our workers, farmers, and indigenous peoples to be used only for the gain of a few. The youth and Gen Z’s calls are to fight for our future, to reject Pax Silica, [and] Trump out now,” said Co in Filipino.

Prominent private universities such as the Ateneo de Manila University, its regional campuses, and the tertiary institutions along Manila’s university belt also staged protest actions in their respective universities.

While protesting in Taguig City, three students from the University of Makati (UMak) were arrested by police personnel over alleged unauthorized assembly. There were also instances of policemen punching and headlocking UMak students.

Read: Cops arrest 3 University of Makati students after anti-Pax Silica protest

Youth Against Pax Silica is expected to launch a series of mass actions during the Philippines-hosted ASEAN Summit, to be attended by Trump and other international state leaders, from November 16 to November 18. (AMU, RVO)

author: Jian Sanz
title: Cops arrest 3 University of Makati students after anti-Pax Silica protest
content:
Police headlocking a UMak studen. (Photo from Anakbayan-UMaK)

Three students of the University of Makati (UMak) who participated in a protest against Pax Silica were arrested earlier today, November 13, in Bonifacio Global City, Taguig City.

According to Panday Sining UMak, uniformed police officers and intelligence personnel in plainclothes surrounded the demonstrators, confronting them over an alleged unauthorized assembly and confiscating their placards.

In a statement, Anakbayan UMak condemned the violent, arbitrary arrest. “This is how the rotten government of Marcos Jr. treats students who are peacefully expressing their sentiments,” the group said.

During the dispersal, police officers blocked the students from both sides and forcibly apprehended one participant. Video footage from Karapatan National Capital Region showed that a police officer punched a female student who attempted to free another arrested student. A police officer was captured headlocking one of the arrested students. who can be seen to be put in a headlock by a police officer in another video report.

Karapatan NCR also reported that a paralegal who responded to the forceful arrest was threatened with charges by police officers.

The three students are currently detained at BGC Police Station 1 and face initial charges of alarms and scandal. The arrests unfolded amid youth-led protests across the country, as students rallied against the expected arrival of U.S. President Donald Trump, the chief architect behind the widely opposed Pax Silica initiative, for the ASEAN Summit. (RVO)

title: Kundgebung für Maja & Zaid
content:
+++Kundgebung vor dem Bundesjustizministerium am 13.11. um 13:00 Uhr in der Anton-Wilhelm-Amo-Str. 37.+++


Am 25.11. soll das Gericht in Paris über Zaids Auslieferung nach Ungarn entscheiden.


Trotz des Machtwechsels in Ungarn können wir aus Majas, Tobis und Ilarias Erfahrungen erahnen, was ihn dort erwartet: Isolation, Gewalt und Willkür, sowie ein politisches Verfahren.


Zudem sind die ungarischen Behörden und das Knastsystem für ihren gewaltvollen Rassismus bekannt.


Wir gehen zusätzlich davon aus, dass Zaid eine Abschiebung von Ungarn nach Syrien drohen würde.


Währenddessen sitzt Maja seit über 2 Jahren in Ungarn im Knast. Zuletzt wurde Majas Urteil zu 7 Jahren Haft unter strengsten Bedingungen rechtskräftig.


Maja wurde eine Rücküberstellung nach Deutschland zugesichert.


Während eine rechtswidrige Auslieferung nur wenige Stunden dauert, schieben sich die deutschen Behörden die Zuständigkeit für die Rücküberstellung hin und her. Es kann sein, dass Maja noch ein weiteres Jahr in ungarischer Haft überstehen muss – und das, obwohl sich Majas Haftbedingungen in der Strafhaft weiter verschlechtert haben!


Wir werden weder das noch eine weitere Auslieferung nach Ungarn hinnehmen!


Deshalb rufen wir für den 13. und 14. November dazu auf, den Druck auf alle verantwortlichen Behörden zu erhöhen!


Besonders wichtig aus deutscher Sicht sind dabei französische Konsulate, das Justizministerium und das Auswärtige Amt.


Gemeinsam wollen wir am Freitag, dem 13.11. möglichst vielen französischen Konsulaten in Deutschland einen offenen Brief übergeben, in dem unsere Forderung klar werden: keine Auslieferung von Zaid nach Ungarn!


Dafür brauchen wir Euch! Organisiert eigene Briefübergaben in Euren Städten!


Am Ende des Aufrufs findet ihr den Brief als Druckvorlage und eine Liste der Konsulate.


Noch ein kleiner Hinweis: Wenn ihr zu den Botschaften geht, kündigt die Übergabe am besten vorher per Mail bei den Konsulaten an!


Am selben Tag wird es auch eine Kundgebung vor dem Justizministerium in Berlin geben, um deutlich zu machen, dass Maja jetzt nach Deutschland rücküberstellt werden muss! Kommt und supportet am 13.11. um 13:00 Uhr in der Anton-Wilhelm-Amo-Str. 37.

author: Keelan Jacobs
title: Indigenous youth, Elders join national protests against Bill C-39 at Prime Minister’s Office
content:
Indigenous youth, Elders, environmental organizations and labour leaders rallied outside the Prime Minister’s Office Thursday as part of a national day of action against Bill C-39, the Building Canada Strong Act.


Opponents say the legislation would override Treaty rights, weaken environmental laws and expand Cabinet power to fast-track major projects.


Hand-drummers from the Ottawa River Singers opened the demonstration. 


Speakers warned the omnibus bill would give the government broad new authority to designate “regions of national interest,” suspend or amend key environmental protections, and override the inherent, Treaty and constitutionally protected rights of First Nations.


Dara Wawatie-Chabot, an Indigenous youth speaker, told the crowd the legislation threatens protections across the board.


Dara Wawatie-Chabot at a rally outside the Prime Minister’s Office on a day of action against Bill C-39 on Nov. 12, 2026. Photo: Mark Blackburn/APTN.


“Bill C-39 would go right through any type of protections, whether it is environmental protections, labour protections or Indigenous rights,” she said. “They are just going to be completely bypassing all of that in order to get access to resources that are going to just make things worse for everybody on this planet.”


Introduced in September, Bill C-39 expands powers created under last year’s Building Canada Act. It would allow Cabinet to designate “regions of national interest” where certain projects — including pipelines, energy infrastructure, telecommunications networks and industrial developments — could be pre-approved or accelerated under a one-year decision timeline.


It’s really not shocking,” she said. “What Mark Carney represents is this legacy of Canadian settler violence and resource extraction, to be honest.”


Prime Mark Carney in effigy huggling a gas container at a rally held outside the Prime Minister’s Office on a national day of action against Bill C-39. Photo: Mark Blackburn/APTN.


Approximately 100 protesters attended the protest carrying signs that read “seniors for climate action now” and “open up your hearts and listen to the people.” Eventually, a teenager came out imitating Prime Minister Mark Carney. The character had many different props that he pulled out from a box titled “Liberal Priorities.” 


The Carney character eventually pulled out and hugged a red gas container while simultaneously stomping on a stuffed fox and orca. 

The Carney character, who used a paper mache mask, was “dragged over to the Senate” to continue the demonstration. 


Elder Naanii Rose Lockyer delivered a direct message to the government.


“Stop the destruction. We’re at a point in time where if we keep on going in the direction we’re going, we can’t turn back,” she said. “They cannot predict what’s coming. And their fear-based response is to amp up surveillance and control of the masses. They’re pushing people over the edge. You have to look at the poverty crisis, the hunger crisis that all people are facing now. It’s not just First Peoples that are being offered up. The poor are on the chopping block as well. We have how many homeless people? It’s crazy.”


“They’ve tried assimilation, that didn’t work. They’ve tried colonization that was moderately successful. He [Carney] basically declared war on all of us, not first peoples but all people. This Mother Earth supports us all, and that’s what people are trying to protect today.”


Naanii Rose Lockyer outside the Prime Minister’s Office on a day of action against Bill C-39 on (Nov. 12, 2026). Photo: Mark Blackburn/APTN.


Her message to the Carney government on Bill C-39 was concise: “Hear the people. Lead with your heart, not your wallet.”


What the bill would do


Critics say C-39 would enable ministers to set aside or amend conditions under the Species at Risk Act, the Fisheries Act and other environmental laws if they are judged too financially or practically challenging. It also strengthens the federal government’s ability to end legal strikes.


The Assembly of First Nations, the Chiefs of Ontario, the British Columbia Assembly of First Nations, the Assembly of First Nations Quebec-Labrador and Nishnawbe Aski Nation have all rejected the bill, arguing it subordinates the honour of the Crown and free, prior and informed consent to commercial timelines.

author: Unknown
title: We Started the School Year with a March on the Principal
content:
At Ferndale High School, nestled in a Detroit suburb, one of our most pressing problems is the dilapidated building, built in the 1950s.


The outdated heating and cooling systems are prone to classroom floods—in the last nine months I've experienced three. Once boiling hot water sprayed out of the HVAC unit during class, nearly injuring a student.


It was late August—our last Sunday night of freedom before our teacher professional development week—when six of my co-workers and I received an email from our principal. She said that a few classrooms had flooded again the previous week, but the damage was limited and our classrooms were “ready for our return.”


“Tomorrow is still the beginning of a fresh school year,” she wrote, “and I’m looking forward to welcoming everyone back and starting the year together on a positive note.”


She made the mistake of including all affected teachers as recipients, instead of blind copying us, so I knew exactly who to reach out to.


That evening I spent lots of time on the phone with my co-workers and my fellow union building representatives. We all had experienced previous flooding, so we were skeptical that our classrooms would

actually

 be ready for our return the following morning.


Ever since I began working at this school in 2024, my mission has been to convince my co-workers we should be compensated in some way when our school administrators fail us. Whenever we’ve asked administrators to address issues like poor attendance or facilities problems, we’ve gotten responses like “That is not my fault” or “I do not have the power to fix that.” This energy has been so demoralizing for our teaching staff, and it seemed to me that my co-workers had gotten used to just accepting the b.s.


But having cut my teeth as a political organizer on my college campus and read

Secrets of a Successful Organizer

, I could tell that

this issue had the juice we needed to lead a workplace action

—everyone cared enough to do something about it. By Monday morning I had

devised a plan

 with the support of my fellow building reps.


INDUSTRIAL FANS


Our suspicions were correct; words can hardly describe the scene we walked into. Each of the seven flooded classrooms had eight to 15 industrial fans blowing on the floor, dehumidifying machines siphoning water out of the classroom windows, and no functioning air conditioning.


Teachers were supposed to spend this day organizing and preparing our classrooms. Most of us spend hundreds of dollars of our own money to purchase supplies, decor, soft lighting, and small comforting touches to make our classrooms the warm, safe environments we know students need. It takes a fair amount of time to unpack those things from the summer months and get the space ready for the school year.


When I saw the state of my classroom, I knew it was going to be impossible to get any sort of work done in that environment. My next step was to walk door to door and check in on my six co-workers who had been looped in on that email. No classroom was even close to being a functional workspace.


I could feel the swelling anger, and knew the moment was ripe to make an ask. “We do not deserve this,” I told my co-workers. “What if we all went to the principal and asked for something in return?”


I told them about the plan the other building reps and I had come up with: The affected teachers could march together to the principal’s office and ask that either we receive pay for the additional hours it takes us to set up our classrooms outside of contract time, or we be excused from a professional development session during the week to set up our classrooms during work hours.


Everyone was too angry to be afraid. All but one agreed to join our march on the boss.


The six of us found our principal in a teacher’s classroom. She stepped into the hall to see us standing there shoulder to shoulder, looking upset. None of us will ever forget her response: She took out her phone, started filming us, and said, “Oh I am going to put this on TikTok, it’s the first day of school and the teachers already want something from me.”


When she saw how deeply stunned we were, she put her phone back in her pocket and asked what was wrong. I reminded her of her email, and informed her that our classrooms were in fact not “ready for our return.”


I told her this wasn’t fair to us, and explained how we felt it could be rectified. She said she understood our frustration and would “look into” …

title: Women demonstrate in Istanbul for the release of sick and elderly female prisoners
content:
Outside the Çağlayan Palace of Justice in Istanbul, MATUHAYDER (Association for Solidarity and Cooperation with Families of Prisoners and Convicts in the Marmara Region) called for the release of sick and elderly women prisoners. The demonstration, held under the slogan “Freedom for Women Prisoners,” was part of activities marking November 25, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women. The protest focused on inadequate medical care in Turkish prisons and the repeated denial of release to prisoners who have completed their sentences.


Sultan Bozkurt, a relative of a political prisoner and a member of the Kurdish Peace Mothers Council in Istanbul, criticized the continued imprisonment of political prisoners despite the ongoing Peace and Democratic Society Process. She stressed that seriously ill prisoners, in particular, must be released immediately.

Life-threatening illnesses under prison conditions


MATUHAYDER board member Elif Taşdöğen drew attention to the situation in the women’s prisons in Sincan, Gebze, Kayseri-Bünyan and Bakırköy: “Many imprisoned women require increased medical care due to their age or serious illnesses but do not receive adequate treatment. Others remain in prison even after completing their sentences because their release is repeatedly postponed.” Taşdöğen described it as unacceptable to continue holding women with life-threatening illnesses in prison conditions that fail to ensure proper medical care.


Women must be able to shape peace


Referring to the ongoing peace process, Taşdöğen emphasized that women must not be regarded merely as those affected by political decisions but must actively participate in shaping a peaceful society. “Women must build peace not behind prison walls, but at the heart of society and in every sphere of life, through their own strength and free will,” she said.


Taşdöğen called for the release of Evin Zapsu, Pınar Tikit, Havva Ak, Hatice Yıldız, Fatma Tokmak and Çiğdem Özlü, along with all other sick women prisoners. “Where women are not free, peace remains incomplete. We insist on women’s freedom, peace and the collective building of a democratic society,” she stated.


The demonstration concluded with applause and slogans.
