author: Shireen Akram-Boshar
title: Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide Calls on ICC to Arrest Trump, Rubio Over Gaza
content:
The alliance accused Trump and Rubio of aiding and abetting “genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity in Gaza.”

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

A delegation of U.S. taxpayers and human rights attorneys has called on the International Criminal Court (ICC) to issue arrest warrants for President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio for their role in the genocide in Gaza.

On Wednesday, the Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide (TAAG) delivered evidence against Trump and Rubio at the Hague, the headquarters of the ICC in the Netherlands, calling for their arrests for “aiding and abetting Israel in the commission of genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity in Gaza.”

The organization announced its submission to the ICC at a press conference at the Hague on Wednesday.

Individuals and organizations working with the Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide collected evidence for nearly a year, including sworn affidavits from doctors who worked in Gaza, firsthand eyewitness testimonies, and whistleblower accounts related to U.S. military, financial, and diplomatic support for Israel throughout the course of the three-year genocide in Gaza.

The submission to the Office of the Prosecutor includes testimony of medical professionals who treated victims of 2,000-pound bombs and victims of shootings at distribution sites of the U.S. and Israel-backed Gaza Humanitarian Foundation — and notes that the Trump administration lifted a hold on 2,000-pound bombs, with Trump personally confirming the release of these bombs in early 2025. Rubio, the document states, also “approved or facilitated major arms transfers” including “large quantities of 2,000-pound bomb bodies or penetrator warheads,” while “waiving or compressing congressional review.” In addition, Rubio “participated in, funded, or defended” activities of the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation, even after Médecins Sans Frontières, the UN, USAID, and other organizations warned that the foundation was involved in “mass casualties, hunger, and aid-site danger.”

Seth Donnelly, co-founder of TAAG, introduced Wednesday’s press conference, explaining that the organization had attempted to utilize the U.S. court system to stop the government’s participation in the genocide — but that the U.S. court system “has proven incapable again, and again, and again, from addressing this crime,” forcing them to turn to the ICC.

“It is not enough to wait for elections, or to vote them out,” Donnelly said, of U.S. government officials including Trump and Rubio. “Those responsible for grave crimes against humanity, including genocide, must be prosecuted — even if they are the most powerful officials in the world.”

Lawyers working with TAAG spoke at the press conference, explaining that the evidence submitted demonstrates that Trump and Rubio “knowingly supplied, released, expedited, and protected the transfer of weapons to Israel after repeated warnings that those weapons were being used to cause mass civilian deaths, destruction, starvation, displacement, and to create conditions that made life virtually impossible in Gaza.”

Trump and Rubio’s attempts to dismantle the ICC were also addressed at the press conference. The Trump administration has “withdrawn from international human rights mechanisms and sought to undermine institutions” that aim to hold the powerful to account, argued Palestinian American human rights lawyer and TAAG member Huwaida Arraf.

Francesca Albanese, human rights expert and UN special rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territories, also spoke at the press conference, saying, “This administration’s attack on the ICC, on UNRWA, and the United Nations as a whole reveal an ambition to entrench global hegemony and extinguish the possibility of justice, not just in Palestine — everywhere.”

Albanese decried Trump’s celebration of the so-called ceasefire, during which the Israeli military has killed more than a thousand Palestinians in Gaza, and his creation of the “Board of Peace,” which, she says, “revives imperial ambitions and colonial tones while securing conditions for Palestine’s continued erasure and Israel’s impunity.”

“Let us be clear: the genocide of the Palestinian people would not have been possible without the unwavering support of the United States,” Albanese said.

author: Kodao Productions
title: Protesters taste early police brutality as ASEAN summit draws near
content:
Three University of Makati (UMak) student leaders were arrested by Taguig City police on Friday during a rally against Pax Silica in a preview of government’s response to protests as the Philippines is set to host the 49

th

 ASEAN Summit.


The UMak chapter of the group Panday Sining said police personnel and intelligence agents surrounded the protesters and violently apprehended one of the students in Bonifacio Global City.


The group added another student was head-locked and was nearly choked. A video circulating online also showed a police officer repeatedly hitting others trying to rescue their distressed fellow student.


Panday Sining added the police confronted them for holding the activity without a permit and seized their placards despite attempts to negotiate.


The three students are currently detained at BGC Police Station 1 and may face alarm and scandal charges, Panday Sining said.


Harassments in Southern Tagalog


In Biñan, Laguna, police and Land Transportation Office personnel blocked a protesters’ caravan from proceeding to Metro Manila and joining the massive protests in the next days.


The caravan earlier complained of punctured tires and cut brake lines it said were likely committed by government saboteurs.


Thousands of students from various universities in Metro Manila and Southern Tagalog have also conducted mass walkouts demanding the rejection of the US-led Pax Silica initiative.


‘P22 billion hypocrisy’


Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (Bayan), meanwhile, condemned Ferdinand Marcos Jr. government’s “overkill security preparations and Imeldific measure” in hosting the regional summit.


Bayan said Marcos hypocritically hides rampant poverty in the country’s capital region while


justifying the eviction of vendors in Pasay and Paranaque by saying the summit would eventually provide livelihood and job opportunities for Filipinos.


“This is insulting to those who make an honest living yet they have been swept aside as eyesores that need to be hidden from visiting foreign dignitaries. If the summit will showcase our local culture, why is the government discriminating against vendors and informal workers?” Bayan secretary general Raymond Palatino asked. #

(Raymund B. Villanueva)

author: Michael Csaszkóczy (konkret 7/26)
title: Ein unpolitischer Prozess? In einem – wie das Gericht betonte – völlig unpolitischen Prozess ist Daniela Klette zu 13 Jahren Haft verurteilt worden.
content:
»Was ist ein Dietrich gegen eine Aktie? Was ist ein Einbruch in eine Bank gegen die Gründung einer Bank?«


Mackie Messer in der »Dreigroschenoper«


In der Berichterstattung über das Urteil gegen Daniela Klette kommt kaum eine Meldung ohne die Bemerkung aus, wer ihr Auftreten sehe, könne fast den Schilderungen der Nachbarn glauben, die sie als freundliche und nette ältere Frau beschrieben. Das müsse allerdings offensichtlich Verstellung sein: »Reue sieht anders aus«, tadelt die »Bildzeitung«, und die »Taz« bemängelt Klettes »schier unerträgliche Hybris«.


Denn anscheinend ist die 67jährige auch heute noch nicht bereit, sich pauschal von der RAF zu distanzieren. Ob Klette Mitglied der RAF war, ist – anders als es die Berichterstattung nahelegt – eigentlich überhaupt nicht Gegenstand des Verfahrens, in dem es ursprünglich um 13 teils versuchte, teils durchgeführte Raubüberfälle geht, die die Angeklagte gemeinsam mit ihren Genossen Burkhard Garweg und Ernst-Volker Staub begangen haben soll, um ihr Leben in der Illegalität zu finanzieren (Staatsanwalt und Gericht nennen das Habgier). Während des Prozesses wurde entschieden, dass fünf Taten nicht weiter verfolgt werden. Damit ging es vor Gericht nur noch um acht Überfälle. Erst in einem späteren Verfahren soll die mögliche Beteiligung an drei Anschlägen in den Jahren 1990 bis 1993 geklärt werden. Der Tatbestand der Mitgliedschaft in einer terroristischen Vereinigung selbst ist ohnehin seit geraumer Zeit verjährt.


»Wir führen hier kein Staatsschutz-, kein Terrorismusverfahren, auch wenn wir im Staatsschutzsaal verhandeln«, hatte der Vorsitzende Richter Lars Engelke gleich zu Beginn der Verhandlung betont und anlässlich der Urteilsverkündung sprang die »Taz« ihm noch einmal bei: Für eine politische Motivation des Verfahrens »spricht wenig. Auch andere wurden wegen ähnlicher Überfälle auf Geldtransporter zu vergleichbar langen Haftstrafen verurteilt.« Das ist insofern nicht völlig falsch, dass es bei erheblich vorbestraften Tätern für Raubüberfallserien schon vereinzelt ähnlich hohe Strafen gegeben hat – wenn es um erhebliche Geldsummen geht, versteht die Klassenjustiz keinen Spaß.


Dass aber der Prozess gegen Daniela Klette ein politisches Verfahren war, müsste selbst für einen »Taz«-Journalisten, für den die Weigerung, einen revolutionären antikapitalistischen Anspruch als Verfehlung einzugestehen, anscheinend eine permanente Provokation darstellt, offensichtlich sein. Dafür sorgt schon der Ort der Verhandlung: Eine ehemalige Reithalle in der Umgebung von Verden wurde eigens für mehrere Millionen Euro zu einem festungsartigen provisorischen Gerichtsgebäude umgebaut. Klette selbst war samt ihren Verteidigerinnen und Verteidigern in einem kugelsicheren Glaskasten plaziert, an den Ausgängen des Gebäudes waren Spezialkräfte mit Sturmhauben und Maschinengewehren postiert. Beim zweieinhalbstündigen Transport zur Verhandlung musste die Angeklagte eine schwere Bleiweste tragen und war an Händen und Füßen gefesselt.


Obwohl bei den verhandelten Raubüberfällen niemand verletzt wurde, beharrte die Staatsanwaltschaft auf dem Vorwurf des »versuchten Mordes«. Die »billigende Inkaufnahme tödlicher Verletzungshandlungen«, die die Bundesanwaltschaft (BAW) Klette vorwirft, ergibt sich allein aus der unterstellten früheren Mitgliedschaft in der RAF. Letztlich ist es auch diese vermutete Zugehörigkeit zu der längst aufgelösten Stadtguerillagruppe, mit der die Indizienkette, aufgrund derer das Urteil gefällt wurde, in irgendeiner Weise plausibel gemacht werden könnte. Die Argumentation beruft sich erkennbar auf die allgemein bekannte Kollektivität in der Entscheidungsstruktur der RAF. Die Zulässigkeit dieser Argumentation wurde 1998 vom Bundesgerichtshof bestätigt und dient nun dazu, Daniela Klette auch die Beteiligung an Raubüberfällen zur Last zu legen, bei denen es für ihre konkrete Tatbeteiligung nur wenige Indizien gibt: Zeugenaussagen oder Überwachungsvideos, die sie klar als Täterin identifizierten, sind nicht vorhanden, und die DNA-Mischspuren, die die Beweisaufnahme in Fluchtfahrzeugen festgestellt hat, sind für sich genommen nicht besonders aussagekräftig.


Obwohl das Thema RAF also den gesamten Prozess beherrschte, sollte es nach dem Willen von Staatsanwaltschaft und Gericht keine Rolle spielen. Erst in einem weiteren Verfahren am OLG Frankfurt wird es um einen versuchten Anschlag auf ein Gebäude der Deutschen Bank im hessischen Eschborn 1990, um Schüsse auf das …

author: Emma Honeybun
title: Newest report from correctional investigator says 10 year review of prison life shows little has changed
content:
The newest report from Canada’s federal prison watchdog says that despite 49 recommendations over 10 years, there has been “an absence of progress” in reducing the over-incarceration of Indigenous Peoples.


Valerie Phillips, who was the interim head of the

Office of the Correctional Investigator (OCI)

, wrote that findings indicated Correctional Services Canada (CSC) “remains predominantly risk-averse, security-driven, and institution-centred, with Indigenous-specific initiatives operating at the margins rather than as core system functions.”


“The central finding of this report is clear and consistent. A persistent gap remains between policy commitments and what is experienced on the ground,” she wrote. “This gap is the defining challenge of federal corrections.”


The OCI acts as a watchdog for the federal corrections system, taking complaints from prisoners and prison workers and visiting prisons to assess living conditions and trends, such as the over-incarceration of Indigenous Peoples.


Every year, the office releases an annual report which summarizes findings from the last year, paired with recommendations for Corrections Service Canada (CSC) to help address issues or gaps.


Phillips released the 2025-2026 annual report on Oct. 26, the first since former correctional investigator Ivan Zinger took his retirement in February.


This time, she wrote her report based on findings from the last decade.


In the

206-page document,

 she concluded that there is no behind-bars support that can replace community-based alternatives.


Indigenous Peoples remain over-represented throughout the entire legal system because of a lack of community-based supports, as well as risk assessment tools which advocates believe are rooted in outdated, colonial practices.


Sen. Kim Pate said she found the report “disheartening.”


“The situation keeps getting worse because we need the courage and the conviction to actually recognize that what has happened for decades has been not only ineffective, it’s been damaging and has made people who already have significant past trauma and histories of abuse in situations of more risk of not having their needs met,” she told APTN News.


“And until we do that and until we address those in the community and provide support to folks to have those, have their needs met, we will continue to see more of the same.”


Nicole Kief, the executive director of

Prisoners’ Legal Services (PLS)

, had a similar reaction and said the report didn’t “surprise her at all.”


PLS is a clinic operated by the Vancouver-based West Coast Justice Society, which offers prison-related legal aid to Indigenous and non-Indigenous clients.


“As I’m reading through these reports, I just find myself nodding and nodding and nodding and nodding, because this is all consistent with what we see in our own work,” Kief said.


From the perspective of an advocate who sees the barriers faced by people in incarceration on the day-to-day, she said what is often the biggest challenge is the “gap between policy and practice.


“That’s what stands out to me,” she said.


Sen. Kim Pate reads a letter from an incarcerated person in her Ottawa office in 2023. She said the 2025-2026 annual report from the OCI was “disheartening.” Photo: APTN File.


In the report’s section on Indigenous corrections, Phillips wrote that there have been gains when it comes to corrections officers being more culturally informed with the help of increased training introduced as recently as the fall of 2025.


For example, a higher number of Indigenous Peoples in incarceration had access to cultural resources because corrections officers were better equipped to recognize and place people in programs at an earlier stage than before.


For example, that year, 37 per cent of high-risk Indigenous offenders participated in the

Pathways initiative

, an Elder-driven cultural healing program for those preparing to transfer to a lower security facility.


In the 2022-2023 fiscal year, fewer than 10 per cent of Indigenous offenders accessed the program, which means there was almost a 30 per cent jump in two years.


However, the progress is undermined by risk assessment tools and written legislation that isn’t being changed, she continued.


In 2025-2026, the Pathways program only increased capacity from 350 to 366 people at one time, nationally, and 76 people “remained waitlisted despite operating at approximately 86 per cent capacity,” Phillips wrote.

author: Unknown
title: Non vogliamo mica la luna, vogliamo l’università!
content:
In seguito all’occupazione di Palazzo della Sapienza e alla partecipatissima assemblea di ateneo ottenuta da quella, si è aperto uno spazio di confronto, in cui ci siamo riconosciutə tra studentə che passano da una lezione all’altra tantissimo tempo al Polo San Rossore.


Da Cua Pisa


Non solo nei problemi e nei disagi di quotidianità universitarie asfissianti e asettiche, ma anche nella possibilità di cambiare il posto dove viviamo e studiamo, e con esso anche il modo in cui lo facciamo. A partire dalla strutturale mancanza di un’aula in cui studiare, sostare e incontrarci, negli scorsi due giorni abbiamo reso l’Aula D un’aula studio, di confronto, in cui ripararsi dalla pioggia, ma un’aula sola non era abbastanza. Il San Rossore è un polo che viene attraversato da moltə studenti, ma non vissuto. La sua architettura invita ad andarsene: non ci sono spazi in comune, mancano sedie, panchine ed un giardino dove possa essere piacevole trascorrere del tempo. E’ un edificio enorme, gestito male, ci sono aule grandi dove fanno lezioni in pochə, il suo atrio è vasto, ma non ci sono tavoli e panchine per permettere agli studenti di studiare. Come studenti occupanti rivendichiamo un’aula studio e uno spazio di confronto e socialità. A questo si aggiungono problemi concreti, come la mancanza di acqua la mattina e la pioggia in alcune aule. La direzione in cui va oggi l’università è ben precisa: una routine monotona e alienante tra lezione, casa e studio, quando invece dovrebbe essere condivisione del sapere, dialogo e dibattito. Siamo stanche di un’istruzione in declino, messa da parte da un governo che ha come priorità profitto e riarmo. Ci chiediamo cos’è, in questo momento, un’università che ci fa crescere? In un contesto in cui l’università e il diritto allo studio vengono definanziati e smantellati, abbiamo bisogno di immaginare davvero una formazione e una didattica diverse, e per farlo dobbiamo partire dal bisogno materiale di vivere un’università dignitosa, guardando a un futuro lontano dalla precarietà e dallo sfruttamento. Ci sentiamo i clienti di un’azienda, in cui paghiamo per un foglio che porta con sé la promessa di un lavoro che ci permetta di sopravvivere in questo tempo di crisi. In cui fare sacrifici significa essere privilegiati, mentre annaspiamo per mantenere la borsa o ci facciamo umiliare nei lavori part-time più assurdi e massacranti, pensando che sia possibile conciliarli con lo studio. In un periodo in cui i tagli del governo colpiscono ogni anno l’università e i suoi servizi, non è accettabile che le difficoltà finanziarie ricadano sulla qualità delle strutture e sulla vita dellə studenti. Poli in cui manca l’acqua o piove dentro, l’impossibilità di accedere a risorse digitali e riviste online necessarie per tesi e ricerca, sono condizioni incompatibili con il diritto allo studio. Al tempo stesso, si investe in poli lontani dal tessuto cittadino e privi degli adeguati spazi e servizi, come il nuovo polo di biologia a Ghezzano, compiendo scelte giustificate dalla scarsità di fondi e dagli appalti a ribasso, che peggiorano attivamente le nostre condizioni di studio e di vita.


Il Polo San Rossore è proprio un esempio di questo modello di università e proprio da qui vogliamo ripartire. Le risorse di cui dispone l’università devono essere destinate a ciò per cui esiste: garantire a tuttə le condizioni materiali per studiare, ricercare e costruire il proprio futuro. Deve essere un luogo e un tempo della vita accessibile a ognunə, in cui crescere collettivamente, approfondire aspetti della vita e della cultura che non solo ci stimolano, ma che possono farci sviluppare come persone e mettere le nostre conoscenze a servizio di un territorio. Questo polo è frequentato da molti studenti di dipartimenti diversi, sfruttiamo questa occasione per confrontarci, parlare e mobilitarci: scriviamo insieme una piattaforma, dove stilare le problematiche riscontrate da ogni dipartimento e risolverle una volta per tutte. L’ università è di chi la vive tutti i giorni: studenti, lavoratorə delle cooperative esternalizzate, personale sba, dottorandə, asssegnistə, professorə, a cui chiediamo di partecipare alla nostra occupazione, collaborando con noi per realizzare lezioni alternative, tavoli di lavoro, per una didattica che non sia solo nozionistica. Con l’occupazione, possiamo rompere la routine frenetica di tutti i giorni, possiamo dedicarci del tempo per ripensare il nostro polo, per rendere nostro il luogo in cui …

author: Shan Kenshin Ecaldre
title: Peasant organizer persists despite surveillance
content:
Jesus Monasterial. (Photo from Photo from Tanggol Magsasaka-TK)

Repeated surveillance restricted his movements and caused anxiety over his family’s safety.

When he was a university student, he questioned the purpose of agricultural education. Now he is organizing landless farmers and fisherfolk.

Jesus Monasterial has spent more than two years working with rural communities in Southern Tagalog. However, his work resulted in repeated surveillance by state forces, peasant groups said.

On October 31, Tanggol Magsasaka–Timog Katagalugan reported that a police intelligence operative identified as “Bruno” had been asking about Monasterial’s whereabouts in Lian, Batangas. The operative was reportedly previously assigned in Nasugbu.

At the time, Monasterial was assisting a protest camp in Barangay San Diego, where farmers, fisherfolk, and residents opposed the possible demolition of several houses.

“I was on my way back to the people’s protest camp in San Diego when news reached us that someone had been asking about my personal information,” he said.

The camp was established by Samahang Mangangawil 1979 and the San Diego Homeowners’ Association, with support from the Katipunan ng mga Samahang Magbubukid sa Timog Katagalugan (KASAMA-TK) and Pambansang Lakas ng Kilusang Mamamalakaya ng Pilipinas–Timog Katagalugan (PAMALAKAYA-TK).

The incident prompted fellow organizers to discuss security measures. They also plan to file a complaint before the Commission on Human Rights (CHR).

Monasterial’s involvement in peasant organizing began at the University of the Philippines Los Baños (UPLB) where he was enrolled in BS Agricultural Biotechnology.

Coming from a family of farmers in Bicol, where his grandparents worked as agricultural tenants, he became increasingly critical of an agricultural education system that he said served the interests of transnational corporations rather than addressing farmers’ lack of land and government support.

Through the League of Filipino Students–UPLB, he became involved in social issues action and joined community immersions with farmers in Tartaria, Silang, Cavite, as well as Mangyan communities in Mindoro and Dumagat communities in Rizal.

These experiences led him to leave his studies and become a full-time organizer. He now serves as deputy secretary-general of KASAMA-TK.

His work involves staying in communities, conducting consultations and political education, and helping establish local farmers and fisherfolk associations.

“Being a full-time organizer means devoting my entire time to the communities and being far from my loved ones,” he said, adding that he had to set aside his plan to finish college.

The October 31 incident was not the first reported surveillance involving Monasterial.

On July 19, 2026, soldiers from the 16th Infantry Battalion of the Philippine Army reportedly sought to identify the organizers of KASAMA-TK’s Regional Peasant Consultation in Barangay Malinis, Lemery, Batangas.

On September 21, a man introducing himself as “Del” Dela Cruz reportedly approached a member of Sugarfolks’ Unity for Genuine Agricultural Reform (SUGAR-Batangas), attempting to persuade the member to leave the organization and provide information about its activities.

According to Tanggol Magsasaka–Timog Katagalugan, the man showed footage of a protest outside the Department of Agriculture regional office led by the Alyansa ng Magsasaka para sa Kumpensasyon (AMK), SUGAR-Batangas, KAISAHAN, and KASAMA-TK. He allegedly warned the member against working with Monasterial, claiming that the organizer was “already drawing attention.”

The protest resulted in a dialogue with government representatives to demand agricultural inputs and implements for farmers and farmworkers affected by successive calamities.

The groups also cited previous incidents in Barangay Casile, Laguna; Lupang Ramos and Tartaria, Cavite; and Coron, Palawan.

Monasterial said that the repeated surveillance restricted his movements and caused anxiety over his family’s safety. “Repeated surveillance limits my movements as an organizer and makes me fear returning home to my family because they might also be targeted by the state due to my advocacy.”

Despite the threats, Monasterial said that his work remains rooted in the struggles of farmers and farmworkers.

In Batangas, he witnessed sugarcane cutters and loaders receiving only P350 to P400 for every ton of cane harvested and loaded onto trucks. Their wages are paid at the …

author: dev
title: Habiter au corps d'un âne mort ou le chemin de Nietzsche
content:
Dans la continuité des très nombreux articles que nous avons publiés afin de déchiffrer l'Intelligence artificielle, le monde qu'elle avale, celui qu'elle charrie et celui qu'elle produit, nous partageons cette semaine l'épatante découverte d'Olivier Chiran et Pierre Muzin. La première occurrence de l'expression IA reviendrait au célèbre philosophe Friedrich Nietzsche dans le tout aussi célèbre

Ainsi parlait Zarathoustra

, un tiret séparait néanmoins les deux voyelles :

« Braire à tout propos I-A, c'est ce qu'apprennent les ânes et ceux qui en ont l'esprit. »


« Donnez-moi du travail, de la fatigue,


de la douleur et de l'enthousiasme. »


George Sand


1.


Pour savoir précisément où nous en sommes, mais aussi faire face à ce qui nous arrive, alors que l'intelligence artificielle étend son emprise sur le monde et les vies, nous avons besoin d'un sémaphore.


2.


On dit que l'expression « intelligence artificielle » a été lancée par John McCarthy, en 1956, lors de la conférence de Dartmouth, coup d'envoi du programme de recherche consacré à la reproduction algorithmique de la pensée humaine. Soixante-douze ans plus tôt, en 1884, Friedrich Nietzsche, le célèbre philosophe allemand, rédige son grand poème philosophique :

Ainsi parlait Zarathoustra

. Dans la troisième partie de cet ouvrage (trouvée « sous le ciel alcyonien de Nice », dira-t-il), il écrit : « Braire à tout propos I-A, c'est ce qu'apprennent les ânes et ceux qui en ont l'esprit

 [

1

]

. » Première apparition de ces deux lettres, longtemps avant Dartmouth. Évidence de leur rapprochement – en même temps que, d'un simple tiret, de leur mise à distance. On pourrait s'étonner que les traducteurs français (Henri Albert en 1903, Geneviève Bianquis en 1969) aient fait le choix, au lieu du « hi-han » conventionnel, de les conserver telles quelles. Mais le texte allemand dit bien : «

Immer I-A sagen – das lernte allein der Esel, und wer seines Geistes ist

 ! » – Nietzche ayant délibérément fait tomber le

h

 de «

iah

 », braiment de l'âne dans la langue de Goethe. Nous dirons donc, quant à nous, que l'histoire de l'I-A commence à la fin du xixe siècle, lorsqu'un philosophe visionnaire, cheminant à flanc de montagne, a compris qu'on pouvait arracher au cri de l'âne sa puissance d'exclamation intempestive – et qu'il y avait là, pour nous, un grand danger

 [

2

]

.


3.


C'est qu'il y a deux ânes. Gilles Deleuze, commentant les propos de Nietzsche : « On aurait pu croire que l'âne, l'animal qui dit I-A, était l'animal dionysiaque par excellence. En fait, il n'en est rien ; son apparence est dionysiaque, mais toute sa réalité est chrétienne

 [

3

]

author: EDRi
title: Data retention is mass surveillance of people’s phone and internet activity
content:
In 2014, the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) declared mass retention of internet traffic and location data as contrary to the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights. Any proposal for a new EU instrument harmonising data retention must respect the boundaries of CJEU jurisprudence and uphold the rights to privacy, data protection and freedom of expression. Read more in EDRi’s new publication.

It is the legal requirement for internet service providers to retain metadata about their users beyond what is necessary for the provision of the service (e.g. billing or network optimisation and security purposes) and to keep it solely so that it can later be accessed by law enforcement bodies and intelligence services.

Metadata is data generated for the purpose of transmitting content in electronic communications services and networks. This includes mobile numbers of the sender and recipient, the time and duration of a call or an internet session, websites accessed, and the location of mobile devices. On a technical level, metadata is no longer needed once the transmission ends.

Metadata is very revealing about people’s private lives.

Systematic recording of location data will reveal a person’s permanent and temporary places of residence, political and religious preferences (e.g. participation in public demonstrations and religious ceremonies), health status (e.g. visit to a specialised clinic), sexual orientation (e.g. LGBT+ venues), or other sensitive aspects (e.g. visit to a lawyer’s office).

Metadata contains information about social or professional relations with other people (“social graph”).

Usage patterns for website visits and other internet services reveal an enormous amount of information about a person’s interest and state of mind.

Metadata is more revealing than the content of communications, especially because metadata is highly structured, which makes it easy to analyse. Governments can easily profile and categorise entire populations solely based on metadata.

The Court of Justice of the EU rightly described metadata retention as creating a feeling of being under constant surveillance. This has a chilling effect on participation in public life, as individuals restrict their own civil liberties to avoid surveillance.

While data access requests may be specific and targeted, general and indiscriminate data retention treats everyone as a potential suspect. Surveillance without suspicion violates the presumption of innocence, which is an essential right in democratic societies.

Retention of vast amounts of personal data inevitably creates huge vulnerabilities to cyberattacks. Malicious actors can gain access to massive amounts of data and abuse it for identity theft or blackmail.

Data retention severely undermines the possibility of online anonymity. Anonymity is a question of safety for many, even a matter of life or death: investigative journalists, whistleblowers, crime survivors, political opponents, refugees, victims of transnational repression, artists, human rights defenders, and more. It supports the exercise of key fundamental rights such as freedom of expression and the freedom to receive and impart information.

US telecom company AT&T was hacked by an attacker who stole the logs of calls and texts to more than 100 million customers over a six-month period in 2022.

In 2024 the Garda Síochána Ombudsman Commission (Ireland’s police watchdog) accessed journalists’ phone records to identify their sources as part of its own investigation into the Irish police, even though the journalists were not accused of any criminal offence.

In 2013, the Polish Central Anti-Corruption Bureau (CBA) obtained access to billing data of a journalist who had reported on irregularities in the intelligence services. The CBA’s aim was to uncover their source’s identity. The journalist won the case in court, and the CBA published an official apology.

The Berlin Data Protection Authority reported that most cell tower dumps (law enforcement requesting information on all the devices that connected to a particular cell site during a specific time period) by German authorities between 2009 and 2011, when data retention was in place in the country, were unlawful. The German police used this surveillance technique as an everyday investigative tool despite its very intrusive nature, and systematically failed to meet several legal requirements. Data retention enabled this abuse.

author: Unknown
title: Lilia Folt - On Anti-Surveillance Mindfulness
content:
Author

: Lilia Folt

Title

: On Anti-Surveillance Mindfulness

Date

: September 27

th

, 2026

Notes

: Originally published in

Dissonant Times

, a grassroots journalism and counter-info project from the Willamette Valley of Oregon.

Source

: Dissonant Times, Retrieved on 11/5/2026 from https://dissonanttimes.org/anarchic-reflections-on-anti-surveillance-mindfulness/


 Surveillance has become a ubiquitous feature of everyday life in America. Cameras watch us from businesses and homes, from bus stops, from cars, from traffic lights. Bluetooth trackers ping our smartphones as we pass by, mapping our movements. The phones themselves illuminate our paths through society by continuously pinging cell towers, providing our cell providers our location data, information that is only a subpoena away, if that. In countless ways, we’ve been made to both passively accept and actively participate in our own surveillance. This vast complex of surveillance doesn’t just gather information about us, it also shapes our behaviors, temperaments, and ways of moving through the world. Surveillance molds us down to the level of subjective, sensory, embodied experience. At that same level we can begin to shake off its hold on us and reclaim ourselves. For that, I am offering a practice I’m calling “anti-surveillance mindfulness,” a form of walking meditation that builds mindful awareness of surveillance cameras. This practice, if taken up consistently, opens onto a broader project of transforming our relationship to the places we live in, a project that itself naturally blossoms into materially transforming public space, as self expands to world in the moment-by-moment practice of mindfulness.


Anti-Surveillance Mindfulness


 Readers may or may not be familiar with the Panopticon. Designed by 18

th

 century English liberal Jeremy Bentham, the Panopticon was a model for an institutional building designed so that a single prison guard can watch all the inmates from a central watch tower. The inmates, meanwhile, cannot tell whether or not they are being watched, and therefore could be watched at any moment. To quote Bentham:


 The more constantly the persons to be inspected are under the eyes of the persons who should inspect them, the more perfectly will the purpose of the establishment have been attained. (...) This being impossible, the next thing to be wished for is, that, at every instant, seeing reason to believe as much, and not being able to satisfy himself to the contrary, he should

conceive

 himself to be so.


 A lot has changed since the 1700’s, but the disciplinary paradigm of surveillance has remained the same. If anything, it has expanded beyond specific institutions to encompass much of society.


 There are cameras everywhere, and we are being watched, and while we are aware of this, we tend to see it as normal and unremarkable, an inevitability we must resign ourselves to. Consciousness of being surveilled fades into the background, becoming a constant assumption of being watched that we internalize. This surveillance consciousness is running us all the more effectively because it is not distinct, because it is

un

conscious. That is why the first step in anti-surveillance mindfulness is becoming conscious of surveillance.


 Mindfulness is at the same time a means and an end, the seed and the fruit. When we practice mindfulness in order to build up concentration, mindfulness is a seed. But mindfulness itself is the life of awareness: the presence of mindfulness means the presence of life, and therefore mindfulness is also the fruit. — Thích Nhất Hạnh,

The Miracle of Mindfulness


 “Mindfulness” is a practice originating in various sects of Buddhism. The mindfulness practices and concepts I’m familiar with have largely been within the school of Zen Buddhism

[1]

.


 The classic mindfulness practice is watching the breath, and that is a great starting point. Take a breath in, the air entering through your nose, your stomach and chest softly expanding as you inhale. Then exhale through the mouth, the stomach and chest settling back down, gently exhaling for a little longer than your inhale. Repeat this several times, deepening your breaths slightly. From there, start to check in with your body. Notice how it feels to be sitting down, or to be standing if you are standing; notice how it feels to be holding this piece of paper, holding your phone, or looking at your computer, however it is that you are reading …

author: Jesse Staniforth
title: Air Creebec hit by administrative data breach affecting employees and passengers
content:
Air Creebec, a regional Quebec airline owned by the Cree Nation of Eeyou Istchee, reported a data breach Wednesday affecting both customers and staff.

In a press release, the company announced “an unauthorized intrusion targeting some of its administrative systems.”

The release stresses that the breach did not compromise any systems associated with aircraft, flight operations or flight safety, noting the company’s administrative systems were not connected with aircraft and flight systems, which it said operate independently.

“Initial findings indicate that administrative files were exfiltrated,” states the release. “These files may contain personal information relating mainly to current and former employees, as well as passengers. Others may also contain operational, administrative or financial information related to customers and partners. The review is ongoing.”

Based in the airport of Val d’Or in the Abitibi-Témiscamingue region of western Quebec, roughly 520 kilometres northwest of Ottawa, Air Creebec offers flights to 16 destinations in Quebec and Ontario. The company’s fleet consists of 21 Dash-8 turboprop regional airliners, along with one ATR 72 turboprop air-freighter for cargo, and carries 200,000 passengers per year.

Cybersecurity experts assessing damage

Air Creebec director for Marketing and Business Development Edward Trahan said the breach was identified in October after which company officials immediately brought in cybersecurity experts to analyze the situation.

“They’re currently evaluating what’s going on and what the breach actually contained,” Trahant told APTN News. “The experts are still conducting their review, so there’s no numbers [of victims] at this time that we can give.”

He added that for security reasons, he was not presently willing to name the cybersecurity team currently helping with post-breach recovery.

He said because the attack was designed to go undetected it was hard to determine the date upon which it began, and for how long attackers were able to access Air Creebec’s systems prior to being discovered.

“What I can assure you of is that as soon as [we were] made aware of [it], we acted immediately and did not wait.”

At the moment, Trahant said the attack appeared to have stolen information “related to our employees, past employees too, and maybe even our passengers.”

“But it’s hard to confirm at the moment.”

Company will contact affected parties

He added that a priority for Air Creebec is contacting every one of their staff or customers whose information has been compromised, which cybersecurity experts would undertake to carry out as soon as possible.

“A part of what the cybersecurity experts are doing for us is gathering information to [determine] what kind of protection packages we can provide to people that had their information involved,” said Trahan.

“Those people will be directly contacted in probably the next few days — [but] probably more like [the next] day — about what package they will receive, what protection they’re going to have and how long it’s going to last.”

Trahan said the cybersecurity team was currently in the process of securing all possible intrusion points, but he said the nature of cybersecurity is that 100 per cent protection is impossible.

“It’s just the way of the world,” he said, “but they are closing every possible way to get in and they are getting to the very end of that. As for how they got in initially, we don’t know yet and I don’t want to speculate while the review is still underway.”

Trahan said he and Air Creebec are taking the situation very seriously and are committed to supporting all those affected, and the company said it would be in touch with affected people to offer “appropriate protective measures,” including the possibility of credit-monitoring and identity-protection services.

“Those services will be based on the nature of the information exposed and the risks that were identified,” he said. “So individuals that are eligible to receive this protection will be informed directly and will be given a list of steps to follow in the very near future.”

Jesse joined APTN as a producer after 16 years as a print and web journalist. During seven of those years, he covered the Cree Nation of Eeyou Istchee for community newsmagazine The Nation. Jesse’s writing on Indigenous issues has also appeared in Canadian Geographic, the Toronto Star, the Rover, The Eastern Door, Metro, and the Huffington Post.

author: Scott Timcke
title: The Stories Shaping Africa’s AI Future
content:
In the boardrooms of Addis Ababa and the tech hubs of Nairobi, a new worldmaking project is underway. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become one of the central arenas where African states negotiate their position in an unequal global order. To speak of “AI in Africa” is not simply to describe the arrival of a technology, but to encounter a set of competing discursive frames through which political desires, developmental ambitions, ethical claims, and governance priorities are translated into technical agendas. As national strategies and regional protocols are rolled out, what comes into view is a struggle over how Africa is imagined within this machine age, and what kinds of futures that imagination makes thinkable.


These frames are not simply different ways of describing a new technology. They are competing scripts for what Africa is, what AI is for, and who ought to shape its future. Some cast the continent as a site of leapfrogging and renewal; others as a zone of exposure, extraction, sovereignty, moral repair, or improvised adaptation. Each brings some actors and possibilities into focus while pushing others to the margins. That is why the issue is not only what AI means for Africa, but what pictures of Africa are being called into view through AI discourse.


The first terrain is shaped by promise and protection. One of the most pervasive registers is promissory. In the African renaissance 2.0 frame, visible in the

AU Continental AI Strategy

, AI appears as a

leapfrogging

 device through which Africa can bypass the chokepoint of traditional industrialization and enter prosperity through technical modernization. Here, the ethical subject is the developmental state or planner charged with delivering growth, inclusion, and renewal. What comes into view is capacity, competitiveness, and beneficial transformation. What recedes from view are the historical and political-economic conditions that make acceleration so attractive in the first place: debt, infrastructural dependence, uneven ownership, and the possibility that AI may deepen rather than overcome inherited asymmetries.


Running alongside this is a protective register. In this vulnerability frame, Africa is not late but exposed to surveillance, bias, exclusion, and systems introduced into settings where safeguards are weak and redress is limited. As the

CIVICUS report on AI surveillance in Africa

 suggests, the issue is not only future risk but already existing forms of technologically mediated harm. The ethical subject here is the harm-bearing population—the data subject, precarious worker, surveilled citizen, and linguistically marginal user most likely to absorb the costs of badly governed AI. This frame is ethically indispensable because it foregrounds rights, harm, and institutional fragility, including the uneven but growing architecture of data protection on the continent. Its limit, however, is that it can cast Africa chiefly as a site to be protected rather than one from which technological futures are actively contested and shaped.


A second terrain is shaped by structure and sovereignty. Alongside these promissory and protective registers sits a more structural critique. In the

anti-colonial frame

, AI appears as a socio-technical order built through unequal material relations: not only data extraction, but also mineral supply chains, outsourced labor, environmental degradation, foreign-owned infrastructures, and asymmetrical control over the institutions that govern digital life. From this perspective, Africa is not outside the AI order looking in; it is already deeply inserted into it, though often on subordinated terms. The ethical subject is the dispossessed worker, community, or polity whose labor, resources, and data are drawn into AI systems while ownership and value are captured elsewhere. What becomes visible is the political economy of AI—an approach that makes it harder to sustain the comforting idea that Africa’s main problem is simply one of readiness or delayed entry. But the frame has limits. In foregrounding dispossession, it can flatten internal differentiation, externalize agency too completely, and become so totalizing that the uneven realities of negotiation and strategic inhabitation recede from view.


The sovereignty frame shifts the question from extraction to control: AI is cast as a problem of authority over infrastructure, procurement, standards, and rulemaking, a concern visible in South Africa’s

author: Dinah Gardner
title: The Other China We Need to Talk About
content:
WHAT IF I told you that there was a chance—not a very high chance, but a real chance nonetheless—that if you visited the People’s Republic of China today you might be kidnapped, blindfolded, driven to a specialized facility and subjected to six months of psychological torture. All on the orders of the state.

It sounds unbelievable, doesn’t it?

But this is what happened to at least several dozen foreign citizens in recent years. It is what happened to American scholar Min Zin this past June, when he landed in Yunnan province on the invitation of a Chinese academic institution to attend a conference. And it is also what happened to half a dozen people who appear in the latest edition of the book The People’s Republic of the Disappeared, which we just published on 28 October.

This important book is a collection of mostly first-person stories that expose the psychological horrors of being held in the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) feared secret detention system called Residential Surveillance at a Designated Location (RSDL). The system permits police to hold an individual in complete isolation, no contact with family or lawyers, to be interrogated for hours at will.

The individual is under 24-hour guard: this includes being watched all day every day, all night every night, whether you are asleep, sitting quietly in your cell or even on the toilet. The CCP intentionally uses RSDL to strip away every last shred of human dignity. RSDL is designed to break a person’s will to extract a confession for crimes imagined by the state

For more than a decade, the CCP has used RSDL against its own people, in particular human rights defenders. It is now increasingly using it against foreign citizens to exert its will across borders and as a kind of hostage diplomacy. Michael Kovrig, a former Canadian diplomat who wrote the foreword to this edition, is one of its most well-known examples.

In editing the stories for this book, I was struck again and again by how similar everyone’s experience was. This speaks to the uniformity of the RSDL system:

The removal of the temporal world. “There are no clocks in RSDL” is the title of Australian TV anchor Cheng Lei’s chapter. She would guess and count breaths to keep track of time.

The removal of the physical world. There are no windows in RSDL or they are covered in thick blackout curtains. Japanese scholar Hideji Suzuki cried when he was granted 15 minutes of sunlight, the only time in his seven months’ incarceration when he was allowed to see the sky.

The removal of yourself. Michael Kovrig noted: “There are no mirrors—not even the reassurance of seeing your own face.” Chinese activist Li Qiaochu writes how she was simply called “target”.

Filling the space left by these absences was a current of fear. Endless rules, the lack of privacy yet total isolation (guards were forbidden from talking to prisoners), reduced nutrition, sleep deprivation, lack of fresh air, and the padded suicide-proofed walls. Several of the detainees wrote while they could never see outside their RSDL facility, at nighttime they would often hear gunfire or the barking of dogs.

“In my mentally exhausted state, the sounds of gunfire would constantly startle me and even cause me to imagine that I was about to be executed,” wrote Taiwanese human rights activist Lee Ming-che.

But something else struck me as I read through their testimonies. However harrowing these stories of suffering are, they are also evidence of human resilience in the face of horror.

Cheng Lei writes about how she would escape into her mind, translating poems, reliving her former TV interviews and making up stories in her head. Similarly, Michael Kovrig meditated, sang songs to himself, and remembered past moments in his life, as if it was a recording playing in his mind.

“I learned to meditate on the movies I had watched and the poems and novels I had read,” wrote Li Qiaochu. “Those precious memories allowed me to gradually filter out the brainwashing, to preserve my vitality and to keep myself from being transformed into their machine.”

Feedback from earlier editions informed us that rights activists use the Chinese editions of The People’s Republic of the Disappeared to prepare for and strengthen their mental resolve and courage in case one day they too are taken into RSDL. Knowing that others have gone through this and come out the other side can be an immense help. It’s for this reason that the Chinese edition of this book will be …

author: Unknown
title: The Third World War, the Middle East and the Kurds
content:
Following the collapse of the Soviet Union in the early 1990s, Britain, the United States and Israel developed a strategy under the concept of the “New World Order,” aimed at restructuring the international system in the interests of global capital. The conflict that began with the war against Iraq in the 1990s continues to this day and has grown increasingly intense, widespread and complex through successive phases. One of the central objectives of this Third World War was to dismantle the Kurdish freedom movement, resolve the Palestinian question in line with hegemonic interests, and reorganize the Middle East under Israeli dominance and the control of the principal hegemonic power.


To prevent the expansion and further development of the Kurdish freedom movement and ultimately bring about its destruction, a federal Kurdish entity was established in Southern Kurdistan (Northern Iraq). In doing so, the powers involved relied on both local collaborationist forces and the states among which Kurdistan has been divided. However, despite all the plots directed against the freedom movement and Abdullah Öcalan, they failed to achieve the objectives pursued through this war.


The geopolitical pressures behind Turkey’s strategic reorientation


The failure of the strategy aimed at dismantling the Kurdish freedom movement was not the only factor that prompted the Turkish state to seek new political options. Other developments following Hamas’s attack on Israel on October 7 also played a role: Israeli military operations in the Gaza Strip and Lebanon, the resulting weakening of Hamas and Hezbollah, the escalation of tensions with Iran into open warfare, and the restructuring of international energy and trade routes, which saw Cyprus included in relevant agreements while Turkey was left out. These developments forced the Turkish state to reconsider its previous strategic orientation.


Another significant factor was the resistance developed by the Kurdish freedom movement under Abdullah Öcalan’s leadership, characterized by a far-reaching willingness to make sacrifices. Without this resistance, the changing regional balance of power alone would not have prompted the Turkish state to undertake such a strategic shift. It was only the combination of geopolitical developments and the struggle waged in Kurdistan that compelled the Turkish leadership to respond to Abdullah Öcalan’s approach to initiating a new political process and to issue a corresponding appeal to him.


The nation-state order in the Middle East is being shaken


The military and political upheavals in the region also caused considerable concern within the Turkish leadership. These include the war waged by the United States and Israel against Iran, the change of power in Syria that saw Baathist rule replaced by a Sunni-dominated government, and the resulting weakening of the so-called Shia Crescent. At the same time, the nation-state order in the Middle East, rooted in the Sykes-Picot Agreement, became increasingly unstable and was called into question even by the dominant powers themselves. These uncertainties were further heightened by the perception that the hegemonic actors were considering partly divergent approaches to resolving the Kurdish question.


With Israel’s growing hegemonic influence, its increasing capacity for military intervention across the region and the extensive support it receives from the United States, these developments came to be perceived by Turkey as an existential threat to the survival of the state. Against this backdrop, the fact that the political resolution process continues to this day and that Abdullah Öcalan remains recognized as a negotiating partner can largely be attributed to the Turkish leadership’s security concerns and fears for the state’s very existence.


The Third World War, which began in the Middle East and particularly in Kurdistan, has gradually spread to other regions of the world. The collapse of the Soviet Union brought an end to the bipolar world order, prompting the United States to develop a strategy aimed at controlling the Middle East and establishing its unchallenged global hegemony. Despite various crises, the US largely succeeded in securing its dominant position through the support and involvement of cooperating governments. In recent years, however, the People’s Republic of China and Russia have steadily expanded their international influence. Their rise as major economic and military hegemonic …

author: labor4pal
title: A fightback is building as crackdown deepens against civil liberties (Workers’ Voice)
content:
Dozens of activists are accused by the federal government of contributing to bogus “criminal conspiracies.” In Minnesota, two separate conspiracy cases accuse 54 people of participating in illegal conspiracies for participating in protest and journalistic activities. The Minnesota 15, Righteous 39, Michigan 8 (now 12), Spokane 3, and Prairieland Defendants are the most well known cases in the ongoing crackdown. All of these cases are attacks on organized labor.

The California Faculty Association and the Graduate Employee Organization at University of Michigan (GEO-AFT 3550) are facing frontal attacks on their unions by the right-wing press and FBI. Doctored video of a CFA meeting was leaked to Trump booster Bari Weiss’s Free Press in an attempt to scandalize the union with false accusations of antisemitism. The Department of Justice first charged GEO President Hiab Teshome with felonious financial crimes. Those bogus charges were dropped the same day that a grand jury subpoenaed GEO’s books, including all member lists, meeting minutes, and financial records. The union is fighting to retain basic privacy rights.

Fueled by National Security Presidential Memorandum-7, U.S. intelligence and police apparatuses are being explicitly targeted at anyone standing for basic democratic rights, immigrant communities, and racial justice. As the world drifts closer to major inter-imperialist conflict and expanding zones of overt imperialist military occupation takes hold in the semi-colonies, Western imperialisms are tightening restrictions on protest, speech, and organizing for progressive movements.

While there are many additional cases of “lawfare” and anti-protest policing, it is worth taking a moment to review two of the cases mentioned above to understand the tactics and scope of the current crackdown.

Around two dozen protesters held a noise demonstration on July 4, 2025, outside of the Prairieland Detention Center in Texas. As the protest was winding down and many of the participants had left, Alvarado Police Officer Thomas Gross sped onto the scene and almost immediately aimed his gun at a demonstrator moving away from him. Video evidence indicates that Gross discharged his weapon, something that would appear to have been covered up by the judge and prosecutors.

In response to seeing a potentially lethal attack on a protester, Marine Corps veteran Benjamin “Champagne” Song let out a warning shot into the ground away from the officers. Gross went to the hospital for superficial wounds that the government alleges resulted from being shot by Song, but video evidence released after sentencing indicates Gross was likely hit by shrapnel produced from his own weapon’s discharge.

Using the presence of guns and defensive action of Song as pretext, 22 people were ultimately indicted as part of an alleged conspiracy to attack cops and carry out an armed prison break. One person, Daniel “Des” Rolando Sanchez Estrada, was not at the protest at all. Des was convicted for “corruptly concealing a document or record” and sentenced to 30 years for possessing legally protected political materials.

After arrests, pressure and legal sabotage was mounted by the judicial system against the defendants. Many were initially held in solitary confinement, with one reporting that human feces coated their cell. U.S. District Judge Mark Pittman blocked the defendants from retaining a private attorney, meaning they had to use public defenders. Song’s legal team was not allowed to make an argument that the warning shot was taken in self-defense. Eight defendants became cooperating witnesses, providing coerced testimony to validate the government’s made-up conspiracy theories.

Before the trial even began, the deck was stacked against non-cooperating defendants. In an explicit “warning” to the left, Judge Pittman laid down ridiculously high sentences of between 30-100 years to non-cooperating defendants.

From the war on drugs to the war on speech: Minnesota 15

The Minnesota 15 are 15 activists accused of a “conspiracy to impede or attack federal agents.” The majority are current or recent union members and all are community activists. They are not accused of participating in or coordinating any acts of violence. Instead, the original 92-page indictment against them lists “evidence” including participating in rapid response group chats, protests, and mutual aid activities. Any successful convictions on the basis of these charges would be a …

author: Sicilia Libertaria
title: La guerra come forma della crisi
content:
Il capitalismo oltre la promessa della crescita infinita


La guerra contro l’Iran racconta qualcosa di più di un nuovo conflitto per il controllo delle risorse energetiche e degli equilibri geopolitici mondiali. Racconta la crisi di un modello economico che ha fatto della crescita senza fine la propria ragione d’essere e la propria promessa di benessere. Un modello che, incontrando i limiti materiali del pianeta, sembra sempre più orientato a trasformare la stagnazione in rendita, la scarsità in profitto e l’instabilità in una condizione della propria sopravvivenza.


Il 13 luglio 2026 l’OPEC ha comunicato, per la terza volta consecutiva, una revisione al ribasso delle previsioni di crescita della domanda mondiale di petrolio: da 970.000 a 780.000 barili al giorno. Nello stesso periodo il prezzo del greggio continuava a subire le violente oscillazioni provocate dalla guerra iniziata il 28 febbraio con i bombardamenti congiunti degli Stati Uniti e di Israele contro l’Iran.


Sono due dati che raccontano aspetti differenti di una stessa contraddizione. Il prezzo del petrolio ci parla della guerra; il rallentamento della domanda ci parla delle difficoltà di un sistema che ha costruito la propria riproduzione sull’espansione permanente dei consumi.


Il secondo numero, insomma, ci dice perché la guerra possa diventare una risposta alla crisi del sistema. Non necessariamente una risposta capace di rilanciare lo sviluppo, ma certamente una possibile occasione per continuare a produrre profitti.


Già nel 2024 il World Energy Outlook dell’Agenzia internazionale dell’energia collocava entro il 2030 il possibile picco della domanda mondiale di petrolio. Per decenni l’ossessione degli analisti era stata quella del picco dell’offerta: quando avremmo esaurito le riserve disponibili? Oggi la questione si è rovesciata. Il problema non è più soltanto quando finirà il petrolio, ma quando il suo consumo smetterà di crescere.


La saturazione di alcuni mercati, la diffusione della motorizzazione elettrica, soprattutto in Cina, i miglioramenti nell’efficienza energetica e lo sviluppo delle fonti alternative stanno modificando le prospettive dell’industria petrolifera. L’Agenzia internazionale dell’energia è arrivata a prevedere per il 2026 una contrazione complessiva dei consumi mondiali, aggravata dalle conseguenze economiche della guerra.


Non siamo ancora alla fine del petrolio, naturalmente. Ma siamo di fronte alla possibilità che uno dei principali motori materiali dell’espansione capitalistica non possa più garantire una crescita indefinita.


Il paradosso più grande è che nemmeno la guerra è riuscita a rianimare questo mercato. Il conflitto ha moltiplicato i prezzi senza produrre una corrispondente ripresa dei consumi. Ha creato occasioni di guadagno per chi riesce a vendere a prezzi maggiorati, mentre ha aggravato i costi per chi deve acquistare energia.


Ci troviamo così di fronte a un capitalismo nel quale la produzione di profitto può separarsi sempre più nettamente dalla crescita della ricchezza sociale. Un sistema che, quando non riesce a espandere sufficientemente i mercati, cerca di aumentare la quota di ricchezza che può appropriarsi.


Non più soltanto produrre, dunque, ma estrarre.


E l’instabilità può diventare una risorsa. Il blocco dello stretto di Hormuz, la sua parziale riapertura, le nuove interruzioni e le continue oscillazioni dei prezzi creano condizioni nelle quali alcuni operatori economici e finanziari possono realizzare guadagni indipendentemente dall’aumento della produzione.


Per produrre occorre stabilità. Per appropriarsi di determinate rendite, invece, l’instabilità può diventare conveniente.


Per comprendere questa trasformazione dobbiamo tornare indietro, alla fine della Guerra fredda e all’emergere della crisi climatica come questione politica mondiale.


Rio de Janeiro, 1992. Durante il vertice internazionale sull’ambiente, il presidente americano George Bush senior ribadì che lo stile di vita degli Stati Uniti non era negoziabile. Quella dichiarazione conteneva una promessa destinata a entrare in contraddizione con i limiti materiali del pianeta.


L’American way of life aveva, e conserva, un presupposto fondamentale: la disponibilità di energia abbondante e a buon mercato. La politica energetica americana si trova davanti a una contraddizione: deve garantire ai propri cittadini la continuità di un modello di consumo che ha dichiarato intoccabile, mentre le condizioni economiche …

author: webdev@democracynow.org (Democracy Now!)
title: "Birds of War": New Film Tells a Story of Love and Journalism from Syria to Lebanon
content:
We speak with Janay Boulos and Abd Alkader Habak, filmmakers and subjects of the new documentary

Birds of War

, which tells their epic love story through years of upheaval in the Middle East. Boulos, a London-based Lebanese journalist working for the

BBC

, and Habak, a Syrian activist and cameraman, first connected while covering the Syrian civil war and stayed in touch through years of war, revolution and exile, forming a relationship that is chronicled in the documentary by drawing on 13 years of their personal videos, voice notes and other correspondence.


The film also examines the unequal relationship between international news organizations and local journalists whose work they rely on, the fraught political history between Syria and Lebanon, and how Boulos and Habak’s personal connection overcame those divisions.


“Without our journalistic relationship, [we] would have never been together. I would have never opened my heart to somebody like him,” says Boulos. “We can be any race, any gender, any religion, any background, but at the same time we’re all humans.”


Birds of War

 premiered at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival, where it won the World Cinema Documentary Special Jury Award for Journalistic Impact.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Unnamed Military Exercises Aim to Intimidate Taiwan Ahead of Elections, While Avoiding International Outcry
content:
ACCORDING TO TAIWANESE Minister of National Defense Wellington Koo, China is currently engaged in area access denial drills around Taiwan.

Such drills involve more than 100 naval and coast guard ships operating in waters around Taiwan. These exercises include the deployment of the Liaoning, China’s first aircraft carrier, and its carrier group.

Last week, on November 3rd, images of Chinese naval vessels deployed around Taiwan were released by National Security Council head Joseph Wu. Wu also drew attention to a large number of air sorties that had taken place on November 3rd, with 49 sorties of Chinese aircraft that entered Taiwan’s Air Defense Identification Zone and crossed the median line of the Taiwan Strait.

Previously, news reports had indicated that China may have been practicing for a potential blockade of Taiwan in late October and early November, through exercises that coordinated between its eastern, northern, and southern theater commands. According to national security officials, these drills were larger than previously named large-scale drills by China, such as the 2025 Justice Mission.

Indeed, it is notable that China has not formally announced any military drills to date. China normally conducts at least two named large-scale military exercises per year, in the spring and the fall. This has not occurred this year yet, though it might be expected that China would conduct a large-scale set of exercises before the end of the year.

It is possible that China is stepping up military activity as a show of force before the Taiwanese local elections set to take place later this month. Indeed, probably as a means of intimidating Taiwan and flexing muscles, one has in short order seen Pakistan briefly revoke permissions for Taiwanese airlines to fly over its airspace, Papua New Guinea order the closure of Taiwan’s representative office, and reports that Lithuania requested that Taiwan change the name of its representative office in what would have been read as a form of diplomatic downgrading.

Likewise, domestically in Taiwan, one has seen incidents of transnational repression. These include political commentator Akio Yaita being attacked at the venue of a talk, a comedian who mocked Chinese president Xi Jinping in his stand-up routine having feces and paint thrown at the venue where he was performing, and a plot to ram the same comedian with a vehicle and hospitalize him.

China may be stepping up efforts to intimidate Taiwan then–including familiar military threats. But not formally announcing a new set of military exercises may be a means of avoiding strong reactions to Chinese military exercises that might backfire for the CCP, in which members of the public rally behind the DPP and Lai administration rather than being cowed into voting for the KMT.

Either way, Chinese naval movements go to show that Chinese threats against Taiwan have not ceased, shortly before elections. Furthermore, that there is little attention from the world in a time of significant military exercises should be concerning, in that the sources of information about military activity remain confined to state actors, and China is able to prevent any outcry about its military activity if it does formally announce military exercises.

title: PETA x Adventsome – vegane Adventskalender: Infos zur Verlosung und die Gründer:innen im Interview
content:
Werbung | Die

Weihnachtszeit

 rückt näher und mit ihr die Vorfreude auf kleine tägliche Überraschungen. Gemeinsam mit Adventsome verlosen wir von PETA Deutschland daher drei vegane Adventskalender voller

pflanzlicher Snacks

 und Infos zur Unterstützung gemeinnütziger Projekte. Der vegane Adventskalender zeigt, wie vielfältig, lecker und kreativ die Weihnachtszeit sein kann – mit vielen rein veganen Überraschungen. 


Über unsere Social-Media-Kanäle verlosen wir insgesamt drei vegane Adventskalender von Adventsome im Wert von jeweils 149 Euro. Mit etwas Glück können Sie sich oder Ihren Liebsten eine ganz besondere tierfreundliche Vorweihnachtszeit schenken. 


Teilnahmezeitraum: 13.11.2026 bis 16.11.2026

 


Inhaltsübersicht


									Interview mit Adventsome: Lea und Josias im Gespräch zum veganen Adventskalender


									Alle Infos zur PETA x Adventsome-Verlosung


									Lust auf noch mehr vegane Adventskalender?


Interview mit Adventsome: Lea und Josias im Gespräch zum veganen Adventskalender


Wir haben mit den Gründer:innen des Start-ups Adventsome – Lea und Josias – ein Interview geführt, um die Menschen hinter dem Projekt und den Gedanken hinter dem veganen Adventskalender vorzustellen: Welche Motivation treibt sie an, welche Rolle spielen Tiere bei Entscheidungen und wie kann ein Adventskalender über die Weihnachtszeit hinaus etwas bewegen? 


Lea und Josias – die Gründer:innen des Start-ups Adventsome.


PETA: Nehmt uns mit an den Anfang: Wie wurde aus eurer persönlichen Begeisterung für Adventskalender die Idee zu Adventsome?


Gab es einen bestimmten Moment, in dem ihr dachtet: „Genau so einen Kalender möchten wir selbst entwickeln“?

 


Adventsome:

 Die Idee kam uns, als wir uns 2017 gegenseitig Adventskalender schenken wollten, aber uns keiner wirklich begeistern konnte. Wir wünschten uns einen, der uns mit jedem Türchen aufs Neue überrascht, ganz viele unterschiedliche Produktkategorien vereint und in einer sinnvollen Verpackung kommt, die nicht nach 24 Tagen im Müll landet. Die zwei Kalender, die wir daraufhin selbst bastelten, haben uns im Dezember so viel Freude bereitet, dass wir beschlossen haben, diese auch mit anderen zu teilen. Ein Jahr später brachten wir unsere ersten 500 Adventskalender auf den Markt, die wir damals alle selbst neben der Uni verpackten – das waren ganze 12.000 einzelne Geschenke! 


PETA: Weihnachten verbinden viele Menschen mit Mitgefühl und Nächstenliebe. Welche Rolle spielen Tiere für euch dabei – und wie hat das eure Entscheidung für einen vollständig veganen Adventskalender geprägt?

  


Adventsome

: Wir lieben Tiere, haben selbst auch zwei

Katzen adoptiert

 und uns jahrelang im Tierschutz engagiert. Mit Adventsome möchten wir daher keine Produkte unterstützen, für die Tiere leiden müssen. Gleichzeitig finden wir es spannend, wie vielfältig das vegane Sortiment mittlerweile ist und wie viele innovative Alternativen es gibt. Genau den Brands, die diese Entwicklung weiter vorantreiben, möchten wir eine Bühne geben und ihnen helfen, bekannter zu werden. Unser Adventskalender soll Menschen dafür begeistern, Neues auszuprobieren und vielleicht auch die eine oder andere Gewohnheit zu hinterfragen! 


PETA: Euer Kalender verbindet 20 Produkte von Start-ups mit vier Spendentürchen. Was sollen Menschen beim Auspacken erleben – und was soll davon nach dem 24. Dezember bleiben?

 


Adventsome

: Wir wünschen uns, dass unsere Kund:innen jeden Morgen mit echter Vorfreude ein Türchen öffnen. Das schönste Feedback ist für uns, wenn uns jemand schreibt, dass er oder sie wieder kindliche Neugier verspürt. Richtige Überraschungen sind im Erwachsenenleben so selten geworden! 


Nach Weihnachten bleiben soll zunächst einmal unsere weiterverwendbare Design-Box, die wir jedes Jahr mit einer Künstlerin gemeinsam kreieren. Außerdem hoffentlich ganz viele neue Gedankenanstöße und Perspektiven und vielleicht auch das ein oder andere Lieblingsprodukt? 


Lea und Josias engagieren sich seit Jahren im Tierschutz und haben selbst zwei Katzen adoptiert.


PETA: Von Snacks über Pflege bis zu Alltagsprodukten: Wo findet ihr die Überraschungen, die es in euren Kalender schaffen?

  


Adventsome

: Die wichtigste Frage ist immer: Würden wir uns selbst darüber freuen, wenn wir morgens das Türchen öffnen? Das Produkt muss zudem vegan, unisex und alkoholfrei sein und auch darüber hinaus mit unseren Werten matchen!

title: Grossdemo gegen Tönnies
content:
Grossdemo gegen Tönnies

Wir demonstrieren am 21.11. in Kellinghusen

Ihr seid wütend auf Tönnies? Wir auch! Wir haben

dokumentiert

Hintergrundinfos


Rideshare-Tool

Damit möglichst viele Menschen zur Demo gegen Tönnies kommen, wollen wir euch bei der Planung eurer Anreise unterstützen. Daher haben wir ein cleveres Rideshare-Tool entwickelt, mit dem ihr Fahrgemeinschaften bilden könnt. So wird die Anreise für euch günstiger, einfacher und spaßiger.


Jetzt einsteigen!

Warum demonstrieren wir?

Anlass für die Großdemo am 21. November ist unsere aktuelle Veröffentlichung „Töten im Takt – Die grausamste Maschine bei Tönnies“. Tönnies ist Deutschlands größter Schlachtkonzern und gilt als eines der mächtigsten Unternehmen der europäischen Fleischindustrie. Als Marktführer tötet Tönnies jedes Jahr 16 Millionen Schweine. Unsere Aufdeckung zeigt den grausamen Erstickungskampf der Tiere in der CO₂-Anlage. Die Schweine schreien vor Angst und versuchen zu fliehen.


Was wir bisher getan haben

Gewalt im Schlachthof aufgedeckt

Verstöße dokumentiert

Tönnies angezeigt

Eine große Welle an Presseberichten ausgelöst

Zahlreiche Interviews geführt

Eine politische und gesellschaftliche Debatte angestoßen

Bei der Tönnies-Zentrale in Rheda-Wiedenbrück protestiert

Hintergrundinfos

Und jetzt?

Die Gewalt im Schlachthaus geht unvermindert weiter! Wir sind wütend. Deshalb fahren wir jetzt nochmal ganz groß auf, bündeln unsere Kräfte an einem Termin und demonstrieren gemeinsam mit euch an genau dem Schlachthof, aus dem die Aufnahmen unserer Aufdeckung stammen:

Kellinghusen!


Unsere Forderung: Der Betrieb muss schließen!


Ablauf und Programm

14:00 Uhr: Auftakt


Wir starten mit einer Auftaktkundgebung mit Redebeiträgen auf dem Unteren Marktplatz.

Demozug


Als großer und lauter Demozug ziehen wir mit Schildern, Bannern und Fahnen durch Kellinghusen, skandieren lautstark und setzen ein starkes Zeichen.

Zwischenstopp am Schlachthof


Die Demoroute führt uns bis zum Schlachthof. Dort gibt es weitere Redebeiträge.

Abschlusskundgebung


Gemeinsam laufen wir zurück zum Unteren Marktplatz, wo die Demo nach einer Abschlusskundgebung endet.

So kannst du mithelfen

Du willst mithelfen, dass die Demo richtig groß wird? Dann unterstütze uns bei der Mobilisierung: Bring deine Freund*innen mit zur Demo, teile unseren

Content auf Social Media

 oder poste selbst unser Sharepic:


Demoregeln

Bitte beachtet unsere allgemeinen Demohinweise, damit sich alle wohlfühlen. Danke für euer Verständnis und eure Mithilfe!


1. Antispeziesistisch und abolitionistisch

Einen Ansatz, die Ausbeutung der Tiere zu reformieren und somit im Grundsatz beizubehalten, verfolgen wir nicht. Unsere Forderungen sind grundsätzlich antispeziesistisch und abolitionistisch. Wir bitten deshalb ausdrücklich darum, auf der Demo vermeintliche „Zwischenschritte“ oder „Reformen“ (z. B. Biofleischkonsum oder Verbesserung der Haltungsbedingungen) nicht als Ziel zu kommunizieren.

2. Kein Platz für Menschenfeindlichkeit

ARIWA lehnt alle Formen allgemeiner und gruppenbezogener Menschenfeindlichkeit (wie zum Beispiel Ableismus, Antisemitismus, Homo- und Trans*feindlichkeit, Rassismus oder Sexismus) sowie verschwörungsideologische Denkmuster ab. Personen mit solchen Hintergründen sind bei der Demo ausdrücklich nicht erwünscht. Mehr Infos:

ariwa.org/selbstverstaendnis

3. Keine Kleidung tierischen Ursprungs

Bitte tragt nach Möglichkeit keine Kleidung tierischen Ursprungs und achtet darauf, dass sie auch nicht so aussieht. Denn Produkte wie Kunstpelz oder Kunstleder können missverstanden werden und für Außenstehende einen falschen Eindruck erwecken.

4. Keine Partei- oder Religionswerbung

Parteiwerbung, Werbung für religiöse Gruppierungen sowie Holocaust-Vergleiche sind nicht erwünscht.

5. Bitte keine Tiere mitbringen

Aufgrund von Lärm, Hitze und Enge bitten wir euch, keine Tiere mit zur Demo zu bringen.
