title: SAVE THE SOUTH SUFFOLK ONE!
content:
Oh, wait… sorry. The Judge already did that in court.


John ‘Pinocchio’ Henty’s case ends in acquittal

.


Thank you to


South Suffolk Hunt Sabs


for this guest article.


A court case brought by former Essex & Suffolk Hunt huntsman John Henty against a hunt saboteur has ended in a resounding victory for the defence, with the saboteur found NOT GUILTY.


John Henty outside court.


Following allegations made to police, former Essex & Suffolk Hunt huntsman John Henty pursued a prosecution alleging abusive and threatening behaviour under Section 5 of the Public Order Act. The case followed an incident on a quiet country lane in which Henty pursued the hunt saboteurs’ vehicle, blocked it in, approached it and attempted to provoke a reaction.


What followed was a lengthy legal process based on Henty’s account of events. However, when his evidence was examined in court, serious questions arose about the credibility of that account and whether the alleged behaviour actually amounted to a criminal offence.


A case that should never have reached court?


The Judge was highly critical of the way the case had been handled by the CPS and the police officers involved, making clear that the alleged actions did not meet the legal threshold required for a criminal offence.


Both the prosecution and the defence barrister sought to discontinue the case on more than one occasion. The case was nevertheless directed to proceed. The circumstances surrounding that decision raise serious questions about why so much time and public money were spent pursuing a prosecution that ultimately failed.


Former Essex & Suffolk Hunt huntsman John Henty is now at The Ludlow Hunt.


The evidence tells a different story


Henty submitted two video clips, recorded by himself, which were played in court. The footage showed Henty pulling his vehicle alongside the hunt saboteurs’ Land Rover, getting out of his own accord and filming the encounter.


Our saboteur told Henty to ‘f*ck off’ before closing the vehicle door. Rather than disengaging, Henty continued filming and engaging with the occupants. Despite claiming under oath that he had been alarmed and distressed, the circumstances captured on his own footage told a different story.


The prosecution was unable to produce further evidence demonstrating that Henty had experienced the alarm or distress alleged.


Henty spun a yarn of lies that should never have made it to court.


The judge’s conclusion


Having heard Henty’s evidence under cross-examination and considered the footage and relevant law, the Judge concluded that:


Henty had parked his vehicle alongside the saboteurs’ vehicle of his own accord.


He had got out of his vehicle voluntarily.


He had chosen to film the encounter.


He had continued the interaction of his own accord.


He had not contacted the police immediately, instead reporting the incident to 101 approximately two hours later.


These circumstances were central to the Judge’s assessment of Henty’s claim that he had experienced fear, alarm and distress. Following Henty’s evidence and cross-examination by the prosecution and defence, the case concluded without our hunt saboteur needing to take the stand.


The verdict

:

Not guilty. Acquitted.


After all the allegations, the police involvement, the CPS proceedings and the considerable expenditure of public resources, the case ended in an acquittal. A considerable amount of time, money and public resources had been spent pursuing this matter, only for the court to reach a conclusion that raises serious questions about why the prosecution was pursued in the first place.


Hunt saboteurs will not be intimidated out of exposing illegal hunting. And they will not be silenced by allegations that cannot withstand scrutiny in court.


The South Suffolk One stands vindicated.


SAVE THE SOUTH SUFFOLK ONE!


South Suffolk Hunt Sabs remain steadfast and will not be intimidated or silenced.

Wolves are also a big part of the trophy hunt which means that their lives will be sold to the highest bidder, both legally and illegally.

Hunt Saboteurs Sweden intends to make the hunting difficult and prevent the killing in every possible way to protect the wolves. We will do everything in our power to protect and save these innocent and amazing creatures from the hunters bloodlust.

WHY DONATIONS ARE NEEDED: Unfortunately it costs a lot to sabotage a hunt. The sabs needs food and shelter but also cars and petrol since the hunt is taking place in the woods and sometimes very far away from the society. We always make sure to choose the cheapest options of everything.

WHY TO PROTECT THE WOLVES: Hunt Saboteurs Sweden is an anti-hunting and antispeciesist organization that fights for and protects the wild animals against hunters and their psychopathy. We are dedicated to animal liberation. This means we work with groups locally, nationally and worldwide who fight to end domination and injustice.

We take direct action peacefully when needed on the fields to stop the hunt and slaughter of our wildlife. Not everyone can join us on the fields but anyone can play an important role. Fundraising and raising awareness are as important as the sabbing itself.

author: Jana Hoger
title: Update: Polizeihund bei Demo misshandelt – Staatsanwaltschaft stellt Ermittlungen ein
content:
Symbolbild


Bei einer Demonstration gegen den AfD-Parteitag am 11. Januar 2025 in Riesa kam es zu

gewaltsamen Einsätzen

 der sogenannten Polizeihunde. Wir von PETA Deutschland kritisieren dies scharf, erstatten Strafanzeige gegen die Verantwortlichen und fordern, dass der Einsatz von Polizeihunden endlich beendet wird. Erfahren Sie hier, was bei der Demonstration vorgefallen ist und warum Gewalt gegen „Polizeihunde“ kein Einzelfall ist.


Update vom 7. November 2026


Staatsanwaltschaft Dresden stellt Verfahren ein


Nachdem im Januar 2026 ein Video für einen medialen Aufschrei sorgte, das zeigt, wie ein sogenannter

Polizeihund

 bei einer Demonstration gewaltsam gegen einen Demonstranten eingesetzt wurde, erstatteten wir von PETA Deutschland Strafanzeige gegen die Verantwortlichen.


Im August 2026 wurde bekannt, dass die Staatsanwaltschaft Dresden in dem Fall nicht weiter ermittelt – angesichts des traurigen Videos mit absurden Begründungen. Die Staatsanwaltschaft erklärt diese Entscheidung in dem Einstellungsbescheid damit, dass ein „Verstoß gegen das Tierschutzgesetz […] nur vorliegen [würde], wenn man einem Tier ohne vernünftigen Grund aus Rohheit erhebliche Schmerzen zufügen würde.“ Der im Video dokumentierte Umgang des Beamten mit dem Hund sei keine „Rohheit“ im Sinne des Tierschutzgesetzes, da die ergriffene „Maßnahme […] zum Aufrechterhalten der öffentlichen Sicherheit und Ordnung erforderlich war […]“ und der Hund „nur kurz eingesetzt“ worden sei.


Die Staatsanwaltschaft begründet die Entscheidung darüber hinaus damit, dass „Diensthunde […] legal bei der Polizei als Hilfsmittel auch in Stresssituationen eingesetzt […]“ werden. Die Tiere würden dabei automatisch Belastungssituationen ausgesetzt. Die Interessen und das Wohl der Hunde rückten jedoch im Verhältnis zu den polizeilichen Interessen der Gefahrenabwehr in den Hintergrund, da die „Diensthunde“ zu diesem Zwecke ausgebildet würden. Der den Hunden zugeschriebene „Nutzen“ rechtfertigt laut Ansicht der Staatsanwaltschaft Dresden, dass die Tiere bewusst in Gefahrensituationen gezwungen werden.


PETA kritisiert Entscheidung der Staatsanwaltschaft: Gesetz erlaubt Gewalt gegen Diensthunde


Die Einstellung unserer Anzeige ist ein weiteres Beispiel dafür, dass das Gesetz die „Diensthunde“ nicht vor einem gewaltsamen Umgang und Missbrauch schützt. Hunde sind keine Einsatzmittel, sondern fühlende Lebewesen, die einen respektvollen, liebevollen Umgang verdient haben – nicht die missbräuchliche Verwendung  als Waffe oder Schutzschild.


Wir vertreten die Ansicht, dass moderne Polizeiarbeit ohne Tiere auskommt und fordern daher Politik und Behörden auf, „Diensthunde“ zu verbieten.


Originaltext vom 13. Januar 2025


Gewalt gegen Polizeihunde bei einem Einsatz gegen Demonstranten in Riesa


Videos von der Demonstration zeigen deutlich wie gewaltvoll einige Diensthundeführer:innen mit den „Polizeihunden“ umgehen. Einer der

Hunde

 wurde von einem der Beamten am Hals gepackt und gegen eine Leitplanke und einen Demonstranten gedrückt. Dadurch sollte der Hund offensichtlich dazu gebracht werden, den Demonstranten zu beißen. Der Hund zeigte hierbei unübersehbare

Anzeichen

 von massivem Stress, Überforderung und Meideverhalten. Ein weiterer völlig überdrehter Hund verbiss sich in den Arm eines anderen Polizisten.


https://www.instagram.com/p/DExO_Z1Mcvv/?hl=de


PETA erstattet Strafanzeige und fordert den Einsatz von Polizeihunden zu beenden


Dieser gewaltsame Umgang der Einsatzkräfte mit den Hunden ist tierschutzwidrig. Hunde sind nicht dazu da, für die Arbeit der Polizei ausgenutzt zu werden. Wir fordern deshalb, den Einsatz von Hunden bei der Polizei endlich einzustellen. Zudem erstatten wir bei der Staatsanwaltschaft Dresden Zweigstelle Meißen Strafanzeige gegen den verantwortlichen Polizisten. Ferat Kocak, Abgeordneter der Linken war als parlamentarischer Beobachter vor Ort und hat sich bereit erklärt in der Strafanzeige als Zeuge aufzutreten.


„Die aktuellen Aufnahmen aus Riesa zeigen eindeutig, dass Hunde bei Polizeieinsätzen nichts zu suchen haben. Wir hoffen, dass es den betroffenen Hunden gut geht und sie keine körperlichen Schäden von dieser grausamen Behandlung davontragen. Die Psyche der Hunde leidet nach solch einem Einsatz ganz sicher. Hunde sind von Natur aus freundliche, soziale Lebewesen. Durch gewaltsame Trainingsmethoden werden sie bei der Polizei ‚scharf gemacht‘ und zu einer Art Waffe konditioniert – gegen ihren Willen. author: hsa_oryx
title: OCTOBER ROUND UP
content:
First conviction under Hunting with Dogs (Scotland) Act 2023


October kicked off with

Glasgow Hunt Sabs

 reporting that Claire Bellamy, ex-huntswoman and former Master of the Lauderdale Hunt, was found guilty under the Hunting with Dogs (Scotland) Act 2023. Footage which was obtained by sabs shows hounds chasing a fox outside the area covered by a licence that had been granted by NatureScot, and was described by the judge as “

gut wrenching

.” This is the first ever conviction under the new Scottish legislation and you can learn more about the legislation in Scotland and what led to Claire’s conviction

here.


Claire Bellamy found guilty of deliberately hunting a fox with dogs in January 2025.

Image: Glasgow Hunt Sabs


Drone theft


On the 3

rd

 of October Dorset Borders Sabs reported that their drone had been stolen by The Cattistock Hunt as they hunted in Corscombe, Dorchester. The last image visible on the drone was a known member of the hunt running towards it in a field. The incident has been reported to the police and thanks to the generosity of supporters

Dorset Borders Sabs

 raised enough funds to replace the drone.


What do you do when you receive a CPW? If you’re a fox hunt then you break it as soon as possible of course


It didn’t take the Four Burrow Hunt long to break their Community Protection Warning (CPW) which had just been freshly issued by Devon and Cornwall Police. On the 10

th

 of October the hunt was caught breaking condition 7 of the CPW, by failing to give police 24 hours’ notice of their meet. As they had failed to give the details of the meet this means they won’t have provided a map of their “trail” meaning they will have broken more conditions that just number 7. It remains to be seen what action the police will take.

Read our recent article about CPW’s.


Four Burrow Hunt were issued with a CPW after years of trespass and livestock worrying.

Image:


Kernow Sabs, Monitors and Animal Rights Team-Cornwall


Stag hunting horror continues


The horror of stag hunting has continued to escalate in the south west. On the 12

th

 of October the Quantock Staghounds hunted a stag towards the A39 between Nether Stowey and Holford. This is a stretch of road where the hunt are continually causing chaos and putting people’s lives in danger.


This particular incident resulted in a

hunted stag running across the road and colliding with a car.

 A witness described how the terrified stag “

was flipped over the top of the car. Its leg kicked out smashing the rear nearside window. The Stag landed heavily on the verge.”

 Luckily the woman driving and her small child were not hurt but were badly shaken up.


The cruelty doesn’t end there. Two weeks later

North Dorset Hunt Sabs

 reported that the Quantock Staghounds had once again inflicted sickening suffering and pain on a stag. This particular large stag had a visibly infected wound on his side and it is also suspected he had a broken leg. These injuries unfortunately indicate that it is likely the stag that was hit by the car. Despite these injuries the hunt continued to torture him, subjecting him to a chase through thick gorse which no doubt would have caused him unbearable pain.


A stag hunted and terrorised by the Quantock Staghounds.

Credit: North Dorset Hunt Sabs


On the 22

nd

 of October hunt master of the Quantock Staghounds, Christopher Gibbons and huntsman Martin Watts, appeared at Taunton Magistrates Court. Gibbons is facing two counts of hunting a wild mammal under the Hunting Act, and Watts is facing one relating to the barbaric five-hour chase and ultimate

killing of a stag on the 23

rd

 of April 2026

. Both have pleaded not guilty and the case has been adjourned until the 18

th

 of January 2027 for a case management hearing; no trial date has been set. In the meantime, the Quantock Staghounds are continuing to commit abhorrent levels of animal cruelty whilst putting the safety of the general public at great risk.


This stag was tortured for five hours and ultimately killed on the 23

rd

 of April by the Quantock Staghounds.

 Huntsman and hunt master have both pleaded not guilty to charges under the Hunting Act.

Credit:


Mendip Hunt Sabs


They’re blatantly hunting foxes


Amidst the CPW’s, convictions, court hearings, road chaos and trespassing, foxes are still being chased, like the one pictured below.


Beds and Bucks Hunt Sabs

 along with

Peterborough Hunt Sabs

 have been keeping the pressure on …

author: PETA-Team
title: Neue Aufdeckung: Kamele in Marokko für Tourismus missbraucht
content:
Recherchen von PETA Asien dokumentieren immer wieder wie

Kamele

 in der marokkanischen

Tourismusindustrie

 ausgebeutet werden. Die Tiere, die für Ausritte ausgenutzt werden, werden geschlagen und ohne Schutz vor der Witterung angebunden. Sobald sie keinen Profit mehr einbringen, werden sie im Schlachthaus getötet. Erfahren Sie hier, wie es den Kamelen in Marokko geht und was Sie dagegen tun können. 


PETA Asien deckt erneut auf: Missbrauch von Kamelen in Marokko  


PETA Asien hat 2026 erneut die Misshandlung von Kamelen am Rande der Sahara in Marokko aufgedeckt, wo die Betreiber:innen sie zwingen, Tourist:innen durch die trockenen Wüstendünen zu tragen:  


Die Tiere sind außerhalb ihrer Einsätze häufig angekettet und schutzlos extremer Hitze, intensiver Sonneneinstrahlung und Sandstürmen ausgesetzt. 


Viele Kamele verbringen einen Großteil ihres Lebens isoliert und haben kaum die Möglichkeit, sich frei zu bewegen oder Sozialkontakte zu pflegen.  


Die Kamele werden meist nur dann von ihren Ketten befreit, wenn sie kurz Wasser trinken dürfen oder um weitere Tourist:innen durch die Wüste zu tragen. Ein Kamel wurde dabei beobachtet, wie es nicht nur zum Trinken, sondern auch zu einem Pfosten rannte, um sich dort zu kratzen. Es wurde jedoch zurück zu seinem Anbindeplatz gejagt.  


Tierhalter:innen schlugen Kamele wiederholt mit Peitschen, traten sie und zerrten gewaltsam an ihren Schwänzen. 


Kamele sind intelligente, soziale Wesen mit eigenen Bedürfnissen, Wünschen und Interessen. Wenn sie frei in ihrem natürlichen Lebensraum umherstreifen, leben sie in Herden und kommunizieren miteinander durch Laute und Körperbewegungen. Als Zeichen der Freundschaft blasen sich Kamele manchmal gegenseitig ins Gesicht. In der Tourismusindustrie müssen diese Tiere ein Leben lang Elend und Leid ertragen.


 PETA Asien Recherche aus dem Jahr 2025


Bereits 2025

veröffentlichte

PETA Asien

 Videomaterial, dass die Ausbeutung und Misshandlung von Kamelen in Marokko dokumentiert.

Das beunruhigende Video zeigt Kamele, die an nur wenigen Meter langen Seilen angebunden sind. Ein Betreiber wurde dabei gefilmt, wie er ein gefesseltes Kamel wiederholt mit einem langen Stock schlug, während das Tier versuchte, den Schlägen auszuweichen. Ein weiterer Betreiber erklärte den

Ermittler:innen

, dass Kamele, die bis zu 40 Jahre alt werden können, in der Regel etwa fünf Jahre lang ausgebeutet werden, bevor sie getötet oder als

Fleisch

 verkauft werden.


Globales Muster der Grausamkeit


Frühere PETA-Untersuchungen von Kamel- und Pferdebetrieben in Ägypten offenbarten ähnliche Misshandlungen: Tiere wurden blutig geschlagen, gezwungen, Menschen in brütender Hitze ohne Zugang zu Schatten oder Wasser zu tragen, und wie Müll entsorgt oder ins

Schlachthaus

 geschickt, wenn sie zu alt, krank oder verletzt waren, um noch „nützlich“ zu sein. Airbnb, booking.com, Klook, Marriott und viele andere Unternehmen erklärten sich bereit, die Werbung für Tierfahrten bei den Pyramiden von Gizeh einzustellen, nachdem sie von PETA über das Leid der Tiere informiert worden waren.


So können Sie Tieren in der Tourismusindustrie helfen


Tourist:innen, die für Kamelritte bezahlen, halten diese herzlose, unmenschliche Industrie am Laufen. Wenn Sie einen Urlaub planen, vermeiden Sie Angebote mit Tieren und entscheiden Sie sich für tierfreundliche Alternativen. Unterstützen Sie unsere Petition, um das Leid der Kamele und Pferde bei den ägyptischen Pyramiden zu stoppen.  


		Jetzt unterschreiben!


The post

Neue Aufdeckung: Kamele in Marokko für Tourismus missbraucht

 appeared first on

PETA Deutschland e.V.

.

title: No Land, No Hunting
content:
Thank you to West Midlands Hunt Saboteurs for this guest article.


On Thursday 8th October, West Midlands Hunt Sabs (WMHS) held a protest outside The Bower House in Shipston on Stour. The restaurant is owned by Andrew Stephen Bower Knight, who continually allows, not only the Warwickshire Hunt to illegally hunt foxes on his land at Compton Scorpion, but the North Cotswold Hunt too.


The protest caused quite a stir amongst the pro-hunt community prompting the British Hound Sports Association (BHSA) to publish a social media post stating

“Rural businesses are under attack by urban saboteurs.”


Visitors to The Bower House in Shipston on Stour were made aware that business owner, Andrew Stephen Bower Knight, enables illegal fox hunting.


The campaign against the Warwickshire Hunt is one that spans back years and is steeped in controversy, including the fact that Warwickshire Police entered into a “secret deal” with the hunt when they withdrew the Community Protection Notice that they had been issued.


WMHS have always highlighted the importance of holding landowners to account, something which featured heavily in the campaign against the now defunct Atherstone Hunt. The Hunting Act stipulates that should a landowner allow the hunting of a wild mammal with dogs on their land then they are breaking the law.


Demonstrations took place outside businesses that supported the now defunct Atherstone Hunt.

© West Midlands Hunt Sabs


Section 3.1 of the Hunting Act 2004 states;

“A person commits an offence if he knowingly permits land which belongs to him to be entered or used in the course of the commission of an offence under Section 1.”

Section 1 of the Hunting Act states;

“A person commits an offence if he hunts a wild mammal with a dog.”


“Trail” hunting does not exist, a fact which was openly discussed during a 2020

webinar

 held by the then Hunting Office, now the BHSA. It was the hunting community who coined the term “smokescreen” to describe “trail” hunting, as they discussed ways that hunts could continue to break the law. Now they are acting the victim, especially when landowners are reminded of their part in this pantomime.


WMHS work alongside other anti-hunt groups such as Locals Against the Warwickshire Hunt and Warwickshire Hunt Watch to use a varied approach to their campaigning. One of which is writing to landowners to remind them of their responsibilities and to inform them of what the Warwickshire Hunt are capable of.


As well as detailing the contents of the Hunting Act, the letters remind landowners that only last year, Ben Halsall of the Warwickshire Hunt was convicted under the Hunting Act after a fox was killed. The letter also states that the presiding judge at the trial made a statement that there was

“no evidence at all of any trail being laid.”


In 2023 this fox was killed by the Warwickshire Hunt, on land owned by Marcus Dill of Idlicote House Estate. Hunt member Ben Field was found guilty; however, no charges were brought against Marcus.


The letter goes on to say that

“The new huntsman, Jack Weedon has previously been caught on camera blocking an active badger sett in a Site of Special Scientific Interest and has recently been cautioned under a Section 4a Public Order offence.”


The protest held on 8th October took place during a book signing event by Dame Prue Leith. The aim; to make people aware of the fact that the business, through its owner, is linked to illegal fox hunting. However, the pro-hunt community have tried to claim that by protesting, sabs are putting people’s livelihoods at risk, rather than focusing on the fact that the only person putting any livelihood at risk is Andrew, by continuing to break the law and enable an illegal fox hunt.


If people choose to not use an establishment or support a business because they facilitate fox hunting, that’s their prerogative.


The Warwickshire Hunt have already lost a lot of land, some of which is through landowners rescinding their permission due to public outcry. In October 2025 Warwickshire Christmas Tree Farm very publicly withdrew permission for the hunt to use their land, stating that due to the public’s disgust at their affiliation with the Warwickshire Hunt they were left with no choice.


Warwickshire Christmas Tree Farm publicly withdrew permission for the Warwickshire Hunt to use their land.

title: Hatimoğulları: Now is the time to expand the ecological struggle
content:
Tülay Hatimoğulları, co-chair of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party), criticized the UN Climate Summit COP31 in Antalya as a platform serving the interests of governments and major corporations. At a press conference with representatives of the ecology movement, she accused those responsible of using climate protection as a pretext to legitimize an economic system based on limitless growth, exploitation and the destruction of the natural foundations of life.


Hatimoğulları spoke during protests against the official climate conference. Alongside COP31, ecological and civil society organizations in Antalya are organizing an alternative People’s Climate Summit. The DEM Party politician welcomed activists who had traveled from various regions and paid particular tribute to the resistance of women, farmers, young people and workers against the destruction of their living environments.


“COP31 is nothing but exploitation”


The DEM Party co-chair fundamentally questioned whether the very governments and corporations whose economic and energy policies have significantly contributed to worsening the climate crisis could be expected to develop solutions to it. “COP31, jointly organized by the state and capital, represents the domination of capital over life, the exercise of power over society and the plundering of nature. It is nothing but exploitation itself,” Hatimoğulları declared.


The climate crisis, she said, is not merely an ecological problem but a reflection of social power relations. “The climate crisis is a question of class exploitation and justice. Its root cause is the insatiable greed for profit.”


In this context, she also recalled the deaths of 19 workers at HABAŞ in Izmir. Hatimoğulları blamed the disregard for occupational safety regulations and the profit-driven interests of company management for the deadly working conditions. She noted that workers who sought to protest against these conditions had reportedly been attacked by the gendarmerie. She stressed that the DEM Party stands alongside the workers and supports their struggle for decent working conditions.


Ecological destruction in Kurdistan is increasing


A particular focus of Hatimoğulları’s speech was the expansion of mining and energy projects in Kurdistan. She warned that the economic exploitation of the Kurdish provinces was accelerating precisely at a time when peace and a democratic solution to the Kurdish question were being discussed. “Today, as we discuss the Peace and Democratic Society Process and the guns have fallen silent, we are witnessing capitalism and capital rapidly advancing into the Kurdish provinces,” she said.


The DEM Party co-chair noted that the government and major corporations have already carried out extensive interventions in nature in the Aegean, Black Sea and Mediterranean regions, and are now increasingly targeting the Kurdish provinces with similar projects.


“This is not merely about exploiting natural resources, but also about destroying long-established social environments and ways of life,” she underlined.


“The village where we were born, the summer pastures we migrate to, and the fields where we earn our livelihoods are living environments. For the people who live there, this land, these trees and natural resources are neither objects nor commodities.” Hatimoğulları pointed to protests against controversial energy and mining projects in Sur in Amed (Turkish: Diyarbakır), Varto and Diyadin, as well as ecological resistance movements in Artvin, Gümüşhane, Uşak and the highlands of the Black Sea region.


She described these struggles as manifestations of a common conflict between the livelihoods and well-being of local communities and an economic policy that subordinates natural resources to corporate exploitation. She sharply criticized Law No. 7554, which ecological initiatives have described as the “Plunder Law.” Remarking that the legislation was passed despite resistance from social movements and the parliamentary opposition, she said: “We do not recognize Law No. 7554. As far as we are concerned, it is null and void.”


Oil discoveries in Gabar and contradictory climate policies

author: Corey Larocque
title: Let’s hope ‘build, baby, build’ doesn’t overshadow environmental protection
content:
We’re starting to see what it means to be “masters of our destiny,” to “build Canada strong” and to “build, baby, build.”


Those are expressions associated with Prime Minister Mark Carney’s bullish approach to strengthening Canada’s economy in the face of uncertainty by building big infrastructure projects — and building them fast.


Two recent Nunavut-related steps signal a willingness to ease off conventional safeguards in the interest of stimulating the economy. Carney’s Liberal government is considering

lifting the moratorium

 on oil and gas exploration in the Western Arctic. And its adviser on the impact of proposed developments in Nunavut says the proposed Iqaluit Nukkiksautiit Hydro Project does not require a

public review

.


In 2016, a Liberal government under then-prime minister Justin Trudeau imposed a ban on offshore oil and gas exploration in the Western Arctic. The risk of spillage could be disastrous to a delicate ecosystem and pristine wilderness.


But when Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne unveiled the 2026-27 budget on Nov. 5, it included funding that will be used to consider lifting that ban. Since taking over as prime minister in 2025, Carney has relaxed his party’s environmental protection standards in favour of strengthening the economy by building so-called “nation-building” infrastructure projects.


Coincidentally, a day before the budget’s release, the Nunavut Impact Review Board issued its screening decision that the proposed hydroelectricity generator near Iqaluit does not require a public review.


The Iqaluit Nukkiksautiit Hydro Project is a proposal to build a $500-million hydroelectricity generator near Iqaluit. It would generate up to 30 megawatts of power and reduce Iqaluit’s reliance on burning diesel fuel to produce electricity.


The federal government referred the hydro project to its Major Projects Office, making it eligible to be fast-tracked through the regulatory process.


But the Qikiqtani Inuit Association — whose own business development arm, Qikiqtaaluk Corp., owns Nunavut Nukkiksautiit Corp., the company pitching the project — said it’s concerned about not having a “full public review.”


Go figure! The proponent of a multimillion-dollar construction project wants a review, but the review board that advises the government doesn’t. It seems a little backwards.


The hydro project is still in the planning stage, and its size, location and design are being finalized, the board said. Environmental, socio-economic and technical studies are underway, and it’s undergoing other reviews, including by the Nunavut Planning Commission. Federal permits will still be needed for specific activities, the board said.


NIRB did note the project will reduce diesel use, support Inuit jobs and business opportunities.


You have to wonder if NIRB would have taken that stance if it had screened the hydro proposal before Carney started talking about “nation-building” and created the Major Projects Office.


Or is the board taking its cue from Ottawa — the government wants to move quickly on what it calls “nation-building projects” like the hydro plant — and not getting in the way?


In any case, Nunavut has recently and quickly encountered two big economic projects with the potential to generate both jobs in Nunavut and government revenue. But they also bring the risk of adverse environmental impacts.


We need to hope that the enthusiasm for building big and fast doesn’t cancel out the safeguards that have traditionally been in place to prevent environmental disasters.

author: Chantal Eco
title: Will the new FPIC guidelines fast-track the Pax Silica hub in ancestral lands?
content:
Indigenous Aytas from different villages in Capas, Tarlac, listen to an environmental advocate during a community gathering on August 16, 2026, to discuss the impacts of the proposed Pax Silica hub on their land. Photo by Chantal Eco / Bulatlat

“It was really built to cater to corporations. Any semblance that it protects IP rights and allows Indigenous peoples to say no is gone.”

Mandor Matias, 45, has lived all his life on his family’s land in Sitio Binyayan in Capas, Tarlac. He and his relatives plant rice and vegetables on about three hectares of land. But on July 15, employees from the Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) came to his house. They pointed to the planted land in front of it, handed him a paper to sign and offered P30 (USD 0.47) per square meter, or about P900,000 (US$ 14,100) for all three hectares.

“They gave me a paper and asked me to sign it. I said I didn’t need to sign it. If I signed it, it would be as if I had accepted payment,” Matias told Bulatlat in Filipino.

He was not told why they were being pushed to sell their land. He later learned through social media and then confirmed by their village head, that the Pax Silica hub, a U.S.-backed hub for artificial intelligence and semiconductor manufacturing, will be built on their land.

Matias is an indigenous Ayta. His home and farm now lie within the area of the proposed Clark Advanced Manufacturing Park, a 1,620-hectare hub in New Clark City that the BCDA is developing with the United States under the Pax Silica framework. Their fate may now be decided under new consent rules. In May, the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples (NCIP) approved the contentious amendments to the guidelines on free, prior and informed consent (FPIC), and a copy was only released publicly in September. The 2026 guidelines shorten deadlines, approve permits automatically when officials fail to act on time, and let some government projects pass with a document review instead of a full community vote. Indigenous groups warn the rules could clear the way for Pax Silica and other “development projects” on ancestral lands.

The FPIC process could take months to years, especially when a project could greatly affect the ancestral land and the community is divided. The new FPIC guidelines run on tight deadlines: seven working days for the NCIP’s field investigation, 10 days for community assemblies on large projects and up to 60 days for the community to decide. If NCIP officials fail to act on time on a completed consent report, the certificate is issued automatically.

Government-funded projects need only a document review if they are “non-commercial.” Those with private partners or long-term impacts go to Category A or B, as the regional director decides. Projects that displace residents fall under Category A, the strictest track. But a project can get its certificate even before it is clear which households will be affected. Protections for those families can be settled later. Meanwhile, even after a community says no, the applicant keeps the right to refile.

Funa-ay Claver, an Indigenous youth leader and spokesperson of Katribu, said the BCDA may avoid FPIC altogether by insisting that no Indigenous people live on the site.

“It was really built to cater to corporations. Any semblance that it protects IP rights and allows Indigenous peoples to say no is gone,” Claver explained in Filipino.

She said the categories depend on a project’s scale, not on how many people it affects, and that manufacturing hubs are not mentioned anywhere. She added that the NCIP never released a draft for public comment.

Katribu said it is wary of even calling on the BCDA to “uphold FPIC.” Under the new rules, Claver said, consent risks becoming a checklist that only clears the way for the project.

At a media forum of the Foreign Correspondents Association of the Philippines (FOCAP) in September, BCDA President Joshua Bingcang claimed that they have always consulted communities whenever there’s a project or development within New Clark City. While showing pictures of what he described as consultations, he did not specifically say that they have already consulted, much less secured the consent of the Aytas living in the area where the Pax Silica hub will be built.

He called the hub site “already BCDA property” and promised, “We will not just kick them out… there will be consultations.”

Trade Undersecretary Ceferino Rodolfo, who was on the panel, said the site’s …

author: Lisa Sorg
title: Critics Slam Department of the Interior’s New Strategic Plan for Public Lands
content:
They say data center developers, mining firms, and energy companies could seize the opportunity to acquire vast tracts.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

The U.S. Department of the Interior could transfer swaths of public lands to state, local and tribal governments through sales or land swaps, according to the agency’s new strategic plan.

Critics are concerned that many states, cities and counties can’t afford to maintain the lands, and would sell them to private interests — the first step toward a wholesale privatization of lands that have belonged to Americans for more than 150 years.

“This is the biggest attack we’ve ever seen on public lands,” said Kate Groetzinger, communications director for the nonprofit Center for Western Priorities.

The Interior Department did not respond to requests for comment.

The agency manages more than 500 million acres of land in addition to 3.2 billion acres of offshore resources and 700 million acres of underground minerals. All told, the department manages 20 percent of the country’s lands, from national parks to wildlife refuges.

Data center developers, mining firms and energy companies — all favored industries of the Trump administration — could seize the opportunity to acquire vast tracts for their environmentally harmful operations, critics say.

The plan says Interior “will work to decrease the size of the federal estate” through the sales. That will allow the department to “focus its resources on primary federal responsibilities and nationally significant federal lands,” according to the plan, with some of the sales proceeds going back to “the purchasing entities to use for conservation purposes.”

The plan also says the agency will “consolidate its workforce to advance operational efficiencies.” Interior has already lost more than 17 percent of its workforce under the second Trump administration.

In the plan’s introduction, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum wrote that the agency will streamline environmental reviews and expedite leasing and permitting for energy companies. Nowhere in the plan does the agency mention wind or solar power. The first goal outlined in the plan is “Increase American Prosperity,” and the opening pages feature pictures of an oil rig and an offshore oil operation.

“Together, we can simplify processes and remove red tape that creates drudgery for our team members and impedes progress,” Burgum wrote. “We can bring forward new ideas and better ways of working. For the first time in human history, we can turn electricity into intelligence.”

Burgum has made millions of dollars off investments in artificial intelligence, powered by data centers, ProPublica reported Nov. 6.

The plan doesn’t specifically identify data centers as potential customers to purchase federal property, but the White House previously asked Bureau of Land Management state offices to identify lands that would be appropriate for these uses.

Last June, BLM approved an AI data center on 81 acres of public land near Boulder City, Nevada. The builder had received federal approval in 2023 to construct a solar farm, but amended its application to include a data center.

A federal judge has halted the project because BLM did not conduct a new environmental analysis but rather used the previous one for the solar project, a likely violation of the National Environmental Policy Act.

Energy and mining interests have long sought — and received — access to the oil, gas and minerals beneath public lands via leases. The new Interior plan would allow BLM to sell or transfer those properties outright to agencies that could then resell them.

The plan runs from fiscal year 2026 to 2030. However, the Trump administration has already begun planning to offload some public lands in particular.

This September, the Forest Service, which is under the U.S. Department of Agriculture, issued a permit to Pitkin County in Colorado to manage a section of the White River National Forest that contains the Maroon Bells Scenic Area, the gateway to stunning burgundy peaks where hundreds of thousands of recreators visit annually. Critics see this move as a trial run for public land transfers.

In Alaska, the federal government is expected to soon open 28 million acres to new development and land ownership, according to the Juneau Independent.

author: Rishika Pardikar
title: African Arguments Interview with Dr Antwi-Boasiako Amoah Ahead of COP31
content:
The 31st climate talks (COP31) began in Antalya,

Türkiye

on 9 November

.

The African Group of Negotiators (AGN), an alliance of all of the 54 countries from the continent, had submitted three agenda proposals to the UNFCCC for the conference. One concerned a demand to triple adaptation finance, the other related to trade-related climate measures like carbon border taxes and the last one was about financing arrangements under the Green Climate Fund (GCF), a climate fund established under the UNFCCC to assist developing countries in mitigation and adaptation. None of the three proposals made it into the final agenda adopted for COP31. However, the COP31 presidents said negotiation tracks concerned with trade-related climate measures and the GCF will take the respective matters under consideration during negotiations in the following days. If the proposals by AGN were accepted, all three themes would have been negotiated as separate agenda items in their own right. 


Nevertheless, the fact that AGN made three submissions shows that the bloc seeks to assert its voice on the global stage.


After the agenda was adopted Dr Antwi-Boasiako Amoah, chair of the AGN from Ghana, said in the plenary ‘Africa comes to Antalya with one clear message: implementation depends on means of implementation. Our continent contributes the least to this crisis and is among the most exposed to its impacts.’ It was in this spirit, the chair added, that AGN had proposed three agenda items and also that it participated actively in the negotiations on the agenda and supported the conclusions that were reached. 


With COP32 scheduled to be held in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, African Arguments interviewed Dr Antwi-Boasiako Amoah about AGN’s priorities for COP31 and the outcomes it hopes to secure to build momentum towards the next climate summit:


AA: What are AGN’s priorities for COP31? 


Firstly, thank you for the interview. We all need to be speaking to each other in this precious space.


Since the adoption of the Paris Agreement, we have been able to set up a number of structures for implementation. There are methodologies and structures for the implementation of Article 6 [on carbon markets]. Countries have submitted their NDCs [Nationally Determined Contributions] and NAPs [National Adaptation Plans]. Over 80 developing countries have submitted NAPs–this is more than half the number of total developing countries. Even on Article 13 on enhanced transparency framework, we have a solid framework to make sure reporting on climate action is taken care of. So, the groundwork for implementation has been laid. The question now is whether we implement it and how we implement it. Our focus for COP31 and COP32 is to actually bring the issue of implementation to reality. And here, we need to talk about finance, technology and capacity. We are coming to COP31 believing we can make progress on the finance work programme and on the goal to triple adaptation finance. We also come to COP with an understanding that trade-related issues impede our development, especially on climate-related measures [like carbon border taxes]. This COP is mainly about support for implementation. Ambition goes not only with NDC targets and creating awareness but also financial support. Because temperature goals can only be met if developing countries have resources to meet their mitigation targets and other long-term strategies.  


AA: AGN was the first group that brought the Global Goal on Adaptation (GGA) to worldwide attention in 2013 with a submission to the UNFCCC that linked global adaptation efforts and costs to temperatures. Then in 2015, GGA was incorporated into the Paris Agreement, as a result of a collective push by the G77+China bloc. Now, more than a decade into this process, do you see progress? What have been the major successes and roadblocks? 


When we first submitted the GGA proposal [in 2013], it sounded strange to a lot of stakeholders, especially developed country parties. I remember it very well because I was a part of the process. The initiative and the understanding from our side, as Africa, was to give visibility to adaptation within the global climate negotiations and provide space for the mobilisation of resources to address adaptation activities across countries. I would say that we have seen success because nobody believed GGA would be adopted as part of the Paris Agreement. But now have a whole Article 7 that focuses on adaptation. Through …

author: Nina Garcia Steel
title: Crossing Dimensions of Pain Without Losing My Soul
content:
A

s I sit here in my—as I like to call it—Oasis in the Desert, looking out my window at the morning clouds gloriously dancing to the tune the songbirds sing every morning is simply a treasure. I can smile at the sun and sway with the wind as it tickles my senses. I enjoy this morning view as I sip a cup of sweet herbal tea and take in the rays of light.


There was a time when such treasures were absent in my mind. I was living with undeniable pain that I could not explain, except in my poetry.


Photo by Nina Garcia Steel


It’s my heart that aches the most.


The feeling of nerves tearing and bones slowly breaking.


Flares of fire running through my veins.


The words that everyone took as metaphorical were literal words of agony from trauma that started decades earlier. It would take over half a century to discover the root cause of the autoimmune conditions that developed, the near dementia scares. At one point, I was having severe neurological attacks where I lost control of my limbs entirely, making them feel as though they were being tossed around like a rag doll. I picked three alcoholic husbands and stayed in abusive relationships. Little did I know that all of this was coming from the same place:

unprocessed trauma

.


It took me by surprise too. I had been making decisions about who I chose to be my mate based on what I thought was normal from what I experienced as a child. I had suffered sexual abuse more than once, starting when I was only 7 at the hands of a friend’s oldest brother, then an uncle who was visiting, with the worst culprit being my own father. What does a horrific experience like that do to the mind of an innocent child? Nobody was ever prosecuted, my therapy was abruptly stopped, and nothing was done. Left without justice or support, I was left to navigate the aftermath entirely on my own. This meant those early patterns quietly and unknowingly dictated my choices for years.


Decades later, the trauma manifested itself as depression. The connection wasn’t obvious because nobody asked the core question: What happened in your childhood?


So many individuals struggle with trauma that they cannot even name, for we are told, even by medical professionals, that we must focus on our future and that going backward is not in their school of thought. However, trauma is the poisonous seed that grows weeds of unnecessary pain that need to be destroyed at the root.


I walked with pride for so many years, challenging the status quo despite what had happened. I buried it without realizing that everything always comes back if not properly addressed. The pain of betrayal is doubly sharp when there’s unprocessed trauma in the background. It is unfortunate that the questions that could have shaped my treatment were not asked.


I always did things differently, even as early as 6 years old when I was selected to teach a kindergartener English, showing a precocious initiative and drive to bridge gaps long before I understood what systemic obstacles even were. I remember thinking that it was important for my student, Alicia, to learn hopscotch as that would make it easier for her to integrate with the other children. I was an ESL assistant from third to sixth grade. Selling shiny rocks door-to-door for ice-cream money at age 6, writing formal letters in Spanish to my grandfather at age 8. At just 14 years old, I served as the inventory buyer for our family shoe store. I was entrusted to travel on buying trips with an adult and curate the shoes for our inventory.


Learning the mechanics of commerce, spatial merchandising and inventory selection at such a young age taught me how to analyze systems, spot value, and exercise practical strategy long before I ever had to apply those skills to my own survival. At 15, that same drive led me to approach my high school principal with a proposal to redesign the school uniform. I saw how the existing uniforms lacked functionality and aesthetic timelessness, so I designed an updated, structurally timeless uniform that my school adopted. I was already practicing the art of seeing what needed change, organizing a solution, and taking decisive action.


I dared not dwell on the horror of the abuse I had experienced, not realizing that my body would keep score. At that stage, blocking the pain was pure survival. I hadn’t yet allowed my mind to acknowledge the true scope of what had happened — confronting it all at once would have destroyed me, so I compartmentalized …

author: Unknown
title: Varto Ekoloji Platformu’ndan, Doğu Anadolu Kalkınma Ajansı’nın toplantı planına tepki
content:
Varto Ekoloji Platformu Varto kültür Merkezinde, Doğu Anadolu Kalkınma Ajansı tarafından düzenlenmesi planlanan etkinliğe tepki gösterdi. Daha önce Muş’ta halktan ve ekoloji örgütlerinden gizlenerek yapılan toplantıda, daha sonra jeotermal güzellemesi yapıldığının ortaya çıkması üzerine, benzer bir etkinliğin de Varto da yapılması tepki çekti. Platform tarafından paylaşılan açıklamada, Varto halkının, toprağını ve suyunu hedef alan, halkın yararına olmayan sömürü projelerine karşı 8 aydan fazladır iradesini direnerek ve mücadele ederek net bir şekilde gösterdiği vurgulandı.

Açıklamada, Varto halkının mücadelesine rağmen düzenlenmesi planlanan toplantıya karşı, “Varto Kültür Merkezi’nde sözde bilim insanı İskender Dölek’in katılımıyla gerçekleştirilmesi planlanan toplantı, halkın aylardır sürdürdüğü bu kararlı direnişi kırma ve doğamızı yıkıma uğratacak projeleri meşrulaştırma çabasıdır. Halka ait kamusal alanların, Varto’nun geleceğini karartmak isteyenlerin propaganda alanı haline getirilmesini kesinlikle kabul etmiyoruz. Bilim; şirketlerin fonlarıyla hareket edenlerin değil, halkın ve doğanın hakikatini savunanların yanındadır” ifadelerine yer verildi.

Açıklamanın devamında, şu ifadelere yer verildi:

“Bu doğrultuda Varto Ekoloji Platformu olarak açık tavrımızdır:

Fonlu ve Şirket Odaklı Anlayışa Soruyoruz:

Sermaye grupları ve maden/enerji şirketleri tarafından fonlanan, talan projelerine zemin hazırlayan bu sözde bilgilendirme toplantılarını hangi çıkarlar karşılığında yürütüyorsunuz?”

STK, kurum ve muhtarlara çağrı yapılan açıklamada, “Varto halkının 8 aydır ilmek ilmek büyüttüğü direniş iradesine sahip çıkın. Şirket fonlarıyla hazırlanan bu meşrulaştırma toplantısına kesinlikle katılmayın, boykot edin” çağrısı yapıldı.

Kamusal mekan vurgusu yapılan açıklamada, “Varto halkının ortak malı olan alanların, halkın onaylamadığı sömürü projelerine tahsis edilmesini reddediyoruz. Varto halkı toprağına, suyuna ve yaşam alanlarına sahip çıkmaya; bu sömürü projelerine karşı mücadelesini kararlılıkla sürdürmeye devam edecektir” denildi.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: groundxero
title: 544 Scientists and Researchers Stand with Siang Valley Anti-Dam Movement; Demand Halt to Mega Project and Release of Detained Activists
content:
“We stand with the people of the Siang Valley in their struggle to protect their river, their lands, their rights and the ability to determine their future. We recognise that the people who call this valley home must have the primary say in determining its future.”


 


Groundxero

 Desk


 


In a strong show of solidarity with the indigenous Adi communities resisting the proposed 11,000 MW Siang Upper Multipurpose Project (SUMP) in Arunachal Pradesh, a group of 544 scientists, researchers, and concerned citizens working in the fields of nature, wildlife, society and the environment has called on the Union and state governments to immediately halt all pre-feasibility activities, withdraw additional security forces from the valley and release anti-dam protesters detained and arrested under the stringent Unlawful Activities Prevention Act (UAPA).


 


The statement, issued on November 9, 2026, comes amid growing resistance in the Siang Valley to the proposed mega-dam and reports of intensified security deployment, restrictions on people’s movement, arrests and the use of force against protesters.


 


The signatories, many of whom have worked in Arunachal Pradesh and the Eastern Himalayas, describe the Siang Valley as an ecologically irreplaceable landscape of immense biodiversity, cultural significance and traditional knowledge. Referring to an earlier statement by 114 scientists issued on June 9, 2025, they point out that 48 new species and 140 new distribution records have been documented in the valley in the past 15 years alone.


 


The statement warns that large-scale construction in an ecologically fragile and highly seismically active river system could have irreversible consequences. It emphasises that the Siang River, its forests and surrounding mountains sustain not only rich biodiversity but also the livelihoods, cultural identity and traditional knowledge systems of indigenous Adi communities.


 


The scientists express particular concern over the Arunachal Pradesh government’s continued efforts to push ahead with the project’s Pre-Feasibility Report (PFR) despite sustained opposition from affected communities. They condemned the militarisation of this otherwise peaceful region, restrictions on movement, arrests and detentions of local anti-dam activists, and the use of tear gas and force against protesters. They also denounce the alleged harassment and intimidation of lawyers, journalists and others standing in solidarity of the movement.


 


Invoking the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP), the signatories assert that the project must not proceed without the free, prior and informed consent of the affected indigenous communities, whose lands, livelihoods, cultural heritage and relationship with the Siang are at stake. They also stressed on the constitutional guarantees of freedom of speech, expression and peaceful assembly.


 


The statement calls on the Arunachal Pradesh and Union governments to stop all PFR-related activities, withdraw additional armed forces from the region, release those detained for participating in the movement, and initiate an open and meaningful dialogue with the affected communities.


 


The signatories affirm that the people who have protected and sustained the Siang Valley for generations must have the primary say in determining its future.


 


The full statement along with the list of signatories is published below:


 


November 9, 2026


 


We, a group of scientists, researchers, conservation practitioners and concerned citizens, many of whom have worked in Arunachal Pradesh and in the Eastern Himalaya, stand in unequivocal solidarity with the people of the Siang Valley in their opposition to the proposed 11,000 MW Siang Upper Multipurpose Project (SUMP).


 


The Siang Valley is not merely a site for a proposed mega-infrastructure project. The Siang River, its forests and the surrounding mountains sustain extraordinary biodiversity, livelihoods, traditional knowledge systems and the cultural identity of indigenous Adi communities.


 


A statement issued by a collective of 114 scientists on 9th of June 2025, noted that the Siang is a rich living landscape of immense ecological, cultural and biological significance. In the past 15 years alone, there have been 48 new species described, as well as 140 new distribution records from the valley.

author: dialogocomospovos
title: Somos Filhos do Tempo
content:
Durante a visita de Moira Millán ao Assentamento Terra Vista, em meio ao intercâmbio com lideranças Guarani, Kaiowá e Terena e à segunda etapa do Curso de Filosofia da Terra, a liderança mapuche aprofundou sua formação sobre a luta do povo Mapuche.


Em outro momento, Moira abordou a liderança como algo que não se reduz a figuras humanas: “O povo Mapuche não tem liderança humana. A liderança é a terra. A terra diz o que temos que fazer”, afirmou, explicando que esse dizer se manifesta por sonhos, sinais e pelo animar da vida. Para ela, os povos indígenas vivem mais de um plano de existência e enxergam além da terra tangível.


A organização social mapuche, disse, é horizontal e circular, e cada pessoa nasce com um propósito e um espírito preparado para cumpri-lo — como as mulheres e homens medicina. O cacique, nesse horizonte, não decide nem é o líder: aconselha e organiza com a gente. Moira também refletiu sobre a Ateja, espaço de identidade e memória que não se limita à produtividade.


Criticando a cultura dominante, que diz que somos filhos da história, ela propôs outra compreensão: “A história é um segmento, um retalho de narrativa que os humanos contam”. Ser filho do tempo, para os Mapuche, é algo muito mais longo e profundo — outro conceito de tempo-espaço.

author: Shannia Cabuello
title: Artists, Ayta sing vs Pax Silica
content:
Photo by Shannia Angel Cabuello

Artists and other advocates amplified their opposition against a US-led initiative through song.

On November 6, an artist group launched the anti-Pax Silica anthem “Get Off Our Lands” in a solidarity night filled with protest songs.

Produced by the Concerned Artists of the Philippines (CAP), the song was accompanied by a documentary music video featuring the Ayta community in Sitio Kalangitan, whose ancestral lands and natural resources are threatened by displacement and plunder.

Through the song, CAP aimed to expose the false promises behind the Pax Silica and to condemn those in power who allowed it.

Cultural performances and solidarity messages completed the program as part of the Trump Out campaign and the ‘12 Days of Protests’, building up the major protest actions on November 16 and 17.

Ayta elders also attended the solidarity night and expressed their strong rejection of Pax Silica, chanting “Ako Labay Ya Pax Silica!” (I don’t like Pax Silica!).

They led a community dance ritual to drive away “bad spirits,” which they associate with the Pax Silica Initiative and the impending visit of US President Donald Trump for the ASEAN Summit.

Ayta Chieftain Nelson De Guzman countered the statement of Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) President Joshua Bingcang that no Indigenous community would be affected by the Pax Silica Initiative. He said that no proper consultation was conducted within their community.

“They learned that they were being driven away from their land even before they knew about the project,” said Sandiwa Network project coordinator Gina Cambronero.

“The Pax Silica will kill our future. We nurtured our lands. We cannot allow foreigners to claim it,” said Ayta Indigenous woman Tessie Sanchez.

Sanchez told Bulatlat that planting rice, taro, and sweet potato helped support her seven children. She feared that the signing of the agreement could dry their water sources and take away their farmlands.

“The ruling class used the term pax which meant peace. But is there peace in it? They use it as instruments for deception,” Cambronero said.

“We just want peace in our tribe and in our land,” De Guzman said in the song’s documentary music video.

Around 20,000 peasants and 15,000 Ayta could be reportedly displaced once its Artificial Intelligence hub was established on the 1,620 hectares of land in Tarlac.

The anthem started by introducing the Philippines as a friendly Southeast Asian country that shares its homeland to everyone, even to foreign ones.

The music video explained that Ferdinand Marcos Jr. volunteered to give the agricultural and ancestral lands in Tarlac to the United States to establish an Economic Security Zone.

CAP said that the establishment of an Artificial Intelligence hub in Tarlac and the Luzon Economic Corridor (LEC) in Subic Bay, Clark, Manila and Batangas that claims of job creation and economic security are false promises. The group said that it only “prioritizes corporate profits and militarization, fueling war for the US benefit.”

“In the past years, we have always been at a disadvantage with US relations. There are already several trade agreements that only lead to our losses,” said Attorney Rey Cortez of National Union of People’s Lawyers (NUPL).

Cortez added in a solidarity message that it only allowed for the United States to mine the country’s lands and determine how to exploit its resources. He described the government’s marketing of the country’s environment and sovereignty as unconstitutional, as only the Filipinos are allowed to explore the Philippines’ critical minerals.

“Development should not be measured by the number of investments, infrastructure, and technology advancements. Its effect on the people, community, and environment must also be analysed,” said College of Social Work and Community Development Dean and CAP member Justin Nicolas.

Arthur Cadungon of CAP and writer of Get Off Our Lands said that the anthem is not just for the fight against the Pax Silica Initiative, but also a song of protest against the reclamation of Manila Bay, Laguna Lake, and Pasig River Expressway (PAREX).

title: Today’s Our Day
content:
By

Rosario Brenda Gonzalez


 


The streets were once more filled with the voices of the young


The cries against what would probably be a done deal


That would displace our Indigenous Peoples


Wreak havoc on our natural resources


Continue the sale of our cheap labor


And without our national sovereignty


Scenes of past betrayals and oppression emerged


Alongside years of strength in struggle


Of lives, rights and cultures lost


With every tear that we shed


Sleep that refused to find us


Nightmares that haunt the consciousness


Are the victorious fights for decreased land rent,


elimination of usury and better working conditions


The organized communities of the marginalized


Asserting and pushing for meaningful change


Scenes that make us look far beyond our lifetime


As today’s events took the young outside their classrooms


With placards, with chants


With dance, songs and poetry


Filling our hearts with hope


Now and for always

author: Aaron Hemens, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: ‘It’s all about taking care of people’: How a smǝlqmíx farmer is building food sovereignty at ntámłqən
content:
Dixon Terbasket, the founder of ntámłqən Community Garden in smǝlqmíx homelands, walks through the farm’s greenhouse on Sept. 15, 2026.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


The potato plants are so tall that their stems reach Dixon Terbasket’s eyes.


He remembers walking through his family’s garden when he was three or four years old, more than 60 years ago, in a community where his mom, all his aunties and uncles, grew food in gardens and orchards — and stored them in root cellars, too.


Now, Dixon finds himself leading his own food sovereignty initiative that he hopes will equip the next generation of smǝlqmíx (Similkameen) people with the knowledge and skills to farm on their own.


“I want to give them at least a running chance, man,” Dixon told IndigiNews.


The ntámłqən garden is in unceded smǝlqmíx territory in the lower Similkameen Valley, in the southern Interior of “B.C.” It shares its nsyilxcən name with the adjacent community elementary school, meaning “gathering place.” Dixon said his people have gathered here since time immemorial.


The ntámłqən Community Garden in smǝlqmíx homelands on Sept. 28, 2026. Photo by Aaron Hemens


At ntámłqən, a 7.5-acre community garden and food hub on Lower Similkameen Indian Band (LSIB) land near “Cawston,” he works with a small but dedicated crew of staff and volunteers to teach people life skills — from growing their own food; to sharing it with the community; and how to preserve what they grow.


At the peak of the harvest season, the garden hosted a free barbeque for the community on Sept. 28, in collaboration with the Indigenous Food Sovereignty Association. 


Rumy Muenala helps prepare food for a community BBQ at the ntámłqən Community Garden in smǝlqmíx homelands on Sept. 28, 2026.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


Staff at ntámłqən Community Garden prepare salads during a community BBQ event at the farm in smǝlqmíx homelands on Sept. 28, 2026.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


Dozens of people — Indigenous and non-Indigenous — came together around meals made with ingredients provided by the garden and its partners. Between all the mingling and laughs, they feasted on stuffed-peppers, colourful salads, watermelon, goat meat, apple pie and more.


“It’s all about taking care of people,” Dixon said, echoing the farm’s slogan of “For The People.”


Hannah Field, who co-manages the ntámłqən Community Garden as its coordinator, stands in a prayer circle before a community BBQ event at the farm in smǝlqmíx homelands on Sept. 28, 2026.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


Community members fill their plates with food during a community BBQ event hosted at the ntámłqən Community Garden in smǝlqmíx homelands on Sept. 28, 2026.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


The garden is working towards giving the community the ability to make decisions about their food — and having the knowledge, land and facilities to provide for one another. A processing facility expected to be completed by March 2027 will add space to prepare and store harvests, with opportunities for community food businesses. 


Dixon’s niece, Coven Terbasket, joined the crew in 2024, a couple of weeks after moving back to her ancestral homelands. She was 29 and looking for work when she ran into Dixon at an insurance office in small-town Keremeos. 


For most of her life, Coven had lived south of the colonial border in “Spokane, Washington.” During childhood summers, her mom would send her up to “roam around” LSIB lands with family, usually in their ancestral community of nkʷrulauxʷ (Blind Creek, Place of Yellow Dirt). 


Like her uncle, she remembers family gardens all around Blind Creek, and the work that kept households fed beyond the growing season.


“Everyone had made the time to grow their own food, can their own food, to preserve,” she said.


Coven Terbasket, the administrative assistant at the ntámłqən Community Garden, is pictured at the farm in smǝlqmíx homelands on Oct. 5, 2026.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


Coven hadn’t seen Dixon since she was a child. As they reconnected in the insurance office two years ago, he learned she needed work and offered her a job at the community garden he had been building with a small crew of workers and volunteers for more than a year.


“He told me to show up at the garden the next day at 10 a.m., so I did,” she said.


Coven describes the encounter as fate, saying her uncle “found me” shortly after her return, during a difficult period in her life. 


“It’s freaky how crazy it worked out … me looking for a job; me …

author: Petala Ironcloud
title: Native Youth Programs Are Building a Different Model of Mental Health Care
content:
These models are employing youth and grounding well-being in culture, relationships, and community.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Growing up in Eureka, a small city in Northern California, provided Roger “Chapreges” Jones an anchor in his Yurok culture. He took public K-12 Yurok language classes and Indian Ed covered school supplies. But when his parents divorced and he moved to Redding at 13, those resources vanished — and so did his appetite.

Chapreges got his first job at a Native American mental health clinic while grappling with an eating disorder hidden in plain sight. His new role at Two Feathers Native American Family Services became a kind of Trojan horse: He walked through the door looking for employment and found therapy waiting inside.

Founded in 1998 by a tribal consortium to strengthen Native family units in Humboldt County, Two Feathers has grown significantly since 2018, when its current executive director, Virgil Moorehead, joined. It went from having four staff members to having 32, including mental health clinicians, substance abuse counselors, and cultural coordinators.

Two Feathers serves a disproportionately large Native population across Northern California, where many Tribes and their citizens are either unrecognized federally or have been disenrolled. Critically, it serves Native families regardless of enrollment status — a stance that resists the disenrollment politics that plague underfunded tribes across Indian Country.

Chapreges is one of dozens of Native youth accessing Two Feathers services in a region where waitlists are long and federal funding cuts have gutted alternatives. A 2022 study from the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health echoes mounting research on the importance of cultural connection to Native youth’s mental health.

Chapreges’s experience speaks to that truth. He had struggled to acclimate to Redding without other Native youth or regular cultural resources beyond the annual Stillwater Powwow. In his sophomore year, he and his father, overwhelmed by the isolation, returned to Eureka, where Chapreges completed high school.

The following year, he became a youth ambassador at Two Feathers, promoting their culturally tailored programming: stick games, flower dance, trips to the local powwow, and the Young Bucks and Spotted Does programs for youth ages 8 to 12.

Moorehead is also a licensed clinical psychologist and has helmed a new era for the organization, implementing circular Native philosophy by creating a continuum of school- and family-oriented treatment services for Native youth and their families. Two Feathers’ approach reflects a broader Indigenous understanding of mental health that recognizes the effects of historical trauma while at the same time accounting for the distinct experiences of different Native communities.

One such program, the Acorn Youth Wellness Program, works with youth individually to bolster their cultural identity. “But I think giving them hope, you know, sense of belonging,” said Moorehead, “Those are all things that are measured.”

Moorehead said the program tracks attendance, cultural identity, and hope for the future. “I always say that if you don’t have kids that come to the program, you don’t have a program. And so through the way we did Acorn, it engaged kids and had them show up in the sense of coming back and back and back.”

In 2020, the California State Assembly’s Select Committee on Native American Affairs conferred the honor of a plaque, letter, and on-site visit recognizing the organization’s work to improve and stabilize the lives of Native youth and families in Northern California. The program’s success has attracted interest from other Native Nations seeking to replicate the model. Moorehead said he’s in early conversations with one tribe planning to launch their own version next year, though he declined to name specific nations in preliminary stages.

Another member of the Two Feathers staff, Jayla, who asked to be identified by first name only to protect her privacy, joined the organization at age 15 after seeing an employment ad. A year into her time at Two Feathers, in 2025, President Donald Trump proposed consolidating behavioral health funding. Despite the fact that Trump’s proposal has only been partially implemented, Jayla still sees the impact of it firsthand …

author: Kerry Smith
title: Socialist Alliance: Funding cuts to Villamanta throw people with disability on scrap heap
content:
Brenden Grull, Socialist Alliance spokesperson and candidate for Geelong, has called for funding cuts to Villamanta, Geelong’s Disability Rights Legal Service, to be reversed.

The community-based service, which is housed in Geelong West but works across Victoria, fights for the rights of people with disability-related justice issues. It has been operating since 1990.

The Department of Health and Ageing said on November 10 that it would be cutting approximately 30% of Villamanta’s total funding and around 50% of its core funding.

“It is almost unbelievable that as the demand for disability advocacy increases and in defiance of the Disability Royal Commission’s recommendations to recognise independent advocacy as a vital safeguard for people with disability that Villamanta’s funds are being cut so significantly,” Grull told Green Left.

“I understand that the decision will have an immediate impact; it will lead to substantial job losses. I presume that this is part of the federal government’s cuts to NDIS services.

“It is particularly shocking when independent reviews have recognised that Villamanta is a leader in best-practice disability advocacy and community legal support.”

Grull said the cuts will “only cause more pain and suffering for clients and workers”. He said as cost of living pressures rise for everyone, these cuts show federal Labor’s “diminishing commitment” to community-based organisations.

“Labor’s preference is for dodgy providers from the private sector.”

Grull said Socialist Alliance backs Villamanta’s campaign to get the funding cuts reversed and to protect access to independent disability advocacy.

“We support the reintroduction of publicly-funded disability services to fix gaps in the National Disability Insurance Scheme. Villamanta has our 100% support and we will be doing everything in our power to help restore its funding.”

author: Chiara Joos
title: Das Recht auf sexuelle Selbstbestimmung
content:
Zwangssterilisation ist verboten. Dennoch erfahren Frauen mit Behinderungen häufig Druck von Angehörigen, Ärzt*innen oder Betreuer*innen, sich sterilisieren zu lassen.

Weißt du, wie viele Menschen ich begleitet habe, die darunter gelitten haben, dass sie sterilisiert wurden?“, fragte mich eine Beraterin am Telefon. Sie schult Menschen mit Behinderungen in Selbstbestimmung. Es war eines von hundert Gesprächen, die meine Kollegin Ramona Arzberger und ich geführt haben, um zur Verhütungspraxis bei Menschen mit Behinderungen zu recherchieren. Nach fast einem Jahr ist daraus der Film „Hauptsache, du kriegst kein Kind“ unseres Magazins „andererseits“ entstanden. Er begleitet mehrere Frauen in Deutschland und Österreich, die mit Lernschwierigkeiten leben und auf Unterstützung angewiesen sind. Drei von ihnen sind sterilisiert. Keine entschied allein. Elf Prozent der Frauen in deutschen Einrichtungen geben an, sterilisiert zu sein, so der Forschungsbericht zu Gewalt und Gewaltschutz in Einrichtungen der Behindertenhilfe des deutschen Bundesministeriums für Arbeit und Soziales von 2024. In Österreich waren es zuletzt 17 Prozent. In Deutschland habe fast die Hälfte der Betroffenen den Eingriff nicht von sich aus gewollt, heißt es in dem Bericht. In Österreich taucht in Befragungen dasselbe auf: Eltern, Ärzt*innen und Betreuer*innen hätten auf die Frauen eingewirkt. „Ich will auch mitmachen!“, platzte die Stimme von Hannelore Trtil ins Telefon, noch ehe meine Kollegin erfuhr, wer da sprach. Die 66-Jährige hatte unseren Flyer gesehen, der Betroffene erreichen sollte. In den 1980er-Jahren wurde sie in Wien „unterbunden“, ein anderes Wort für sterilisiert. „Die haben alle gesagt, man darf keine Kinder kriegen. Das habe ich nicht richtig gefunden. Und das habe ich nicht gewollt“, sagt sie im Film. Heute verbringt sie oft Zeit mit Kindern. Ihre OP-Akte hat das Krankenhaus vor etwa zehn Jahren vernichtet, nach Ablauf der Frist für Schadenersatz. Sie wird nie erfahren, welche Art von Sterilisation bei ihr gemacht wurde. Hannelore sagt auch, sie habe nie Sex gehabt, aus dem ein Kind hätte entstehen können. Diesen Satz haben wir in unseren Recherchen nicht nur von ihr gehört. Thea, die in Wirklichkeit anders heißt, wurde 2025 sterilisiert, in einem Alter, in dem manche noch nicht an Kinder denken. Sie auch nicht. „Weil für uns schon klar war: Das lassen wir.“ Gemeint sind sie und ihre Mutter. Das Wohnhei…Teile diesen Artikel
