author: Sharon Zhang
title: Fresh Off Electoral Defeat on Iran War, Trump Floats New Military Front in Cuba
content:
The Trump administration’s fuel blockade has already been likened to an act of war by critics.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

President Donald Trump said this week that he wants to “get Cuba done” before his term is over, casually saying that he is considering opening yet another military front in a country whose civilian population is already being killed and starved by his sweeping sanctions campaign.

When asked by conservative talk show host Hugh Hewitt on Thursday whether or not he would use military force in Cuba, Trump said he “would certainly consider” a military campaign on the small island nation.

“I want to get Cuba done before I leave, yeah,” said Trump.

“We have a very good, talented guy for Cuba named Marco,” Trump went on. “Because Marco’s parents are from — Marco Rubio, his parents are from Cuba, as you probably know and he would love to do that. So we’re watching it very closely. It’s doing very poorly, it’s essentially a failed place, nation, whatever you want to call it, it’s failed. And we’re watching it. I would like to be able to do it.”

The suggestion to open a new military front comes despite voters delivering Trump and the Republicans a historic loss in last week’s midterm elections, due in large part to his failed war on Iran.

Cuba is indeed “doing very poorly” due in large part to the U.S.’s decades-old sanctions regime. The U.S. has held an embargo prohibiting U.S. businesses and citizens from conducting trade with Cuba since the 1960s, which had already had severe deleterious effects on the country.

Trump’s severe escalation in the sanctions regime, including the fuel embargo, is currently killing even more people in Cuba. As of June, childhood cancer survival rates in the country had declined from 85 percent to 65 percent since Trump’s sanctions were imposed, with medicine supplies reaching critically low levels. Infant mortality also doubled in that time, to 9.9 per 1,000 births, compounding on the existing effects of U.S. sanctions; according to an analysis this April by the Center for Economic and Policy Research (CEPR), the U.S.’s sanctions regime caused 1,800 excess deaths of infants between 2017 and 2025.

“The Trump policy of ‘maximum pressure’ on Cuba has killed a lot of babies — and, although we don’t yet have data for the last few months, it’s highly likely that more babies are dying now, and at an even higher rate than last year as a result of the current U.S. fuel blockade targeting Cuba,” said CEPR report coauthor Alexander Main at the time.

The U.S.’s fuel blockade, meanwhile, has led to numerous near-total or total blackouts across Cuba this year, leaving Cubans literally in the dark as they clamor for basic food and medicine supplies. Experts have said that the blockade is akin to an act of war.

The Trump administration has not shown any signs of letting up on Cuba. Just last week, Rubio and the Trump administration instituted yet another wave of sanctions targeting Cuba. Trump and Rubio have openly called for regime change. Two weeks ago, Rubio issued an open call on X for people to open a “discrete [sic] partnership with the CIA” if they seek change in Cuba, in concert with the CIA’s Cuba task force set up earlier this year.

In remarks on Monday, Trump said, on Cuba, that he “imagine[s] it will fall fairly soon.” The same day, Rubio criticized the Cuban “regime” and said that the U.S.’s goal is for Cubans to “wake up and realize that there is no future on the path they are on right now.”

author: CMI Argentina
title: La inflación de octubre fue del 2,2 por ciento y suma 26,3 en el año
content:
La inflación de octubre volvió a superar el 2% y alcanzó el 2,2%, según informó el Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Censos (INDEC). Con este resultado, el Índice de Precios al Consumidor (IPC) acumuló un incremento del 26,3% en los primeros diez meses de 2026 y del 33,1% en los últimos doce meses.


El dato de octubre fue el más alto desde abril, cuando la inflación había alcanzado el 2,6%. Además, se ubicó 0,3 puntos porcentuales por encima del registro de septiembre y terminó superando las previsiones de analistas y consultoras privadas.


El mayor aumento se registró en vivienda, agua, electricidad, gas y otros combustibles, con una suba del 4,2%, impulsada principalmente por el incremento del gas. Le siguieron Recreación y cultura, con el 3,3%, y Bienes y servicios varios, con el 2,3%. Las tres divisiones se ubicaron por encima del promedio general.


En tanto, prendas de vestir y calzado aumentó un 2,2%; Transporte, un 2,1%; y Comunicación y Alimentos y bebidas no alcohólicas, un 2% en ambos casos. Por debajo del nivel general quedaron Salud (1,8%), Restaurantes y hoteles (1,5%), Equipamiento y mantenimiento del hogar (1,4%), Educación (1,3%) y Bebidas alcohólicas y tabaco (0,8%).


En la división por regiones, tres jurisdicciones superaron el índice nacional: la región Pampeana registró una inflación del 2,6%, la Patagonia del 2,5% y Cuyo del 2,3%.


Por otra parte, el informe del INDEC detalló que los precios estacionales tuvieron el mayor incremento, con un 5,5%, mientras que los precios regulados subieron un 2,9%. La inflación núcleo, que excluye los componentes estacionales y regulados, fue del 1,5%.


De esta manera, el índice continúa con una dinámica de subas y bajas que se observa desde julio, cuando había sido del 2,1%. En agosto llegó al 1,7%, el registro más bajo del año, mientras que marzo continúa siendo el mes de mayor inflación, con un 3,4%.

title: Trump Subpoenas Teachers Union for Info on Pro-Palestine Students (The Intercept)
content:
The expansive subpoena asked the American Federation of Teachers headquarters for information related to a vandalism case against Michigan students.

Activists gather at a pro-Palestine encampment at the University of Michigan’s campus on April 24, 2024, in Ann Arbor, Michigan.Photo: Adam J. Dewey/Anadolu via Getty Images

The Trump administration quietly broadened its crackdown on campus pro-Palestine protests over the summer, moving to ensnare one of the largest unions in the country in a case revolving around alleged incidents of vandalism.

The national headquarters of the American Federation of Teachers, or AFT, received a grand jury subpoena in August as part of an ongoing federal investigation into protests at the University of Michigan. Twelve pro-Palestine activists have been charged with felonies in the case.

The subpoena against the AFT, which has not been previously reported and was obtained by The Intercept, shows the administration casting a wider net in its investigation into student protesters than was previously known.

“They’re using this language around conspiracy and trying to draw in all of these different organizations.”

The Graduate Employees’ Organization, or GEO, an AFT local at the university, also received a notice to provide information and testimony to a grand jury around the same time, according to a copy of the previously unreported subpoena obtained by The Intercept.

The effort to draw a powerful, liberal union into a case that revolves around spray-painting charges represents a dramatic escalation in Donald Trump’s war on the left.

“They’re using this language around conspiracy and trying to draw in all of these different organizations that are taking stances against fascism, against the government, and anything that’s counter to their ideology,” said Natalie Chen, who serves as GEO’s communications director. “This is perhaps another ‘in’ for them to broaden their attack

As pro-Palestine protests swept campuses across the country in 2024 and widespread demonstration broke out against U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement this year, the Trump administration has sought to paint left-of-center protest, nonprofit work, and labor organizing as a nefarious far-left conspiracy, even labeling some activists and groups as terrorists.

Critics of the administration’s crackdown on Palestine solidarity and protests against ICE see moves like the ones against AFT and GEO as part of an effort to silence dissent.

“Historically, federal grand jury subpoenas have been used against social movements and political dissent to gather information, to isolate individuals, and of course to try and prosecute people,” said Xavier de Janon, executive director of the National Lawyers Guild. “What is different in politicized cases is the extent of people and places that get subpoenaed, which many people see clearly goes way beyond what they’re supposedly trying to prosecute.”

Activists at the University of Michigan said the effort to extract information about students from the union was an attempt to further target pro-Palestine protesters and their relationships with labor organizers.

“What is different in politicized cases is the extent of people and places that get subpoenaed.”

The grand jury subpoenas came as part of a case that has seen a dozen protesters become caught up in serious federal charges against the students, dubbed “the Michigan 12.” They allege that protesters committed illegal acts like vandalism as part of a pressure campaign seeking to push university officials to divest school holdings tied to the Israeli genocide in Palestine.

The subpoenas against the GEO and AFT were requested by federal prosecutor Margaret Smith with assistance from FBI agent Kara Phipps — two federal officials deeply enmeshed in the investigation into the Michigan 12. (The Department of Justice declined to comment for this story.)

The subpoenas were issued as the GEO was already reeling after its president, Hiab Teshome, was charged with felony embezzlement by local prosecutors working in conjunction with the University of Michigan Police Department.

Authorities alleged that Teshome, who was a bargaining team member in the middle of intense contract negotiations between the union and the school, misused organizational funds to purchase laptops for a campus club.

author: Chris Walker
title: Poll: Most US Voters Want a Popular Vote Model for Picking Future Presidents
content:
Democrats in several states have indicated support for the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

New polling demonstrates that a majority of registered voters in the United States support changing the method through which presidents are selected.

Currently, the Electoral College is the mechanism used to pick presidents. Each state receives electoral votes equal to its number of congressional representatives — the number of House districts in the state plus its two Senate seats. These electors are directed by their states to vote for a presidential candidate following an election.

For most states, their entire slate of electors is given to the presidential candidate who won the most votes in their state. To win the presidency, a candidate must receive a majority of the tallied Electoral College votes, which is currently 270.

Due to significant population differences among states that are not accurately reflected in the Electoral College, the model can sometimes choose a presidential winner who did not win the popular vote among voters nationwide. Indeed, there have been five elections in U.S. history — including two elections since 2000 — in which the popular vote winner did not end up becoming president.

The post-midterm Economist/YouGov poll, conducted November 9-11, asked respondents whether they favored keeping the Electoral College or preferred to replace it with a popular vote system. Among registered voters, 51 percent said they wanted presidents to be selected through a popular vote, while only 28 percent said they wanted to keep the current system in place. Another 21 percent said they were unsure.

According to the poll, one in five registered voters (22 percent) have either heard of the Electoral College but don’t know how it works, or have never heard of it at all. It’s possible that a large segment of this population of voters would also support a popular vote model if they learned more about the undemocratic way in which the Electoral College functions.

With the results of the midterms flipping several state governments to Democratic Party control, there now exists a real opportunity for lawmakers to implement a popular vote system.

Complete abolition of the Electoral College would require a constitutional amendment. But advocates for a plan called the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact say the rules of the Electoral College can actually be used to create a popular vote system.

Per the Constitution, each state determines for itself how its electors are chosen. If the compact was implemented, states totaling a majority of Electoral College votes would direct their electors to the candidate who won the majority of votes nationwide, rather than the candidate who won the majority of votes in their state.

The compact doesn’t kick in until states totaling a majority of Electoral College votes sign on. As it stands right now, just 48 electoral votes are needed for the compact to go into effect.

In this month’s midterm elections, Democrats won new trifecta governments (e.g., states in which Democrats have control of the state legislature and governor’s office) in Wisconsin, Michigan, Nevada, Arizona, and Pennsylvania. Each of those states has yet to back the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact — but if they do, they would represent more than enough of the remaining electoral votes needed to put it in place.

Lawmakers from those states have indicated that they are planning to pursue that route or are open to the idea of doing so.

Even if those states pass the compact, there’s one more hurdle: Article I Section 10 of the Constitution also requires Congress to approve most interstate compacts. That means the incoming Democratic-controlled Congress must pass a resolution to approve the idea — and that a filibuster by Republicans in the Senate could block it.

That is, unless Democrats change rules in that chamber to limit how and when a filibuster can occur, a matter that is presently dividing members of the party.

En este contexto, organizaciones de jubiladas y jubilados junto a movimientos sociales y partidos de izquierda realizarán una jornada nacional de protestas contra el Gobierno de Javier Milei. La convocatoria central será el próximo miércoles 18 de noviembre, frente a las oficinas de la Administración Nacional de la Seguridad Social (ANSES) en distintas provincias. Los organizadores definieron la iniciativa como un “miércoles federal”, en continuidad con las movilizaciones que los jubilados sostienen desde diciembre de 2023 y que ya acumulan más de 140 semanas consecutivas de reclamos frente al Congreso.


En la Ciudad de Buenos Aires, la protesta comenzará a las 11 frente a la sede de ANSES ubicada en avenida Córdoba 1144. Desde allí, los manifestantes marcharán hacia el Congreso, donde está prevista una concentración a partir de las 15. El principal reclamo apunta a un aumento urgente de las jubilaciones mínimas, que se ubican en $444.158,46, más un bono de $70.000 que permanece congelado desde 2024. De esta manera, el ingreso bruto de quienes cobran el haber mínimo no supera los $514.158,46.

author: Joseph Lee
title: Indigenous leaders at COP31 say it’s past time to turn promises into action
content:
The annual United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change gathering drew historic levels of Indigenous attendance in Belém, Brazil last year, leading some to dub it “the Indigenous COP.” But the event was marked by frustration and

protest

, with many Indigenous leaders calling it little more than a continuation of a longstanding pattern of exclusion from international negotiations. 


This year’s gathering in Antalya, Turkey, is billed as an “implementation” conference

focused less on sweeping new pledges

 than on the procedural work of turning previous agreements into action. For Indigenous advocates, that makes COP31, which started November 9, a test of whether the promises made last year translate into tangible changes, including greater authority over climate action.


“It is still a struggle,” said Edward Porokwa, who is Maasai and a member of the United Nations Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues. “I’m yet to really determine whether there will be any more progress that is made in terms of realization of the rights of Indigenous people.”


Indigenous advocates are pressing governments to follow through on their commitments to secure and strengthen Indigenous land rights on 400 million acres in tropical forest countries, provide

$1.8 billion in funding

, and respect rights to free, prior, and informed consent in the energy transition. 


Despite those pledges, funds have been

slow to reach affected communities

 and Indigenous land defenders say their rights and

lives remain under constant threat

. Porokwa said that he feels that responsibility to address climate change continues to fall on smaller countries and Indigenous peoples. 


The stakes have been particularly stark over the last year. In Nepal, massive floods and landslides in August killed more than 1,500 people and destroyed entire villages. In Canada, a

historic wildfire season

 saw millions of acres burned, causing thousands of evacuations. And in Indonesia, wildfire smoke alone has

caused thousands of deaths

 and led to school closures and other emergency measures across Southeast Asia.


“The recent large-scale mountainside collapse on the border of Nepal and Tibet should serve as a wake-up call to the global community,” said Biswash Chepang, who is a founder of the Institute for Indigenous Affairs and Development in Nepal.


Climate-driven threats to Indigenous peoples and their lands continue to mount as a historically powerful

El Niño

 threatens to drive famine, heat-related deaths, and other catastrophes across the globe.


Read Next


DOGE cuts cost tribes $470M, gutting funding for climate projects


Joseph Lee


The conference comes in the wake of a recent United Nations report that said it will be virtually

impossible to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees

, the goal set under the landmark

2015 Paris Agreement

. Indigenous delegates find that reality particularly frustrating because they see it as a direct result of decision makers ignoring their knowledge and

all the ways

 their

stewardship has been proven

 to

benefit the environment and climate

. 


“For over 30 years we have brought Indigenous knowledges and sciences to these negotiations,” Māori activist Quack Pirihi said in an opening statement on behalf of the International Indigenous Peoples Forum on Climate Change. “Yet emissions continue to rise, putting 1.5 degrees C beyond reach.”


While the work of reducing emissions and protecting Indigenous rights in the energy transition continues, securing funding for nations and communities most impacted by climate disasters is also a priority. In October, the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage approved $21.6 million for Nepal — its first disbursement and less than 1 percent of the nearly $5 billion in damage the country sustained. But the process to receive and administer those funds is

ongoing

, and Indigenous leaders say the fund must work faster. Their push comes as wealthy countries face renewed scrutiny over climate-finance pledges they have failed to deliver.


“Loss and damage is not simply a question of humanitarian assistance,” Chepang said. “It is also a question of climate responsibility, historical emissions, equity, and the right of affected communities to recover with dignity.” 


Indigenous peoples also hope to hold polluters to account. Bianca Ranson, who is Māori and a board member of the Aotearoa Climate Action Network, is attending COP31 in part to highlight the landmark climate …

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: John Amagoalik squares off with GN in court over home-care funding
content:
Nunavut Chief Justice Susan Cooper reserved her decision after hearing lawyers for John Amagoalik argue the territorial government should pay for his private medical care in Iqaluit while government lawyers argued it shouldn’t.


Lawyers for the man many consider the “Father of Nunavut” were in civil court Friday, trying to secure emergency funding to allow him to receive medical care in Iqaluit while

a lawsuit

 he brought against the Nunavut government proceeds.


At issue is the retired politician’s request for approximately $16,000 a month to pay for private support care workers and housing.


Amagoalik says he needs that money so he can live with his wife and family in Iqaluit instead of at a long-term care facility in Ottawa, where he had been living for a year and a half until he returned North in August.


Nunavut’s Health Department has declined the request, saying it’s outside the government’s

legislative authority

 to provide the amount of in-home care Amagoalik needs to stay in Nunavut.


Last month, Amagoalik, 79,

filed an application

 for a judicial review of the Health Department’s decision, which the court will consider at a later date.


The department has so far offered to cover two hours a week of private support care for Amagoalik, which his lawyer Dougald E. Brown said is unacceptable. He currently receives up to 10 hours of care a day.


“This is for an individual who is described in the plan of care as medically fragile,” Brown told Cooper in an Iqaluit courtroom Friday morning. “That is not a scenario that ends well. Mr. Amagoalik would be left vulnerable, and at risk of serious, adverse medical consequences – and I say this candidly – death.”


Brown cited sections of the territory’s Hospital Insurance and Health and Social Services Administration Act and its Boards of Management Dissolution Amendment Act, which he said appear to give the department the authority to fund his care and housing.


Brown told the judge “it is clear” the Health Department does have the legislative authority to grant Amagoalik’s request.


The way the Government of Nunavut has chosen to handle Amagoalik’s pleas for help infringe upon his Charter of Rights and Freedoms rights, Brown said.


Since the 1970s, Amagoalik had lived in Iqaluit with his family, until a surgery resulted in him being sent to the care home in February 2025.


Amagoalik has described his life at Embassy West as lonely and says he was unsatisfied with the care he was receiving.


He cannot and will not return to Embassy West in Ottawa, Brown told the judge.


“A return to Embassy West is not a Charter-compliant option,” he said. “John Amagoalik already experienced life at Embassy West to be psychologically distressing and painful.”


In the afternoon, lawyers for the government took their turn.


“How public dollars are spent and the delivery of public health care is for the legislative assembly” to decide, not the courts, said Craig Boyer, a lawyer for the GN.


Exercising discretion in a way that goes against values in the Charter is not the same as infringing upon someone’s Charter rights, he also said.


“[The Charter] does not provide an unqualified right to healthcare,” he said.


Using that logic, Iqaluit’s hospital would not be considered Charter-compliant, because some higher levels of care, such as certain kinds of cancer treatments, aren’t available there, Boyer said.


Brown, Amagoalik’s lawyer, said however they are “not asking for a restructuring” of the government’s home-care program delivery. Rather, they want the court to assess the reasonableness of the Health Department’s decision not to fund Amagoalik’s home care.


Cooper did not say when she will give a decision on Amagoalik’s application.

author: Andrés
title: Explosión en Remedios de Escalada por negligencia y precarización de METROGAS
content:
Foto: Nico Kobane


En trabajos con una tuneladora, Exgadet SA, una empresa tercerizada de Metrogas, rompió un caño de gas. En lugar de activar  los protocolos de seguridad, llamaron a METROGAS. La cuadrilla de la empresa se acercó al lugar y convino en seguir con el trabajo. El gas se acumuló y la explosión voló en pedazos toda la esquina. 21 personas fueron traladadas, 8 ya fueron dadas de alta. 6 permanecen en estado de gravedad en el Hospital Evita, 5 son empleados de Exgadet. Y 7 quedaron en observación. Hay un muerto y dos desaparecidos. Se demoraron a dos administrativos no jerárquicos y se está realizando la investigación administrativa. Pasadas las dos de la mañana lograron obturar el caño y se apagó el fuego.

Por ANRed.


Foto: Nico Kobane


Los trabajos los estaban realizando este mediodía (13.11.26) en el centro de Lanús, luego de que vecinos sintieran durante días el permanente olor a gas. Con una tuneladora, la empresa EXGADET SA rompió un caño de gas. Llamaron a METROGAS, acudió la cuadrilla, dijo que estaba controlada, pero poco después estalló luego de que el gas se hubiera acumulado, provocando heridas en más de 30 personas, que fueron trasladadas en su mayoría al Hospital Evita, en Lanús.


«Hubo una violación en los protocolos de emergencia. En este momento METROGAS está realizando los cortes al Este, Oeste, Norte y Sur. Por eso en este momento la llama ha disminuido, aunque deben cortar aún sobre la calle Iberlucea. Por el momento, la fiscal ordenó la detención de dos personas jerárquicas de METROGAS. No han disipado con líneas de agua el gas que se fue derramando. La empresa METROGAS decidió mantener en reserva, a pesar de que vecinos dijeran que percibían desde ayer el olor a gas.», testimonIó desde el lugar Claudio Arale, director de Defensa Civil de Lanús.


Foto: Nico Kobane


Hay personas con quemaduras y politraumatizadas por la explosión. 5 cinco obreros de la empresa tercerizada Exgadet S.A. (tercerizada de Metrogas), tienen quemaduras y lesiones de gravedad, entre los que contamos un muerto y dos desaparecidos.


Ante una falla en los protocolos de actuación, la justicia deberá determinar qué sucedió. En el lugar está establecido un comando de operaciones y gracias a los cuarteles de bomberos hermanos ya está todo controlado.


Foto: Nico Kobane


Desde hace días, los vecinos venían avisando sobre el fuerte olor a gas en la zona. Nuevamente, los trabajadores, comerciantes y vecinos son víctimas de la negligencia de las empresas, del gobierno nacional, del provincial y del municipal, que tercerizan trabajos de alto riesgo sin garantizar la adecuada seguridad.


Varias dotaciones de bomberos siguen intervininedo para disminuir las llamas.


Los suministros de gas y luz se encuentran cortados.


Casas, comercios, escuelas y bibliotecas de la zona fueron evacuados.

author: Amy Goodman
title: Nvidia Scandal Has Exposed “How Precarious the Governance of This AI Truly Is”
content:
Tech critic Paris Marx and Professor Ramesh Srinivasan discuss the centrality of Nvidia to the whole AI industry.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including with an employee and a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence officials accuse of spying for Beijing. The company says Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO as the board searches for a permanent replacement.

Nvidia’s computer chips are at the heart of the artificial intelligence boom, driving the company’s value above $4 trillion and making Huang one of the most influential business leaders in the world. His spectacular fall from the company he co-founded in 1993 comes as the U.S. stock market has become highly dependent on a handful of AI-related companies and amid intense competition between the United States and China over control of the technology, with access to Nvidia’s chips becoming a major point of contention between the two countries.

Tech critic Paris Marx notes that the AI industry’s “circular financing,” in which companies are both clients and investors for one another, has created systemic risk.

We also speak with Ramesh Srinivasan, director of the AI Futures Lab at UCLA, who says the “soap opera” of the Huang scandal has exposed “how precarious the governance of this AI truly is,” with only a handful of people and firms controlling “incredibly powerful technology that feeds off of all of us and the planet.”

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: We begin today’s show looking at the fallout from Jensen Huang’s resignation as the CEO of Nvidia, one of the world’s most powerful companies. Nvidia’s advanced AI computer chips have powered much of the artificial intelligence boom. Huang cultivated close ties to President Trump and is credited with helping to shape U.S. policies around artificial intelligence and rules around the export of advanced AI chips.

Huang’s resignation came days after reports emerged he had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman named Alice Huang — no relation — whom U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspected of spying for Beijing and helping China obtain advanced Nvidia chips, which are banned by U.S. export controls. The Information news outlet reports Alice Huang helped route at least $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips to China via a Singapore-based cloud computing company called Megaspeed International. Jensen Huang confirmed he had an affair with the woman. Later, published reports revealed he also had affairs with two employees at Nvidia, including with a senior executive who reported to him.

Nvidia has announced its longtime chief financial officer, Colette Kress, would serve as interim CEO as the board searches for a permanent replacement.

On Thursday, U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche took questions about Nvidia.

REPORTER: When did the Justice Department learn, with regard to Nvidia, that Alice Huang might be a suspected Chinese asset? And there’s been concerns raised that the Commerce Department was giving favoritism to Nvidia and Megaspeed, which is Alice Huang’s company. Do you share the concerns that maybe the Commerce Department was impeding the ability to uncover the smuggling network that Alice Huang was involved in?

ATTORNEY GENERAL TODD BLANCHE: Well, your first question assumes something that I have never said and that I don’t know to be true. So, you assume that DOJ learns that she is, in fact, a spy. I’m not — nobody said that. I certainly haven’t said that. And I don’t — all I said a minute ago, and all that I think I will say, is that, of course, DOJ is investigating or looking at it. So, there’s no — there’s no conclusions reached by the Department of Justice or by me or by Director Patel around who she is or is not.

I don’t have concerns with the Commerce Department. I don’t. We have a good relationship with the Commerce Department. I’ve read some of the stories, which, you know, are sourced or not sourced, and so I don’t have any — but, no, I don’t have — the answer to your question is, no, I don’t have any — I don’t have any concerns.

author: Golnar Nikpour
title: To End Iran War, Democrats Need New Leadership — and a New Approach
content:
Democrats must now reject Schumer and Jeffries’s hawkish status quo on Iran and fully embrace diplomacy.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Tens of millions of voters across the United States issued an unequivocal rebuke to the administration of Donald J. Trump this November by voting for Democratic candidates, including dozens of democratic socialists. The so-called blue tsunami was so thorough that Republican strongholds like Texas and Georgia and Mississippi flipped key offices, while swing states and districts from Pennsylvania to Arizona to Michigan moved comprehensively leftward.

As pundits and politicians have rushed to explain the electoral sea change, one interesting point of consensus has emerged: The U.S.’s and Israel’s war of choice against the Islamic Republic of Iran — an unpopular effort that has spiked gas prices and exacerbated inflation — has proven disastrous for the Republican Party.

On election night, Trump himself stated that “Iran was a piece of” the GOP’s midterm drubbing. Vice President JD Vance echoed this point, calling Iran “the real reason” for the electoral bloodbath. Exit polls confirmed this, showing that 74 percent of voters called the war a “crucial” or the “major” factor behind their vote.

Meanwhile, numerous Democratic candidates made opposition to the war a key part of their campaign messaging. Democratic socialists including Claire Valdez, Melat Kiros, and Darializa Avila Chevalier campaigned on staunch antiwar platforms. On Election Day, hours after news broke of the U.S. again bombing Iran’s Qeshm Island, Michigan’s soon-to-be Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed stated, “We need less war, not more.” North Carolina’s Annie Andrews shared a similar message, calling for an end to “this illegal, unconstitutional, billion-dollar-a-day war overseas.”

This messaging hasn’t been limited to the left wing of the Democratic coalition. Centrist party stalwarts have also claimed that voters have provided a mandate to end Trump’s folly in Iran. In a post-election interview, New York Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand put it succinctly: “We have to end this war in Iran.”

Despite Democrats’ current antiwar messaging and an electoral mandate to end the war, the hawkish logic that undergirds Trump’s approach to Iran has decades of bipartisan support.

But what would it mean to end this war, and are Democrats currently led by those who would earnestly endeavor to do so? Amid questions over future party leadership, key Democrats have promised to pluck off the lowest-hanging fruit in Trump’s war cabinet, such as “Secretary of War” Pete Hegseth. This is welcome news for opponents of a war that has seen Hegseth’s leadership bring an endless litany of alleged war crimes and the mass killing of Iranian civilians.

But ending the war will be more difficult than simply ridding the Trump administration of Hegseth. To halt a standoff that has the potential to spiral into a yearslong slog of pointless violence and global economic devastation, the Democratic Party needs change in its leadership and in its overall approach toward the Islamic Republic.

Despite Democrats’ current antiwar messaging and an electoral mandate to end the war, the hawkish logic that undergirds Trump’s approach to Iran has decades of bipartisan support. This posture was briefly evidenced in unhappy responses to the Trump administration’s short-lived June memorandum of understanding (MOU) to end the war. Even members of the GOP loath to critique Trump lashed out at the MOU upon its release.

Like their Republican counterparts, some powerful Democrats described the terms of the MOU, particularly its financial concessions, as an unacceptable capitulation. While Democratic responses centered Trump’s recklessness in starting a costly war of choice, they nonetheless described Iran in pointedly hostile terms and challenged the wisdom of offering the Islamic Republic diplomatic compromises. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, then the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, called the MOU a “catastrophically bad outcome for a war that should have never happened.” Shaheen continued, “President Trump has offered concession after concession to the Iranian regime for next to nothing in return.” Problematic concessions, per Shaheen, included “sanctions relief, billions in unfrozen funds, $300 billion in fresh investments facilitated by the …

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Schumer, Who’s More Unpopular Than Trump, Gets a Challenger for Majority Leader
content:
Trump has hit record low approval ratings during his second term, but even fewer Americans approve of Schumer.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Maryland) announced on Thursday that he is running for Senate majority leader, posing competition for Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-New York), who is one of the most unpopular congressional leaders this century with an approval rating even lower than Donald Trump’s.

Van Hollen announced that he is vying for the seat in an interview with MS NOW on Thursday evening, saying that voters have handed Democrats a “generational opportunity for the Senate to respond to the call of the American people for change.”

In the half-hour interview about his platform, Van Hollen called for a break from the status quo, saying that he backs numerous progressive populist priorities, like “get[ting] rid of super PACs,” refusing AIPAC funding, and “tak[ing] on a broken economic system that’s rigged” against the working class.

Van Hollen and Democratic advocacy groups have called for the process of choosing a leader to be more democratic, creating a space for the caucus to come together to lay out a plan for the new Congress and have debates on what that may look like. Schumer, on the other hand, has spent the last week speaking as though his leadership is a foregone conclusion.

“I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead,” said Schumer in a statement after Van Hollen’s announcement. “I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader. I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people.”

It’s currently unclear whether or not Van Hollen has the votes to win. He has the support of Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont), one of the most popular politicians in the U.S., and numerous freshman senators who have called for new leadership.

However, polling has found that the public is ready for new leadership in the Democratic Party.

Schumer, who has been the Senate Democratic leader for nearly a decade, is extremely unpopular. NBC polling done late last month found that only 13 percent of voters view Schumer positively, compared to 53 percent who view him negatively — a 40-point gap. This is even worse than Trump’s dismal approval ratings, which have hit new lows in his second term; that same poll found that 60 percent of people disapprove of Trump while only 40 percent approve, a 20-point gap.

Other polls have yielded similar results. A poll by The Economist/YouGov found earlier this month that 54 percent of voters view Schumer unfavorably, compared to 23 percent who view him favorably — giving him a -31-point rating. That poll found that more voters disapprove of Trump, but also that more voters approve of him, at 62 percent to 36 percent, respectively, giving him a -26-point rating.

Schumer is also one of the most unpopular congressional leaders in recent history. According to Gallup polling, 67 percent of respondents said they disapproved of Schumer’s performance in December 2025, compared to 28 percent who approved. This is far lower than his approval rating in 2021, when Schumer had 44 percent approval, and 53 percent disapproval.

Between Rep. Mike Johnson (R-Louisiana), Rep. Nancy Pelosi (D-California), Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-New York), Rep. Kevin McCarthy (R-California), Sen. John Thune (R-South Dakota), and Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Kentucky), only McConnell had worse favorability at any point in his leadership than Schumer, Gallup found. In his last year as leader of the Senate Republicans, McConnell had a 71 percent disapproval rating, compared to 27 percent approval in 2023.

Voters are hungry for change. Polling by Reuters/Ipsos in June 2025 found that the vast majority of Democrats, 62 percent, want the party leaders to be replaced, with only 24 percent saying the leaders should stay the same.

This may be due, in part, to Schumer’s opposition to many of the populist progressive policies that Van Hollen extols. Last year, he taunted Trump for not being more aggressive against Iran and twice folded on a government shutdown while extracting little to no concessions from Republicans on issues like ICE funding. He is a staunch supporter of Israel, including amid its genocide in Gaza, and has not backed proposals like Medicare for All; rather, in recent months, he has backed the pro-data center legislation …

author: Jesse Staniforth
title: 70% of Inuit children live in households that skip meals, eat less to make ends meet: report
content:
A new report on access to food in Nunavut says the territory continues to be in a “food security crisis” and children are most affected. 


“Existing survey data show that 7 in 10 Inuit children in the territory live in households that make sacrifices — skipping meals, eating less, and/or eating lower-quality food to make ends meet,” the report said.  


The 146-page report was written by more than two dozen researchers looking into grocery supports and the Hamlet Food Voucher Program for Nunavut Inuit. 

 


Researcher Vandna Sinha told APTN News that she hopes the new report will be the last word on the subject. 


“We brought together a really great team of researchers from across disciplines and across universities so that we could look at food insecurity, and the effect of these initiatives on food insecurity, in a really comprehensive way and put something out that would hopefully eliminate the need for people to say we need more research,” said Sinha, an associate research professor at the University of Colorado Boulder’s Faculty of Education. 

 


The report,

Strengthening Food Access in Nunavut: Lessons from the Inuit Child First Initiative funded Grocery Supports and the Hamlet Food Voucher Program

,

is the product of work by four researchers from Qupanuaq, which advocates for Nunavut children and youth in partnership with 22 researchers from six universities along with the Institute for Circumpolar Research and BetterCart Analytics.


Sinha, who began research on Jordan’s Principle while working at McGill University in Montreal, said Qupanuaq contacted her to discuss potential research about food supports in Nunavut. She said the research team and the number of local advisors has expanded over the years.

 


Rankin Inlet, Nunavut. Photo: APTN


Beginning with five pages of quotes from Nunavummiut about the strain and challenge of struggling to get enough food — and sacrifices that parents make to give their children better access to food — the report is unequivocal in its findings.


“Food insecurity surveys usually ask about events during the year,” the report noted, “but families in Nunavut faced much more consistent challenges: 8 out of 10 families we interviewed faced daily, weekly or monthly struggles to make ends meet.”

 


New report about an old problem

 


Hunger, food access, food security and food sovereignty are all longstanding concerns in Nunavut, the report noted.


In 2019, the federal government launched the Inuit Child First Initiative (ICFI) — an Inuit parallel to the Jordan’s Principle program designed to provide First Nations children with equal access to health, social and educational services.

 


Initially, the ICFI offered “Grocery Supports” to individual Inuit families who requested them. By 2023, the report notes, individual-family requests for Grocery Supports were overwhelming bureaucrats and creating a large backlog, which led Nunavut hamlets to apply for funding for food-voucher programs that would feed all Inuit children and youth in the communities. 


This was known generally as the Hamlet Food Voucher program (HFV).

 


Baker Lake, Nunavut. Photo: APTN


“By the end of 2024, these programs reached Inuit children in 24 of 25 communities, for an estimated annual cost of just under $100 million,” the report said. “They operated without complex or time-consuming application processes and allowed families to use the funds in ways that complemented their other budget-stretching strategies.”

 


The consequence was immediate; the report found the HFV seems to have reduced physical and psychological harms “by reducing hunger, increasing nutrition, improving physical health, improving quality of life and giving both families and communities greater resources to devote to needs that extended beyond nutrition.”

 


In March 2025, Indigenous Services Canada ended the program, forcing families to make requests for Grocery Supports once again.

 


However, the report notes, “After that, very few requests for individual Grocery Supports have been approved. The treatment of ICFI-funded Grocery Supports requests does not appear to meet the legal standards for responding to urgent cases that have been established for services to First Nations children through Jordan’s Principle, the southern parallel to ICFI.”

 


The number of people seeking daily meals from Iqaluit soup kitchen Qajuqturvik Community Food Centre saw a steady decline after HFV — which reversed when the …

title: “En el conurbano no hay ni pan ni trabajo”: organizaciones movilizaron a municipios y gobernación
content:
13.11.26 Organismos sociales se movilizaron a la gobernación de La Plata


Organizaciones territoriales de la provincia de Buenos Aires se movilizaron en diferentes distritos y en la capital provincial, de manera coordinada, en simultáneo, en reclamo de trabajo y alimentos para miles de familias que vienen siendo afectadas por las crisis social y política que atraviesa el país.

Por corresponsal popular, para ANRed.


A media mañana se concentraron en las puertas de los municipios de La Matanza, Esteban Echeverría, Presidente Perón, Moreno, y una columna de más de 600 personas se movilizó a la Gobernación de La Plata.


“Somos organizaciones independientes que hace años trabajamos en los barrios más humildes de diferentes distritos de la provincia de Buenos Aires, luchando por la defensa de nuestros postergados derechos y desarrollando tareas comunitarias y sociales de lo más diversas. Llevamos adelante espacios comunitarios culturales y de encuentro. Realizamos propuestas productivas y de trabajo, culturales, radios populares, espacios para mujeres y disidencias, ludotecas, diversos talleres, apoyo escolar y alfabetización para niñeces, jóvenes y personas adultas”, relataron los diversos movimientos en la convocatoria.


13.11.26: Movilización a La Matanza


En la capital provincial, además de la Coordinadora por el Cambio Social se sumó al reclamo el movimiento Justicia y Libertad.


“Las políticas del gobierno nacional vienen dinamitando nuestros barrios, donde crece la desocupación y la pobreza.  Esta situación no quita responsabilidad a las autoridades provinciales sobre el abordaje de lo que viene pasando. Venimos a movilizarnos reclamando trabajo para nuestras cooperativas y para miles de familias que hoy comen una vez al día y hacen malabares para llegar a fin de mes”, aseguró Karina Sebastián, integrante del Frente de Organizaciones en Lucha (FOL) durante el corte de cla calle 6, frente a la Gobernación.


13.11.26: Movilización a la Municipalidad de Presidente Perón


Por otra parte, dentro del pliego de reivindicaciones se planteó la necesidad de trabajar un plan de contingencia para las inundaciones y el fenómeno de “El niño” a partir de la generación de puestos de trabajo para la limpieza de arroyos y erradicación de basurales en las zonas bajas de gran parte de los barrios, villas y asentamientos del territorio bonaerense.


13.11.26: Movilización a la Municipalidad de Esteban Echeverría


Según señalaron en la totalidad de los distritos como en los diálogos generados en la capital provincial se dio el compromiso verbal de dar respuestas a las demandas en las próximas semanas.


Por último, los movimientos dejaron planteado el reclamo para que desde el gobierno de Axel Kicillof se construya una mesa de trabajo interministerial destinada a abordar tanto las problemáticas de trabajo y alimentación como las posibles consecuencias que genere el fenómeno de “El Niño”.

author: Shahad Ali
title: 1.4 Million People in Gaza Live in Tents. Winter Storms Can Be a Death Sentence.
content:
Making unlivable conditions even more dire, flooding in Gaza is just the first disaster of a long winter to come.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

The recent deep low-pressure system that struck the Gaza Strip earlier this month resulted in a widespread humanitarian disaster. According to Gaza’s Government Media Office, flooding inundated 70,000 tents, leaving 350,000 people without shelter. The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) also stated that more than 26,000 Palestinian families in the Gaza Strip had requested assistance after their shelters and belongings were damaged by rainfall. In addition, Gaza’s Civil Defense reported that a mother and three of her children died after a rain-soaked sand embankment collapsed onto their tent in Deir al-Balah.

Around 1.4 million people in Gaza — roughly 65 percent of the population — are currently living in tents in overcrowded camps after the Israeli assault destroyed 82 percent of residential buildings. Most are living in worn-out tents that they have been using for years but cannot afford to replace or repair to make them more resistant to heavy rainfall. Shelter materials are extremely expensive in Gaza. For example, a single tent costs around $350, while a tarpaulin costs approximately $50.

For the fourth consecutive winter, Israel continues to restrict the entry of essential winter supplies, including blankets, warm clothing, proper tents, tarpaulins, basic materials needed to repair damaged homes, and heavy machinery required to drain floodwater and repair sewage networks. According to the Al Mezan Center for Human Rights, approximately 200,000 tents across the Gaza Strip have become completely worn out and can no longer provide even minimal protection against cold and rain. The International Organization for Migration has also confirmed that currently available shelter stocks cover only 17 percent of Gaza’s actual winter needs. The organization has stressed that Palestinians in Gaza need more durable and sustainable shelter solutions, including wooden structures, prefabricated housing units, and caravans.

In addition to this suffering, many families have few options but to pitch their tents in areas near the beach, as Israeli forces still control roughly 70 percent of the Gaza Strip within what is known as the “Yellow Line,” leaving more than 2 million Gazans confined to approximately 30 percent of the territory. These coastal areas are particularly vulnerable to flooding. Strong waves can reach far inland, flooding tents and washing them away. The lack of adequate rainwater drainage systems in these areas makes matters worse, as floodwater often mixes with sewage and accumulates around tents, turning their surroundings into pools of contaminated water.

According to OCHA, approximately 950,000 displaced people in Gaza are living in areas exposed to flooding, including more than 400,000 in locations considered at extremely high risk of flooding.

Aya Alshami, 25, a mother of two who is now living in a tent near the Gaza City port, told me that when the deep low-pressure system struck the Gaza Strip, her tent and all her belongings were flooded:

The rain was very heavy. I felt the top of the tent starting to sag and lean towards us. I tried to lift it, but the water had made it so heavy that I couldn’t manage on my own.

Then I heard my children shouting from inside, “Water is coming in!” We wondered where it was coming from. We thought we had secured everything, but then we found water seeping in from all sides.

My husband and I desperately tried to push the water out using a squeegee, but all our efforts were in vain. The mattresses were submerged, our belongings were soaked, and everything was flooded, turning the tent into a pool.

Alshami added that after her tent was flooded, she sat with her children in the street, drenched and shivering, with nothing to keep them warm:

These have been the worst days I have ever experienced. Before the war, winter was my favorite season. We lived in a warm home. I used to prepare sahlab and watch the rain falling while wrapped in a warm blanket. Now, I am literally homeless and helpless.

Although I received a new tent from a humanitarian organization after my previous one was flooded, I am certain it will not withstand the next rainfall. No matter how much you try …

author: Kiara Green
title: Eight Black Women Make History in Georgia Statewide Elections
content:
On November 3, Georgia voters elected eight Black women to statewide office, marking a historic milestone for representation in state government. The victories came as Democratic candidates across the country made significant gains in congressional and state elections, reflecting a shift in the political landscape. Georgia’s results stand out not only for their historic significance, but also for the growing political influence and leadership of Black women across the South.

Over the last decade, Georgia has become increasingly competitive for Democrats, electing Senators Jon Ossoff and Raphael Warnock to the US Senate. This year, the state elected Keisha Lance Bottom, the former mayor of Atlanta, as governor. Bottoms will become the first Black woman governor and the state’s first Democratic governor elected since 1998.

In her victory speech, Bottoms recognized the broader significance of the results, saying, “And just for the people of Georgia, for us to have had the blue wave, or the blue tsunami, as it’s being described in this state, really represents a shift in Georgia, throughout the South, I believe, that’s going to reshape who we are as a party, as a state for many years to come.”

Bottoms shares this historic moment with seven other Black women who have won statewide races in Georgia, marking a historic moment for the South as the political landscape begins to change.

Penny Brown Reynolds, former Fulton County judge and Biden administration USDA official, becomes the first Black woman to hold the position of Secretary of State in Georgia. Tanya Miller, former federal prosecutor and Georgia state representative, becomes the state’s first Black woman elected attorney general.

The other historic winners include Keisha Sean Waites, elected as Georgia’s Insurance and Safety Fire Commissioner; Nikki Porcher as Labor Commissioner; Lydia Powell as State School Superintendent; and Katherine Juhan-Arnold as Agriculture Commissioner. Sheila Edwards was elected to the Georgia Public Service Commission’s District 5 seat. Together, these victories mean Black women will hold seven of Georgia’s eight major executive offices, alongside a seat on the state’s public utility regulatory commission.

The elected candidates now replace Republican white men in a state President Donald Trump led by more than 2 percentage points in 2024.

This victory was championed by Black voters who have been a pivotal voting group despite efforts to redistrict and disenfranchise their vote. In the Georgia state election, 95% of Black eligible voters voted for Democrats. Young Black women aged 18-29 outperformed men and other racial groups with 96% of their votes going to Democrats.

Georgia’s results were part of a broader series of Democratic gains across the South, including elections in North Carolina, Virginia, Mississippi, South Carolina, and Texas. Voters, specifically Black voters, showed up demanding accountability, affordability, and change.

In 2018, the late civil rights activist and Georgia Congressman John Lewis spoke about the future of political representation in the South. During a rally supporting Stacey Abrams, he said, “When the state of Georgia becomes blue, along with the state of Texas, they will not be able to hold us down. It’s gonna happen.” Lewis’s words reflected the longstanding fight for political representation and the power of voter participation. Eight Black women winning statewide office in Georgia marks another historic chapter in that ongoing struggle.

title: Over 200,000 Debtors and Their Allies Demand Student Loan Repayment Pause
content:
The Federal Reserve Bank of New York reports that outstanding student loan debt has hit approximately $1.66 trillion.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

More than 200,000 student borrowers and their allies, as well as a coalition of advocacy groups, demanded Thursday that Democratic congressional leaders seize the moment of their soon-to-be majorities in both houses of Congress to win a student loan repayment pause.

A petition circulated by the Student Debt Crisis Center (SDCC) demanding President Donald Trump act to pause all federal student loan repayments and interest had collected 209,359 signatures as of Thursday afternoon.

The petition accuses the Department of Education under Education Secretary Linda McMahon — who has said she shares Trump’s goal of abolishing the DOE — of having “failed Americans” by moving the student loan portfolio to the US Treasury Department, creating lengthy delays in and “egregious account errors” in application processing, not granting loan forgiveness to qualified borrowers, making repayment less affordable, announcing the end of the Saving on a Valuable Education plan, and restarting interest accrual on SAVE plans. Dozens of Democratic lawmakers last week pressed McMahon to answer for these failures.

“Amid an affordability crisis and the current state of affairs, student loan payments should be the last thing on anyone’s mind,” the petition states. “Student loan payments are an unacceptable source of additional stress for Americans who are already stretched thin.”

Our payment pause petition surpassed 200,000 signatures, but we aren't stopping there. Read the full press release here: www.studentdebtcrisis.org/post/student…Add your name to the petition: actionnetwork.org/petitions/pa…

“We called for a payment pause in 2025, which the Department of Education chose to ignore, but we are resuming our call for a pause right now,” the document adds. “Given the growing economic anxiety and hardship facing Americans, an immediate payment pause is not just necessary; it is imperative.”

SDCC said in a statement announcing the petition:

Following the midterms, affordability is top of mind for millions of Americans. With a new Congress opening the door for real change, beginning with a payment pause would give student loan borrowers necessary relief while the 120th Congress legislates and conducts oversight. Lawmakers are already demanding answers from the Department of Education on their extensive failures managing the federal student loan system. Now, borrowers are holding those in charge accountable.

“The results of the midterm election are undeniable — Americans need relief from the burden of unaffordable living, and they need it now,” said SDCC founder and president Natalia Abrams.

“Implementing an immediate pause on student loan payments and interest wouldn’t just be an effective way of providing relief, it would also free up room in the paychecks of over 43 million borrowers to pay bills, care for their families, and revitalize their local economies,” Abrams added. “It’s a no-brainer.”

The Federal Reserve Bank of New York reported Tuesday that outstanding student loan debt reached approximately $1.66 trillion in the third quarter of 2026, making it the second-largest category of household debt after mortgages.

Meanwhile, Federal Student Aid, a DOE agency, highlighted earlier this year that more than 42 million people hold federal student loans, with the federally managed portfolio alone exceeding $1.64 trillion.

On Wednesday, around 20 advocacy groups wrote to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, both New York Democrats, urging them to pressure Trump to sign legislation pausing student loan repayments after Democrats take back control of Congress in January.

“The student debt system is on the brink of breakdown, and today it functions worse than it did before the COVID-era payment pause,” the groups contended in their letter, referring to the suspension of repayments during the first Trump administration that continued during former President …

author: Chris Walker
title: DHS Brags That It Has Deported Over 483,000 People Over the Past Year
content:
During Trump’s second term, immigrants have frequently been deported to countries where they face immediate danger.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

On Thursday, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announced that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) “broke the record for the highest number of deportations and arrests in any fiscal year.”

ICE conducted “more than 491,000 immigration arrests,” the department said in a press release. Furthermore, the agency deported “more than 483,000” people over the past year.

DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin gleefully celebrated the numbers.

“I couldn’t be prouder of the brave men and women of ICE, who just broke more historic records,” Mullin said.

The numbers were announced just over a week after the midterm elections, in which millions of Americans voted against Republican policies, including many who indicated they were troubled by the Trump administration’s mass deportations. Indeed, in one exit poll, 58 percent of voters said the White House’s immigration enforcement has gone too far.

Even President Donald Trump himself acknowledged in a post-midterm interview that his positions on immigration may have hurt him and his party in the elections, stating that he may have been “too tough.” Despite that assessment, however, Trump has promoted Stephen Miller, the architect of many of his draconian immigration policies, to become his chief of staff.

While the announcement by DHS touted deportations of “the worst illegal aliens,” the department has often targeted people living legally in the U.S. or asylum seekers who have little or no criminal background. Indeed, an assessment by TRAC Immigration finds that more than 7 in 10 of those imprisoned in ICE jails have no criminal conviction at all.

Children have also been detained in immigrant jails under deplorable conditions. Perhaps the most infamous example is the detention of 5-year-old Liam Conejo Ramos, who was abducted after returning home from school and sent to a prison in Texas, where he subsequently became ill due to horrid conditions.

Other prisons have had torturous conditions — at a Florida-based prison nicknamed “Alligator Alcatraz,” for example, guards beat immigrants imprisoned there for merely requesting access to phones. Detainees were also placed in small cages for many hours at a time, and there is evidence that the Trump administration withheld documentation of its torture campaign.

DHS’s human rights violations, lack of respect for due process, and medical neglect have resulted in dozens of deaths of people being detained. Federal immigration raids have also resulted in the deaths of protesters, including Minneapolis residents Renee Good and Alex Pretti, both of whom were killed by federal agents.

During Trump’s second term, immigrants have frequently been deported to countries where they face immediate danger. Many individuals have been deported to countries they have no connection with, and LGBTQ immigrants have been sent to countries where their lives could be at risk.

Immigrant advocates have criticized the Trump administration’s actions, noting that they aren’t just harmful to immigrants living in the U.S. but to all Americans.

“We must reject fear and division and choose policies that promote dignity, safety, and health for all. Our communities and our country deserve better,” read an October 2025 explainer from the National Immigration Law Center.

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

We are fundraising right now for those basic operating expenses — we need $39,000 in the next 5 days. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference.

author: Clare Hymer
title: X Suspends Palestinian-American’s Account After He Launches Senate Bid
content:
A Palestinian-American running for the US Senate has had his campaign account suspended by the social media platform X just days after launching his bid.


Ahmed Moor, a democratic socialist who was born in Gaza, announced on Monday that he would run in the primary to be the Democratic nominee in Pennsylvania in 2028. 


The seat is held by John Fetterman, a pro-Israel Democrat who has voted with Republicans on issues related to Israel rather than with his own party.


On Wednesday,

Moor said

 that his X campaign account had been suspended. “It’s official! We’re a threat,” he posted on his personal X account.


The account had gained over 33,000 followers within three days of its launch. X has not provided an explanation for its suspension.


Moor, who has criticised US support for Israel and how “wars and tariffs that have driven up costs for working Pennsylvanians”, has said he wants to unseat Fetterman and

“chart a new path for America”

. 


Fetterman has not yet announced whether he will run again.


“I’m running to end the war in Iran and to promote the dignity agenda: free healthcare, free childcare, and affordable housing,” Moor said in his campaign announcement. 


“I’m calling for accountability for genocide, for ICE and for corruption. And finally, for the protection of our civil liberties in America.”

author: Leanne Sanders
title: First Nations Leadership Council sends open letter to the prime minister, Indigenous Services over delay in passing Bill S-2
content:
In an open letter to Prime Minister Mark Carney and Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull Masty, the First Nations Leadership Council (FNLC) is calling for an immediate end to the second-generation cut-off.

The FNLC is made up of the B.C. Assembly of First Nations, First Nations Summit and the Union of B.C. Indian Chiefs. It’s calling for an end to sex and race-based discrimination in the Indian Act, and removal of the second-generation cutoff.

“We fully support the amendments to Bill S-2 made by the Standing Senate Committee on Indigenous Peoples and adopted by the Senate of Canada on December 4, 2025,” the FNLC said in the letter.

“Further, we are concerned with the Minister of Indigenous Services Canada’s (ISC) use of a secretive process regarding the new standalone legislation, which violates the legal duty to consult in good faith.”

The second-generation cutoff is when a person, under section 6(1) of the Indian Act, passes status to a child no matter who the other parent is. But a person under section 6(2) can pass it on only if the other parent is also registered as “status” under the Indian Act.

After two generations of parenting with someone who is not registered, the third generation is out. That is the second-generation cut-off.

The FNLC maintains that the immediate elimination of the second-generation cut-off is supported by UN human rights bodies including the UN Human Rights Committee, the UN Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination Against Women, and, in May 2026, the UN Expert Mechanism on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples.

“For months, Bill S-2 has been stalled in the Standing Committee on Indigenous and Northern Affairs (INAN Committee), while the Minister insisted upon further consultations and then argued for broader registration reform and confused the issues of band membership and self-determination over citizenship with Indian status, and is now proposing new draft legislation. These deceptive tactics are a red herring to distract and delay the passage of Bill S-2,” the letter stated.

First Nations Summit Political executive Robert Phillips said in an interview with APTN News that it’s frustrating that “we’ve governed ourselves for thousands of years. And to remove second-generation cutoff and maybe replace it with universal one parent rule, or introducing legislation-and then it’s stalling?”

“We’re getting to the point where now we’re in argumentative stage…I do believe we need to be at a table and say that the authority should rest with First Nations and those that have treaties or those that have Aboriginal rights like here in British Columbia…,” Phillips said.

According to Phillips, Gull-Masty has invited “select First Nations leaders” to consult with ISC on new draft legislation to address the second-generation cut-off.

In the letter to Carney and Gull-Masty, the FNLC said, “we understand that… the minister has invited select First Nations leaders to consult with ISC regarding new draft legislation to address the second-generation cut-off, on the condition that they sign a Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA), which binds them to not disclose any information that is shared with them for a period of five years, unless that information is disclosed to the public by the Minister.”

That doesn’t sit well with the FNLC.

“Using NDAs to convene meetings with selected leaders blocks First Nations leaders from consulting their Nations, members, technical and legal advisors. This secretive and selective process is an alarming escalation of the government’s tactics to undermine the broad support of First Nations.”

Senators vote to end the second-generation cutoff for ‘status Indians’

According to a statement from Gull-Masty’s office, a “collaborative process” on the second-generation cut off and section 10 voting thresholds concluded at the end of July, where the government invited First Nations to “put forward their own proposals and solutions to address these inequities in the Indian Act.

“We heard a range of perspectives, proposals, and priorities, alongside a shared sense of urgency: the second generation cut-off must be addressed,” according to a statement provided by Gull-Masty’s office. “While the Collaborative Process has now concluded, the work continues. We are currently reviewing the proposals, feedback and perspectives shared through the process to inform next steps, including legislative reform.”

The FNLC said the process goes against “the vast majority of First Nations …

author: Sophia Sheera
title: Katy Perry Performs for Tech Firm Founded by Ex-IDF Soldiers
content:
Katy Perry put on a private show for employees from American-Israeli cybersecurity company Wiz in Thailand earlier this month.


Staff at the company were enjoying a five-day luxury getaway in Khao Lak on Saturday, 7 November when the American popstar arrived by surprise, Israeli news outlet

Israelim reported

.


Wiz was founded in 2020 by “four tech musketeers” who “met in the Israeli army and served together in the IDF for almost a decade”,

the Times of Israel reports

. All four are graduates of Unit 8200, the Israeli army’s cyber-security arm responsible for the mass surveillance of Palestinians living in apartheid conditions. 


In March 2026, Wiz was acquired by Google parent company Alphabet for $32bn. Google’s links to the Israeli government were already well-established through Project Nimbus, the cloud computing project signed in 2021. 


Perry is yet to comment on the online backlash garnered by her performance. But in May 2024, she shared a Unicef post calling for a ceasefire and condemning the “unconscionable” killing of children in Rafah.

ᓱᕋᒃᓯᒪᔪᖅ ᓱᕈᓯᕐᓂ ᐃᓄᓕᕆᓂᖅ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᐱᒋᐊᕐᕕᖃᕐᒪᓐ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᒐᕙᒪᒃᑯᑦ ᓄᓇᓕᙳᖅᑎᑕᐅᑎᓪᓗᒋᑦ ᒪᓕᒃᑕᐅᓯᒪᓂᒃᑯᑦ ᓈᒻᒪᙱᓕᐅᕈᑎᖃᓗᐊᕐᒪᑕ, ᐃᓚᖏᑦ ᐅᖃᕐᓯᒪᔪᑦ ᐊᕐᕌᒍᒐᓴᖕᓂ ᑕᒪᑐᒥᖓ ᐊᑐᕐᓯᒪᓂᑰᔪᑦ ᓱᕈᓯᓕᕆᓂᕐᒥᑦ.


“ᓄᓇᖃᖅᑳᖅᑐᑦ ᓱᕈᓯᖏᑦ ᐱᔭᐅᖃᑦᑕᕐᓂᖏᑦ ᓄᖅᑲᖅᓯᒪᙱᒻᒪᑦ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕆᐊᕐᕕᐅᕙᓚᐅᖅᑐᓂ,” ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ ᔨᐅᕆᒥ ᔭᖕ, ᐊᓈᓇᖓᓂ ᐱᔭᐅᓂᑯ ᓱᕈᓯᐅᑎᓪᓗᒍ. “ᑲᔪᓰᓐᓇᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ ᓱᕈᓯᕐᓂ ᐊᖓᔪᖅᑳᕆᙱᑕᖏᓐᓄᑦ ᑲᒪᒋᔭᐅᑎᑕᐅᓕᕌᖓᑕ.”


ᔭᖕ ᐅᖃᓪᓚᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ ᓄᓇᑦᓯᐊᕐᒥ ᐱᕙᓪᓕᐊᔪᓄᑦ ᐊᑐᖃᑦᑕᖅᓯᒪᔭᕕᓂᕐᒥᓂᒃ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᐊᖓᔪᖅᑳᕆᙱᑕᖏᓐᓄᑦ ᑲᒪᒋᔭᐅᖃᑦᑕᕐᓂᐅᔪᒥᑦ ᓄᕕᐱᕆ 5-ᒥ ᐅᖃᐅᓯᖃᖅᖢᓂ ᑭᖑᓪᓕᖅᐹᒥ ᐊᑐᖅᑕᐅᕙᓪᓕᐊᔪᓂᒃ ᖃᐅᔨᓴᖅᑎᓄᑦ ᐊᖓᔪᖅᑳᑉ ᐅᓂᒃᑳᓕᐅᓚᐅᖅᑎᓪᓗᒍ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᒐᕙᒪᒃᑯᑦ ᑲᒪᒋᔭᖃᕈᓯᖏᓐᓂᒃ ᐃᓅᓱᒃᑐᓂ ᑲᒪᒋᔭᐅᑎᑕᐅᔪᓂᒃ ᐊᖓᔪᖅᑳᕆᙱᑕᖏᓐᓄᑦ.


ᐱᓇᓱᐊᕈᓯᐅᓚᕐᑐᒥ ᐅᓂᒃᑳᓕᐊᕆᔭᐅᔪᖅ, ᑕᓪᓕᒪᒋᔭᐅᔪᖅ ᐊᕐᕌᒍᑦ 15 ᐃᓗᐊᓂ, ᓴᖅᑭᑎᑦᑎᓯᒪᖕᒪᑦ ᐊᓯᔾᔨᖅᓯᒪᓗᐊᒋᓐᓂᖓᓂ. ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᒐᕙᒪᒃᑯᑦ ᑲᒪᒋᔭᐅᑎᑕᖏᓐᓂ ᓱᕈᓯᕐᓂ ᖃᐅᔨᒪᓗᐊᙱᒻᒪᑕ ᖃᔅᓯᐅᓂᖏᓐᓂ, ᖃᐅᔨᓴᖃᑦᑕᙱᓗᐊᖅᖢᑎᒡᓗ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᒃᓴᕆᒐᓗᐊᖅᖢᒍ ᑕᒪᒃᑯᐊ ᓱᕈᓰᑦ ᐊᖓᔪᖅᑳᕆᙱᑕᖏᓐᓄᑦ ᑲᒪᔨᒋᔭᐅᔪᑦ ᓈᒻᒪᒃᑐᒥᑦ ᐊᖏᕐᕋᕆᔭᐅᔪᒧᐊᕋᓗᐊᕐᒪᖔᑕ.


ᔭᖕ, ᒫᓐᓇ 26-ᓂ ᐊᕐᕌᒍᖃᓕᕐᑐᖅ ᐊᓈᓇᖓᓂ ᐱᔭᐅᓚᐅᕐᓯᒪᖕᒪᑦ ᓱᕈᓯᐅᑎᓪᓗᒍ ᐸᓐᓂᕐᑑᒥ ᑲᒪᒋᔭᖃᑦᑎᐊᕋᓱᒃᑲᓗᐊᖅᑎᓪᓗᒍ, ᔭᖕ ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ.


ᐱᔾᔪᑎᖃᓗᐊᕋᓱᒋᓚᐅᕐᑕᖓ ᐃᓄᒋᐊᓗᐊᖅᑐᒦᓐᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᓂᕿᖃᕈᓐᓇᑦᑎᐊᙱᖢᑎᒃ ᐃᓚᒌᑦ, ᐅᖃᖅᖢᓂ ᐊᓈᓇᖓ ᐊᕐᕌᒍᓂ 12-ᓂ ᐃᒡᓗᑖᕋᓱᓚᐅᕐᓯᒪᓂᖓᓂ ᐃᓚᖏᓐᓄᑦ ᑭᓯᐊᓂᓕ ᐊᔪᖅᑎᑕᐅᖏᓐᓇᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ.


“ᓄᓇᖃᑎᒌᓕᕆᔩᑦ ᓄᓇᖃᖅᑳᖅᑐᓂ ᐃᑲᔪᙱᓗᐊᕐᒪᑕ,” ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ. “ᑕᐃᒪᓐᓇ ᐊᔪᕐᓴᑲᑕᓗᐊᖅᐳᒍᑦ. ᑕᐃᒪᓐᓇ ᐊᒃᓱᕈᕐᓇᖅᑐᒃᑰᑲᑕᓚᐅᖅᑐᒍᑦ.”


ᔭᖕ ᐃᓱᒪᔪᖅ ᐃᓄᐃᑦ ᓇᖕᒥᓂᖅ ᒐᕙᒪᖃᕐᓂᖓ ᓈᒻᒪᙱᓕᐅᕈᑎᓂ ᐋᖅᑭᒋᐊᕈᑎᐅᔪᓐᓇᖅᑐᖅ ᓱᕈᓯᕐᓂ ᑲᒪᒋᔭᖃᖃᑦᑕᕐᓂᕐᒧᑦ. ᑲᖏᖅᖠᓂᖅᒥ ᖃᐅᔨᓴᖅᑎ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕐᑐᓕᕆᔨ ᐲᑕ ᕗᐃᓕᐊᒻᓴᓐ, ᐊᒻᒪ ᐋᓖᓐ ᕼᐊᓯ, ᐊᕐᕌᒍᒐᓴᖕᓂ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᑐᐃᔨᐅᔪᖅ ᐱᓕᕆᖃᑎᖃᖅᐸᒃᖢᓂ ᓄᓇᖃᖅᑳᖅᑐᑦ ᐊᕐᓇᖏᓐᓂ ᑕᒪᑐᒥᖓ ᐊᖏᓚᐅᕐᒥᔪᖅ.


ᕗᐃᓕᐊᒻᓴᓐ ᐅᖃᓚᐅᕐᒥᔪᖅ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᒐᕙᒪᒃᑯᑦ ᐊᑐᖅᑕᐅᕙᓪᓕᐊᔪᓄᑦ ᖃᐅᔨᓴᖅᑎᓄᑦ ᐊᖓᔪᖅᑳᕐᒥ ᑐᓵᓪᓚᕆᓕᖅᐸᑕ ᐃᓱᒪᓕᐊᖏᓐᓂ ᓱᕈᓯᓕᕆᓂᖅ ᐋᖅᑭᒃᑕᐅᖁᔭᐅᓪᓗᓂ, ᑖᓐᓇᓗ ᐃᓚᖃᖅᖢᓂ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᖑᕙᓪᓕᐊᔪᑦ ᑐᓴᐅᒪᔭᐅᑦᑎᐊᕈᑎᒃᓴᖏᓐᓂ, ᑕᒪᓐᓇᓗ ᐱᒋᐊᕈᑎᐅᔪᒥᑦ ᐋᖅᑭᒋᐊᕈᑎᐅᓇᔭᙱᖢᓂ ᒪᑯᓂᖓ ᓱᕈᓯᕐᓂ ᐃᓚᖏᓐᓂ ᐊᕐᓵᖅᑕᐅᖃᑕᕐᓂᕐᒨᖓᔪᓂ. ᑕᒪᓐᓇᓕ ᐋᖅᑭᒋᐊᕈᑎᑐᐃᓐᓇᐅᖕᒪᑦ.


“ᓇᓗᓇᐃᕐᓯᑲᑕᖕᒪᑕ ᒪᑦᑐᑎᑐᐃᓐᓇᕐᓂ ᐋᖅᑭᒋᐊᕈᑎᓂ ᒐᕙᒪᒃᑯᓐᓂ ᐱᒋᐊᕈᑎᖏᓐᓂ ᐋᖅᑭᒃᓯᙱᖔᖅᖢᑎᑦ ᓄᓇᓕᖕᓂ,” ᕗᐃᓕᐊᒻᓴᓐ ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ.


ᐃᒡᓗᖃᑦᑎᐊᙱᓗᐊᕐᓂᖅ, ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕐᓯᒪᑦᑎᐊᙱᓗᐊᕐᓂᖅ, ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔮᒃᓴᖃᙱᓐᓂ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐊᔪᕐᓴᑲᑕᖕᓂᖅ ᐅᓗᕆᐊᓇᕈᑎᐅᖕᒪᑕ ᓱᕈᓯᕐᓂ ᐃᓚᖏᓐᓂ ᐊᕐᓵᖅᓯᖃᑦᑕᕐᓂᕐᒧᑦ, ᕗᐃᓕᐊᒻᓴᓐ ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ, ᐅᖃᐅᓯᖃᖅᖢᓂ ᕿᒥᕐᕈᐊᖃᑦᑕᕐᓂᕐᑯᑦ ᖃᐅᔨᓴᖅᑕᐅᓯᒪᔪᓂᒃ ᓄᐊᑦ ᐊᒥᐊᓕᑲᒥ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐅᑭᐅᕐᑕᖅᑐᕐᒥ ᖃᐅᔨᓴᖅᑎᓄᑦ.


“ᐅᑯᐊ ᐊᑐᖅᑕᐃᓗᐊᕐᒪᑕ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ,” ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ.


ᐊᓈᓇᒋᔭᐅᔪᑦ ᑐᐊᕕᕐᓇᖅᑐᓕᕆᓂᒃᑯᑦ ᐃᒡᓗᖃᖅᑎᑕᐅᔪᑦ ᐅᓗᕆᐊᓇᖅᑐᒦᓐᓂᕐᓴᐅᖕᒪᑕ ᓱᕈᓯᖏᑦ ᐱᔭᐅᓇᔭᕆᐊᒃᓴᖏᓐᓂ, ᐅᖃᒃᑲᓐᓂᖅᑐᖅ.


ᕼᐋᓯ ᑕᒪᑐᒥᖓ ᐊᖏᓚᐅᕐᒥᔪᖅ, ᐅᖃᖅᖢᓂ ᒫᓐᓇ ᐱᓕᕆᔾᔪᓯᐅᔪᖅ “ᑐᖁᕋᐃᓂᕋᖅᖢᓂᒋᑦ” ᓄᓇᖃᖅᑳᖅᑐᓂ.


“ᐅᑯᐊ ᒐᕙᒪᒃᑯᑦ ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔭᖅᑎᖏᑦ ᐃᓚᒌᓄᑦ ᐅᐸᒍᑎᔭᕌᖓᑕ ᐅᕝᕙᓘᓐᓃᑦ ᓄᓇᓕᖕᓄᐊᖅᐸᑕ ᑕᒪᑐᒃᑯᓂᖓ ᕿᒥᕐᕈᐊᖃᑦᑕᕐᒪᑕ ᓈᒻᒪᙱᓕᐅᕈᑎᐅᕙᒃᑐᓂᒃ,” ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ. “ᓲᖃᐃᒻᒪ ᐃᓱᒪᖏᑦ ᐃᓄᒋᐊᓂ ᐋᖅᑭᒃᓱᐃᓯᒪᓇᓱᖕᓂᖏᓐᓄᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐃᓅᖃᑎᒌᙱᑕᖏᓐᓂ ᐱᐅᒃᓴᖃᑦᑕᙱᓐᓂᕐᒧᑦ.”


ᐊᓯᐊᒎᕈᑎᐅᔪᓐᓇᖅᑐᕐᓕ ᐃᓄᖕᓄᑦ ᐊᐅᓚᑕᐅᔪᓂ, ᓄᓇᓕᖕᓃᑦᑐᓄᑦ “ᐃᑲᔪᖅᑐᐃᓂᕐᒥ ᐃᓚᒌᓂᒃ, ᖃᐅᔨᒪᓗᑎᒃ ᐱᒻᒪᕆᐅᓂᖏᓐᓂᒃ ᐊᒻᒪᓗ ᒪᒥᓴᕈᓐᓇᕐᓂᖏᓐᓂᒃ, ᐊᒻᒪ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᑐᐃᕙᒡᓗᑎᒃ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐊᔪᕈᓐᓃᕐᓴᖅᐸᒡᓗᑎ,” ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ.


“ᐃᓄᐃᑦ ᖃᐅᔨᑎᑕᐅᔭᕆᐊᖃᕐᑐᑦ ᐱᕈᕈᓐᓇᕐᓂᖏᓐᓂ ᒫᓐᓇ ᐅᐸᒃᓯᒪᔭᖏᓐᓂ ᓄᑖᒦᖔᓕᕈᑎᒃ. ᑕᐃᒪᓐᓇ ᐃᓐᓇᐃᑦ ᐃᓱᒪᖕᒪᑕ ᐃᓄᐃᑦ ᓄᓇᖏᓐᓃᑦᑐᑦ.”


ᓄᓇᕗᑦ ᐱᒋᐊᓕᓵᕐᓯᒪᑎᓪᓗᒍ 1999-ᒥ, ᓄᓇᒥᑦ ᒐᕙᒪᒃᑯᑦ ᖃᐃᖁᔨᓚᐅᕐᓯᒪᖕᒪᑕ ᕼᐋᓯᒥ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᐳᓚᕋᖁᔭᐅᓪᓗᓂ ᓄᓇᓕᖕᓂ ᐊᒻᒪ ᑕᒪᓐᓇ ᑐᓴᐅᒪᔭᐅᔪᖅ ᑐᓴᖅᑕᐅᑎᓪᓗᓂᒋ ᒪᑐᒧᖓ ᓱᕈᓯᕐᓂ ᐊᖓᔪᖅᑳᖏᓐᓂ ᐊᖅᓵᖅᑕᐅᓯᒪᔪᑦ ᒥᒃᓵᓄᑦ, ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ.


ᐅᓇ ᐃᓱᒪᒋᔭᐅᓕᓵᙱᑦᑐᖅ. ᐋᖅᑭᒃᓱᐃᓂᖅ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐊᑐᓕᖅᑎᑦᑎᓂᖅ ᕼᐊᕗᐊᐃᒥ 1979-ᒥ, ᓱᓕ ᒫᓐᓇ ᐊᑐᖅᑕᐅᖕᒪᑦ.


“ᐅᓇ ᖃᐅᔨᓇᓱᕈᑎᑦᑎᐊᕙᒃ ᓄᓇᕐᔪᐊᕐᒥ ᓄᓇᖃᖅᑳᖅᑐᓂ ᑐᑭᓯᓯᒪᔭᐅᓂᖓ ᐃᓚᒌᑦ ᒥᒃᓵᓄᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᓱᕈᓯᕐᓂ,” ᕼᐋᓯ ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ. “ᐅᓇ ᑕᐃᒪᐃᖃᑦᑕᕐᓯᒪᔪᖅ ᐅᕝᕙᓘᓐᓃᑦ ᓄᑖᖑᙱᖢᓂ. ᑭᓯᐊᓂᓕ ᐅᑭᐅᕐᑕᖅᑐᕐᒥ ᑕᐃᒪᐃᖃᑦᑕᓕᑕᐃᓐᓇᕐᒪᑦ ᐃᓄᒋᐊᓃᓕᖅᑕᐅᓯᒪᙱᑉᐸᑦ.”


ᓄᓇᕗᑦ ᑖᔅᓱᒥᖓ ᐊᑐᖅᑕᐅᕙᒃᓯᒪᔪᒥ ᐊᑐᖁᔨᓚᐅᙱᑦᑐᑦ.

author: Software Architektur im Stream
title: Warum Schichten? Und wie viele?
content:
Schichten sind ein Erfolgsmodell in der Software-Architektur. In der Realität hat dieser Ansatz oft Herausforderungen. In dieser Episode geht es um die Ideen hinter dem Schichten-Modell und verschiedene Nutzungen: 3-Schichten-Architektur, das Anti Corruption Layer aus DDD und wann Schichten wirklich entkoppeln.
