title: YPJ spokesperson Ruksen Mihemed: We can only achieve our freedom through our own struggle
content:
What does self-defense mean for women whose identity, history and social existence have been subjected to attacks for generations? And what conditions must be established to ensure that women no longer have to depend on others to make decisions about their security, their rights and their future?


According to Ruksen Mihemed, spokesperson for the Women’s Protection Units (YPJ) in Rojava, these questions lie at the heart of a struggle that extends far beyond armed resistance.


In an interview with ANF, Mihemed reflected on 15 years of women’s organizing and self-defense in Northeast Syria. She discusses the establishment of the YPJ, the experiences of the women’s revolution and the challenges arising from the ongoing restructuring of Syria.


“When a woman defends herself, there is life. But if she entrusts her defense to others, she cannot protect her life. The consequence is death,” Mihemed said.


https://video.anf-news2.com/live/firat/7e263871_20261110221245_2026-11-10-qamislo-ruksen-mihemed-ypj-komutani-jpj-ve-25-kasim_1.mp4


Self-defense begins with awareness of one’s own identity


The emergence of independent women’s defense structures was closely linked to the social organizing that developed during the Rojava Revolution. Women began establishing their own institutions, taking responsibility in political decision-making processes and organizing independently in the field of defense.


“With the Rojava Revolution, women began to organize, and their participation in defense became a necessity. But first, women had to recognize their own identity and existence, learn about their history, understand themselves and develop an awareness of self-defense,” the YPJ spokesperson said.


She continued: “Our fundamental principle was that women should gain confidence in themselves, be able to express their thoughts freely and make their own decisions. On this foundation, they subsequently became increasingly involved in the field of defense.”


YPJ wrote a new chapter in the history of women’s struggle


With the formation of the YPJ, an independent women’s military organization emerged within the Kurdish freedom movement in Rojava. Its development was part of a broader social process in which women established their own political and institutional structures.


“With its establishment, the YPJ also wrote a new chapter in history: the history of a new women’s struggle. For the first time, an autonomous women’s force was established. This gave women the opportunity to create their own representation in all areas,” Mihemed noted.


“If self-defense has no place in a woman’s life, neither her rights, her legal status nor her life are protected. This is precisely where the YPJ took action. It created a system intended to ensure security, dignity and a life free from violence.”


Mihemed also emphasized the international impact of the YPJ: “Over these 15 years, the YPJ’s struggle has brought together not only women in Rojava and the Middle East, but also women around the world under a common banner of struggle. It has helped foster a shared stance and a spirit of solidarity among women.”


Women’s rights as a point of contention in Syria’s restructuring


As negotiations continue over Syria’s political and institutional future, questions are also emerging about the preservation of the women’s structures established in Northeast Syria over the past several years. Mihemed directed her criticism particularly at the Syrian transitional government, saying: “Damascus is still not convinced that the women’s question and women’s freedom are fundamental issues. It has failed to recognize that no country can be built without women’s organizing and that lasting stability in the fields of defense and security is impossible without their participation. Instead, a male-dominated mentality continues to prevail.”


According to the YPJ spokesperson, negotiations over the country’s future political system are therefore inseparably linked to women’s legal status: “This mentality must change. We must not forget that injustice committed against women is also an injustice against society as a whole. Women’s political and legal rights must be guaranteed within the emerging system.”


‘Appointing a few women to official positions does not mean recognizing women’s will’

title: “Shared Stories, Free Cinema”: 6th Rojava Film Festival opens on Friday
content:
The 6th International Rojava Film Festival will open on Friday, November 13, with the screening of “Heval Kekê Min” by Haşim Aydemir. Under the theme “Çîrokên Hevpar, Sînemaya Azad” (Shared Stories, Free Cinema), the festival will bring filmmakers from various countries together with audiences in Rojava through November 20. Alongside feature films and documentaries, the program includes discussions on the social significance of cinema, collective filmmaking and the conditions for independent cultural production.


The main venue will be the Mihemed Şêxo Center in Qamişlo, where the film screenings will take place. Workshops, expert discussions and panel discussions will be held at the TEV-ÇAND, Sine Jin and Hunergeha Welat cultural centers. A special focus will be the “Ji Rojava” (From Rojava) section, featuring five productions from the region. The program will also include Kurdish-language short films, international feature films and documentaries.


Opening with music, dance and “Heval Kekê Min”


Friday’s opening ceremony will begin at 5:00 p.m. at the Mihemed Şêxo Center. MA Music will provide the musical program, while Narin Dance will present a dance performance. At 7:00 p.m., the opening film “Heval Kekê Min,” directed by Haşim Aydemir, will be screened.


The accompanying program of professional events will begin on Saturday, November 14. From 10:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. at Sine Jin, documentary filmmaker and editor Sasha Ayoub will introduce the work of Stories Film Lab. The program supports independent filmmakers in Syria in developing their projects. Films produced through the lab will also be screened during the event.


Film screenings will begin at 11:00 a.m. with “The Country Judge.” Other selections include the Kurdish-language short films “House of the Moon” and “Dorpêç,” as well as the documentary “The Wedding of the Pirs.”


From 3:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. at TEV-ÇAND, cinematographer Cemil Kızıldağ will lead a workshop on the visual language of cinema. The session will explore the creative possibilities of visual composition and cinematic storytelling.


Filmmaking practice and stories from Rojava


On Sunday, November 15, two multi-day workshops will begin. Cinematographer and lighting designer Jafar Amin Al-Betar will provide theoretical foundations and practical training in film lighting at Hunergeha Welat from 9:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. The workshop will continue on November 16 and 17. Meanwhile, documentary filmmaker Guevara Namer will lead a workshop at Sine Jin focusing on the documentary filmmaking process and her experiences in international film production. The second part of her workshop will take place on November 16.


The “Ji Rojava” section will also begin that day. “Rêwiyên Ser Riya Agir” will be screened at 11:00 a.m., followed by “Keziyên Berxwedanê” at 11:50 a.m.


At 3:00 p.m., director Sêvînaz Evdikê, known for her film “Berbû,” will introduce the Nûjîyan Women’s Film Festival at TEV-ÇAND. At the same time, the documentary “Kî me ez?” will be screened at the Mihemed Şêxo Center.


The evening program will feature two more documentaries: “04.17 Adıyaman” at 6:00 p.m., followed by “Pêlên Kurdan” at 7:10 p.m. Both screenings will be followed by discussions with the audience.


Ten years of collective filmmaking in Rojava


On Monday, November 16, the experiences of the Rojava Film Commune will take center stage alongside the film screenings. “To Fetch a Pail of Water” will be screened at 11:00 a.m., followed by the documentary “Under the Flags the Sun” at 3:00 p.m.


From 3:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m., a panel discussion on the collective filmmaking practices of the Rojava Film Commune will take place at TEV-ÇAND. Since its establishment in 2015, the commune has been developing collectively organized approaches to filmmaking.


Moderated by Mirzan Bekir, the discussion will bring together founding members Diyar Hesso and Şêro Hindê and sound designer Coni Docolomansky, who worked on the films “Kobanê” and “Berbû.” The discussion will focus on experiences with collective production processes and the development of an independent filmmaking practice in Rojava.


Screenwriting and the Kurdish Question in Cinema


On Tuesday, November 17, screenwriter Önder Çakar will lead a workshop on developing film protagonists at Sine Jin from 10:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. The workshop will explore the process of developing a character from an initial concept to its full realization in a screenplay.

title: Shengal People’s Council calls for the recognition of the will of Yazidi society
content:
On the 11th anniversary of the liberation of the Yazidi region from the terrorist organization Islamic State (ISIS), the Shengal People’s Council called for the recognition of the will of Shengal and the Yazidi community.


In a statement on Thursday, the council recalled the resistance against ISIS and the social and political structures established since 2014. It emphasized that the ongoing process of democratic integration into the Iraqi state must be based on recognition of these achievements.


Shengal was liberated on November 13, 2015, following more than a year of fighting against ISIS. The People’s Council particularly honored the efforts of the Kurdish guerrilla forces and Yazidi defense units. It specifically commemorated the fallen commanders Dilşêr Herekol, Egîd Civiyan, Berfîn Nûrhaq, Nûjîn Amed, Çeko Çatak, Saît Hesen, Berxwedan Tolhildan, Dijwar Feqîr and Zerdeşt Şengalî.


“Just as the history of our people has been marked by attacks and fermans, its courageous people have repeatedly written stories of victory through their resistance,” the statement said. The Yazidi community uses the term

Ferman

to refer to the historical campaigns of persecution and extermination directed against its people.


‘Liberation of Shengal marked the beginning of a new phase in Yazidi history’


The People’s Council pointed out that the liberation of Shengal marked the beginning of a new phase in the history of Yazidi society. According to the council, the establishment of democratic and social institutions has enabled the Yazidi population to increasingly take control of its own affairs. In this context, the People’s Council referred to the political ideas of Abdullah Öcalan, whose philosophy, it said, has played a decisive role in shaping independent organization and social reconstruction. The council also views the current steps toward democratic integration into Iraq in connection with the Peace and Democratic Society Process initiated by Öcalan.


“Our struggle is for recognition of Shengal’s will”


The People’s Council stated that the progress achieved so far has created an opportunity to establish relations between Shengal and the Iraqi state on a new foundation. Central to this is the demand for recognition of the independent political and social structures established by the Yazidi population. According to the council, this also includes the ability to defend its own society against renewed attacks.


“Shengal was liberated through the efforts of its own sons and daughters and has now, within the framework of democratic integration, developed the capacity to defend its own society,” the statement said.


Young Yazidi women and men are taking responsibility for defending their community to prevent further campaigns of extermination, the council said, noting that Yazidi society possesses the will and determination to shape its own political representation.


“Our goal and our struggle are directed toward securing recognition of the will of Yazidi society and Shengal. As the Yazidi community and the social forces of Shengal, we have spent twelve years building our social structures with great determination and continuing our work on the basis of the will of a free society.”


The council stressed that recognition of this political will would not contradict Iraq’s territorial unity. On the contrary, it could strengthen the Iraqi state and reinforce social cohesion within the country, it said.


Call for a joint celebration on November 13


The People’s Council called on the people of Shengal, as well as members and supporters of the Yazidi community, to celebrate the anniversary of the liberation together. A central celebration is scheduled for Friday, November 13, at 2:00 p.m. in front of Medreseya Sor in the center of Shengal. The People’s Council invited the public to participate in the celebrations marking the 11th anniversary of the liberation.

title: Koçyiğit: Rojin Kabaiş case extends into state institutions
content:
Gülistan Kılıç Koçyiğit, deputy parliamentary group chair of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party), called for a full investigation into the death of university student Rojin Kabaiş during a press conference at the Turkish parliament. Her remarks followed an attack and threats against the young woman’s uncle in Istanbul. Koçyiğit expressed suspicions that the case involved connections to state institutions and drew parallels with the unresolved disappearance of university student Gülistan Doku.


At the beginning of her press conference, Koçyiğit addressed the explosion at the HABAŞ steel plant in the Aliağa district of Izmir province, which claimed the lives of 19 workers. She criticized the failure to hold those responsible accountable and the lack of adequate state oversight of workplace safety.


“There are no independent inspections, and no one talks to the workers. Instead, they talk to the business owners. Not a single concern raised by employees is heard. Workers are dying because these safety measures would impose costs on employers,” Koçyiğit said.


Another issue addressed at the press conference was the sinking of the Tuğberk İmamoğlu vessel in the Sea of Marmara in September. The families of nine people whose bodies have still not been recovered visited several parliamentary groups the previous day to draw attention to their situation. Koçyiğit criticized the authorities’ inaction, saying: “A state that knows when a sheep goes missing on the banks of the Euphrates has failed to recover the bodies from the Sea of Marmara for months.”


Corruption allegations and criticism of COP31


The lawmaker contrasted the deadly working conditions faced by workers with the latest revelations surrounding the investment fund scandal. While people work under life-threatening conditions for a monthly wage, millions were transferred through fraudulent financial transactions, Koçyiğit said, adding that she had received numerous messages from victims seeking public attention.


Regarding the arrest of former Minister of Family and Social Affairs and AKP deputy chair Fatma Betül Sayan, she stated: “We say, finally. But we know that attempts are being made to cover up this affair by sacrificing a handful of individuals.”


The DEM Party politician also criticized the UN Climate Change Conference COP31, currently taking place in Antalya. She accused companies such as Cengiz, LİMAK and SİMPAŞ, which are sponsoring the event, of engaging in greenwashing. “On the one hand, you destroy nature and wipe out olive trees through hydroelectric power plants, geothermal facilities and mining projects. On the other hand, you present yourselves at COP31. We do not accept this,” she stated.


“This is about women’s right to life in this country”


Referring to the recent armed attack and threats against an uncle of Rojin Kabaiş in Istanbul, Koçyiğit leveled serious accusations against state institutions. She drew parallels with the unresolved disappearance of Gülistan Doku: “As in the case of Gülistan Doku, this is also a case with connections extending into state institutions and the structures operating within them.”


Emphasizing the broader social significance of the case, Koçyiğit said: “The case of Rojin Kabaiş is not merely about the loss of one person. It is about women’s right to life in this country. We will continue to demand justice for Gülistan Doku and Rojin Kabaiş.”


The DEM Party politician called on the Ministry of Justice to ensure that both cases are fully investigated and those responsible are identified.


Criticism of extended prison terms


Finally, the DEM Party politician criticized the practices of the Administrative and Observation Boards in Turkish prisons. She said these boards continue to prevent the release of prisoners who have been incarcerated for more than 30 years and have already completed their sentences.


Koçyiğit appealed to the Minister of Justice: “We are now genuinely ashamed of having to raise these issues over and over again. I once again call on this country’s Minister of Justice: Stop keeping people in prison after they have served their sentences and allowing the Administrative and Observation Boards to make arbitrary decisions.”


Koçyiğit stressed that the ongoing violations of prisoners’ rights must end. “Do not become complicit in depriving people of their freedom,” she said.

title: Students in Rojava: We will not back down until our right to education in Kurdish is recognized
content:
Protests against restrictions on Kurdish-language education continue across Rojava. On Thursday, students, parents and residents demonstrated in Hesekê, Dirbêsiyê and Rimêlan, demanding recognition of Kurdish as an official language of Syria and constitutional guarantees for the right to education in their mother tongue.


In Hesekê, hundreds of people took part in a march that began at the Kevok roundabout and continued to the Şehîd Serhed intersection. Demonstrators carried banners bearing slogans such as “Our language is our identity,” “Our rights must be guaranteed in the constitution,” “Kurdish is our red line” and “Our language is our dignity.”


PYD: Damascus must reverse its decision


At the rally that followed, Ebdulxenî Oso of the Democratic Union Party (PYD) addressed the demonstrators. He recalled the development of Kurdish-language education since the beginning of the Rojava Revolution.


“The identity of peoples is closely linked to their language and culture. In Rojava, the Kurdish language has made significant progress over the past 14 years. Kurdish has been used as the language of instruction in schools, institutes and universities. Today, our language is also used in civilian institutions and public offices,” Oso said.


Oso continued: “Any restrictions on these achievements are unacceptable. Syria is a country with a rich diversity of peoples, languages and cultures. Preserving this diversity requires a democratic system that guarantees the rights of all communities. I call on the government to reverse its decision and correct this mistake. If it does not recognize the Kurdish language, it means that it does not recognize the existence of the Kurdish people either.”


Students demand recognition of Kurdish as an official language


Students in Dirbêsiyê also protested against the restrictions. Children and young people from the Şehîd Cemil Ehmed Hesen School in the village of Til Kerem issued a statement, which was read aloud by student Sozdar Hemê.


In the statement, the students called for the protection and development of the Kurdish language and its recognition as one of Syria’s official languages. They emphasized that Kurdish is inseparable from the identity, history and culture of the Kurdish people. “Preserving and promoting our mother tongue is a fundamental human right that must not be restricted,” they underlined.


“Without language, there is no life”


Another demonstration took place in Rimêlan. Students from Girkê Legê and Rimêlan gathered in front of the Şehîd Şîlan School and marched through the city. Outside the Silêman El Helebî School, student Zîlan Berekat read a joint statement. She described education in one’s mother tongue as a fundamental right and demanded that the Kurdish language and the right to Kurdish-language education be explicitly enshrined in the Syrian constitution.


The students vowed to continue their protests until the Kurdish language and the right to education in Kurdish are recognized: “We will not back down until our right to education in our language is recognized.”


The rally concluded with the slogan “Bê ziman jiyan nabe” – “Without language, there is no life.”

title: Women in Arzoxlî continue resistance against solar power project
content:
Resistance against the construction of solar power facilities continues in the village of Arzoxlî (Turkish: Kervanpınar) in the province of Amed (Diyarbakır). Residents have been holding a protest vigil against the Zenkar 1 project for 22 days. During a march from the village square to the planned construction site, Turkish gendarmerie units blocked the path of the protesting women.


The demonstrators chanted slogans such as “Our land and our water are our existence,” “We will prevail through resistance” and “No to the company.” When soldiers prevented them from entering the site, the villagers questioned the legality of their actions: “On what legal grounds are you preventing us from entering our own land?”


“They have bought everything with money”


Emine Eren, who has been participating in the protest vigil, accused the security forces of prioritizing the company’s interests over the rights of the villagers. “There is no humanity left here. People have no heart anymore. They have bought everything with money. There is no justice left to speak of,” she said.


Eren criticized the fact that residents have to protest every day against encroachments on their living environment. “Do we really have to come here every day? Our village has its own resources. If this were a good project, we could implement it ourselves.” Following the confrontation with the soldiers, the women returned to the protest tent and continued their vigil.


Legal victory against another solar energy project


Alongside their protests against Zenkar 1, residents of Arzoxlî recently secured a legal victory against another solar energy project. The Administrative Court in Amed ordered the temporary suspension of the Zenkar 2 project. However, resistance against the planned solar installations and the associated encroachment on agricultural land continues.

title: Two political prisoners released after decades of imprisonment
content:
Political prisoners Aydın Kudat and Zübeyir Idem have been released from Turkish prisons after serving 34 and 30 years, respectively. In both cases, the responsible Administrative and Observation Boards had repeatedly blocked their release despite the completion of their regular prison terms.


Aydın Kudat released after 34 years


Aydın Kudat was released from the T-type prison in Karabük on Wednesday and was welcomed by his family outside the facility. He was arrested in 1992 in the Bismil district of Amed (Turkish: Diyarbakır) and subsequently sentenced to life imprisonment by the then State Security Court (DGM).


His release was originally scheduled for September 6, 2022. However, the responsible prison board denied his release a total of six times. The stated reason was Kudat’s refusal to sign the so-called declaration of remorse demanded by the prison administration.


The long-term prisoner was finally able to leave prison following a new decision by the board. He was scheduled to return to Amed on Wednesday evening on a flight via Istanbul.


Zübeyir Idem released after two postponements


Zübeyir Idem has also regained his freedom after 30 years in prison. He was released from the prison in Espiye, Giresun province, after the responsible Administrative and Observation Board approved his release.


Idem had already completed his 30-year prison term on June 2, 2026. Nevertheless, two separate decisions by the board postponed his release by three months each.


Following his release, Idem was welcomed by family members. He then traveled to Adana to visit the graves of his mother and father, both of whom had died during his decades of imprisonment.

author: CMI Argentina
title: Milton Tolomeo en huelga de hambre: exigen al SPF que cumpla lo ordenado por el Poder Judicial
content:
Desde la Coordinadora contra la Represión Policial e Institucional (CORREPI) y la Gremial de Abogados y Abogadas denuncian el grave empeoramiento de las condiciones de detención de los presos políticos y el incumplimiento del Servicio Penitenciario Federal y su superior, el Ministerio de Seguridad Nacional, de lo ordenado por el Tribunal Oral Federal nº 6.


Milton Tolomeo


Compartimos el comunicado:


Informe sobre la situación de Milton Tolomeo, preso político en huelga de hambre: EXIGIMOS AL SPF QUE CUMPLA LO ORDENADO POR EL TRIBUNAL ORAL FEDERAL


El 8 de noviembre, Milton Iván Tolomeo, preso político por haberse manifestado contra la infame reforma laboral el 11 de febrero de 2026, inició una huelga de hambre en su actual lugar de alojamiento, el nuevo Complejo Penitenciario VIII de Marcos Paz.


Milton, igual que Eneas Gallo, permanece detenido, con prisión preventiva, desde el 14 de febrero pasado. Se lo acusa por los delitos de resistencia a la autoridad, intimidación pública y tenencia de material incendiario. Los primeros dos delitos son parte del “combo” habitual aplicado a manifestantes, y el tercero surge de una irregular identificación efectuada por las fuerzas de seguridad a partir del ciberpatrullaje y tecnología de reconocimiento antropométrico altamente cuestionable.


No conforme con eso, el fiscal de instrucción, el inefable Stornelli, agregó la agravante genérica de “acto terrorista” al propiciar la aplicación -por primera vez a nivel nacional desde su sanción en 2011 y ampliado en 2024- del art. 41 quinquies, que duplica el mínimo y máximo de la pena en expectativa, con lo que ambos enfrentan hoy una sanción penal de hasta 30 años de prisión.


Esa agravante ya había sido descartada por el juez instructor inicial de la justicia de Ciudad y la Cámara de Apelaciones, pese a lo cual fue incorporada al requerimiento de elevación a juicio. Cabe agregar que esa agravante, conforme la letra del mismo artículo, no es de aplicación cuando el hecho ocurre en el marco de la defensa de derechos humanos o constitucionales, como, en el caso, los derechos laborales.


Después de un largo mes recluido en el SIGPPLAR (Sistema Integral de Gestión para Personas Privadas de la Libertad de Alto Riesgo), verdadero Guantánamo “a la Bullrich” creado en 2024, que significó la privación de todo contacto personal o telefónico con familiares y hasta sus defensores, con 20 horas de aislamiento y sólo 4 al día de “recreo” para acceder al patio, a los sanitarios y a los sectores para preparar alimentos, logramos que Milton fuera trasladado a pabellón común en el CPF II de Marcos Paz, donde pudo retomar el derecho a las visitas familiares y de organismos de DDHH, la comunicación telefónica y el acceso a alimentación adecuada provista por sus allegados, elementos de higiene personal y limpieza.


Pero el 11 de octubre pasado, de manera totalmente discrecional, el Servicio Penitenciario Federal decidió su traslado al nuevo complejo federal, inaugurado a las apuradas para descomprimir la superpoblación de la cárcel de Devoto en vísperas de la anunciada visita del papa León XIV a ese penal, donde hoy apenas 70 internos quedan alojados.


El traslado, entre gallos y medianoche, se produjo dejando atrás la totalidad de sus pertenencias (ropa, calzado, libros, elementos de cocina, de higiene y limpieza, radio, etc.). En el nuevo lugar de alojamiento hay elementales carencias básicas de infraestructura y servicios. No hay libre acceso al agua potable, a los depósitos de mercadería de sus familiares las instalaciones sanitarias no están terminadas y se limitaron los días y horarios de visitas.


Desde su defensa denunciamos el grave empeoramiento de las condiciones de detención al Tribunal Oral Federal nº 6, que de inmediato envió varios oficios al servicio penitenciario exigiendo resolver esa situación y requiriendo informes, y los propios internos interpusieron un recurso de Habeas Corpus correctivo que tramita ante el Juzgado federal nº 1 de Morón.


Ante la falta de respuesta del SPF, el 8 de noviembre Milton decidió iniciar una huelga de hambre, negándose a ingerir alimento alguno.


Informado de la situación, en el día de ayer el Tribunal Oral Federal inmediatamente requirió al servicio penitenciario que las autoridades del CPF VIII efectúen los controles médicos correspondientes cada 24 horas, remitiendo informes periódicos; insistió en el cumplimiento de lo ordenado en lo ordenado por el Tribunal con fechas 13 y 15/10/2026 y …

author: Lilli Akpaleeapik
title: Iqaluit Skating Club receives $5,000 grant
content:
The Iqaluit Skating club has $5,000 to spend after being named a recipient of this year’s Canada Post Community Grant.


Canada Post presented the grant to the local skating club on Monday morning at Astro Hill in Iqaluit.


Following the presentation of a $5,000 cheque, the Canada Post Community Foundation held an event for all attendees to celebrate the work that the Iqaluit Skating Club does for the community.


The non-profit distributes grants to schools, community organizations and other charities across the country that provide services for youth up to age 21.


The club provides programs and lessons and facilities for the community year round, with the grant aimed at supporting its inclusive skating programs.


The event also highlighted the importance and positive impacts created by community partnerships, according to Mahmooda Ahmed, who works for Canada Post.


This year, the Canada Post Community Foundation awarded over $1.3 million to 113 organizations across the country. The Iqaluit skating club was the only grant recipient from Nunavut.

author: Shireen Akram-Boshar
title: ICE’s Own Investigations Reveal Deaths in Custody Caused by Medical Neglect
content:
Internal ICE investigations have found that 23 individuals died in 2025 after a lack of proper medical care.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

The San Francisco Chronicle has obtained internal ICE investigations into the deaths of dozens of people in its custody during the first year of President Donald Trump’s second term, finding that 23 of the 29 individuals died after a lack of proper medical care.

Guards, medical providers, and staff at Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facilities failed to provide emergency care, failed to send individuals to the emergency room, or ignored other critical warning signs, the report indicates. According to ICE’s own investigations, deficient medical care directly contributed to 20 of 23 of the deaths. The six other individuals who died in 2025 had received care within sufficient limits, the agency claims.

The Chronicle acquired the reports through a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request. The findings contradict the Department of Homeland Security (DHS)’s claim that its immigration jails provide “timely and appropriate medical care” and that “the medical care in ICE detention is the best care” that many immigrants “have received in their entire lives.”

The Chronicle previously reported on 48 deaths in ICE custody since Trump’s second term began, finding that delayed medical care and failure to provide critical care contributed to 17 of these deaths and that there was not enough information on at least 15 cases. This report, from April, came before the outlet obtained ICE’s own investigations into the 2025 deaths, which reported an even larger number directly caused by medical neglect.

At least 62 people have died in ICE custody since the start of Trump’s second term, more than double the amount of deaths from the first Trump administration and the highest rate in over a decade.

ICE has not investigated all of the deaths caused by the agency and its immigration jails. For example, Prisciliano Trejo Ricano died shortly after ICE released him from custody while he was in a coma; his name has not been counted among those who died in custody after the agency changed its policy in June to no longer report and investigate deaths of individuals who died within 30 days of release. Similarly, at least two disabled people died in 2026 shortly after ICE released them into freezing weather, and were not counted among ICE’s official death count.

In the second half of October alone, three people died in ICE detention: Emiliano Andrade-Covarrubias, a 56-year-old permanent resident from Mexico who died on October 17 at the Rio Grande Processing Center in Laredo, Texas, whose family reported that he was denied medication and care; Luis Sandoval, a 48-year-old Salvadoran who died on October 23 in ICE detention in Georgia and, according to DHS, died by suicide; and Roberto Jimenez Gutierrez, a 43-year-old Guatemalan who was found unresponsive on October 24.

In some cases, prison staff mocked individuals who called for help and who later died after their neglect. In others — like the deaths at Camp East Montana in Texas, which have been referred to as suicides — conditions included medical neglect, solitary confinement, and physical and sexual violence.

People imprisoned inside ICE jails have launched hunger strikes in protest of the conditions inside, including medical neglect and unlawful, prolonged detention. In May, over 300 detained people launched a hunger and labor strike at New Jersey’s Delaney Hall, which lasted approximately a month and brought national attention to conditions in immigration jails. In September, immigrants being detained at the El Valle Detention Facility in Texas launched a hunger strike; and in October, at least 73 people launched a hunger strike at a processing center in Georgia. Other hunger strikes have been reported in immigration jails in Pennsylvania, Michigan, California, and Washington — with one immigration jail in Tacoma, Washington, witnessing at least 20 hunger strikes in 2026.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share …

author: Diana Varenik and Natascha Elena Uhlmann
title: Lessons from an 85-Day Hotel Strike
content:
You’d be forgiven for worrying, 12 weeks into a strike, that the boss is hell-bent on waiting you out. But after more than 80 days on the picket line at Seattle’s Embassy Suites by Hilton in Pioneer Square, Aspen Desmarais was undeterred. “I can live on a budget,” she said. “Been doing it since day one.”


After 85 days, on September 10, workers won the longest hotel strike in Washington state history. Their union, UNITE HERE Local 8, represents 4,000 hospitality workers in Oregon and Washington.


Desmarais, a strike captain and bartender at the hotel, worked to keep others motivated throughout the fight. She and her co-workers were “tired of people talking down to us and not treating us with respect,” she said, “when we’re the reason that place stays running the way that it does.”


Hilton’s offer, two weeks into the strike, of

one cent per hour over its previous proposal

 helped fuel outrage. The union held open bargaining, so members heard the offer firsthand. “I [felt] frustrated and disrespected,” Desmarais said. “Especially with how much hard work my co-workers put into making sure the hotel and its guests have clean spaces and stays that are welcoming.”


Fritzie Corral, an Embassy Suites breakfast attendant, had only worked at the hotel for two months before walking out. As the strike went on, she said, her son worried that she had made a mistake in taking the job.


“You see other employees that decided to stay in the hotel working," she said. “Even during that time, I still believed I made the right choice. It’s my right to voice out what I feel and to fight for my rights.”


Hilton did not respond to requests for comment.


PROTECTION FROM ICE


Workers won significant pay increases, lowered barriers for health care eligibility, and highly sought-after protections for immigrant workers. Hilton, which manages the hotel, drew protests earlier this year for housing ICE agents and for

cutting ties with

 a Minneapolis hotel that canceled ICE bookings during Operation Metro Surge.


The union’s leaders criticized Hilton throughout the strike for dismissing contract language that would protect immigrant workers. “With ICE-related killings in the news for months causing immigrant workers to worry, why is Hilton refusing to give immigrant workers’ union a heads up if ICE is staying at the hotel?” Local 8 President Anita Seth

asked

Businesswire

.


Ultimately workers won a commitment from Hilton not to punish workers who call out due to an immigration enforcement surge, plus language binding the hotel to an expedited resolution process in such an event. Workers who lose their work authorization due to immigration enforcement will now be able to return to their jobs if their work authorization is restored within four years, and retain their seniority for up to two.


Desmarais told

Labor Notes

 that making sure immigrant co-workers missing work because of ICE “knew they would have a job still and a safe place to come back to” was the “most important” win strikers fought for.


Starting in 2027, housekeepers will make over $31 an hour—a giant step above the $17.63 an hour that housekeepers make on average across the country, per the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The new contract makes them the highest-paid housekeepers in the state, according to the union. Embassy Suites workers classified as “tipped” will now make $1 more per hour than the city’s minimum wage.


Health care eligibility was also a core demand for the union. Many hotel workers under collective bargaining agreements must meet a minimum threshold of hours worked to qualify for health benefits in a given period. Seasonal layoffs, a hallmark of hotel work, often mean inconsistent coverage for workers and their families.


The new contract replaces the month-to-month eligibility standard with an annual threshold of 1,250 hours, or around 24 hours a week, to qualify.


MASS CANCELLATIONS


The strike coincided with five of the six World Cup soccer matches held at Seattle’s Lumen Field this summer, directly across from the Embassy Suites. World Cup-related leverage helped produce

quick contract wins

 this summer for service and hospitality workers in Philadelphia, New York, and Los Angeles, but not so in Seattle.


How did strikers there keep up the pressure for another 63 days after the games ended? The hotel’s proximity to Lumen Field makes it a destination for football fans when the season starts in September. On game days, the hotel sets up a …

author: Julia Conley
title: Fossil Fuel Giants Have Sued States for Over $443 Billion Under Trade Deals
content:
Critics say the companies are weaponizing provisions to siphon money from public budgets that are already stretched.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

Ahead of an official side event at the United Nations Climate Change Conference in Antalya, Türkiye, campaigners on Thursday released an analysis of UN data regarding secretive deals within trade agreements aimed at protecting the profits of corporations, including fossil fuel giants, which have now claimed at least $443 billion from the legal provisions.

Investor-state dispute settlements (ISDS), which allow corporations to sue governments over their investments and profit losses as the result of laws and regulations, have increasingly been used by the fossil fuel industry as countries have started taking action to regulate planet-heating oil and gas emissions, according to data from the UN Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD).

The data was analyzed by the British campaign group Global Justice Now and the German research organization PowerShift, which found that based on 987 publicly disclosed ISDS cases, corporate investors have demanded a total of $1.177 trillion up to 2025.

That represents a 37.5% increase, or $321 billion more, from the amount investors were attempting to claim at the end of 2023.

$1.177 trillion is nearly equivalent to the total global climate finance needs, including mitigation costs, for 2021-22, said the campaigners.

The total compensation demanded by fossil fuel investors, $443.8 billion, “is equivalent to the estimated minimum amount of economic losses developing countries will face due to climate change in 2030,” said Global Justice Now and PowerShift.

In fossil fuel cases, the amount demanded rose by $80 billion, or 22%, compared to 2023.

Fabian Flues, investment policy lead at PowerShift, pointed out that by “weaponizing” ISDS, fossil fuel giants are siphoning “money from public budgets that are already stretched,” and Nick Dearden, director of Global Justice Now, compared the ISDS payouts to “the owners of enslaved people being compensated for their grotesque harms following abolition in the early 19th century.”

“We know fossil fuel corporations are making a fortune out of global crises, hitting ordinary people hard,” said Dearden. “But they are also using obscure international agreements to bully governments out of responding and drain money from the public sector. It’s obscene that the very corporations which have created the climate crisis are demanding eye-watering payouts when governments take much needed climate action.”

This week, US company ExxonMobil launched a legal challenge to the European Union’s Net Zero Industry Act, under which the company is required to pay for carbon storage.

The law would saddle Exxon with “unrealistic timelines,” the company said in a statement.

A UK-based mining company and its Singapore-based majority shareholder also sued the UK government last year for £300 million ($398 million) after officials blocked their “unviable” coal mine planned for Cumbria.

“This legal challenge is a last, desperate attempt by investors to make some money out of a project which belonged in the last century,” Niall Toru, a senior lawyer at Friends of the Earth, told Land and Climate Review in May.

According to Global Justice Now and PowerShift, the total amount of compensation awarded to corporate investors through ISDS cases reached $123 billion last year, with fossil fuel investors receiving “the lion’s share of $85.9 billion, representing almost 70% of all payouts to investors.”

$123 billion is “equivalent to the entire bilateral development aid given by [Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development] countries in 2025,” said the campaigners.

The groups are among those calling on leaders at the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) to agree to a coordinated phase-out of ISDS.

Next Monday, Global Justice Now and the Netherlands-based group Both ENDS are organizing an official side event in Antalya featuring Vanuatu Climate Minister Ralph Regenvanu, representatives from communities at the center of ISDS disputes, and a senior government official from Australia, which announced a new policy in 2022 of excluding ISDS mechanisms from future trade deals.

author: Gustavo Faleiros
title: COP31: que a semente de Belém brote na Turquia
content:
Quer receber os textos desta coluna em primeira mão no seu e-mail? Assine a newsletter Ligando os pontos, enviada toda quinta-feira. Para receber as próximas edições,

inscreva-se aqui

.


Iniciada esta semana em Antália, na Turquia, a 31ª Conferência das Partes da Convenção das Nações Unidas sobre as Mudanças Climáticas (COP31) não está gerando o mesmo burburinho que sua versão anterior, realizada em Belém. No ano passado, ativistas do mundo todo viajaram ao Pará. A

COP30

, a primeira a ser realizada na Amazônia, teve um simbolismo enorme, com intensa mobilização popular. Ainda que as esperanças por soluções ousadas contra o aquecimento global não tenham se concretizado naquele momento, vemos agora que as negociações ocorridas no Brasil abriram alguns caminhos promissores.


O marco alcançado em Belém foi evidenciar o buraco nas negociações sobre o uso de combustíveis fósseis. Parece uma loucura que os países se recusem até agora a falar em um mundo sem petróleo e carvão, considerando que esse objetivo levou à criação da Convenção Quadro das Nações Unidas para as Mudanças Climáticas (UNFCCC) na Cúpula da Terra, a Rio 92.


Em grande medida, a proposta de pôr fim aos combustíveis sujos só se tornou possível  através da pressão da sociedade civil, que teve presença histórica na COP de Belém. A mobilização conseguiu empurrar a pauta um pouco além da exasperante inércia do atual arranjo multilateral.


Além disso, a aceleração do processo global de aquecimento, levando ao registro do ano mais quente da História em 2024 contribui para criar um senso de urgência. Da maneira como as coisas caminham, com o Super El Niño atingindo o auge nestes últimos meses, 2026 deve ser o novo ano mais quente de todos os tempos. 


Também faz pouco que

soubemos que, pela primeira vez

, o limite de 1,5 °C da temperatura média global, estabelecido como um teto de segurança, será ultrapassado. Ainda não sabemos por quanto tempo ficaremos acima deste limite, mas já temos indícios de que desastres climáticos de grande magnitude seguirão ocorrendo.


Por isso, a COP31 deve ser importante para confirmar o compromisso dos países em achar um caminho de transição a um mundo com menos emissões de carbono. O problema, como sempre, é se essa busca vai ocorrer em tempo hábil e com que recursos financeiros.


Representantes de povos indígenas durante a Cúpula de Líderes sobre Florestas da COP31, no Centro de Exposições de Antália, na Turquia


O mapa do caminho


Em Antália, o tema sobre o fim da era dos combustíveis fósseis continua sobre a mesa, embalado pela iniciativa do Brasil de apresentar o chamado mapa do caminho. Foi uma iniciativa voluntária da presidência da COP30 para não deixar a discussão sobre como banir os combustíveis fósseis minguar. Uma menção explícita sobre este objetivo ficou de fora do texto acordado em Belém, mas o governo brasileiro se uniu a outros governos para apresentar uma proposta sobre como os países podem fazer uma transição para uma economia mais limpa.


Apresentado poucos dias antes da COP31, o mapa do caminho sugere que todos os países  façam nos próximos anos grandes avaliações sobre a complexidade de mudar a demanda de energia, o suprimento de energia e a economia.

 A partir destes diagnósticos, cada nação deve, até 2030, incluir metas para extinguir o uso de combustíveis fósseis em seus planos nacionais de redução de emissões. A iniciativa brasileira foi bem recebida pela sociedade civil organizada. O

Observatório do Clima elogiou a liderança brasileira

 e mencionou que ela deve servir de guia para ações daqui para frente para os países membros da Convenção do Clima.


Livrar o mundo da dependência de petróleo e do carvão não é realmente trivial. Não há economia nas quais a gasolina e o diesel não estejam presentes. Térmicas a carvão ainda geram eletricidade nas nações mais populosas, China, Índia e Estados Unidos. O Brasil, com suas vantagens comparativas – sol, vento e potencial hidrelétrico – pode clamar certa liderança, ainda que na prática esteja investindo no aumento da produção de petróleo. Não creio que haverá pressão popular que poderá reverter a exploração de petróleo na Foz do Rio Amazona, o que mostra a contradição em curso das políticas energéticas de Lula.


As análises mais recentes do perfil de emissões do Brasil, lançadas esta semana

pelo Sistema de Estimativas de Emissões e Remoções de Gases de Efeito Estufa (Seeg),

 mostram que o Brasil não está cumprindo inteiramente a meta …

author: Harrison Stetler
title: Is France Prosecuting a Palestinian Refugee on Evidence Extracted by Israeli Torture?
content:
How might a hostile state pursue a refugee beyond its borders? This is a question some fear is at the heart of a case currently inching its way through

France’s special-track antiterrorist justice system

. 


Four UN special rapporteurs have warned that 2024 charges brought against “Ali O”, a Palestinian national who held refugee status in France, are built on compromised evidence provided by Israel. 


“We are concerned that Ali’s arrest, detention and prosecution appear to be based on information obtained through the use of torture and other forms of abuse against Palestinians by Israeli authorities,” wrote the UN experts, including human rights lawyer Francesca Albanese, in a 28 August communication issued to France and

published in late October

.


After fleeing Palestine, Ali O settled in France in 2016 and obtained formal recognition as a refugee in 2020. Married to a French citizen and the father of French children, he was arrested at his home in Strasbourg in May 2024. He was subsequently indicted for charges of terrorist financing and conspiracy connected to militant activity in the occupied West Bank in early 2023. 


A memo from the French intelligence services to the country’s refugee administration, and included in the litigation file seen by Novara Media, claims the defendant “participated in the transfer of funds and weapons with military aims” to Palestinian armed groups.


The investigation against Ali O was opened in late 2023. Though French criminal procedure precludes the defence from uncovering certain state evidence, the French state alleges that the defendant was a past member of the Fatah Hawks, a militant group linked to the al-Aqsa Martyrs’ Brigades and affiliated with the Fatah faction of the Palestine Liberation Organisation. It also claims that the defendant conducted online searches on websites used for the dissemination of guerilla tactics and weaponry. 


“[Ali O] committed several crimes incompatible with refugee status. Our service proposes withdrawing refugee status for the concerned party,” wrote the French intelligence bureau. Authorities revoked Ali O’s refugee status in February 2025, even though he has yet to be convicted and is therefore presumed to be innocent.   


Dismissing these accusations, Ali O’s counsel claimed allegations like these would be difficult to construct without close collaboration with outside state sources, notably Israeli. “Ali’s dossier demonstrates the degree to which the French justice system has accepted the role of a subcontractor for Israeli authorities,” attorney Raphaël Kempf told Novara Media, placing his client’s case in the wider crackdown and surveillance of Palestinian nationals residing in Europe. 


Irregularities in the case file also point to Israeli influence in the case against Ali O. The French intelligence memo stipulates he participated from France in militant activity in “Judea and Samaria,” i.e. the Israeli state’s official designation for the West Bank, which is internationally recognised as Palestinian territory, including by France. 


France’s anti-terrorism prosecutorial service (PNAT) declined

 Novara Media’s request for comment. 


Ali O isn’t an unknown quantity for the Israeli state. 


Born in 1990 and raised in the Balata refugee camp on the outskirts of the West Bank city of Nablus, Ali O was 14 years old when he witnessed his younger brother’s killing by an Israeli soldier. Two years later, he was arrested and held in extrajudicial detention before receiving a four-year prison sentence for throwing stones at Israeli occupation forces. It was the first of many stints in jail, according to the biographical information compiled by activists with the Free Ali committee. After his last release from Israeli detention in 2014, he fled to Europe, passing through Italy and Switzerland before making it to France. 


“France recognised [Ali O] as a refugee because of his well-founded fear of persecution by Israeli authorities,” UN special rapporteur on torture Pau Pérez-Sales said at a 29 October press conference following the publication of the co-signed notice to the French government. 


The case against Ali O is based on evidence gathered by Israel from three Palestinian sources. The UN memo warns that one witness, Ali O’s brother, was tortured on several occasions and there are grounds to presume that the other two sources were tortured as well, habitual practices for Palestinians held in Israeli captivity. title: Di fronte alle (finte) bombe, non ci sono interessi comuni.
content:
Le evacuazioni in massa delle scuole di ieri e oggi non sono il primo tentativo di imporre la logica dell’emergenza e dell’interesse nazionale per portarci alla guerra, ma per la prima volta si abbattono su un movimento di massa giovanile e studentesco che sta facendo tremare il governo e vacillare la sua tenuta. Oltre il panico e la paura, si apre una sfida inedita per chi si è messo in movimento: trovare risposte diverse e dal basso, che parlino la lingua del contropotere rifiutando la retorica dell’unità nazionale e della difesa della Repubblica. Forse una sfida che arriva “troppo presto”, ma alla quale non è tardi per provare a rispondere.


Una cosa è certa: la

“guerra ibrida”

 svela la vulnerabilità, inietta la paura, confonde le idee.

Il punto è chi la vuole.

 Il governo italiano è in prima fila per beneficiare degli effetti della guerra ibrida in modo tale da giustificare la spesa e la retorica sulla “difesa”. Non si discosta infatti da nessun governo europeo su questo,

il mantra è prepararsi alla guerra alla Russia mascherata dalla guerra della Russia nei confronti dell’Occidente.

 


Da frigoriferi alle scuole, dai droni agli allarmi sui voli internazionali. Il metodo è quello di disorientare e legittimare le operazioni di riarmo europeo su vasta scala. Il punto non è tanto quanto un allarme o un episodio sia vero o falso ma il fatto che resti ignota la sua origine e che di fatto il governo italiano e in generale l’Unione Europea ci stanno trascinando in una guerra che diventa sempre più reale e concreta. 


Oggi l’allarme scatta nelle scuole italiane, nelle stesse ore si stanno svolgendo i colloqui Kiev -Usa- Mosca ad Abu Dhabi, ed è difficile pensare che sia casuale. La prima domanda che dobbiamo porci è: a chi giova?

 L’allarme scatta e immediatamente le scuole vengono evacuate, perché in fondo prima ancora che sia possibile pensare in maniera razionale al da farsi, è necessario delegare a chi ha pensato piani di emergenza per noi la scelta. Per ora, questo avviene in maniera grossolana, manuale, alla vecchia maniera con carabinieri e forze armate che devono finalmente poter entrare a scuola. 


In queste settimane i carabinieri si sono fatti largo in una scuola di Firenze con le pistole puntate per sgominare un allarmante tentativo di occupazione. Forze di polizia a Torino si sono sbizzarrite nel trovare vari modi per penetrare nelle scuole dove poter arrestare studenti e applicare una presenza significativa agli ingressi, dove è possibile anche che una mattina qualsiasi si venga identificati “perché è prassi”. Di questo passo quando i docenti, i dirigenti, i rettori, accoglieranno l’uso dell’intelligenza artificiale per controllare queste “emergenze”? Tutto lo sproloquiare a destra e sinistra sull’importanza della cybersecurity non è altro che la preparazione del prossimo passo in cui la “tecnologia” dovrà salvarci con l’innovazione, invece che affrontare politicamente il problema.


Lo stesso pseudonimo utilizzato in queste mail che hanno svuotato le scuole italiane era comparso negli attacchi ai voli aerei, in Bulgaria, era stato utilizzato per costruire un allarme simile in scuole e asili. Uno pseudonimo che ricorda l’immaginario sovietico, come hanno ben da sottolineare i media nostrani, e così alla Russia si abbina anche l’immaginario misogino e di violenza contro le donne: questo presunto leader della Vilayat di Misoginistan non è distante dalla sigla dei “Combattenti dello Stato Maschile” che hanno firmato i messaggi minatori dei voli aerei nelle scorse settimane.

Insomma sigle di rivendicazione che ricordano più dei meme che dei gruppi hacker. 


La guerra ibrida, quando si è in guerra, è uno degli strumenti che vengono messi in campo, non c’è molto da stupirsi.

Ma ci sembra di essere di fronte ad una guerra ibrida rivolta all’interno,

 Nord Stream docet. La guerra ibrida oggi allarga i confini e il campo di chi combatte e chi no, lo è inglobando progressivamente ogni ambito del reale, anche se la genesi si attiene al campo del virtuale. Se queste a cui assistiamo sembrano operazioni “false flag”, anche quando arriveranno risposte, simmetriche o no, da chi lo stato attacca militarmente da anni, anche senza soldati dichiarati sul campo, la colpa sarà comunque di chi ci ha trascinati in questa situazione.

author: Wolfgang
title: Kündigungen nach Krankenhausstreik 2013 im Spital „La Providence“ in Neuenburg/Neuchâtel
content:
Dossier


Auf einen ersten Warnstreik am 18. September 2012 reagierte die Geschäftsleitung mit Repression, Drohungen und Verschleppung der Verhandlungen. Auch der Staat versuchte gegen die Kampfbereitschaft vorzugehen und erklärte einen ersten Streikversuch für illegal.  Die Angestellten des Spitals haben sich nicht einschüchtern lassen und sind am 26. November in den Streik getreten. Sie kämpfen damit für den Erhalt des geltenden GAVs Santé 21, gegen die drohende Auslagerung und gegen aktuelle Entlassungswellen. Die Kantonsregierung gerät zunehmend in die Kritik… Siehe dazu:


Nach 15 Jahren bestätigt der internationale Gerichtshof für Menschenrechte das Grundrecht auf Streik der 22 ehemalige Angestellten des Privatspitals La Providence


Wegweisendes Urteil gegen die Schweiz: EGMR stärkt Streikrecht


„

Der Schweizerische Gewerkschaftsbund (SGB) begrüsst das heutige Urteil des Europäischen Gerichtshofs für Menschenrechte (EGMR) zum Streik am Neuenburger Privatspital La Providence. Der Gerichtshof stellt fest, dass die Schweiz die Gewerkschaftsfreiheit verletzt hat. Das Urteil ist ein wichtiger Erfolg für die Beschäftigten und ihre Gewerkschaften. Es macht deutlich: Wer für bessere Arbeitsbedingungen streikt, muss sich auf den Schutz seiner Grundrechte verlassen können.


Die Beschäftigten des Privatspitals La Providence wehrten sich 2012 und 2013 gegen eine Verschlechterung ihrer Arbeitsbedingungen. Sie kämpften insbesondere für die Weitergeltung ihres Gesamtarbeitsvertrags. 22 Streikende wurden fristlos entlassen, weil sie ihren Arbeitskampf fortsetzten. Das Bundesgericht hatte die Entlassungen geschützt und den Streik als unverhältnismässig beurteilt.


Der EGMR verurteilt die Schweiz im heutigen Urteil. Der Gerichtshof kritisiert insbesondere, dass für die Beschäftigten nicht ausreichend vorhersehbar war, unter welchen Voraussetzungen die Fortsetzung ihres Streiks als rechtswidrig beurteilt werden konnte. Die Schweizer Gerichte hätten die Bedeutung des Streikrechts und die Interessen der Beschäftigten stärker berücksichtigen müssen. Auch die strafrechtlichen Verurteilungen von vier Gewerkschaftssekretärinnen und -sekretären wegen eines friedlichen Streikpostens verletzen gemäss EGMR die Gewerkschaftsfreiheit.


Der SGB würdigt den beharrlichen Einsatz der Gewerkschaften VPOD und Syna – sowie insbesondere der betroffenen Beschäftigten. Sie haben fast 15 Jahre für ihre Rechte gekämpft und damit einen wichtigen Beitrag zum Schutz der Gewerkschaftsrechte in der ganzen Schweiz geleistet.


Das Urteil hat Bedeutung weit über den Einzelfall hinaus

…“

SGB-Meldung vom 6. November 2026

 


Urteil aus Strassburg: Endlich Genugtuung für Spital-Streikende


„

Im Jahr 2013 hat das Privatspital La Providence 22 Streikende in Neuenburg fristlos entlassen, weil sie sich gegen die Verschlechterung ihrer Arbeitsbedingungen gewehrt hatten. Erst jetzt, fast 15 Jahre später, bestätigt der internationale Gerichtshof für Menschenrechte ihr Grundrecht auf Streik. (…) Das Urteil ist ein klarer Sieg für die Gewerkschaften und eine Klatsche für die Schweiz. Es bestätigt, dass das Streikrecht ein Grundrecht ist und von den Gerichten nicht ausgehöhlt werden darf.


Auf der Seite der Arbeitgeber


Geklagt hatten ehemalige Angestellte des Privatspitals La Providence in Neuenburg. Ihnen drohten massive Verschlechterungen ihrer Arbeitsbedingungen. Dagegen hatten sie sich mit den Gewerkschaften in den Jahren 2012 und 2013 gewehrt. Wegen dieses Arbeitskampfes wurden 22 von ihnen fristlos entlassen. Und vier Gewerkschaftssekretärinnen und -sekretäre strafrechtlich wegen Hausfriedensbruchs verurteilt. Weder die Geschassten noch die Gewerkschaften akzeptierten diese Verletzung des Streikrechts und zogen vor Gericht. Doch die Schweizer Justiz stellte sich auf die Seite der Arbeitgeber. Auch das Bundesgericht urteilte 2019, dass der Streik illegal gewesen und die Entlassungen sowie die Verurteilungen somit rechtens seien.


Versammlungsfreiheit verletzt


Jetzt das klare Verdikt vom Europäischen Gerichtshof: Der EGMR hat einstimmig entschieden, dass die Schweiz Artikel 11 (Versammlungs- und Vereinigungsfreiheit) der Europäischen Menschenrechtskonvention verletzt hat. Und weiter: Weder die Schweizer Bundesverfassung noch die nationale Rechtsprechung würden eine Grundlage für das Gericht bieten, einen rechtmässigen Streik für unrechtmässig zu erklären, nur weil der Arbeitgeber ein Angebot unterbreitete. Für den EGMR ist klar: Es ist in erster Linie …

title: The Midterms Have Changed the Game. Now What?
content:
“It’s important to keep in mind that elections remove people, but they don’t remove infrastructure,” says Scot Nakagawa.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

The midterms delivered a stunning rebuke of Trump and the MAGA movement, but what will it take to turn electoral victories into lasting change? In this episode of “Movement Memos,” host Kelly Hayes talks with anti-authoritarian strategist Scot Nakagawa about the opportunities and dangers of this political moment, the enduring power of tech oligarchs, and how movements can build the solidarity and infrastructure needed to defeat authoritarianism and transform our political culture.

title: From Ranked-Choice Voting to Dumping Electoral College: Rob Richie on Election Reform Movement
content:
Alaska is the only Senate race yet to be called. Democratic challenger Mary Peltola is narrowly leading Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan with about 86% of votes counted. Alaska uses ranked-choice voting, a system where voters choose not only their top candidate, but can also indicate an order of preference for remaining candidates on the ballot. If no candidate wins a majority as the top choice, then second-choice votes are added to the totals and so on until there is a winner.


Rob Richie, president and founder of Expand Democracy and a senior adviser with FairVote, explains how ranked-choice voting has shaped the Alaska race and how it is “a system that promotes [candidates] reaching out, engaging, and, for voters, a lot of freedom.”


Richie adds that Peltola is “heavily favored to win at this point.”

title: Şaredariyên Amedê starta xebatên xwe yên 25ê Mijdarê dan: "Demokratîkbûn tenê bi îradeya rêxistinkirî ya jinan mimkun e"
content:
Şaredariyên DEM Partî yên Amedê, ji bo 25ê Mijdarê Roja Têkoşîna Li Dijî Tundiya Li Ser Jinan li Parka Anîtê daxuyanî dan û starta çalakiyên xwe dan.


Di daxuyaniyê de pankarta “Bi hêza xwe û bi îradeya azad niha dema jinê ye” hate vekirin. Şaredarî, nûnerên rêxistinên jinan û gelek jin beşdar bûn û dirûşma “Jin, Jiyan, Azadî” hate berzkirin.


Daxuyanî bi Kurdî û Tirkî hate xwendin. Metna Kurdî ya daxuyaniyê ji aliyê Midûra Siyasetên Jinan a Şaredariya Peyasê Fatma Budak Guler ve, ya Tirkî jî ji aliyê Seroka Daîreya Siyasetên Jinan a Şaredariya Bajarê Mezin a Amedê Ozden Gurbuz Sumer ve hate xwendin.


Jinan di daxuyaniyê de tekez kirin ku jin ji bo jiyaneke ku ew dikarin bi ziman, çand û nasnameyên xwe yên dayikê bi azadî bijîn, parêzvaniyê dikin. Di daxuyaniyê de hat destnîşankirin ku demokratîkbûna Komarê û aştiya mayînde tenê bi îradeya rêxistinkirî ya jinan mimkun e.


"Em ê têkoşîna xwe li dijî her cûre tundkariyê mezin bikin"


Her weha di daxuyaniyê de hat gotin ji bo avakirina jiyaneke demokratîk, ekolojîk û rizgariya jinan a bi hev re têkoşîn didome û hat gotin:


"Îro, em destpêkirina çalakiyên xwe yên 25'ê Mijdarê radigihînin! Em ê li tax, kolan û gundan bi jinan re bicivin da ku dengê xwe yê hevpar û têkoşîna xwe li dijî her cûre tundûtûjiyê mezin bikin. Bi rêya kombûnên jinan, atolyeyan, çalakiyên hişyarkirinê û bûyerên hevgirtinê, em ê ezmûn, daxwaz û çareseriyên pêşniyarkirî yên jinan bikin kevirê bingehîn ê têkoşîna me ya hevpar. Bi hev re, em ê qadên ku jin dikarin bi azadî li ser jiyana xwe biryarê bidin, têkiliyên hevgirtinê xurt bikin û jiyana civakî bi îradeya xwe ya rêxistinkirî veguherînin zêde bikin."


Piştî daxuyaniyê, jinan belavok belav kirin û banga beşdarbûna meşa ku dê di 25'ê Mijdarê de saet di 17:30'an de li Çerxerêya Dinyayê were lidarxistin, kirin.

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: Judge to consider motion to dismiss lawsuit by Igloolik Inuit alleging harmful medical experiments
content:
This story was updated on Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026, at 11:52 a.m. ET.


A Nunavut judge will have to decide whether to hear or dismiss the claims of five Inuit who allege the federal government subjected them to medical experiments in Igloolik in the 1960s and 1970s.


Former Nunavut premier Paul Quassa, filmmaker Zacharias Kunuk, Lazarie Uttak, Lydia Inooya and the late artist Madeline Ivalu, who died in May, are suing the federal government for more than $1 million each in damages.


But lawyers representing the federal government and three universities appeared in the Nunavut Court of Justice before Justice Mark Mossey this week to argue

the 2019 lawsuit

 should be dismissed because it was brought too late.


“Applicable limitations periods under the limitations legislation in effect at the time have long since expired,” Chris Bernier, the federal government’s lawyer, wrote in a motion to the court in August 2025.


The federal government, University of Toronto, University of Manitoba, and University of Alberta are requesting a summary judgement, which if granted would prevent the case from going to trial.


The universities have also motioned to dismiss Canada’s third-party claims against them.


Steven Cooper, the plaintiffs’ lawyer, said Mossey is expected to decide by the end of the year. He said if his clients’ lawsuit is dismissed, it would set a harmful precedent.


“If this case is allowed … to be dismissed in this fashion, this will have an impact across the country, especially in the North,” he said in an interview Tuesday.


The five plaintiffs are among approximately 30 Inuit who say they underwent harmful experiments, including ones that included skin-grafting and ones that were aimed at evaluating their tolerance to extreme cold.


Court documents filed by the federal government’s lawyer note the universities were among the partners involved in the experiments, conducted under a research program called the International Biological Program.


“Our position to the court was simply that the conditions in the North, the knowledge of the plaintiffs, and the law as it stands all suggest that this has to go to trial,” Cooper said. “The world of Igloolik in the ’60s and ’70s was very different than it is now, we have to be careful about applying southern case law to northern realities.”


A spokesperson for the federal Justice Department said it couldn’t comment on the government’s motion for dismissal, saying the Crown-Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs departments would be better suited. Spokespeople for the departments were not immediately available to comment. The representative for Crown-Indigenous Relations mentioned the Remembrance Day holiday.


The three universities involved are not targeted by his clients’ 2019 lawsuit, Cooper noted. They came in as third parties, and filed motions alongside the federal government last August to dismiss the case.


Cooper said he believes lawyers for the federal government persuaded the universities to join the legal dispute as a delay tactic.


Nunatsiaq News reached out to the three universities and the lawyers representing them for comment. Only the University of Alberta did not respond.


Janesca Kydd, lawyer for the University of Manitoba, said that the university is not a defendant in the case and that it denies being involved in the experiments. She declined to comment further as the matter remains before the courts.


An unnamed spokesperson for the University of Toronto said its researchers “were not involved in the research at issue.”


“The Government of Canada […] provided the University of Toronto and other universities with a notice of Third-Party Claim,” the university wrote in a statement. “The University of Toronto disputes Canada’s claim against it.”


Cooper said the federal government’s actions go against the spirit of a 2021 civil litigation directive by the former Attorney General of Canada Jody Wilson-Raybould, which noted limitations should be pleaded only in exceptional cases when dealing with historical abuses brought forward by Indigenous Peoples.


Update:

 

This story has been updated to include comment from the University of Manitoba and the University of Toronto. It has also been updated to include the fact that the universities have motioned to dismiss Canada’s third-party claims against them.

author: webdev@democracynow.org (Democracy Now!)
title: Relatives of Slain Freedom Summer Activists Celebrate Scott Colom's Historic Senate Win in Mississippi
content:
Democrat Scott Colom has defeated incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first African American senator since the post-Civil War Reconstruction era. The electoral breakthrough is particularly meaningful given Mississippi’s history in the civil rights movement. In 1964, three civil rights activists — James Chaney, Michael Schwerner and Andrew Goodman — were murdered by the Ku Klux Klan after traveling to the state to register Black voters. We speak with two of their relatives about Colom’s stunning upset.


“I believe that people were voting for help. And they evidently saw something in Mr. Colom that made them feel like that they could hope again and that he was the help that was needed,” says Angela Lewis, the daughter of James Chaney.


“The people of Mississippi have spoken,” adds David Goodman, the brother of Andrew Goodman. “And we have to cease and desist this divide-and-conquer business, because it’s not in our collective interest as the United States of America.”

author: webdev@democracynow.org (Democracy Now!)
title: Scott Colom Wins Stunning Victory, Becomes Mississippi's First Black Senator Since Reconstruction
content:
Democrat Scott Colom has made history as Mississippi’s first Democratic senator since 1982 — and its first African American senator since the post-Civil War Reconstruction era. Colom narrowly defeated Republican incumbent Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith in a state that President Trump won by nearly 23 points in 2024. Colom’s victory brings the incoming Senate Democratic caucus to 55. Colom gave his victory speech on Wednesday at the historically Black Tougaloo College, just miles from where civil rights activist Medgar Evers was murdered in 1963 by a member of the Ku Klux Klan.


“There were times that I couldn’t get donors to answer the phone; they did not believe a moment like this was possible. But I kept the faith,” said Colom. “There are so many people that had faith in Mississippi at times where it seemed impossible, people like Medgar Evers.”

title: Union Busting bei Hark Recycling: Wenn der Chef Dich mit Drohnen bespitzelt und strafversetzt
content:
„

Und wieder schwebte eine Drohne über ihnen: Wie Beschäftigte bei Hark Recycling sich die Bespitzelung nicht gefallen lassen, einen Betriebsrat gründen, dafür an einen verwahrlosten Standort voller Schimmel strafversetzt werden – und sich mithilfe der IG Metall wehren. (…) Die Drohnen-Installation wirft angesichts der Vorgeschichte des Unternehmens erhebliche Fragen auf: Welche Funktion hat die neue Anlage? Soll sie erneut zur Überwachung der Beschäftigten eingesetzt werden? Das ist nicht der erste Drohnen-Vorfall bei Hark Recycling. Vor anderthalb Jahren hatte der Chef sie bereits auf dem Betriebsgelände in Hamm mit einer Drohne bespitzelt. „Die Drohne schwebte vor meinem Bagger und filmte mich“, erinnert sich der heutige Betriebsrat Waldemar B. (*Name von der Redaktion geändert). Der Hauptgeschäftsführer von Hark Recycling forderte dann die Belegschaft dazu auf, mit ihm über das Gelände zu laufen und konfrontierte einzelne mit Fotos seiner Drohne: Warum hast Du hier so lange Pause gemacht, Kaffee getrunken, geraucht?

…“ Umfangreicher Bericht der

IG Metall vom 28. Oktober 2026


 aus Dortmund und Hamm, aktualisiert am 10. November 2026


Der Beitrag

Union Busting bei Hark Recycling: Wenn der Chef Dich mit Drohnen bespitzelt und strafversetzt

title: Μαζικές διαδηλώσεις στην Ισπανία για τη στεγαστική κρίση και το αυξημένο κόστος ζωής
content:
Εκατοντάδες χιλιάδες πολίτες και εργαζόμενοι διαδήλωσαν στην πρώτη γενική απεργία μετά από 14 χρόνια σε όλη την Ισπανία, με βασικό αίτημα το δικαίωμα στη στέγαση και την αύξηση μισθών. Τα συνδικάτα ανεβάζουν τη συμμετοχή σε περίπου

4 εκατομμύρια

, ενώ όπως

σημειώνει

 η CGT πραγματοποιήθηκαν 2.500 πικετοφορίες σε μια μαζική και άνευ προηγουμένου κινητοποίηση, με πρωτοφανή καταστολή από πλευράς της αστυνομίας. Ιδιαίτερα μεγάλη συμμετοχή καταγράφηκε στην

 Καταλονία

 και την

Ανδαλουσία,

με δυναμικές διαδηλώσεις σε Μαδρίτη, Βαρκελώνη και σε περισσότερες από 50 πόλεις, παρά τις άσχημες καιρικές συνθήκες (καταιγίδα Charles) που οδήγησαν σε ακύρωση των απογευματινών πορειών που είχαν προγραμματιστεί στις πόλεις Σεβίλλη, Κόρδοβα, Κάντιθ και Ουέλβα.


Αυτή η άνευ προηγουμένου γενική απεργία,  η οποία καλέστηκε λιγότερο από

τρεις εβδομάδες πριν από τις βουλευτικές εκλογές της 29ης Νοεμβρίου,

 ξεκίνησε ως απάντηση στην κρίση στέγασης —που σημαδεύτηκε από την έξωση της

Maricarmen Abascal

, μιας 87χρονης γυναίκας, η οποία εκδιώχθηκε από το σπίτι όπου ζούσε επί περισσότερες από επτά δεκαετίες, μετά από αύξηση του ενοικίου της. Πέθανε λίγες ημέρες αργότερα.


Η υπόθεσή της έγινε σύμβολο της στεγαστικής κρίσης και πυροδότησε ένα κύμα διαμαρτυριών και καταλήψεων δημόσιων χώρων.


Κοινό μέτωπο


Στη γενική απεργία της 11ης Νοεμβρίου συμμετείχαν οι συνδικαλιστικές οργανώσεις της χώρας, CCOO (Comisiones Obreras), η UGT (Unión General de Trabajadores), η CNT, η CGT, η Co.Bas και άλλες συνδικαλιστικές και κοινωνικές οργανώσεις, καθώς και τα συνδικάτα ενοικιαστών. Παρά τις διαφορές τους, οι οργανώσεις αυτές βρέθηκαν σε

κοινό μέτωπο

 για τη

γενική απεργία,

 αν και η συνεργασία δεν ήταν παντού ομαλή. Στη Σαραγόσα, για παράδειγμα, η CGT, η CNT και το Συνδικάτο Ενοικιαστών πραγματοποίησαν ξεχωριστή πορεία από εκείνη των CCOO και UGT.


Η συμμετοχή CGT, CNT και των μεγάλων συνδικαλιστικών οργανώσεων σε μια κοινή γενική απεργία δείχνει ότι υπάρχει δυνατότητα συγκρότησης ευρύτερων κοινωνικών και εργατικών μετώπων. Ταυτόχρονα, οι αντιθέσεις που εμφανίστηκαν αποκαλύπτουν ένα διαχρονικό πρόβλημα του συνδικαλιστικού κινήματος, του πώς μπορεί δηλαδή να συνεργάζεται με ευρύτερες πολιτικές και κοινωνικές δυνάμεις χωρίς να χάνει την αυτονομία και τον ταξικό του χαρακτήρα.


Για την

 CGT,

 το πραγματικό διακύβευμα δεν είναι μόνο η επιτυχία μιας απεργίας, αλλά η

οικοδόμηση ενός κινήματος ικανού να συνεχίσει τον αγώνα και την επόμενη ημέρα και να ενισχύσει τη δυνατότητα συλλογικής δράσης.

Spain is holding a nationwide general strike today over the housing affordability crisis, less than three weeks before a snap general election that could bring the right to power.


It is the country’s first general strike in 14 years, called by Spain’s two largest unions, UGT and CCOO.


Because of the timing, the conservative Popular Party and Vox have accused the unions of acting with electoral motives, a charge UGT and CCOO reject.


Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez hopes to capitalize on the issue to shift the political narrative away from the corruption cases involving his inner circle and the immigration crisis.

title: Rechte Strukturen bei (Bremer) Feuerwehr aufgedeckt
content:
Dossier

Staatsschutz und Verfassungsschutz ermittelten nun, wie weit die Strukturen reichten (…) Die Vorwürfe umfassten zwei Komplexe: Im ersten gehe es um rechtsextreme und rassistische Bilder, die in der privaten Chatgruppe einer Wachabteilung verteilt wurden, in einem zweiten Komplex gehe es um frauenfeindliche und sexistische Vorfälle auf einer anderen Wache.
